Abstract Abstract. This Latin–English reading and reference edition presents Vitruvius’s De architectura with translation, notes, and historical and architectural commentary. The English derives from Diego Kurilo’s authorial Spanish translation; the Latin is checked against Krohn (1912). Documentary testimony, editorial reconstruction, architectural explanation, and the author’s hermeneutic proposals are distinguished. The editorial principles define the scope of the selective apparatus. References follow the Chicago Manual of Style, 18th edition (2024), with American English spelling. Keywords. Vitruvius; De architectura; Roman architecture; architectural theory; bilingual critical edition; Latin philology; history of architecture; proportion; symmetria; Vitruvian Man. iii

PRELIMINARY STUDY The Vitruvian Man Figure 1. Modern line rendering after Leonardo da Vinci, Vitruvian Man, c. 1490. Historical original: Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice, Gabinetto dei Disegni e delle Stampe, inv. 228r. Vector source: Wikimedia Commons, Da Vinci Vitruve Luc Viatour 2.svg; public domain. Leonardo’s Vitruvian Man, c. 1490, is an individual drawing preserved in the Gabinetto dei Disegni e delle Stampe of the Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice, inv. 228r. The modern line rendering reproduced here derives from that sheet and illustrates the relationship between bodily measure and geometric construction. The Geometric Dilemma Leonardo's drawing is, in essence, an exercise in proportional reconciliation rather than an attempt to solve the squaring of the circle. In Book III of De architectura, Vitruvius had proposed that the human body could be inscribed 1

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY within both a square and a circle. Mathematically, however, this posed a difficulty: the squaring of the circle is impossible by means of elementary Euclidean geometry. Through his drawing, Leonardo proposed a graphical interpretation of Vitruvius’s description: • The square represents the earthly realm—stability and the human measure derived from height, since the span of the outstretched arms equals the height of the body. Its center lies at the groin. • Leonardo places the center of the circle at the navel and that of the square at the groin. These distinct centers allow him to reconcile the figures graphically. The construction does not provide a geometrical solution to squaring the circle. In the interpretation proposed here, the body mediates between the stability of the square and the cosmic associations of the circle. 2. Anatomical and Technical Characteristics Leonardo did not base this drawing on Vitruvius’s text alone; he enriched it with his own anatomical research: • Proportion and modularity. The drawing reflects Leonardo's preoccupation with the module. He divides the body into sections governed by the head (approximately one-eighth of the total height) and the hand (approximately one-tenth), confirming the Vitruvian measurements through dissection and the study of proportion in living men. • Canon and mechanism. The superimposition of two poses—arms outstretched horizontally and raised in a V-shape—presents the body at once as a static canon and as a dynamic mechanism. The lines serve not as decoration but as axes of symmetry and proportional guides. 3. Philosophical and Symbolic Interpretations Leonardo’s drawing may be read as a link between earthly and cosmic orders. The square, centered at the groin, suggests material stability and human measure. The circle, centered at the navel, suggests perfection and the celestial realm. These symbolic associations belong to the interpretation proposed here. • This reading aligns with the Neoplatonic and Pythagorean tradition, widely diffused in Renaissance intellectual circles, according to which a 2

PRELIMINARY STUDY correspondence was held to obtain between the microcosm (man) and the macrocosm (the universe). • Such symbolic interpretations, however culturally significant, represent a later interpretive layer rather than a direct reconstruction of Vitruvius’s own intentions, which were proportional and technical. • In the author's own interpretive proposal, Leonardo's graphic solution — the shifting of the two centers — constitutes not merely an anatomical study but a visual meditation on the tension between ideal geometry and embodied reality. 4. A Critical Reading: Art or Science? In scholarly terms, the drawing must be classified as a document of technical research. Through the precision of his line, Leonardo transforms an ancient theoretical text into a manual of practical application. Where Vitruvius had proposed the body as a norm—a rule to be followed—Leonardo presents it as evidence: something that can be measured, tested, and observed. The Vitruvian Man should be read as a visual exegesis of the classical canon, in which the anatomical figure functions as a system of coordinates. Leonardo does not merely illustrate Vitruvian theory; he submits it to empirical verification, employing geometry as the language through which the human subject is integrated into the cosmic order. The superimposition of the two figures, far from being a mere aesthetic device, constitutes a study of the body’s operation in space, and it reaffirms the architect’s role as the agent charged with harmonizing the laws of nature with the construction of the human habitat. 3

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Preliminary Note: Scope and Methodology Purpose and audience. The central aim of this edition is to offer Englishspeaking readers—and architects, architecture students, and art historians in particular—a complete bilingual Latin–English edition of Vitruvius's Ten Books, accompanied by a study that gathers and orders the treatise's architectural doctrine together with the anecdotes that illustrate it. It is not conceived as a new recension of the Latin text—which is drawn from the established critical editions (Krohn 1912, checked against Rose 1899 and the Budé edition)—but rather as a means of presenting the English translation derived from the author’s original Spanish version, checked against the Latin where necessary and annotated, within reach of the professional and the scholar, for whom, to the best of our knowledge, a complete and accessible bilingual version of this kind has not hitherto existed. Alongside this philological and pedagogical purpose, a separate and clearly distinguished section sets out a personal interpretive proposal. On the place of this edition within the publishing tradition: it is important to situate this edition honestly within the tradition of Vitruvian editions, so as to make clear what it contributes and what it does not claim to be. The definitive critical edition remains that of the Collection des Universités de France (the “Budé,” Les Belles Lettres, 1969–2009), directed by Pierre Gros and prepared by Louis Callebat, Jean Soubiran, Philippe Fleury, and other specialists: it establishes the Latin text from the manuscripts, book by book, with a critical apparatus and a monographic commentary. Anyone seeking a definitive textual constitution of Vitruvius should turn to it. Kr. abbreviation of Krohn in the apparatus. Bud. abbreviation of the Budé edition in the apparatus. Gr. abbreviation of Granger in the apparatus. edd. recent. editiones recentiores: the later (Renaissance and modern) editions, as opposed to the manuscripts. In the bilingual sphere, Frank Granger’s Loeb edition (Harvard University Press, 1931–1934) presents the Latin and English on facing pages, based on the Harleianus 2767; its usefulness is undeniable, even if its translation and notes have aged. In English, the version by Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas Noble 4

PRELIMINARY STUDY Howe (Cambridge University Press, 1999) is today the standard, with a sound commentary and Howe’s technical reconstructions, although it does not reproduce the Latin on facing pages. In Italian, the edition by Antonio Corso and Elisa Romano, under the direction of Gros (Einaudi, 1997), is notable for the breadth of its commentary. Complete bilingual editions — presenting the Latin alongside a fluent modern translation for reading and reference — remain comparatively few. In Spanish, for instance, the available versions are translations rather than complete bilingual editions. The most widely circulated—that of José Luis Oliver Domingo, with an introduction by Delfín Rodríguez Ruiz (Alianza, 1995)—is a Castilian version without the Latin text; Francisco Manzanero’s translation for Gredos covers only the first five books; and the historic translation by José Ortiz y Sanz (1787), of great value, is likewise monolingual and now linguistically remote. To the best of our knowledge, no complete Latin–English bilingual edition of all ten books, designed specifically for the architect-reader and uniting critical apparatus with architectural analysis, yet exists. It is precisely this gap that the present edition aspires to fill. It is offered, therefore, not as a new critical edition—a domain in which the Budé remains unsurpassed—but as a bilingual edition for reading and reference: it reproduces the Latin text already established by philology (Krohn 1912, checked against Rose 1899 and the Budé edition), accompanies it with an English translation derived from the author’s original Spanish version and an apparatus of notes, analytical indexes, and indexes of Greek words, places, and names, and places it at the service of the English-speaking architect, student, and historian. Its ambition is not to rival French textual criticism, but to place at the service of the English-speaking reader—as a contribution from the Hispanic scholarly tradition—a bilingual reference edition that unites an up-to-date philological apparatus with the architect's technical and symbolic analysis. This work seeks to explore the intersection between the architectural practice of classical antiquity and the systems of meaning that shaped its symbolic world. To that end, it is essential to set out the methodological framework underpinning the study, so that the reader may clearly grasp the nature of the materials presented. The method operates on two distinct levels. 5

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY This work therefore proceeds on two distinct but complementary levels, which are kept apart throughout: historically verifiable data and technical analysis on the one hand, and interpretive proposals of a more speculative nature on the other. The first level adheres to the canons of architectural historiography and classical philology, drawing on material evidence, epigraphy, and textual sources—such as Vitruvius’s De architectura or the writings of Pliny the Elder—to reconstruct the techniques of layout and setting-out and the roles of the building professions in the Greco-Roman world. Here documentary rigor governs throughout, subordinating the analysis to archaeological verification and established scholarly consensus. The second level is hermeneutical, addressing the symbolic and cultural dimensions of architectural form. The readings it proposes — of sacred space and of numerical iconography — are offered expressly as the author’s interpretive contribution, clearly signalled as such, and are not presented as a substitute for the philological and archaeological consensus. The author is fully aware that such approaches, in proposing semantic links beyond archaeological literalism, belong to the realm of scholarly speculation. Every effort has therefore been made to separate historical data precisely from symbolic inference, leaving the reader to judge the validity of these correlations. Ultimately, the work aspires not to a single, definitive truth but to the opening of an interdisciplinary dialogue between the precision of constructional data and the depth of symbolic thought in antiquity. PRELIMINARY STUDY Introduction This book centers on the figure of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the most influential surviving architectural theorist of antiquity. De architectura is by no means confined to technical matters. Clearly inspired by Hellenism, and with explicit references to inventors such as Ctesibius, the treatise treats, in encyclopedic fashion, the architectural orders, building materials, decorative techniques, building types, hydraulics, the use of color, gnomonics (Book IX), and both civil and military machinery (Book X). Vitruvius describes, for instance, the workings of the water-wheel and of various lifting and siege engines, displaying an exceptional command of the engineering of his day. The influence of De architectura has endured across the centuries. First printed in Rome in 1486 by the humanist Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli, the treatise became one of the foundational texts of the Renaissance. Petrarch was a major force behind its rediscovery, and its influence reached figures such as Leon Battista Alberti, Andrea Palladio, and Leonardo da Vinci, who based his celebrated Vitruvian Man on the human proportions described in the treatise. For Vitruvius, the ideal architect had to command a broad range of knowledge: writing, drawing, geometry, arithmetic, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law, and astronomy. Only through this comprehensive formation—which he called encyclios disciplina [encyclopedic education; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.1.12]—could one attain the summum templum architecturae [the summit of the art of architecture; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.1.11], the .highest peak of the discipline This book seeks to present both the historical and technical dimensions of Vitruvius and the rich symbolic readings his work has prompted over time. The historical and philological sections rest on primary sources and specialized critical literature; the hermeneutic and interpretive sections, clearly identified as such, set out the author’s proposals on Pythagorean symbolism and the architectural traditions of antiquity. The aim, ultimately, is a comprehensive approach to one of the most influential thinkers in Western culture. 9

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY The Six Fundamental Principles of Architecture In Book I of his treatise (De architectura 1.2.1), Vitruvius holds that architecture is composed of six essential principles (principia), which form the theoretical foundation of the entire discipline. These six concepts are not isolated elements; they operate in an interdependent, organic way, articulating the technical, aesthetic, and ethical dimensions of building. 1. The Vitruvian triad: firmitas, utilitas, and venustas Before setting out the six principles, Vitruvius affirms that every building must satisfy three fundamental conditions (De architectura 1.3.2): • Firmitas (solidity): structural stability and the durability of materials. • Utilitas (utility): functionality and fitness for the intended use. • Venustas (beauty): aesthetic grace and visual harmony. These three requirements form the basic triad of architecture and must be met simultaneously for a work to be deemed accomplished. The Six Operative Principles (principia) On this basis, Vitruvius defines six technical and aesthetic concepts by which the three foregoing requirements are achieved: Principle Greek Term Core Meaning Domain Ordinatio τάξις (taxis) Modular ordering according Quantitative and to a common unit Modular Dispositio διάθεσις (diathesis) Arrangement; the Intellectual / Projectconception and graphic based representation of the design Eurythmia εὐρυθμία Visual harmony and graceful Aesthetic (eurythmia) proportion as perceived by the eye Symmetria συμμετρία Commensurability: the Mathematical (symmetria) proportional relationship of the parts to the whole and to a common module Decor τὸ πρέπον (to Propriety, appropriateness prepon) and contextual fitness Distributio οἰκονομία Economic and functional Practical / Ethical (oikonomia) distribution of resources 10

The six operative principles of architecture Note. The Greek equivalents follow the Budé edition (Pierre Gros et al.). The term decor corresponds to τὸ πρέπον (that which is fitting), a concept central to Vitruvian aesthetics and ethics. The Greek word θεματισμός that appears at 1.2.5 properly renders statio —ritual or institutional rule—, one of the three modes by which decor is achieved (together with custom and nature), and not decor itself. 2.1. Ordinatio (τάξις) – Ordering It is the correct disposition of the members of the work according to a common unit of measure (modulus or rata pars). It constitutes the quantitative, modular aspect of architecture. 2.2. Dispositio (διάθεσις) – Disposition It consists in the intellectual conception of the building and its graphic representation, expressed through three modes of representation: • Ichnographia (the plan) • Orthographia (the elevation) • Scaenographia (the perspective view) It is the creative, design moment par excellence. 2.3. Eurythmia (εὐρυθμία) – Eurythmy It is the pleasing, harmonious appearance that arises from the correct application of proportion. It is not mere mathematical proportion, but the agreeable visual effect that proportion produces. 2.4. Symmetria (συμμετρία) – Symmetria / Commensurability It does not denote modern bilateral symmetry, but the proportional correspondence between the parts and the whole, established from a common measure (rata pars). It is the mathematical, rational principle par excellence. 2.5. Decor (decor) – Decorum / Propriety The aesthetic, functional, and cultural appropriateness of the work. Vitruvius distinguishes three kinds: • by convention (statio); • by custom (consuetudo); 11

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY • by nature (natura). It governs, among other things, the choice of architectural order according to the divinity or the function of the building. 2.6. Distributio (οἰκονομία) – Distribution / Economy It is the sound management of material, financial, and spatial resources. It comprises the rational distribution of spaces according to use and social standing, as well as the prudent control of costs. Scholarly Note These six principles form a coherent, hierarchical system. While ordinatio, symmetria, and eurythmia concern quantitative and aesthetic relationships, dispositio and decor address the qualitative and intellectual dimension, and distributio introduces the practical and ethical dimension of architecture. Their formulation has exerted an extraordinary influence, from the Renaissance (Alberti, Palladio) to contemporary architectural theory. “Theories that attribute a sacred or esoteric meaning to the number 216 should be treated with caution. While Vitruvius clearly valued Pythagorean proportions, such speculative interpretations exceed the strictly technical and geometric framework of his text. Scholarly analysis ought to be confined to the technical and geometric function of the number in building practice, thereby avoiding any slide towards interpretations that lack empirical support.” References Vitruvius, De architectura 1.2.1-9. PRELIMINARY STUDY Vitruvius: Life and Work The name of Vitruvius The name by which tradition knows the author —Marcus Vitruvius Pollio— follows the tripartite structure of the Roman name: praenomen, nomen, and cognomen. Of the three elements, only the nomen Vitruvius is securely attested by the treatise itself; the praenomen Marcus and the cognomen Pollio derive from later sources and are accepted with reservations. The praenomen Marcus, one of the commonest at Rome, is usually connected with the god Mars; its attribution to Vitruvius rests on the medieval manuscript tradition rather than on any direct ancient testimony. The nomen Vitruvius denotes the gens or family line and is of uncertain Italic origin: it has been linked to vitrum (glass, or the dyer’s plant woad), which would suggest a remote occupational origin, but the etymology is not secure. It is, in any case, the only component of the name the author himself confirms. The cognomen Pollio —from pollere, “to be strong or influential”— is first associated with Vitruvius in the epitome of Marcus Cetius Faventinus (s. III– IV AD). Hence some scholars have read the phrase “Vitruvius Pollio” not as a single name but as the juxtaposition of two authors —Vitruvius and (Asinius) Pollio—; the hypothesis, however, lacks firm proof. The coincidence with Gaius Asinius Pollio (76 BCE – AD 4), orator, historian, and founder of the first public library at Rome, has fed speculation; yet nothing in the ancient sources indicates that the architect took the cognomen through any connection with him. It is safest to understand Pollio as an ordinary Latin family name, without honorific connotation. It should be remembered, finally, that “Vitruvius” is not a surname in the modern sense but the nomen of the gens Vitruvia: the inscriptions bearing Vitruvius or Vitruvia (collected in the CIL and in epigraphic databases such as the EDR) belong to other members of the line, not to the architect, whose tomb and personal circumstances remain unknown. According to tradition, Vitruvius served as a military engineer under Julius Caesar, most likely during the Gallic Wars (c. 58–51 BCE). After retiring from military service, he dedicated himself to civil architecture and engineering. During this period, he built the only building he explicitly claims as his own 13

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY work, the Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (modern-day Fano, in the Marche region of Italy), described in detail in De architectura 5.1.6–10. However, his most enduring legacy is the treatise De architectura, the only comprehensive theoretical compendium on architecture and engineering that has survived from classical antiquity. PRELIMINARY STUDY Analysis of the work "De architectura" (also known as "Ten Books on Architecture, " De architectura libri decem) is a treatise written by the Roman architect and military engineer Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80–70 BCE – d. after 15 BCE. This work is dedicated to his patron, Emperor Caesar Augustus, and his sister Octavia Minor, to whose commendation Vitruvius attributes his introduction to the emperor. The treatise serves as a guide for building projects. Notably the only architectural treatise to have survived from antiquity, it has been considered, since the Renaissance, as the first known book on architectural theory. Furthermore, it has been recognized as a fundamental source on the canon of classical architecture.11 " That reward, which you initially granted me, you have maintained on the recommendation of your sister. Therefore, being obliged by this favor that allows me to live without hardship until the end of my life, I began to write these books for you, for I realized that you had erected many buildings, that you were currently erecting others, and that in the future you would put your effort into building public and private buildings in accordance with the magnitude of your deeds, so that your memory may endure in posterity. " Vitruvius, De architectura (written between 27 BCE and 23 BCE). In that location, Octavia also erected two public libraries, one for Latin books and the other for Greek books. It is plausible that the collections from Marcellus's private library served as the basis for these. The ancient map of Rome, the Forma Urbis Severiana, reveals the presence of an exedra connecting the temples and the libraries, possibly a space intended for recitations and, occasionally, for Senate sessions. Within the portico, Octavia incorporated a gallery of statues, among which was a representation of Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi. This statue gained renown for being the first female statue publicly displayed in Rome. Vitruvius, who likely had knowledge of this work and whose treatise Octavia was familiar with, wrote about porticoes in cities: "The spaces between 11Octavia the Younger (c. 69–11 BCE) was Augustus’s sister. The Porticus Octaviae, rebuilt in her honor after 27 BCE, housed the libraries she established in memory of her son Marcellus. 31

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY the porticoes should be open to the air and, in my opinion, should be adorned with green plants, since open walkways offer greater health benefits." He expounds the idea that open-air walkways are beneficial to visual and physical health, providing a clear connection between architecture and public health. Vitruvius advocated for the creation of wide and decorative open-air walkways in all cities, highlighting their advantages in both times of peace and war. These walkways, according to him, contribute to the health and safety of cities. According to Plutarch's account, Octavia, between 27 and 23 BCE, dedicated her resources to the construction of a portico in honor of her deceased son. This portico took the form of a colonnaded quadrilateral, encompassing approximately 119 by 135 meters, and surrounded the temples of Juno Regina and Jupiter Stator. The last temple, highlighted by Vitruvius in his treatise, was located near the Theater of Marcellus. Although it was common for Roman women to commission the construction of small temples and sanctuaries, the Portico of Octavia stands out as possibly the first urban-scale intervention carried out by a woman in Rome. The contemporary wording at the time of the portico's construction raises the intriguing question of whether Vitruvius was present during the work and, if so, in what capacity he participated? Did he perhaps play an advisory or consultative role in the realization of this architectural project? Architectural program of the portico was later replicated by Livia, Octavian's wife, around 15 BCE on the Esquiline Hill. The shared choice of this type of building, which served functions related to health, culture, and memory, does not appear to have been accidental. Both women, Octavia and Livia, demonstrated a shared appreciation for a multifunctional architectural space that addressed diverse needs of Roman society. Over the years, the portico underwent several transformations, faced fires and earthquakes, and finally, in the year 770, it was built on top of the entrance propylaeum of the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, evidencing its evolution and adaptation over the centuries. The death of Octavia, which occurred in 11 BCE (although some ancient sources offer slightly different dates), highlights her importance in Octavian's life. The emperor bestowed upon her the highest funeral honors, granting her exceptional treatment as a state hero, which was unusual for 32

Vitruvius and his principles. It is worth clarifying a common misconception: although Vitruvius does explicitly state the triad of firmness (firmitas), utility (utilitas), and beauty (venustas) in De architectura 1.3.2, he does not present it as a universal and abstract axiom upon which all architecture "depends," but rather as the three qualities that a well-made work must possess, within the specific context of building construction. The interpretation of the triad as a canonical and autonomous formula was consolidated later. However, after the publication of a summary of the work by Claude Perrault in 1673, which showed little respect for the original, the so-called Vitruvian triad became established and became a veritable "legend" repeated by generations of architects. In fact, when Vitruvius dares to attempt an analysis of the art he writes about, he proposes to understand architecture as composed of four elements: architectural order (relationship of each part with its use), arrangement (" The kinds of arrangement [...] are the layout in plan, in elevation and in perspective "), proportion (" Uniform concordance between the whole work and its parts ") and distribution (in Greek oikonomía, it consists " in the proper and best possible use of materials and land, and in ensuring the lowest cost of the work achieved in a rational and balanced way "). It must be realized that his doubts on this matter are quite intense, since four pages later he divides architecture into three parts: construction, gnomonics, and mechanics (Vitruvian Royal Framework [Artus Vitruviani regii: expression of the author's interpretation; in classical Latin, artus means " joints, " not " conceptual framework " ]). However interesting and suggestive this may be, it should not be forgotten that this treatise is the only classical treatise that has come down to us, and the probability that it is the best of its time is small. The history of the various versions of Vitruvius's treatise aptly summarizes the conflict surrounding the definition of architecture. In 1673, Claude Perrault, a physician and physiologist specializing in cadaver dissection and a skilled draftsman, published his abridged translation of Vitruvius's treatise, which was completely reorganized. However, it was through Perrault 's 33

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY " summary " that Vitruvius was disseminated and influenced the treatises and theories of subsequent centuries. And it is in this summary that the Vitruvian triad emerged: firmitas, the concepts of firmitas (firmness), utilitas (utility), and venustas (beauty). Public buildings must satisfy three conditions: firmitas (structural soundness and durability), utilitas (functional convenience and proper distribution of space), and venustas (elegance and beauty of appearance). Critical note: The translation of " firmitas " as " strength " is inaccurate; the Latin term designates the stability achieved through the correct selection of materials and the solidity of the foundations. " Venustas " is not simply " beauty " but the visual grace that results from correct proportions; cf. Vitruvius, De architectura 1.3.2, and the discussion in Rowland and Howe, 1999, 66. • The stability of any building is intimately linked to its structure. • Regarding utility, a more abstract concept, consideration is given to both the minimum requirements to guarantee comfort and functionality in the use of an independent space and the efficient relationship and communication between the different spaces that make up the architectural program, which shapes a typology (i.e., the function - space relationship). • On the other hand, beauty, an aspect that can be considered subjective and inherent, is linked to the aesthetic value that arises from the interaction between various design elements. These elements encompass the proportions used to dimension the building's components, the architect's characteristic style, the building's personality, the materials used in its finishes, and the design of the architectural elements, whether functional, structural, or decorative. The substantial difference between Perrault's version and the previous ones lies, according to José Luis González Moreno-Navarro, in that Perrault misrepresents " the synthetic character of architecture in a strictly analytical vision and fragmented into three autonomous branches [which] is a consequence of his mental structure [.] formed throughout a dedicated life to 34

Vitruvius's work, "De architectura," was published in printed editions after its manuscript. Among the printed editions, the following stand out: Incunabula edition (editio princeps): The first printed edition of "De architectura" was published by Fra Giovanni Sulpitius in 1486. This edition was the original version, without illustrations. A second edition was published in 1495 or 1496. Illustrated edition by Fra Giovanni Giocondo: Fra Giovanni Giocondo, a Dominican friar, produced the first illustrated edition with woodcuts in Venice in 1511. This edition featured magnificent illustrations and a meticulous philosophical approach. Italian translations: Italian translations began to circulate in the 1520s. The first printed edition of an Italian translation, with new illustrations, was produced by Cesare Cesariano in Como in 1521. Cesariano was a friend of the architect Bramante. Translations into other European languages: Vitruvius's work was quickly translated into other European languages. The first French version was published in 1547, and the first German version followed in 1548. The first Spanish translation was published in 1582 by Miguel de Urrea and Juan Gracián. The most authoritative and influential edition was published in French in 1673 by Claude Perrault, commissioned by Jean-Baptiste Colbert in 1664. English adaptations and translations: John Shute based his book "The First and Chief Grounds of Architecture" on Vitruvius's text in 1563. Sir Henry Wotton published " The Elements of Architecture" in 1624, an adaptation heavily influenced by Vitruvius. The first complete English translation of the first five volumes was completed in 1771, and the entire work was published in 1791. Later editions: Over the years, many later editions of "De architectura" were published, with detailed and interpretive illustrations. Vitruvius's work became a popular subject of hermeneutics thanks to printing and widespread dissemination. 41

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY There is a story and a certain mythology associated with Archimedes 48that Vitruvius mentions in his book about the discovery of the principle that bears his name. Legend has it that the genius from Syracuse uttered the word Eureka 49(today synonymous with achievements of all kinds) when he entered his bathtub and realized that the volume of water displaced fell over the circular edge of the tub. This displacement was equal to the volume of his body. In this way, he created the theoretical basis for what later became known as Archimedes Principle.This principle describes: A body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid at rest experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Vitruvius’s anecdote concerns displaced volume and the composition of a crown; it does not formulate the modern law of buoyancy in these terms. Vitruvius recounts how King Hiero of Syracuse suspected that silver had been substituted for some of the gold supplied for a votive crown. He asked Archimedes to investigate the suspected fraud. While entering a bath, Archimedes noticed that the water displaced corresponded to the volume of his submerged body. The account then describes comparative tests with equal weights of gold, silver and the crown. The details about sleepless nights and advice from his wife do not occur in Vitruvius’s narrative and should not be treated as part of his testimony. 48Archimedes of Syracuse (in ancient Greek) Ἀρχιμήδης (Syracuse (Sicily), ca. 287 BC – ibid., ca. 212 BC) was a Greek physicist, engineer, inventor, astronomer and mathematician. 49Εὕρηκα (heūrēka), ‘I have found it’, is the exclamation traditionally associated with Archimedes in the story of the crown. The narrative belongs to the later biographical tradition. 64

Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was the first known mathematician to use regular n-sided polygons as a method of approximating the number π by both underestimation and overestimation. Starting with hexagons inscribed and circumscribed about circles and progressively doubling the number of sides until reaching 96-sided polygons, he obtained the value 3 < π < 3 1/7 (approximately 3.1416). This method, known as the " method of exhaustion, " is one of the most significant mathematical achievements of antiquity.51 The Eureka anecdote concerns the principle of buoyancy, not the value of π. The calculation of π by means of inscribed and circumscribed polygons is a separate achievement, set forth in his treatise Measurement of the Circle (Περὶ κύκλου μέτρησις), where he bounds π between 3.1408 and 3.1428 using polygons of up to 96 sides. PRELIMINARY STUDY The presence of Pythagoras in Vitruvius: Vitruvius does acknowledge the Pythagorean influence on the theory of music and proportion. When Vitruvius speaks of harmony and mathematical ratios (such as the proportions that temples or the human body should maintain), he is operating under the same theoretical framework as the Pythagoreans. However, he does so through technical terms from architecture and geometry (such as module, ratio, proportion), not through the numerical mysticism characteristic of the Pythagorean sect. Although Vitruvius does not cite the tetraktys, modern commentators on De architectura sometimes invoke it to describe the logic of his proportional ratios. Such readings belong to the interpretive literature rather than to Vitruvius’s own statements, and are reported here as that. Difference in approach: Vitruvius is a technician and engineer who writes from a practical and pragmatic perspective for a Roman professional audience. The tetractys belongs to a more esoteric and metaphysical realm of Greek philosophy, a field that Vitruvius prefers to set aside in favor of the constructive applications of geometry.52 The devir and the holy of holies A current of Pythagorean origin in Greco-Roman thought associated number, and the cube in particular, with order; within it the number 216 (6³) carried weight as the cube of the “perfect number” six. Vitruvius alludes to this tradition in the preface to Book V, where he remarks upon the standing of Pythagorean doctrine in the formation of the architect. Vitruvius is the main and almost only source that mentions this practice of organizing texts into blocks of 216 verses (6³). 2. Other mentions related to the number 216 in ancient or Neopythagorean Pythagoreanism: ◦ Cycle of transmigration: According to later doxographical accounts (attributed to Aristoxenus and collected by Iamblichus), the Pythagorean tradition associated the number 216 with a period between reincarnations. This information comes from ancient biographical literature about Pythagoras and is cited here for documentary purposes to illustrate the numerological connotations that Antiquity attributed to this number; its value is testimonial, not doctrinal. ◦ The number 216 was held significant as 6 × 6 × 6, the cube of six; in Pythagorean number theory cubic numbers were taken as figures of stability. This symbolic valuation is recorded here as a feature of that tradition, not as a claim advanced by Vitruvius himself. 3. Rich preserved Pythagorean texts: ◦ Golden Verses → 71 verses (not 216). 80

Vitruvius nowhere names the golden section (sectio aurea), and the symbolic and proportional resonances explored here are offered as the editor’s reflective perspective, clearly distinct from the critical text, the apparatus criticus, and the consensus of modern scholarship set out elsewhere in this edition. The reader concerned only with the technical and historical Vitruvius may proceed directly to the ten books. When we speak of the “divine proportion,” 56we are referring to a numerical relationship of spaces and a way of articulating geometries. It involves cutting a line into two unequal parts, such that the larger segment is to the whole line as the smaller is to the larger. In this way, a relationship of sizes is established, with the same proportionality between the whole divided into larger and smaller parts. Figure 7. Year 1528 This way of proportionally sectioning a line or a rectangle is called the “Golden Proportion.” The numerical representation of this size relationship is called the golden number. The parts creates in the whole a correct articulation of different spaces and uses whose proportion is the golden number.57 The extent to which the architecture of antiquity was actually composed according to the golden ratio is much debated and far from settled. Vitruvius himself nowhere invokes it: his system of proportion is modular and commensurable (symmetria), founded on whole-number ratios derived from a common unit rather than on the irrational ratio Φ. The golden ratio (Φ ≈ 1.618) is a mathematical relationship that expresses the division of a segment into two unequal parts such that the ratio of the whole segment to the larger part is equal to the ratio of the larger part to the smaller. Its geometric expression in logarithmic spirals — known as " golden spirals " — appears in numerous natural forms. Vitruvius does talk extensively about proportions, symmetry (symmetria) and harmony in architecture, especially in Book III (proportions of the temple and the human body), but he uses rational proportions (simple fractions such as 1:2, 1:3, 2:3, 3:5, etc.), not the irrational proportion φ. What Vitruvius does mention in relation to this: • Proportions of the human body and their relationship to the circle and the square (famous passage that inspired Leonardo da Vinci). • The Ionic volute of the capital, which has a spiral shape. However, Vitruvius describes how to construct it using geometric methods of compass and straightedge, not using the golden ratio. The Vitruvian triad: firmitas, utilitas and venustas. Comparative diagram from the illustrative material supplied for this edition; conceptual reference: Vitruvius 1.3.2. It is an explanatory image, not an illustration preserved from the ancient treatise. For Vitruvius, architecture may be defined as the equilibrium of three governing demands — durability (firmitas), serviceability (utilitas), and grace (venustas) — no one of which should override the others, each rather sustaining and completing the rest. To weigh any building without holding all three in view at once would be to judge it only in part. The canon established by Marcus Vitruvius in De architectura constitutes the most influential formulation of this triad in Antiquity. Its principles served as the basis for classical architectural composition, visually and conceptually organizing buildings through modular proportions, symmetry, and eurhythmy. Although Vitruvius does not mention the golden ratio (φ), his system of anthropomorphic proportions exerted a profound subsequent influence on architectural theory. Geometric and modular model for the division of architectural space based on traditional Roman units such as the cubit (cubitus) and the palm (palmus). This drawing, which is not preserved in the ancient manuscripts of De architectura, was reinterpreted and popularized during the Renaissance, reaching its highest expression in Leonardo da Vinci's famous version. During the Renaissance, the rediscovery and translation of De architectura had a decisive impact on architectural theory and practice. Among the most important editions is that of Cesare Cesariano (Como, 1521), the first illustrated translation into Italian, notable for its visual richness. Cesariano reinterpreted the figure of the Vitruvian man in poses ad quadratum and ad circulum, attempting to graphically solve the classic problem of squaring the circle. These illustrations contributed significantly to the dissemination of Vitruvian principles and the consolidation of the humanist ideal of Homo Universalis.59 60 61 The meaning of the Vitruvian Man and the squaring of the circle The Vitruvian Man (also known as Homo ad circulum and Homo ad quadratum) is one of the most emblematic images in the history of architecture and Western thought. Its origin lies in Book III of De architectura by Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, where the Roman author describes the ideal proportions of the human body and its relationship to perfect geometric forms. " Vitruvius did not include a drawing in his original treatise. The image we know today is a Renaissance interpretation, the most famous being the one created by Leonardo da Vinci around 1490. Symbolic and philosophical meaning The figure of the man inscribed simultaneously in a circle and a square represents several levels of meaning: 1. Harmony between the Microcosm and the Macrocosm: Man is seen as a perfect reflection of the universe. The circle symbolizes the divine, the celestial, and the perfect (the cosmos), while the square represents the earthly, the material, and the human. 2. Squaring the Circle. The image alludes to the ancient geometric problem of squaring the circle: constructing a square with the same area as a given circle. This problem, considered unsolvable with classical tools, acquired a profound symbolic meaning: the reconciliation between the finite (square) and the infinite (circle), between matter and spirit. 3. Proportion and Beauty: It represents the classical ideal that beauty arises from harmonious proportion (symmetry). The human body becomes the measure of all things. Why was the Renaissance so obsessed with this image? The Renaissance saw in the Vitruvian Man the perfect embodiment of Homo Universalis (Universal Man), a central ideal of Renaissance humanism. The main reasons were: • Anthropocentrism: Man was no longer just a creature of God, but the measure of all things (as Protagoras stated). Leonardo and his contemporaries saw in this figure the dignity and unlimited potential of humankind. • Reconciliation between Science and Art: The image united geometry, anatomy, architecture and philosophy, fields that the Renaissance sought to integrate. • Revival of Classicism: It represented the recovery of ancient wisdom (Vitruvius) adapted to the new humanist spirit. 86

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Spiritual symbolism: Man's ability to be inscribed both in the circle (divine perfection) and in the square (material reality) symbolized the human being's aspiration to unite the earthly and the celestial. Cesare Cesariano’s illustrated edition of Vitruvius (1521) presents a Renaissance interpretation of the body in relation to circle and square. It postdates Leonardo’s drawing of c. 1490 and therefore cannot be cited as a direct influence on that drawing. Definition of Homo Universalis The expression Homo Universalis (Universal Man) refers to the Renaissance ideal of an individual who develops all their faculties to the fullest: intellectual, artistic, scientific, and physical. Leonardo da Vinci is the paradigmatic example: painter, anatomist, engineer, architect, inventor, and theorist. Thus the Vitruvian Man became the visual symbol of Homo Universalis: a harmonious, proportional being capable of encompassing both the material and spiritual worlds.62 Figure 9. This concept reached its full maturity during the Italian Renaissance, finding one of its most prominent theorists in Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472). Alberti, an architect, humanist, and writer, argued that the artist should not be limited to the traditional role of craftsman, but rather should be a well-rounded intellectual, versed in all disciplines of knowledge. In his treatise De re aedificatoria (1452), Alberti asserted that the architect should possess a comprehensive education encompassing the arts, sciences, and humanities, far surpassing mere technical skill. This vision encapsulates one of the essential principles of Renaissance Humanism: the dignification of humankind as beings capable of harmoniously cultivating all their faculties. For Alberti and his contemporaries, architecture was not only a practical art, but the supreme discipline where scientific knowledge, artistic creativity, and humanistic wisdom converged. In this light, it can be said that the Renaissance was, to a large extent, a product of architectural thought. Architecture became the quintessential all-encompassing art, in which the ideal of Homo Universalis was materialized: the harmonious man, capable of measuring, understanding, and beautifying the world. " The Renaissance was defined by a renewed anthropological conception that placed humankind at the center of the cosmos, endowing it with an unlimited capacity for understanding and transforming reality. This humanist imprint urged the individual to cultivate encyclopedic knowledge, promoting the flourishing of the arts and sciences as a manifestation of human potential." Within this framework, the interest in "squaring the circle" transcended mere mathematical curiosity to become a symbol of intellectual apotheosis: the attempt to reconcile earthly finitude (the square) with divine infinity (the circle). In this quest, the figure of the Vitruvian Man, embedded in the ad quadratum paradigm, was consolidated as the archetype of the Uomo Universale, becoming the ethical and aesthetic guiding principle of the era. The reevaluation of Vitruvian thought was fundamental in this process, materializing in critical translations and commentaries on De architectura that allowed the integration of ancient theory into modern practice. Under this paradigm, the canon of human proportions did not operate merely as a rule of measurement, but as the key to architectural composition; a sacred geometry where the human body, as a microcosm, was established as the guiding axis that 64 dictated the order and proportion of universal architecture.63 Classical architecture was conceived as an expressive synthesis of the intelligible universe, in which idea, form, and number converge. In this worldview, humankind occupied a central and guiding place, acting as the measure and axis of architectural composition. The great works of the past have endured precisely because they were created according to the principles of nature: with logic, economy, and efficiency. Through a minimum of intelligently organized matter, a maximum of effect and stability was achieved. In this context, the golden ratio was understood as a universal principle of balance between the part and the whole, present both in the structure of the cosmos and in human creation. Buildings of the magnitude of the Pantheon in Rome or the great Roman villas were conceived according to Vitruvian principles of proportion; beyond their utilitarian function they came to be regarded as architectural archetypes, embodying enduring models for human experience. Proportion was thus understood, in the classical conception, as a principle of harmony in which the parts are resolved into a coherent whole. The association of this harmony with the golden ratio, however, belongs to later interpreters — from the Renaissance onward — and is not warranted by Vitruvius’s own modular system. “It is plausible to conjecture that the cosmos is not a static entity, but the phenomenological materialization of an original geometric idea-form, fertilized 63Ad Quadratum is a constructive method that relates geometry to architecture in a system of proportions, and a numerical form of light, as well as the representation of a state of consciousness. 64The universal man is the absolutely polished man, as a symbol of the center of the universe. 89

Under this premise, reality becomes a 'ship under eternal construction,' a dynamic system organized through incessant mutation.” This vision finds a fundamental echo in the thought of Johannes Kepler, who in his work Mysterium Cosmographicum postulates the ontological primacy of geometry in the creative act: “Geometry provided God with the model for creation; geometry precedes the existence of divinity or, better yet, is the very essence of God.” This perspective transforms the architectural practice: if geometry constitutes the grammar of the divine logos, the architect, in designing their work, is merely participating in the process of “precipitation” of the intelligible into the sensible. Architecture is revealed, then, as an act of cosmic emulation, where measure and form act as the necessary bridge between the immutability of the idea and the fluidity of the material world.65 The best way to find definitions of Vitruvian Man or Geometric Man is through Pico della Mirandola's discourse on the dignity of man.66 “I have not given you, Adam, a fixed place, nor a proper form, nor a particular gift,” God says to man, “so that you may possess the place, the form, and the gifts you desire, according to your will and your own decision. The first can be compared to a measure of gold; the second should be called a precious jewel.”67 Johannes Kepler Reception and exegesis of the Vitruvian canon: From Homo bene figuratus to sacred geometry The "Vitruvian Man" constitutes a paradigmatic synthesis of human proportions, originally articulated under an architectural and geometric logic in the treatises of the Roman theorist Vitruvius. While contemporary iconography has been dominated by Leonardo da Vinci's celebrated illustration (c. 1490), it is imperative to recognize that this figure represents only one of the many interpretations that emerged during the Renaissance. Among these, Cesare Cesariano's version (1521) stands out, whose technical precision and compositional rigor position it as one of the most comprehensive treatises on the representation of the human canon. The nature of Da Vinci's sketch — originating from his personal notes — transcends mere anatomical observation by superimposing two geometric configurations: quadrature (homo ad quadratum) and circularity (homo ad circulum). This duality underlies the Vitruvian principle of homo bene figuratus, which postulates a harmonious correlation between anatomy and the laws of cosmic order. As Vitruvius explains in De architectura (Book III, 1, 3): 67Kepler 's Platonic model of the solar system has aroused the highest interest throughout the ages. 91

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY “Likewise, the central point of the human body is naturally the navel. For if a man be laid upon his back, with his hands and feet outstretched, and a compass is placed on his navel, when a circle is drawn, the fingers and toes will touch the circumference. Similarly, when the shape of the square is applied to the body, it is observed that the height from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head is equal to the wingspan of the outstretched arms. ” Historically, the absence of illustrations in Vitruvius's original manuscripts acted as a creative catalyst, encouraging scholars and artists, such as Albrecht Dürer and Villard de Honnecourt, to develop systems of visual representation. In architecture, the construction method known as ad quadratum transcended the artistic realm to become the governing system of spatial composition. This paradigm, based on Euclidean geometry, was decisive in the construction of Roman temples and Gothic cathedrals, where the square functioned as the generating module for the arrangement of columns, the span of arches, and the height of vaults. The persistence of this model in the history of art and architecture underscores the convergence between mathematical metrics and humanist aesthetics. Da Vinci's representation, beyond being an anatomical study or a possible selfportrait, embodies the Renaissance aspiration to grasp the order of the universe through bodily measurement. Thus, what began as a note in a technical treatise has transformed into a universal canon of Western culture, symbolizing the moment when geometry ceased to be an abstraction and became the foundation of human existence. 92

Francesco di Giorgio Martini (1439–1502) is a pivotal figure in the transition of architectural thought during the Quattrocento, acting as the necessary bridge between humanist theory and the practice of military engineering. His work is remarkable not only for its technical skill but also for its profound attempt to systematize architecture based on anthropomorphic analogy. Francesco di Giorgio's Treatise: Architecture as Body To systematize Vitruvian theory through an original visual exegesis. In his Trattato di architettura civile e militare, he not only interprets Vitruvius's canon but actively develops it. 95

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY His famous drawing of the "Church-Man" is an illustration of the hypothesis about the cubus rationalis: • The anthropomorphic analogy: Francesco di Giorgio argues that the plan of a temple should be directly based on the proportions of a recumbent human body. The altar, for example, should correspond to the position of the head or the heart. • Structure as an organism: Unlike other theorists, his approach was less speculative and more "constructive." For him, the building possessed nervi (nerves), ossa (bones), and articuli (joints), legitimizing the idea that architecture is a living organism governed by strict geometric laws. “Architecture is a science that, through proportion and measure, imitates divine creation; therefore, the architect must be, above all, a geometer who translates the order of the universe into stone.” > — (Conceptual attribution based on the principles of Francesco di Giorgio). 96

Albrecht Dürer occupies a privileged place in the historiography of art and the theory of Renaissance architecture, not only as an artist, but also as the principal architect of the theoretical systematization of human proportions in the Germanic world. His work is the meeting point where the geometric rigor of the Italian Quattrocento merges with the analytical precision of Nordic humanism. Dürer: The geometric synthesis of the canon To understand the figure of women in Dürer's studies, it is necessary to situate it as the result of a convergence of intellectual sources: 97

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY 1. The Vitruvian and Euclidean influence: Dürer assimilated Vitruvius's concept of homo bene figuratus, but elevated it to a higher mathematical dimension by applying the logic of Euclid's Elements. For Dürer, beauty was not merely a matter of visual harmony, but a demonstrable geometric construction. 2. The mathematical legacy (Alberti and Pacioli): Dürer not only drew upon Alberti's theory of perspective, but also incorporated Luca Pacioli's research on the Divine Proportion. The application of the golden section and regular polygons in the representation of female anatomy allowed Dürer to "rationalize" the body, moving it away from a casual, organic representation and placing it within a system of precise measurements. The Female Figure as a metric canon In his treatise The Four Books on Human Proportion (Vier Bücher von menschlicher Proportion, 1528), Dürer establishes a system where the female figure is articulated through a complex network of geometric proportions. This study stands out for two fundamental contributions: • Variability of the canon: Unlike Vitruvius's static and universal canon, Dürer proposes a "variability of proportions." He classifies different types of bodies according to their constitution, anticipating a more scientific and empirical view of the subject. 98

PRELIMINARY STUDY • The geometry of the female body: For Dürer, the female figure corresponds to a geometry of curves that, nevertheless, are derived from perfect rectangles and circles. The integration of these forms reflects his interest in the quadratum and the circulum, where the female body becomes the "container" of these mathematical laws. Figure 13. Taccola: The « Archimedes of Siena » and technique as Logos Taccola was not just a compiler of machines; he was one of the first to conceptualize technology as a graphic language. His treatises, De ingeneis and De machinis, represent a qualitative leap in the history of architecture and engineering. 1. Illustration as a means of transmitting knowledge: Unlike the manuals of his time, Taccola used drawing not as decorative illustration, but as a tool for technical communication. His diagrams of pulleys, lifting mechanisms, and hydraulic systems allowed engineering knowledge to be standardized. 2. Engineering as the basis of architecture: For Taccola, there was no rigid distinction between architecture and mechanics. The construction of a building required a deep understanding of forces, which directly links him to Vitruvian firmitas. His studies on motion (gears and transmissions) are, in essence, a practical application of geometric reason to the material world. 3. The background of Francesco di Giorgio: It is essential to note that Francesco di Giorgio Martini was an indirect disciple and heir to Taccola's legacy. Many of the technological principles that Francesco integrated into his fortification projects were taken directly from Taccola's notebooks. 100

Cesare Cesariano (1483–1543) represents an unavoidable milestone in architectural historiography: his translation and commentary on Vitruvius's De architectura, published in Como in 1521, is the first edition of the treatise in a vernacular language (Italian). This work is not a simple translation; it is a technical and visual exegesis that consolidated the Vitruvian canon in the Renaissance imagination. Cesariano and the materialization of the canon the study of the cubic ratio (216) and the tradition of geometric proportion in architecture, Cesariano's contribution is doubly relevant: 101

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY 1. Illustration as a theoretical tool: In the absence of Vitruvius' original plans, Cesariano — drawing on his experience as an active architect on the Milan Cathedral — reconstructed the Roman treatise writer's principles through detailed illustrations. His edition is one of the first to offer a visual interpretation of architecture as a metric system. 2. The precision of Homo ad quadratum: On folio CXLIX r, Cesariano presents one of the most rigorous interpretations of the squaring of the circle. His approach is fundamentally pragmatic: man is not only an aesthetic figure, but a geometric module whose proportions dictate the commensuratio (the necessary symmetry between the parts and the whole) of any building. 102

This drawing, a synthesis of pen, ink, and wash on paper, transcends mere anatomical representation to become a visual treatise on applied cosmology. 103

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY The geometric synthesis: Homo ad quadratum and Homo ad circulum The intellectual value of this piece lies in the superposition of two geometric systems that, for the 15th-century mindset, represented the relationship between the finite and the infinite: 1. Homo ad quadratum. In Leonardo’s drawing, the square has its center near the groin; the navel is the center of the circle. The association of the square with terrestrial stability and firmitas is the author’s symbolic interpretation. Within the proposed reading of the cubic ratio and 216, it may be understood as a planar base for a volume; that association is not an explicit doctrine of Vitruvius. 2. Homo ad circulum. Leonardo places the center of the circle at the navel. The association of the circle with the celestial realm, divinity and perfection belongs to the symbolic reading proposed here. It should be distinguished from the anatomical and geometric instructions of De architectura 3.1.3. Figure 16. PRELIMINARY STUDY Agrippa: Geometry as Operative Magic His De occulta philosophia (1533) is the compendium where geometry ceases to be a drawing tool and becomes a language of invocation. For the study of the cubic ratio (216), Agrippa provides a fundamental perspective: 1. The harmony of the microcosm and macrocosm: Agrippa maintains that the human body is a mirror of celestial proportions. His famous representation of man on the pentagram is the mystical extension of Vitruvius 's Homo ad quadratum. Where Da Vinci sees mathematics, Agrippa sees spiritual correspondences. Claude Perrault represents the turning point where Renaissance thought is subjected to the rationalist and critical examination of the early Enlightenment. His work as translator and commentator of De architectura (1673) not only marks a key date in the history of architecture, but also introduces a paradigm shift: architecture is no longer governed solely by Pythagorean dogmas, but by scientific reason. 105

Perrault's figure is fundamental to understanding the decline (or transformation) of the concept of the cubus rationalis (216) and the canon of proportions: 1. The critique of "positive" vs. "arbitrary" beauty: Perrault introduced a revolutionary distinction in his treatise. He argued that there are two types of beauty: 106

PRELIMINARY STUDY ◦ Positive beauty: That which depends on the quality of the materials and the technical execution. ◦ Arbitrary beauty: That which depends on taste and conventions (this is where he classifies Vitruvian proportions). For Perrault, the canon of "perfect proportions" (based on numbers like 216 or the golden section) was a cultural convention and not an absolute truth inscribed in nature. 2. Geometric symbolism: While Renaissance theorists (such as Agrippa, Cesariano, and Dürer) sought a divine or alchemical message in geometry, Perrault demystified these systems. For him, Vitruvius's De architectura was a text that needed to be corrected and adapted through the use of logic and physics, moving away from esoteric interpretations. 3. Translation as a tool for modernization: His French translation, profusely illustrated and commented upon, was the one that finally "cleaned" Vitruvius's text of the Neoplatonic interpretations of previous centuries, preparing the ground for French academicism. The classical orders of architecture The classical orders of architecture are distinguished by their ornamental characteristics, their treatment of the module, and the organic nature of their composition. Classical antiquity bequeathed three main orders: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. Later, the Romans incorporated two additional orders: the Tuscan and the Composite. The Tuscan order, more austere and simple than the Doric, represents a Roman reinterpretation of the Etruscan column. Each order is defined by its own system of proportions, characteristic capitals, and entablatures. The column shafts often featured vertical flutes along their surface. In the case of the Doric order, the number of flutes was usually 20, a figure with clear symbolic significance within the Pythagorean and Vitruvian traditions. One of the characteristics common to the three Greek orders is entasis: the columns are slightly wider at the base and gradually narrow imperceptibly 107

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY towards the capital, giving the column an organic elegance and vitality, avoiding the visual rigidity of a perfect cylindrical shape.68 The gradual narrowing of the column shaft as it rises is called entasis. This technical and aesthetic feature has the main purpose of correcting an optical illusion: without this correction, the straight column would appear slightly concave to the observer. According to Heron of Alexandria, entasis precisely compensates for this visual distortion, making the column appear perfectly straight and structurally sound. For his part, historian Vincent Scully has emphasized that this subtle bulging of the shaft produces the visual effect that the column, aware of the weight it bears, seems to yield slightly under its own load, generating an impression of organic tension and vitality.69 This interpretation coincides with the etymology of the term: the Greek word ἔντασις (éntasis) derives from the verb ἐντείνω (enteínō), which means " to stretch firmly ", " to tighten" or " to put under tension ". The height of columns in the classical orders was determined and visually organized in relation to their lower diameter, used as the basic module of proportion. Doric column has a height-to-diameter ratio of between 6 and 7 meters, giving it a robust and compact character. The Ionic column reaches a ratio of 8 meters, while the Corinthian, the most slender of all, rises to 10 meters. In this last case, the diameter of the base is repeated ten times in the total height of the column. These modular relationships were not mere technical conventions, but possessed a profound symbolic meaning, closely linked to the character and aesthetic expression of each order. 68Doric, Ionic and Corinthian forms belong to the Greek architectural tradition discussed by Vitruvius. His Tuscan arrangements are treated at 4.7. The later five-order scheme, including the Composite as a separate order, belongs to the history of classical architectural theory and must not be attributed as such to Vitruvius’s own classification. 69Hero of Alexandria (Ἥρων ὁ Ἀλεξανδρεύς), probably active in the first century CE, was a mathematician and engineer. His treatises on pneumatics, mechanics and automatic devices are fundamental sources for the history of ancient technology. 108

PRELIMINARY STUDY De architectura, Vitruvius explicitly associates the architectural orders with divine attributes and cosmic principles. According to the Roman author, the Doric order, due to its shorter height and its appearance of robustness and solidity, was the most suitable for male deities. In contrast, the Ionic order, more slender and elegant, was primarily reserved for goddesses. The number 6, characteristic of the Doric column, occupied a prominent place in Pythagorean symbolism, associated with cosmic fire and deities such as Poseidon (Neptune), to whose temples this order was usually dedicated. The number 8, characteristic of the Ionic column, was linked in Indo-European antiquity to the movement of the planet Venus. This order was frequently used in temples dedicated to maternal goddesses, such as Hera or Athena Nike (Ἀθηνᾶ Νίκη), the Victorious Athena.70 Ionic order The Ionic order emerged in the 6th century BC in the region of Ionia, located on the coastal and island strip of Southeast Asia Minor. It achieved great popularity during the Archaic period (c. 750–480 BCE). Vitruvius, in his treatise De architectura, establishes a symbolic distinction between the orders, stating that the Doric is inspired by the robust proportions of the male body, while the Ionic is based on the more elegant and slender forms of the female body (De arch. IV, 1, 6-7). Although the Roman author does not cite his direct sources, this interpretation is probably rooted in the Hellenistic theoretical tradition, particularly in the ideas of architects such as Hermogenes of Priene, author of the famous Temple of Artemis at Magnesia on the Meander (present-day Turkey). The Ionic order spread from the east to the Greek mainland. It is closely related to the Aeolic order, which fell out of use at the end of the Archaic period. Its most distinctive features are the slender shaft with finer and more numerous flutes, a wider and more elaborate base, and above all, the capital with two 70Hera (in ancient Greek Ἥρα H ē ra, or equivalently: Ἥρη Hera (Hērē in Ionic and Homeric Greek), the legitimate wife of Zeus and one of his three sisters in the Olympian pantheon of classical Greek mythology. She also held the title of Queen of the Gods. Her Roman equivalent was Juno. The cow, and later the peacock, were sacrificed to her. Her mother was Rhea and her father Cronus. 109

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY opposing volutes (called helices). Between these volutes, a closed palm leaf was often carved, an element that evokes ancient symbolic poles of Eastern origin, related to the idea of the axis of the world. Vitruvius explains in Book IV that three basic tools are sufficient for drawing and subsequently carving the volutes: a ruler, a set square (to establish the midpoint), and a compass (De arch. IV, 1, 7). Below the volutes, the capital frequently features a collar or astragal that separates the echinus from the fluted 71 shaft. The upper abacus is often decorated with oval and dart motifs. Between the volutes and the abacus of the Ionic capital are ornamental elements that enrich the transition, while the Ionic abacus adopts a rectangular shape, unlike the Doric, whose abacus is a perfect square. This formal difference invites interesting reflections of a geometric nature. If we observe the column from its base, looking through its vertical axis, the Doric column visually suggests the ancient problem of squaring the circle: a square that circumscribes a series of concentric circles. Vitruvius explains the origin and character of the Doric order in the following terms: “(Ion) conquered the territory of Caria and founded magnificent cities there… These cities, after having expelled the Carians and the Leleges, called this part of the land Ionia after their leader Ion, and, having designated precincts consecrated to the immortal gods, they began to build temples. The first temple they saw built in this way was in a Dorian city. Since they wanted to place columns in this temple and did not know the proper proportions, they investigated how to make them so that they would not only be suitable for bearing the load, but also pleasing in appearance due to their proportions. They measured the footprint of a human foot and related it to the height of the man. When they learned that the foot was one-sixth of a man's height, they transferred this ratio to the column. They made the height of the shaft, including the capital, six times greater than the width of its base.” This is how the Doric column brought to buildings the proportions of a male body and its solidity and beauty. " 71The molding of the cornice of an entablature, located just below the crown and immediately above the frieze. Also called a bed molding. 110

PRELIMINARY STUDY (De architectura, 4.1.4-6) Ionic order embodies the symbolism of the spiral and the numbers 8 and 5, closely associated with the movement of the planet Venus in antiquity. The Corinthian order, for its part, represents a more elaborate and ornate synthesis of the two previous orders, constituting a formal culmination linked to the idea of light and spiritual elevation, frequently interpreted as a symbol of immortality. The Corinthian order is the last of the three classical Greek orders and developed during the 4th century BC. It takes its name from the city of Corinth. The oldest known example is found in the Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae (Arcadia), dating from between 450 and 420 BCE. It is not the main order of the temple — which features an exterior Doric colonnade and an interior Ionic one — but appears exceptionally within the cella.72 On the Corinthian order Vitruvius describes the Corinthian order as one that imitates the slenderness of a maiden, for its form evokes the most delicate and graceful adornments of a young woman in the bloom of her youth: “The third style, called Corinthian, imitates virginal slenderness, because its form recalls the most beautiful adornments of a maiden, depicted with the most slender limbs due to her tender age. It is said that the discovery of this capital occurred thus: a maiden of Corinth, already of marriageable age, fell ill and died. Her nurse gathered the toys with which the girl used to play in life, placed them in a small basket, and, taking it to her tomb, placed it upon her. To protect these objects from the open air, she covered the basket with a tile. By chance, this basket fell upon an acanthus root. When spring arrived, the acanthus root, pressed by the weight, sprouted leaves and stems which, as they grew along the sides of the basket and met the edges of the tile, bent outwards, forming volutes. ” Explanatory note — Bk. 4.1 (origin of the Corinthian capital). Vitruvius credits the invention of the Corinthian capital to the sculptor Callimachus, active in Athens and Corinth in the later fifth century BC. The Athenians 72It was created as a representation of the cult of Apollo-Asclepius. It can be interpreted as the Greek version of the fundamental pillar, also a philosopher 's sun. 111
