STUDY OF THE TEN BOOKS Academic Restitution and Writing (Books I and II) The structural breakdown of the first two books of De architectura reveals the epistemic matrix upon which Vitruvius builds the entirety of his treatise. Far from constituting a mere summary of trades, the index of these foundational books traces the ontological transition that runs from the training of the scholar and the geopolitical delimitation of territory (Book I) to the physico-chemical analysis of raw materials and the anthropology of building (Book II). The systematic organization of these chapters is reconfigured under the following academic standard: BOOK I: De architectura et de urbis ordinatione (From architectural science and the organization of urban space) • Chapter I: The epistemology of building and the propaedeutics of the architect. Definition of the discipline through the coexistence of the fabric and the ratiocinatio; breakdown of the encyclopedic training of the professional. • Chapter II: The constitutive axioms of architecture. Analysis of the six theoretical principles that govern classical design: ordinatio (arrangement), dispositio (arrangement), eurythmia (eurhythmy), symmetria (symmetry), decor (decorum) and distributio (distribution or economy). 174

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter III: The parts of architectural science and the ontological triad. Division of knowledge in the construction of buildings (aedificatio), gnomonic (gnomonice) and mechanics (machinatio). Introduction of the three universal requirements: firmitas, utilitas and venustas. • Chapter IV: Environmental Teratology and Selection of Urban Sites (De electione locorum sanissimorum). Hygienist and Hippocratic Criteria for the Founding of Cities; Analysis of Winds, Marsh Fogs, and the Salubrity of Humours. • Chapter V: Poliorcetics and Fortification: The erection of walls and towers. Deep foundation techniques (substructio) and defensive geometry to repel enemy siege engines. • Chapter VI: Climatic urbanism and street orientation. Street layout and interpolation of walls based on the wind rose (anemometry) to neutralize harmful currents in public space. • Chapter VII: Sacred and civil zoning (Dispositio moeniorum). Spatial distribution and allocation of plots for the temples of the immortal gods and the common spaces of the citizens according to liturgical decorum. BOOK II: De materiae facultatibus (From the physical and chemical properties of materials and the origin of tectonics) • Chapter I: Cultural Anthropology and the Genesis of Building. Account of the primitive hut; the domestication of fire as the origin of human society and the transition from the cave to the geometric order. • Chapter II: Cosmology of the elements according to the philosophical schools. Theory of matter based on the pre-Socratic principles (Thales' water, Anaximenes' air, Heraclitus ' fire and Democritus' atoms) as the key to understanding building materials. • Chapter III: The adobe brick (De lateribus). Modular typologies (Lydian, pentador, tetrador), seasonal drying processes and quality control of clay. • Chapter IV: Sand (From harena). Mineralogy classification of quarry sands (fossicia), river sands (flumina) and sea sands (marina), and their suitability for mortar cohesion. 175

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY • Chapter V: Lime (From calce). Chemistry of the calcination of limestone and the agglomeration of the stone components. • Chapter VI: Pozzolan (De pulvere puteolan). The discovery of volcanic dust from the regions of Baiae and Vesuvius; the technological miracle of hydraulic setting (mortar capable of solidifying underwater). Critical Notes 1. On the rendering of pulvere puteolanum: the Roman term pulvere puteolanum corresponds directly to modern pozzolana. This chapter (II.6) is among the most important in the history of Roman civil engineering: pozzolana allowed the Romans to build ports, docks, and bridge foundations submerged directly in water, breaking the limitation of Greek architecture, which always relied on dry rock. 2. Chapter VI of Book I as cosmic geometry: The layout of streets according to the winds was not merely a matter of convenience. Vitruvius describes the placement of a gnomon (a vertical pillar) in the center of the future city to mark the line of the shadow in the morning and afternoon. By joining these points, the East-West line was obtained, and from there the city was divided into a perfect octagon corresponding to the eight principal winds. The Roman city is, therefore, an inhabited sundial, a sacred space perfectly oriented with the axes of the cosmos. 3. From Atom to Brick: In the order of the chapters of Book II, Vitruvius does not jump directly to explaining how to build a wall; he first dedicates an entire chapter (Chapter II) to the philosophy of matter. He explains that to be a good architect, one must understand the behavior of the four elements of nature, because brick, lime, and wood expand, contract, and react according to the invisible laws of pre-Socratic physics. Knowledge always precedes technique.100 Books III and IV of De architectura constitute the dogmatic core of the theory of sacred design in Antiquity. Vitruvius articulates a system where beauty (venustas) is not a subjective criterion, but an emergent mathematical property based on the module (M). Book III takes the human microcosm as its starting 100Pozzolans are siliceous or aluminosiliceous materials of volcanic origin which, mixed with lime, set in the presence of water. They are fundamental to Roman opus caementicium. 176

PRELIMINARY STUDY point to dictate the laws of the Ionic order, while Book IV expands this grammar to encompass the vigor of the Doric and the slenderness of the Corinthian, establishing altar typologies according to liturgical decorum. The systematic organization of these chapters is established under the following academic standard: BOOK III: De sacrorum aedium symmetria (On the symmetries and proportions of sacred temples) • Proem: Apology for the merits of the architect in the face of the injustice of political favor; the immortality of classical treatise writers through the written word. • Chapter I: Anthropometry as the matrix of sacred design (homo bene figuratus). Study of the proportions of the human body and its exact inscription in the perfect figures of the circle and the square; derivation of the perfect numerical system (6, 10 and 16) from anatomy. • Chapter II: Typological classification of temples according to their facades. Geometric definition and distribution of the colonnade: temple in amphiprostyle, prostyle, in antis, dipterous, pseudodipterous and peripterous. • Chapter III: Classification of temples according to the intercolumniation (Modulatio). Analysis of the five types of temples based on the distance between columns measured in modules: pycnostylos (thick), systylos (narrow), diastylos (wide), araeostylos (dilated) and eustylos (ideal harmonic proportion). • Chapter IV: Stereobate and deep foundation (De fundamentalis). Excavation techniques and foundation engineering in firm soil or artificial ground using charred wooden piles; construction of the steps (stylobata) and the calculation of the odd scamilli to correct the optical illusions of subsidence on the horizontal line. • Chapter V: The Ionic Order: From the shaft to the entablature. Laws of proportion of the Ionic column: the layout of the base, the reduction of the shaft by means of the entasis (optical curvature), the geometric design of the volute of the capital, and the measurements of the architrave, the frieze and the cornice. BOOK IV: De corinthio et dorico ordine 177

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY (On the architectural orders and the arrangement of the cellas) • Proem: Justification of the continuity of Book III; the need to exhaust the study of the three architectural orders of Hellenic tradition before addressing civil spaces. • Chapter I: The Corinthian Order and the Mythological Genesis of its Proportions. Origin of the Corinthian capital through the anecdote of Callimachus in Corinth and the acanthus basket on the maiden's tomb; analysis of the slenderness of the order as an imitation of the graceful figure of a virgin. • Chapter II: Archaeology of wood and the petrification of the Doric order. Exegesis of tectonic mimesis; how the stone elements of the Doric order (triglyphs, metopes, mutules and drops) are the direct translation and memory of the beams, rafters and wooden joints of the primitive hut. • Chapter III: The metric laws of the Doric order and its design difficulties. The problem of the corner triglyph (Doric angular conflict); exact distribution of modules in the metopes, columns and entablatures to avoid spatial asymmetry. • Chapter IV: Internal arrangement of the temple: The cella and the pronaos. Geometric distribution of the interior walls, the proportions of the naves and the metric relationship between the space of the divinity and the exterior facade. • Chapter V: Cosmic Orientation of Sacred Architecture. Astrological and Liturgical Prescription: The cellas of the temples must be inexorably oriented towards the west, so that the faithful approaching the altar face the east, from where the sunlight originates. • Chapter VI: The doors and openings of the temples. Proportions and profiles of the openings according to three classical typologies: Doric, Ionic and Tuscan (Attic). • Chapter VII: The temples of the Tuscan order (De tuscanicis aedibus). Structural features and proportions of the temple of Italic or Etruscan tradition, characterized by its wide wooden eaves and its almost quadrangular plan. • Chapter VIII: Circular Temples and Altars of the Gods. Geometry of centrally planned temples (tholos) and round peripteral temples; rules for the erection of altars (arae) placed according to the celestial, terrestrial, or chthonic rank of the invoked deity. 178

PRELIMINARY STUDY Critical Notes 1. The Scamilli Impares as a Geometric Secret: In Book III, Chapter IV, Maufras translates the technical term scamilli impares as "unequal bearings." This is one of the most debated passages among Renaissance architects. It refers to the subtle upward curve given to the stylobate (the temple platform). If the platform were perfectly straight in the geometric plane, the human eye would perceive it as sunken due to an optical distortion. By curving it slightly towards the center, the temple appears perfectly stable and regular to the observer. True symmetry requires curving the material straight line. 2. The Doric Angular Conflict as a Mathematical Dilemma: Chapter III of Book IV explains why Greek architects (such as Tarcesius) abandoned the Doric order for the Ionic: due to the rigidity of the triglyph. By law, a triglyph must be positioned exactly over the center of each column and the center of each intercolumniation. However, at the corners of the temple, the triglyph must be placed at the very edge of the frieze, which misaligns the last metope. This dilemma forced the shift from a two-dimensional approach (the façade) to a three-dimensional adjustment of the intercolumniation (corner contraction). Classical geometry prefers to change the physical module rather than disrupt the visual harmony of the whole. 3. The Altar as a Cosmic Interface: The final chapter of Book IV eloquently concludes the hypothesis concerning Delphi and the archetypes. Vitruvius details that the altars of Jupiter and the celestial gods should be elevated; those of Gaia and the underworld (chthonic) deities should be rustic and at ground level; and those of the water nymphs should be intermediate. The altar is the vanishing point where the geometry of the temple communicates with the invisible forces of nature, the same principle that united the ashes of the serpent Python beneath the oracular omphalos of Delphi. From the interior of the cells and the distribution of the pronaos101. Regarding the orientation of the temples. Temple doors and door frames; their proportions 101Pronaos (πρόναος, from πρό, ‘before’, and ναός, ‘temple’) denotes the space in front of a temple’s naos or cella. It forms the temple’s vestibule or entrance and commonly continues the cella’s principal axis. The Latin forms are borrowings from Greek, not the source of the Greek word. 179

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY of the Tuscan order102. We now turn to the middle block of the corpus: Books V, VI, and VII. In these books the text makes the great leap from the rigidity of sacred architecture to the flexibility of Roman civil life and technological pragmatism. The transmission of the passage concerning the palaestra requires care: corrupt readings may obscure its reference to the covered porticoes called xysti (xystos). The title of Book VII, De vitiis, likewise denotes the defects and faults of construction, not any matter of conduct or instruction. “Books V, VI, and VII of De architectura depict the transition from the cosmic space of the gods to the anthropocentric stage of the Roman citizen. Book V regulates the monumentality of the civil fabric (theaters and ports); Book VI theorizes about domestic intimacy (the domus and the villa), adapting it to the climate and social status; and Book VII functions as a rigorous manual of applied chemistry, analyzing coating techniques and the nature of pigments.” The organization of these chapters under a contemporary critical standard is structured as follows: BOOK V: De publicis locis (Of civil architecture and monumental public spaces) • Proem: Justification of the brevity of technical books; defense of the plain and instructive style against the traditional literary rhetoric of philosophers. • Chapter I: The Roman Forum and the legal basilicas. Proportions of the forum in relation to gladiatorial spectacles; geometry of the judicial basilica and case study of the lost Forensic Basilica of Fano erected by Vitruvius himself. • Chapter II: State Logistics: The Treasury, the Prison and the Curia. Technical arrangement of the offices of the public treasury (aerarium), the state prisons and the town hall or municipal palace (curia), guaranteeing their visual harmony with the forum. 102The Tuscan arrangement described by Vitruvius at 4.7 derives from the Etrusco-Italic temple: a column with a simple base, an unfluted shaft and an undecorated capital, with robust proportions. Renaissance theorists, including Serlio, Vignola and Palladio, codified it as the first and simplest of the architectural orders. 180

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter III: The Theater: Environmental Hygiene and Seating Geometry. Criteria for selecting the theater site; exclusion of unhealthy areas to protect the throat and breathing of spectators from harmful air currents. • Chapter IV: Science of music and canonical harmony. Mathematical digression based on the Pythagorean theories of Aristo Xeno; division of musical intervals (harmonic, chromatic and diatonic) essential for architectural acoustics. • Chapter V: The resonating vessels of the theater (Echeia). Symmetrical placement of bronze or clay vases in niches under the seats; tonal calibration in intervals of fourth, fifth and octave to mechanically amplify the human voice. • Chapter VI: Geometric layout of the Roman theater. Inscription of four equilateral triangles within a regular circle to determine the width of the stage (proscaenium), the pulpit (pulpitum) and the accesses of the orchestra. • Chapter VII: Design Variations: The Greek Traditional Theater. Metrical differences with the Roman model; expansion of the orchestra and reduction of the stage for the Hellenic chorus. • Chapter VIII: The roof and porticoes of the theater stage. Aerial acoustics of the stage; inclination of the upper roofs and their function as reflectors of sound waves. • Chapter IX: Public walkways and post-stage porticoes. Design of porticoes behind the theater (porticus post scaenam) as a refuge for citizens from sudden rain; planning of green areas and tree-lined walkways for their therapeutic and hygienic virtues. • Chapter X: The Baths: Hydraulics and thermodynamics of the Roman bath. Arrangement and solar orientation of the saunas and pools; construction technique of the hypocaust (hypocastum or radiant floor) and distribution of the caldarium, tepidarium and frigidarium. • Chapter XI: The Palaestra: Architecture of athletics and the Xysti. Organization of the training courtyards; design of the covered porticoes or xysti intended for physical exercise during the winter. • Chapter XII: Port engineering and submerged hydraulic structures. Construction of docks, dikes and breakwaters; use of wooden caissons (arcae) for water drainage and application of pozzolan hydraulic mortar for the solidification of concrete underwater. 181

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY BOOK VI: De privatis aedificiis (On domestic architecture and the organization of private buildings) • Proem: Praise of education and knowledge as the only wealth that survives the shipwreck; the dignity of the profession in the face of the speculation of upstart builders. • Chapter I: Architectural Climatology and Medical Geography. Suitability of dwellings according to the latitude of the imperium; thick walls and shady orientations for the southern provinces (Egypt), and wide openings oriented to the south for the cold northern regions (Gaul and Germania). • Chapter II: Eurythmy and optical corrections in residential scale. Modification of theoretical proportions based on the actual dimensions of the plot, ensuring that the eye perceives the rooms as balanced despite the constraints of the terrain. • Chapter III: Anatomy of the Domus: From the Atrium to the Peristyle. Modular typologies and measurements of the cavaedium or atrium (Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate); dimensions of the wings (alae), the office of the pater familias (tablinum), the dining rooms (triclinia) and the reception rooms (exedrae). • Chapter IV: Heliothermal orientation of private rooms. Prescription for health and comfort: bedrooms and libraries should face east to take advantage of the morning light; winter dining rooms should face west to capture the heat of the sunset; and art galleries or painting galleries should face north to maintain a constant luminosity that does not degrade the colors. • Chapter V: Sociology of residential space. Distribution of housing in relation to the public rank of the inhabitant; need for majestic private vestibules and basilicas for magistrates and nobles who receive clients, versus modest houses for moneylenders or artisans. • Chapter VI: Rural Architecture: The Rustic Villa. Planning of farms and country houses; arrangement of stables, wine cellars, oil presses (torcularia) and barns according to ventilation and prevention of dampness. • Chapter VII: The Hellenic house and its differences with the Roman one. Structure of the Greek house; strict division between the gynaeceum (women's space) and the andronitis (men's hall); the porticoed courtyards, foreign to the Italic atrium system. 182

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter VIII: Structural Engineering of Residential Foundations. Guidelines for ensuring structural stability and avoiding construction defects in load-bearing walls and archways. BOOK VII: De expolitionibus (From coatings, structural pathology, and pigment chemistry) • Proem: History of technical and scientific literature; catalog of the great treatise writers of classical antiquity (the great bibliographical digression on literary plagiarism and optics). • Chapter I: Pavement and soil engineering. Soil foundation techniques; placement of the stone layer (statumen), the mortar core (rudus) and the final mosaic or marble plaster (nucleus) to prevent settlement cracking. • Chapter II: Scientific preparation of lime for fine stucco. Prolonged slaking process of the lime; mixing and maturation techniques of the paste to avoid granulation that ruins the surfaces. • Chapter III: Construction of vaulted ceilings and plastering. Creation of false vaulted ceilings using reed trusses and wooden profiles; application of the three layers of sand mortar and the three layers of marble dust to achieve a reflective finish. • Chapter IV: Building Pathology: Treatments against Dampness. Solutions for walls in contact with damp ground; erection of double walls with air chambers (muri duplicati) and drainage channels to isolate the painting rooms. • Chapter V: Theory and decline of mural painting. Rules for the decoration of rooms; evolution of pictorial styles and Vitruvius' severe moral criticism against the rise of the fantastic and whimsical frescoes of the "Third Style" (monsters, impossible architectures) to the detriment of classical realistic mimesis. • Chapter VI: Preparation of marble powder. Marble grinding techniques to achieve the characteristic shine and mirror polish of noble stuccos. • Chapter VII: Mineral pigments and natural colors. Location and extraction of chromatic earths: ochres, clays and green earths extracted directly from the imperial quarries. • Chapter VIII: The Metallurgy of Cinnabar and Mercury. Physical properties of bismuth ore and extraction of quicksilver or liquid mercury from the Almadén mines. 183

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY • Chapter IX: Preparation and Fixation of Artificial Cinnabar. Laboratory processes for purifying the intense red pigment (vermilion) and encaustic techniques with beeswax (punica) to protect it from degradation by sunlight. • Chapter X: Artificial pigments and the chemistry of fire. Manufacture of carbon black by controlled combustion of resins in special furnaces. • Chapter XI: Alexandrian Blue and Burnt Ochre. Metallurgy of copper silicate blue (Egyptian blue) invented in Alexandria and the thermal roasting process of yellow ochre to transform it into deep red. • Chapter XII: Chemical Corrosion Processes: Whitewash, Verdigris, and Minium. Obtaining lead white (cerussa) and copper green by exposing metals to vinegar vapors; production of minium from heating lead. • Chapter XIII: Imperial Purple and Marine Mollusks. Extraction of the most valuable dye of antiquity from the glands of murex snails, intended exclusively for the decoration of emperors and the highest-ranking temples. • Chapter XIV: Substitution Pigments and Adulterations. Techniques for imitating purple and expensive colors using cheap vegetable dyes (madre root, yellow) mixed with gypsum. Critical Notes 1. The Palaestra and the Xysti. The technical term xystos (plural xysti) denotes covered porticoes discussed in Book V, Chapter XI.Xystos were the covered, elongated porticoes where Greek and Roman athletes trained during winter storms. The technical vocabulary of the palaestra belongs to the spatial organization of ancient gymnastic architecture and its reception in the Augustan cultural setting. 2. On the title of Book VII (De vitiis): the phrase denotes the material defects, hidden flaws, and faults in the execution of a work — not pedagogy or morality. Chapters I and IV of Book VII treat of how a careless mason who fails to slake the lime properly, or who does not protect the walls from ground damp, ruins the physical fabric of the wall. It is, in the strict sense, the engineering of construction pathologies. 3. Third Pictorial Style as Geometric Transgression: Chapter V of Book VII contains Vitruvius's famous moral complaint against the painters of 184

PRELIMINARY STUDY his time. Vitruvius hated the fantastic Pompeian style because it depicted thin reeds supporting heavy roofs, or human figures sprouting from flowers. For him, this was a violation of structural truth. If a reed cannot support a roof in material reality (firmitas), painting that reed supporting a roof on the wall is an aesthetic lie that destroys ratiocinatio. Decoration must be subordinate to the immutable laws of physics and statics. These two books demonstrate that Roman architecture was not confined to the earth’s surface: Book VIII descends into the depths of the crust through hydraulic engineering, while Book IX rises to the celestial vault through analemmatic and gnomonic astronomy. It is essential to clarify that Vitruvius’s astronomical digression is not an ornamental addition, but the necessary mathematical basis enabling the architect to measure time (sundials) and to orient buildings with respect to the solstices and equinoxes. " Books VIII and IX of De architectura represent the expansion of the discipline of building to encompass the two great fluids of the cosmos: subterranean water and celestial light. Book VIII functions as a treatise on applied geology and fluid engineering, systematizing everything from hidden prospecting to the construction of cisterns; meanwhile, Book IX operates as a compendium of geocentric astrophysics, dictating the mechanical laws that allow the capture of the sun's shadow to regulate the time of civilization." Contemporary analytical standard is broken down as follows: BOOK VIII: De aqua hydraulic engineering and water prospecting) • Proem: Praise of water as the primordial element of the cosmos; its absolute necessity for the survival of life and ritual purity in the face of the other elements of nature. • Chapter I: Geological prospecting and detection of hidden sources (De inventione aquae). Techniques of observing the terrain at dawn; analysis of indicator vegetation (rushes, willows, ivies) and methods of test excavation using inverted bronze vessels to capture the condensation of telluric vapor. • Chapter II: The hydrological cycle and rainwater. Physics of evaporation and condensation; analysis of the purity and safety of rainwater compared to surface runoff or clay infiltration water. 185

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY • Chapter III: Thermalism and chemical properties of springs. Study of hot, sulphurous and mineral waters; analysis of the geological nature of the great rivers and lakes of the imperium, and their impact on the health of the populations. • Chapter IV: Water Teratology: Springs with extraordinary qualities. Catalog of springs with psychotropic, toxic or medicinal effects depending on the minerals (acids, alkalis, iron) present in the underground strata. • Chapter V: Quality control and organoleptic analysis of water. Methodology to verify the safety of the water before its channeling: visual inspection of the transparency, taste, speed of cooking of legumes and clinical examination of the physical constitution and viscera of the animals that inhabit the area. • Chapter VI: Topographic Leveling Engineering: The Chorobates. Technical description and calibration of the chorobates (the twenty-foot-long leveling rule provided with plumb bobs and water channel) and of alternative optical instruments such as the dioptra and the water level (libella). • Chapter VII: Conduction systems, wells and cisterns of opus signinum. Water transport techniques using three systems: masonry channels (specus), lead pipes (fistulae) operating on the principle of the inverted siphon (venter), and fired clay conduits (tubuli). Methodology for excavating wells and waterproofing cisterns using beaten hydraulic mortar. BOOK IX: De gnomonica analemmatic astronomy, and sundials) • Proem: Praise to the inventors of athletic games and to the wise men of letters; the preeminence of the mathematical discoveries of Pythagoras (his theorem), Democritus and Archimedes (the hydrostatic principle of the golden crown) as the true glories of humanity. • Chapter I: Geocentric Astronomy and the Zodiac System. Configuration of the universe according to the model of the celestial spheres; the movement of the sun and the seven planets (wandering stars) through the twelve zodiacal constellations. 186

PRELIMINARY STUDY • Chapter II: Selenography: The phases of the Moon. Geometric explanation of the lunar waxing and waning according to the theory of the half luminous and half opaque sphere (theory of Berossus the Chaldean). • Chapter III: Heliochrony: Solar declination and the variation of hours. Analysis of how the sun's transit through the signs of the Zodiac modifies the length of days and nights, varying the duration of temporal (Roman) hours according to the seasons of the year. • Chapter IV: Northern Uranography: The Northern Constellations. Catalog and coordinates of the stars located between the plane of the Zodiac and the north pole (Ursa Major, Ursa Minor, Draco and Boötes). • Chapter V: Southern Uranography: The Southern Constellations. Description of the stars visible in the southern hemisphere, located between the Zodiac and the Antarctic pole (Orion, Canis Major, Argo Navis). • Chapter VI: Chaldean Astrology and Weather Prediction. Introduction to the sciences of astral divination and meteorological forecasting based on planetary conjunctions and eclipses. • Chapter VII: Descriptive Geometry: Drawing the Analemma. The fundamental mathematical method for projecting the three-dimensional curve of the sun's path onto a two-dimensional flat surface using a ruler and compass, serving as a matrix for any latitude on Earth. • Chapter VIII: Gnomonics: Typologies of sundials and water clocks. Catalog of inventors and models of sundials (horologia): the hemicycle of Berossus, the scaphe of Aristarchus, the plinth of Scopinas, and description of the complex mechanisms of clepsydras or automatic water clocks driven by gears and regulated floats (inventions of Ctesibius). Critical Notes 1. Opus Signinum and Roman hydraulic waterproofing: In Chapter VII of Book VIII, Vitruvius treats lime and cement cisterns. Philologically, the Roman term is opus signinum (lime mortar mixed with fragments of pottery and crushed tiles). The addition of the pottery triggers a chemical reaction that renders the mortar absolutely impermeable. This detail is technically significant: the channeled water is retained without seepage within a watertight lining of opus signinum. 187

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY 2. The analemma of Book IX: geometric projection in gnomonics: Chapter VII of Book IX is a scientific core for the study of regulated space. The analemma is not an artistic drawing; it is a pure geometric construction that projects the apparent annual motion of the Sun, mapping it onto the twodimensional plane of the dial. By mastering the analemma, the Roman architect could calculate the exact shadow a building would cast at any time of day and on any day of the year (equinoxes and solstices). The method thus allowed the architect to represent, on a plane surface, the geometry governing the Sun's apparent course throughout the year. 3. The Inverted Siphon (Venter) and the Mastery of Gravity: In Book VIII, Chapter VII, the description of the lead pipes crossing the valleys demonstrates that Roman engineers understood the physics of communicating vessels. To prevent water pressure from breaking the pipes at the bottom of the valley, they constructed a horizontal section called a venter (belly). Roman engineering did not evade the forces of gravity, but rather balanced them through the symmetry of the watercourse. Astronomy is used to predict changes in the weather, and what will happen to men, based on the appearance of the stars at the time of their birth. How to make an analemma103. Since the invention of summer clocks or sundials; Clepsydras and winter or anaphoric clocks.104 105 103In Vitruvius (9.1.1; 9.7), the analemma (ἀνάλημμα) is a geometrical projection used to lay out a sundial’s hour lines. It is distinct from the figure-of-eight curve also called an analemma in modern astronomy. 104 A clepsydra (from the Greek κλεψύδρα, kléptein,"To steal, and ὕδωρ hydōr," water") is any mechanism for measuring time by the regulated flow of a liquid into or out of a graduated container, thus giving rise to two different types of clocks depending on the direction of the flow. Clepsydras date back to ancient Egypt (mrḫyt) and were used especially at night, when sundials were no longer useful. The earliest water clocks consisted of a ceramic vessel filled with water to a certain level, with a hole at the base of a suitable size to ensure the liquid flowed out at a specific rate and, therefore, in a predetermined time. The container had several markings inside, so that the water level indicated the different periods, both day and night. 105Ctesibius (Κτησίβιος), active in third-century BCE Alexandria, was an inventor and hydraulic and mechanical engineer. The ancient tradition credits him with work on compressed air, pumps and the improvement of water clocks. His writings do not survive intact, and exact birth and death dates should not be inferred from the chronology of other Hellenistic scientists. 188

PRELIMINARY STUDY This final book distils Vitruvius’s pragmatism in its purest form — that of a legionary military engineer. One technical term calls for care: the Latin cochlea must be rendered as the Archimedes’ screw (the water-screw, or auger pump for raising fluids), not by any popular nineteenth-century equivalent. We also systematise the direct influence of this book on the seminal treatises of antiquity and the Renaissance. Book X of De architectura crowns the work not as a technical appendix, but as the dynamic manifestation of physics and geometry applied to the service of the Roman state. Vitruvius breaks down the laws of elementary kinematics, distinguishing between large traction machines and precision devices, before turning to industrial hydraulics and military torsion ballistics, whose mathematical calibration depended directly on the geometric solution of doubling the cube. The organization of these chapters is reconfigured under the following contemporary critical standard: BOOK X: De machinis (From mechanical science, fluid engineering, and poliorcetics) • Proem: Ethical and economic considerations on the budgets of public works; the severe laws of the city of Ephesus that forced architects to answer with their own assets in case of financial deviations, and an apology for prudence in the administration of the State's resources. • Chapter I: Epistemology of mechanics and definition of machine. Conceptual distinction between the machine (machina), which requires the participation of several operators and displays high mechanical performance, and the instrument or organ (organum), operated by the skill of a single individual. • Chapter II: Kinematic lifting and traction devices. Description and breakdown of the loading cranes (trispastos, pentaspastos and polyspastos) used in temple construction; calculation of pulleys, winches, capstans and the physics of levers. • Chapter III: Kinematic Theory: The Straight Line and Circular Motion. Analysis of the physical principles of motion; how the combination of rectilinear and circular forces governs the operation of all machines, exemplified in ship rudders and scales. 189

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY • Chapter IV: Hydraulic lifting engineering: Drums and waterwheels. Mechanisms designed to extract water from rivers and shallow wells by means of paddle wheels and compartmentalized drums powered by human traction (tympana). • Chapter V: Watermills and industrial waterwheels. The automation of milling; description of the Roman angle gear that transmits the movement from the vertical shaft of the waterwheel to the horizontal shaft of the millstones for grinding the grain. • Chapter VI: The Archimedes’ screw (cochlea). Analysis of the waterscrew: the geometric design of the helix wrapped about a wooden cylinder to raise large volumes of water through a low lift, as used in draining mines and fields. • Chapter VII: Ctesibius's impeller pump. Pneumatics and precision engineering; description of the double - cylinder bronze machine provided with pistons, valves and suction pipes capable of raising water to great heights for fire extinguishing. • Chapter VIII: The Hydraulic Organ (Hydraulus). The pinnacle of ancient mechanical precision; application of the laws of hydraulic pneumatics to regulate air pressure by means of water, making flutes and pipes sound through a mechanical keyboard. • Chapter IX: Odometry: Measurement of distances on land and sea. Description of the mechanical odometer or classical taximeter; a system of reducing gears coupled to the wheels of a cart (or to the paddles of a ship) that dropped small bronze spheres into a container for each mile traveled. • Chapter X: Military Torsion Ballistics: Catapults and Scorpions. Principles of Poliorcetics; Calculation of the diameter of the torsion cord module (made of tendons or human hair) based on the weight of the projectile or arrow that the scorpion was to fire. • Chapter XI: Engineering of the Ballista (Ballistae). Mathematical proportions and calibration tables for the construction of large pieces of artillery intended for launching heavy stones to demolish walls. • Chapter XII: Calibration and tempering of torsion cords. Methodology for symmetrically tensioning the arms of catapults and ballistae using acoustic nut wrenches, ensuring that both torsion modules vibrate with the same musical note to guarantee a straight trajectory for the shot. 190

PRELIMINARY STUDY Vitruvian Tradition and the Family Tree of Architectural Theory The disappearance of the original figures (estimated at a minimum of ten modular plates affixed to the ends of the papyrus scrolls by Vitruvius himself) forced 16th-century editors to undertake a colossal graphic reconstruction. This hermeneutical effort gave rise to the creation of the great modern treatises, which adopted the Vitruvian theoretical framework and adapted it to the needs of their respective eras. • Pliny the Elder (Natural History, 1st century AD): An immediate contemporary in the historiographical record. Pliny absorbed and indexed Vitruvius's mineralogical and metallurgical investigations (particularly the data in Book VII on cinnabar, lime, and marbles) within his books dedicated to geology and the plastic arts, validating the soundness of science during the time of Augustus. • Leon Battista Alberti (De re aedificatoria, 1452): The first great treatise of Renaissance humanism. Alberti adopts the decemviral structure (ten books) and cardinal concepts of Vitruvius, but purifies the medievalized technical Latin of the Roman under the lens of Ciceronian prose and Platonic philosophy, transforming the Vitruvian triad into the supreme concept of Concinnitas. • Andrea Palladio (I quattro libri dell'architettura, 1570): The apotheosis of visual codification. Palladio synthesizes Vitruvius's abstract theory and translates it into a practical system illustrated with engravings of perfect geometric symmetry. Through his four books, Palladio applies the module and proportions of Vitruvian temples (Books III and IV) to the design of urban palaces and residential villas, universalizing the classical canon in Western architecture. Critical Notes 1. The cochlea (Archimedes’ screw): the Latin cochlea designates the water-screw and must be rendered accordingly, not by any popular nineteenthcentury term. It effects the transformation of continuous circular motion into an upward linear flow of fluid — one of the great achievements of applied helical geometry, showing that the Roman architect had mastered the principles of hydraulics. 191

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY 2. Music as a regulator of warfare: Chapter XII of Book X. Vitruvius details how military engineers had to tune the catapult strings by musical ear. If one arm of the ballista was tighter than the other, the projectile would be deflected. This demonstrates that the harmonic music of Book V (designed for theaters) and the physics of warfare in Book X share the same mathematical framework. Music is not an art of entertainment; it is the physical law that balances both the voice in the sacred space and destructive energy on the battlefield. 3. Odometry as the Metric of the Empire: The invention of the odometer (Chapter IX) is the materialization of the control of Roman space. By inventing a machine that mechanically counts miles, architecture aligns itself with Agrippa's cartography: the untamed territory of the barbarian provinces is fragmented, measured, and dominated by the geometric regularity of the odometer. Measured space is space conquered by Ratio. De architectura, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80 – 70 BCE – d. after 15 BCE), probably written around 15 BCE The chronology agreed upon by modern philologists (such as Pierre Gros and Louis Callebat) places the birth of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio around 80–70 BCE and his death around 15 BCE. His magnum opus, De architectura, was written progressively and dedicated to Octavian Augustus between 27 BCE and 23 BCE (coinciding with the consolidation of the Principate and the great urban renewal program of Rome), although some technical appendices could be revised until 15 BCE. " The treatise De architectura, the only theoretical corpus of Greco-Roman architecture preserved in its entirety, was composed by the engineer and military architect Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80/70 BCE – 15 BCE). The internal chronology of the text places its main phase of writing between 27 BCE and 23 BCE, a critical period in the history of the West marked by the transition from the Roman Republic to the Principate of Octavian Augustus." Vitruvius conceived his ten books not as a descriptive manual a posteriori, but as a programmatic and legitimizing manifesto of the new political order. By dedicating the work to the Imperator, the author aligned geometric science and construction techniques with the official program of the Restitutio Reipublicae. The treatise served as the conceptual framework for the 192

PRELIMINARY STUDY monumentalization of public space, providing Augustus with the architectural tools necessary to fulfill his celebrated historiographical maxim: to have received a Rome built of brick (latericia) and to bequeath to posterity a metropolis clad in marble (marmorea). The dating of the work, fixed in its definitive edition around 15 BCE, closes the era of Hellenistic influence on the Italian peninsula and inaugurates the construction canon of the global Empire. Critical Notes 1. The significance of 27 BCE: In this year, Octavian received the sacred title of Augustus from the Senate. This is the precise moment when Vitruvius decided to present him with the treatise. This is not a chronological coincidence: Vitruvius knew that a new Empire needed a new architecture that reflected stability, order, and eternity (firmitas). It should be emphasized that the ten books constitute the geometric constitution of Augustus's Empire. 2. The Pax Romana as a technical requirement: Vitruvius confesses in the Proem of Book I that, while the Roman state was mired in civil wars (against Julius Caesar, Mark Antony, and Pompey), he dedicated himself to artillery and legionary ballistics. Only when Augustus pacified the world (Pax Romana) could the architect withdraw the siege engines and devote himself to theorizing about temples and forums. The order of sacred space was only possible when the chaos of war ceased. 3. The transition from the papyrus scroll (volumina) to the modern book: around 15 BCE, Vitruvius presented Augustus with ten separate papyrus scrolls (volumina). The concept of a single bound book is a late antique and medieval development. This physical separation explains why each book has its own independent preface (proemium): each scroll was opened and read before the emperor as a separate discursive and scientific unit. This edition not only functioned as a collector's item, but also as a hermeneutical bridge where classical prescriptions regarding the hygienic environment, materials, and modular symmetry were reread through the lens of the 20th-century architectural avant-garde. The Rowland-Morgan duality: the collation of Morgan (1914) with Rowland (1999) covers the entire hermeneutical arc of the twentieth century. Morgan reflects the rigid, engineering reading of the nineteenth century; Rowland integrates the discoveries of latetwentieth-century construction archaeology (the findings at Pompeii, Herculaneum, and the forums). The result is a balance between statics and material history. 3. Fernando Higueras and the modern reception: the technical revision of the Vitruvian edition entrusted to the architect Fernando Higueras is a point of interest for the twentieth-century Hispanic reception of the treatise. Known for his reinforced-concrete structures of complex geometry and organic imbrication (such as the Crown of Thorns in Madrid), Higueras illustrates the continued relevance of the principles of firmitas and modular venustas in modern architecture, which returned to the discipline of the Vitruvian module and the analemma in contemporary design. To definitively close the history of the transmission of De architectura, we delve into the 17th and 18th centuries, the golden age of enlightened codification and the academic institutionalization of the classical canon. These two references represent the two monumental milestones of translation and critical editing in the Modern Age: the French edition by Claude Perrault (1673/1684), which represented a scientific revolution by applying Cartesian rationalist physics to the Roman text, and the Spanish edition by José Ortiz y Sanz (1787), printed by the Royal Printing House, which constitutes the pinnacle of the Hispanic Enlightenment and the birth of scientific archaeology in Spain. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY and European rationalism, periods marked by two publishing ventures of universal significance: • Claude Perrault's rationalist recension (1673/1684): Published under the title Les dix livres d'architecture de Vitruve, corrigez et traduits en françois, the work of the physician, scientist, and architect Claude Perrault transformed the foundations of the discipline. Perrault applied the Cartesian method and the rigor of the Académie des Sciences to the Latin text. His fundamental contribution lay in the demystification of the mystical character of classical proportions; the French scholar argued that beauty (venustas) did not respond to divine or immutable laws of nature, but to a cultural and arbitrary pact of architects (the invention of taste). His sumptuous array of engravings not only illustrated the elusive lost figures, but also served to legitimize the design of the Louvre colonnade, establishing the canon of French Classicism. • The pinnacle of the Hispanic Enlightenment: José Ortiz y Sanz (1787): Following the partial attempts of the preceding century, the priest and Enlightenment thinker Joseph Ortiz y Sanz completed the monumental translation: The Ten Books of Architectura by Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, translated from the Latin and annotated. Printed in Madrid by the prestigious Royal Printing House in an imposing folio format of 42.5 cm, this work marked Spain's entry into modern architectural philology. Ortiz y Sanz did not limit himself to translating; he collated the Vatican codices by hand, corrected the errors accumulated by the Italian translators, and endowed the volume of 56 copperplate engravings with millimeter - level archaeological precision. Sponsored directly by the Bourbon reforms of Charles III and Charles IV, this edition served as the obligatory reference text for the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando, eradicating the decorative excesses of the late Baroque and establishing the rigor of Neoclassicism on Iberian soil. PRELIMINARY STUDY Vitruvius Pollio, M. The Ten Books of Architecture by Marcus Vitruvius, 1787. Pollion (J. Ortiz y Sanz, Trans. and Com.). Madrid: Royal Printing Press. (In-folio, XXVIII, 277 pp., LVI plates). Exegetical notes 1. Claude Perrault's theoretical fracture: this point is crucial for assessing the persistence of a sacred geometry or cosmic order. Perrault opens a wound in the history of architecture: he argues that the golden ratio and the homo bene figuratus are not divine truths. For Perrault, the eyes become accustomed to seeing buildings in a certain way, and that is why they seem beautiful to us, not because they reflect the order of heaven (Book IX). Perrault thus marks the shift from architecture as mysticism and cosmology to architecture as an engineering science and cultural convention. 2. The Royal Printing Press and the Political Control of Order: The Ortiz y Sanz edition (1787) was not a literary whim. The enlightened Spanish state needed to standardize architecture to control its territory (just as Augustus did in 15 BCE). By decreeing that all churches, town halls, and hospitals in the Spanish Empire (including Spanish America) had to follow the 56 plates of Ortiz y Sanz, the Crown used Vitruvian principles to visually standardize the urban landscape and bury the Churrigueresque style. Geometry once again became an instrument of political sovereignty and the ordering of matter. 3. The value of the 56 plates by Ortiz and Sanz: Unlike the Renaissance illustrations of Cesare Cesariano or Palladio (who adapted Vitruvius to their own architectural tastes), the plates by Ortiz and Sanz are characterized by obsessive philological rigor. The Spanish Enlightenment thinker measured ancient monuments, striving to understand the precise mathematics of the texts without adding Baroque or modern embellishments. They represent the birth of modern archaeological technical drawing in the Hispanic world. Regarding the name of the treatise: For the palaeographical and philological assessment, particular attention must be given to Harley MS 2767 (H), held by the British Library. The manuscript, 197

Medieval manuscripts identify works through opening and closing formulas, conventionally called incipit and explicit, as well as through rubrics. Opus Marci Vitruvii Pollionis, De architectura, quod non modo antiquae constructionis rationes, sed etiam universam artium liberalium disciplinam complectitur, diu sub umbra translationum vitiosarum delituit. In hac editione nostra, quae anno bis millesimo vicesimo sexto in lucem profertur, propositum nostrum fuit textum ex editionibus criticis receptum diligenter exponere, lectiones incertas indicare et rationes architectonicas studiosis explanare. Non ignoramus, in hoc vetusto opere, multos locos ob linguam technicam, quae Graecis vocabulis abundat, difficiles esse intellectu. At vero, cum machinae nostrae aetatis echeia pro echo vel chorobaten pro saltatore vertissent, philologiae officium erat verum sensum mechanicum et geometricum restituere. Non est enim vitruvianus textus ad voluptatem legentis scriptus, sed ad aedificandum et ad machinas movendas; unde oportet verba eius tamquam instrumenta ipsa — sicut perpendiculum, regulam, aut circinum — percipi. Speramus igitur hanc nostram operam — Sophia Lux Publishing auspice edita — non modo architectis et ingeniariis, sed etiam philologis et historiae cultoribus, tamquam firmum fundamentum ad opus vitruvianum intellegendum inservituram esse. PRELIMINARY STUDY Praefatio editoris · Editorial principles This section sets out, for the benefit of the scholarly reader, the nature of the present edition, the text that underlies it, the scope of its critical apparatus, and the orthographic and translational conventions adopted throughout. Nature and base text This is a bilingual reading edition with a selective critical apparatus. The authorial Spanish translation by Diego Kurilo is the source of the English translation. Its Latin base is Fritz Krohn’s edition (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), checked against Valentin Rose (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899); the Budé volumes provide further critical and architectural reference by book. A printed or electronic edition is distinguished from a direct reading of an individual manuscript. Where the text departs from the adopted edition, or where a reading remains disputed, the difference must be identified in the apparatus. Scope of the apparatus The critical apparatus of this edition is selective and illustrative rather than exhaustive. It does not record every variant of every witness lemma by lemma, as the great systematic editions (Teubner, Budé) do; instead it concentrates on the passages of decisive importance for the constitution, the dating or the interpretation of the text, which are treated in the Apparatus criticus (Appendix M) and in the analytical restitution of the Greek vocabulary (Appendix N). The reader who requires a full positive apparatus is referred to the editions of Rose, Krohn and the Collection Budé. This limitation is stated openly so that the edition may be judged for what it is: a critical reading edition addressed to the architect and the historian of architecture, uniting the philological apparatus with the technical and architectural analysis. Orthographic conventions In the running Latin text the consonantal u/v is normalized in the modern manner (utilitas, Vitruvius), the classical majuscule V being retained only in display titles and rubrics that reproduce the epigraphic and manuscript usage (DE ARCHITECTVRA). The diphthong ae is written in full; consonantal i is not distinguished as j. Greek words are given in their restored polytonic form, 201

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY with the correct breathings and accents, accompanied where useful by a Latin transliteration; the principles of restitution are set out in Appendix N. Translation The English translation derives from Diego Kurilo’s original Spanish translation, itself made directly from Latin. Its governing aim is fidelity to that authorial interpretation, with Latin used to check doubtful technical terms, concepts and numbers. Granger and Rowland–Howe are comparative references rather than replacement source translations. Technical terms without exact modern equivalents—firmitas, utilitas, venustas, symmetria, ordinatio and dispositio—are retained in Latin where necessary and defined in the Glossary (Appendix A). 202

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I ARGUMENTUM LIBRI I — AFTER THE dedicatory proem to Augustus, Vitruvius defines the encyclopedic training of the architect and the six fundamental principles of the discipline (ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, distributio); he explains the parts of architecture, the choice of healthy sites, the layout of walls and towers, the orientation of streets according to the compass rose and the arrangement of public buildings. Note. — Book I establishes the architect’s education and professional competence, sets out the six categories of I.2.1 (ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor and distributio), formulates the triad firmitas–utilitas– venustas in I.3.2, and then develops questions of health, fortification, winds and urban planning. Its importance for subsequent architectural theory is exceptional, but its categories must be read within their ancient technical and linguistic context. [I.praef.1] Cum divina tua mens et numen, imperator Caesar, imperio potiretur orbis terrarum invictaque virtute cunctis hostibus stratis, triumpho victoriaque tua cives gloriarentur et gentes omnes subactae tuum spectarent nutum populusque Romanus et senatus liberatus timore amplissimis tuis cogitationibus consiliisque gubernaretur, non audebam, tantis occupationibus, de architectura scripta et magnis cogitationibus explicata edere, metuens ne non apto tempore interpellans subirem tui animi offensionem. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I The meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this first paragraph of the preface, Vitruvius uses an extremely elaborate Latin period (a typical construction of rhetorical prose) to address Augustus with great reverence. The fundamental meaning is as follows: Vitruvius justifies the delay in publishing his work De architectura. He explains that, while Augustus was at the height of his power — having pacified the Roman world after the civil wars — he did not dare to distract him with his writings on architecture. The author uses language laden with courtly flattery (typical of Augustan literature): • He describes Augustus's mind as divine and mentions his numen (divine force). • His undefeated military virtus stands out. • It presents the emperor as absolute ruler of the world (imperio potiretur orbis terrarum). • He describes how the Roman people and the Senate, freed from fear, are guided by Augustus’s judgment. With this rich rhetoric, Vitruvius achieves two objectives: 1. Demonstrate humility and respect before the princeps. 2. Carefully choosing the moment to dedicate his work: precisely when Augustus has achieved universal peace and can dedicate himself to cultural and construction projects. This introduction sets the tone for the entire treatise: a technical work presented under imperial protection and seeking to contribute to Augustus's program of architectural and cultural renewal. M. Academic translation “But when I observed that you were concerned not only with the common welfare of all and the organization of the state, but also with the proper arrangement of public buildings — so that, thanks to you, the city had not only grown larger through the annexation of provinces, but also that the majesty of the Empire had the exalted authority of its public buildings — I considered that I should not delay any longer in dedicating these writings to you on such matters at the first opportunity. This is because, in the first place, I was known to your father precisely for this reason and was devoted to his virtue. Now, when the council of the gods consecrated him in the abodes of immortality and transferred your father’s power to your authority, my own loyalty, which remained alive in his memory, transferred its favor to you.” Therefore, I served, along with Marcus Aurelius, Publius Minidius, and Gnaeus Cornelius, in the preparation of ballistae, scorpions, and the repair of other war machines, and I received the corresponding emoluments along with them. These rewards, which you initially granted me, you subsequently maintained on the recommendation of your sister. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this second paragraph of the preface, Vitruvius explains the reasons that prompted him to dedicate his work to Augustus. 210

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I The text develops two main ideas: 1. Thematic justification: Augustus not only concerns himself with military and political matters, but also with urban beautification and architectural monumentality. Vitruvius thus links his treatise to Augustus's political and propagandistic program, centered on the maiestas imperii through public works. 2. Personal justification: Vitruvius reveals his career path. He appears to have served as a military engineer in the time of Julius Caesar (parenti tuo), worked alongside three colleagues in the manufacture and repair of artillery (ballistae, scorpiones and tormenta), and received rewards that Augustus maintained even after Caesar's death, thanks to the recommendation of Octavia (Augustus' sister). Latin text M. Conscripsi praescriptiones terminatas, ut eas attendens et ante facta et futura qualia sint opera per te posses nota habere; namque his voluminibus aperui omnes disciplinae rationes. Since this favor bound me to you and freed me from the fear of poverty for the rest of my life, I began to write these books for you. I had observed that you had built many works and were still building, and that you would continue to care for public and private buildings on a scale commensurate with your achievements, so that they might be handed down to posterity. I have set down precise rules so that, by attending to them, you may judge for yourself the quality of works already completed and of those yet to come; for in these volumes I have explained all the principles of the discipline. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I • De architectura offers as a useful technical manual for the emperor: a guide that will allow him to evaluate the quality of the works already built and supervise those that will be carried out in the future. • It reinforces the idea of architecture as a vehicle for imperial memory, that is, as a means for the greatness of Augustus to endure before posterity. This paragraph marks the transition between the personal dedication and the beginning of the technical content of the treatise. 213

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I M. Vitruvii Pollionis De architectura Book I, Chapter 1.1 Chapter 1 Comparative apparatus — I.1.1. “Architecti est scientia…” is the lemma under discussion. Scientia is translated as “knowledge” or “disciplinary knowledge” wherever “science” might suggest a modern institution. Fabrica and ratiocinatio are not isolated theory and practice, but two dimensions whose conjunction defines the competence of the architectus. Architecti est scientia pluribus disciplinis et variis eruditionibus ornata, cuius iudicio probantur omnia106quae ab ceteris artibus perficiuntur opera. Ea nascitur ex fabrica et ratiocinatione. Fabrica est continuata ac trita usus meditatio, quae manibus perficit[ur] e materia cuiuscumque generis opus [est] ad propositum deformationis. Ratiocinatio autem est, quae res fabricatas sollertiae ac rationis pro portione demonstrare atque explicare potest. The architect’s knowledge embraces many disciplines and varied forms of learning; by its judgment, all works accomplished by the other arts are assessed. It arises from fabrica and ratiocinatio. Fabrica is the continuous, practised exercise of making: through manual work and materials of whatever kind, it brings a work into being according to its intended design. Ratiocinatio, by contrast, enables one to demonstrate and explain constructed works according to the proper proportion of skill and reason. COMPARATIVE CRITICAL NOTE — I.1.1. The manuscript tradition and modern editions do not agree on every detail of this definition. This edition retains cuius iudicio probantur omnia, a transmitted reading also adopted in the modern critical text consulted; Granger, by contrast, regarded the clause as a possible interpolation and proposed different punctuation. For fabrica, the readings perficit[ur] and opus [est] retain editorial brackets. The concluding phrase is given as sollertiae ac rationis 106 cuius iudicio probantur omnia] A disputed passage in the editorial tradition. Krohn (1912) prints these words in the text; other editions have marked them as doubtful or enclosed them in brackets. This edition retains them, but records the discussion without attributing a deletion to the manuscript tradition where the apparatus for the passage has not been verified. 214

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I pro portione, rather than the smoother normalization sollertia ratione proportionis. These distinctions separate transmitted readings, editorial conjecture and syntactic regularization. Exegetical note — Fabrica and ratiocinatio. The distinction does not set manual skill and intellect apart as sealed compartments. Vitruvius presents two inseparable dimensions of the profession: experience in execution and the ability to justify rationally what has been built. Scientia here means the disciplinary knowledge of the architectus, not “science” in its modern institutional sense. Critical Apparatus • Architecti est scientia ] Adopted reading. The genitive architecti indicates “the science proper to the architect” or “the knowledge of the architect”, not “the architect is a science”. • pluribus disciplinis et variis eruditionibus ornata ] Standard reading. Ornata = enriched, decorated. • cuius iudicio probantur omnia] This edition retains the transmitted phrase. Granger questioned its authenticity and proposed treating the passage differently; the manuscript evidence should not be described as unanimous without reference to a critical apparatus. • Ab ceteris artibus] “By the other arts”. This is the adopted phrase. The alternative ex ceteris lacks an identified witness in the sources cited here and is not assigned to a manuscript. • continuata ac trita usus meditatio ] Preferred reading. Trita = worn by use, exercised, habitual. • ad propositum deformationis ] Adopted reading. The distinction is textual, not merely typographical. Academic translation “The architect’s knowledge is enriched by many disciplines and varied forms of learning; by its judgment all works carried out by the other arts are assessed. It arises from building practice (fabrica) and theoretical reasoning (ratiocinatio).” 215

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I practice is the continuous meditation exercised by use, through which the work is carried out with the hands, from any type of material, according to the projected design. Theoretical reasoning, on the other hand, is that which can demonstrate and explain, with technical skill, through method and proportion, works that have already been built. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) This is one of the most important and frequently cited paragraphs in all of Vitruvius's work. In it, he establishes the dual nature of architecture: • Fabrica → The practical and manual dimension of the architect’s work: construction informed by accumulated experience. • Ratiocinatio → Theoretical, intellectual aspect: the ability to explain, justify and project works through reason, mathematics and proportion. From the outset, Vitruvius argues that architecture is not merely a trade, but a scientia (an intellectual discipline) requiring encyclopedic training. The architect must possess profound knowledge in multiple fields (which will be detailed later), as their judgment serves as the supreme criterion for validating the works of other arts. Key concepts: • Architecture as a synthesis between praxis and theoria. • The importance of the proportio (proportion) as a rational principle. • The architect as an intellectual figure and not just as a builder. This paragraph lays the theoretical foundations of the entire treatise and exerted an enormous influence on Renaissance architectural theory (Alberti, Palladio, etc.). M. Vitruvii Pollionis De architectura Book I, Chapter 1.2 Itaque architecti, qui sine litteris contenderant ut manibus essent exercitati, non potuerunt efficere ut haberent pro laboribus auctoritatem; qui autem ratiocinationibus et litteris solis confisi fuerunt, umbram non rem persecuti videntur. At qui utrumque perdidicerunt, uti omnibus armis ornati, citius cum auctoritate quod fuit propositum sunt adsecuti. 216

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Therefore, architects who sought to train their hands without acquiring literary learning could not gain recognition commensurate with their labors; those who relied on reasoning and books alone seem to have pursued the shadow rather than the substance. Those, however, who thoroughly mastered both, equipped as though with every weapon, attained their aims more swiftly and with authority. Critical Apparatus • sine litteris contenderant ] Adopted reading. Litterae = theoretical studies, literary and scientific culture. • ut manibus essent exercitati] Refers to exclusively practical and manual training. • pro laboribus auctoritatem] Means “authority or professional standing commensurate with their efforts”. • umbram non rem persecuti] Platonic metaphor: they pursued the “shadow” (appearance) and not the “reality” (rem). • uti omnibus armis ornati] Comparison of the complete architect with a fully armed soldier (very Roman image). • citius cum auctoritate] Emphasizes that those who master both forms of training achieve their aims more quickly and with greater authority. Academic translation " Therefore, those architects who strove to practice solely with their hands, without the support of letters, could not achieve an authority commensurate with their efforts. On the other hand, those who relied only on theoretical reasoning and letters seem to have pursued a shadow and not reality itself. But those who thoroughly mastered both disciplines, like soldiers equipped with all weapons, achieved their goal more quickly and with greater authority. " Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this paragraph, Vitruvius develops and exemplifies the thesis presented in the previous section. He establishes a clear typology of architects and defends an intermediate position: 1. Purely practical architects (sine litteris): They have great manual dexterity, but lack intellectual authority and social prestige. 2. theoretical architects (rationationibus et litteris solis): They possess speculative knowledge, but their proposals lack real foundation. Vitruvius 217

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I criticizes them with the Platonic metaphor of the “shadow” versus the “reality ”. 3. Ideal architects (qui utrumque perdidicerunt): Those who combine practice (fabrica) and theory (ratiocinatio). These are the only ones who achieve complete success, described with a very eloquent military image: “like soldiers equipped with all weapons.” Importance of the paragraph: • It reinforces the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as a complete and comprehensive professional. • It combines the Roman tradition of the vir bonus (practical and cultured man) with the technical demands of his discipline. • This passage was highly influential during the Renaissance, especially upon the figure of the humanist architect. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio On architecture Book I, Chapter 1.3 Cum in omnibus enim rebus, tum maxime etiam in architectura, haec duo insunt: quod significatur et quod significat. Significatur proposita res, de qua dicitur; hanc autem significat demonstratio rationibus doctrinarum explicata. Quare videtur utraque parte exercitatus esse debere qui se architectum profiteatur. Itaque eum etiam ingeniosum oportet esse et ad disciplinam docilem. Neque enim ingenium sine disciplina aut disciplina sine ingenio perfectum artificem potest efficere. For in all things, and especially in architecture, two elements are present: what is signified and what signifies. What is signified is the proposed subject under discussion; what signifies it is a demonstration explained through the principles of the disciplines. Whoever professes to be an architect must therefore be trained in both. He must possess natural talent and be receptive to instruction, for neither talent without training nor training without talent can produce an accomplished practitioner. Et ut litteratus sit, peritus graphidos, eruditus geometria, historias complures noverit, philosophos diligenter audierit, musicam scierit, medicinae non sit ignarus, responsa iurisconsultorum noverit, astrologiam caelique rationes cognitas habeat. 218

Since this edition offers no new recensio, variants are not attributed here to particular manuscripts, nor are formulas such as “codd.” reproduced without direct verification in an identifiable critical apparatus. He must therefore be literate, skilled in drawing and trained in geometry; he must know historical narratives, have listened attentively to philosophers, understand music, possess some knowledge of medicine, be acquainted with the opinions of jurists, and understand astronomy and the workings of the heavens.
