Etiam is retained in the Spanish edition and Krohn’s text; no omission of etiam is adopted without a documented manuscript witness. • haec duo insunt: quod significatur et quod significat] Vitruvius distinguishes the subject or matter under discussion from its demonstrative explanation through the principles of the disciplines. This is a semantic explanation, not a claim of manuscript unanimity. • docilem] The word denotes a disposition or capacity to learn. No particular textual judgment is added where a relevant variant has not been documented. The Spanish edition heads this lexical note ingenio et disciplinae docilem; the running text has ad disciplinam docilem. • peritus graphidos] Graphidos is a Greek genitive used in Latin by Vitruvius and refers to skill in drawing. It is translated according to its function in I.1.3–4. • eruditus geometria] The meaning is “trained in geometry”. No alternative form is reconstructed when it is unnecessary for the translation. • responsa iurisconsultorum noverit] Vitruvius requires knowledge of the jurists’ responses or opinions: sufficient familiarity with legal questions relevant to architectural practice. Academic translation “Indeed, in all things, but especially in architecture, these two elements are found: what is signified (quod significatur) and what signifies (quod significat). What is signified is the proposed thing being discussed; what signifies is the demonstration explained through the principles and reasoning of the 219

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I disciplines. Therefore, it seems that whoever proclaims himself an architect must be skilled in both. Thus, it is necessary that he possess natural talent and be receptive to teaching. For neither talent without discipline nor discipline without talent can produce a perfect craftsman.” Furthermore, he must be a man of letters, an expert in drawing, versed in geometry, familiar with numerous historical works, have listened attentively to philosophers, know music, be knowledgeable in medicine, be familiar with the opinions of legal experts, and have knowledge of astrology and the laws of the heavens. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) This paragraph is of great importance because Vitruvius delves into the semiotic and epistemological nature of architecture and establishes the ideal educational program for the architect. Main ideas: 1. Theoretical distinction: Vitruvius introduces the conceptual pair quod significatur (the real object, the thing itself) and quod significat (the theoretical representation, the rational demonstration). This distinction underscores that architecture is both a material reality and a body of knowledge that must be able to be rationally explained and justified. 2. Balance between talent and instruction: Neither innate genius (ingenium) without systematic training, nor study without natural ability, is sufficient. A combination of both is required. 3. Encyclopedia of the Architect: Vitruvius presents the first known list of knowledge that an architect must master. This encyclopedic training includes: • Humanities (litteratus, history, philosophy) • Arts (graphics, music) • Exact sciences (geometry, astrology, caeli rationes) • knowledge (medicine, law) M. Vitruvii Pollionis De architectura Book I, Chapter 1.4 Quae cur ita sint, haec sunt causae. Litteras architectum scire oportet, uti commentariis memoriam firmiorem efficere possit. Deinde graphidis scientiam 220

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I habere, quo facilius exemplaribus pictis quam velit operis speciem deformare valeat. Geometria autem plura praesidia praestat architecturae, et primum ex euthygrammis circini tradit usum, ⟨regulaeque⟩ e quo maxime facilius aedificiorum in areis expediuntur descriptiones, normarumque et librationum et linearum directiones. Item per opticen in aedificiis ab certis regionibus caeli lumina recte ducuntur. Per arithmeticen vero sumptus aedificiorum consummantur, mensurarum rationes explicantur, difficilesque symmetriarum quaestiones geometricis rationibus et methodis inveniuntur. The reasons for these requirements are as follows. The architect must be literate so that written notes may strengthen his memory. He must also know drawing, so that he can more easily represent the intended appearance of a work through drawings. Geometry provides architecture with many aids: first, it teaches the use of the straightedge and compasses, which facilitate the setting-out of buildings on their sites and the alignment of set squares, levels and lines. Optics enables light to be admitted correctly into buildings from particular quarters of the sky. Arithmetic is used to calculate construction costs, explain systems of measurement and resolve difficult questions of commensurability through geometrical reasoning and methods. Critical Apparatus • Quae cur ita sint, haec sunt causae] An explanatory transition introducing the reasons for the educational requirements. • graphidos scientiam] Graphidos (Greek genitive) = art of technical and design drawing. • euthygrammii et circini] This is the heading used by the Spanish edition’s lexical note, which explains euthygrammium as a ruler for drawing straight lines. The adopted running text instead reads ex euthygrammis circini tradit usum ⟨regulaeque⟩; the heading must not be mistaken for an independently verified manuscript reading. • in areis expediuntur descriptiones ] Adopted reading. In areis = on the ground, in the lot. • normarumque et librationum] Normae are set squares; librationes are leveling operations or levels. • per opticen] It refers to optics (perspective and lighting). 221

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I • per arithmeticen] Arithmetic applied to the calculation of costs and measurements. • symmetriarum quaestiones] Vitruvian central concept: harmonic proportions. Academic translation " Here are the reasons why this is so. The architect must know how to read and write, in order to strengthen his memory through written notes. Likewise, he must have knowledge of drawing, so that he can more easily represent, through exemplary drawings, the appearance of the work he wishes to design." Geometry, for its part, provides architecture with numerous aids: firstly, it teaches the use of the ruler and compass, thanks to which the plans of buildings, as well as the directions of set squares, levels, and lines, can be drawn much more easily on the ground. Likewise, optics allows for the correct direction of light from certain regions of the sky towards buildings. Arithmetic allows for the calculation of construction costs, the explanation of the reasons for measurements, and the resolution of difficult questions of symmetry through geometric reasoning and methods. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius begins to justify in detail why the architect must master each of the disciplines mentioned. Main points: 1. Letters (Litterae): They are used to take notes and consolidate memory (commentarii). 2. Drawing (Graphidos scientia): An essential tool for visually materializing the ideas of the project. 3. Geometry: A fundamental discipline that provides practical tools (ruler, compass, set square, level) for drawing plans and carrying out construction work. 4. Optics: Allows for the correct management of natural lighting in buildings according to their orientation. 5. Arithmetic: Necessary for calculating costs, measurements and, especially, for solving problems of symmetria (harmonic proportion), one of the most important concepts of Vitruvian theory. 222

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Vitruvius presents architecture here as a technical-scientific discipline requiring a solid foundation in the liberal and applied arts. This encyclopedic approach distinguishes the Roman architect from the mere faber (craftsman) and elevates him to the status of intellectual. M. Vitruvii Pollionis De architectura Book I, Chapter 1.5 Historias autem plures novisse oportet, quod multa ornamenta saepe in operibus architecti designant, de quibus argumenti rationem, cur fecerint, quaerentibus reddere debent. Quemadmodum si quis statuas marmoreas muliebres stolatas, quae caryatides dicuntur, pro columnis in opere statuerit et insuper mutulos et coronas conlocaverit, percontantibus ita reddet rationem: He must also know many historical narratives, because architects often include ornaments in their works and must explain the reasoning behind them to anyone who asks why they were used. Thus, if someone sets up marble statues of robed women, called caryatids, in place of columns, and places mutules and cornices above them, he will give the following explanation. Carya, civitas Peloponnensis, cum Persis hostibus contra Graeciam consensit. Postea Graeci, per victoriam gloriose bello liberati, communi consilio Caryatibus bellum indixerunt. Itaque, oppido capto, viris interfectis, civitate deflagrata, matronas eorum in servitutem abduxerunt, nec sunt passi stolas neque ornatus matronales deponere, non uti una triumpho ducerentur, sed aeterna servitutis exemplo gravi contumelia pressae poenas pendere viderentur pro civitate. Ideo qui tunc architecti fuerunt aedificiis publicis designaverunt earum imagines oneri ferendo conlocatas, ut etiam posteris nota poena peccati Caryatium memoriae traderetur. Caryae, a city in the Peloponnese, allied itself with the Persians against Greece. After their glorious victory had freed them from war, the Greeks jointly declared war on the inhabitants of Caryae. They captured the town, killed the men, laid waste to the city and carried its matrons into slavery. They did not allow the women to remove their robes or matronly ornaments: they were to be displayed not in a single triumph but as an enduring example of servitude, burdened with humiliation and paying the penalty for their city. The architects of that time therefore represented them in public buildings as figures bearing a load, so that 223

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I the punishment of the offense of the people of Caryae might be remembered by posterity. Critical Apparatus • Historias autem plures nosse oportet] Historias denotes historical and mythological narratives. • argumenti rationem, cur fecerint] The expression means “the reason and rationale for the motif”. • Carya, civitas Peloponnensis] The passage names Caryae in the Peloponnese, distinct from Caria in Asia Minor. • Gloriose bello liberati] “Gloriously freed from the war”. Gloriose is the adverb in the adopted wording; the alternative glorioso is not attributed to an individual witness without documentary support. • civitate deflagrata] The running text describes the city as burned down. the Spanish edition’s lexical note instead uses the heading civitate desacrata and glosses it as “razed” or “ritually destroyed”. These different expressions are distinguished here; no manuscript variant is inferred from the discrepant heading. • oneri ferundo] Gerundive: “destined to bear a burden”. • Caryatium] Genitive plural referring to the people of Caryae. The association of their women with load-bearing figures belongs to Vitruvius’s explanatory narrative. Academic translation “Furthermore, it is advisable for the architect to know many historical narratives, because he frequently designs numerous ornaments in his works, and he must be able to give an account of them — and explain the basis of his decision — to those who ask him.” Thus, for example, if someone places marble statues of women dressed in long tunics — called caryatids107 — in place of columns, and places mutules and 107 Caryatids are sculpted female figures that replace columns as supports for an entablature; the canonical example is the porch of the Erechtheion on the Acropolis at Athens (c. 421–406 BC). In 1.1.5 Vitruvius offers an aetiological explanation intended to show why architects must know history: the women of Caryae, a town in Laconia that sided with Persia, were supposedly enslaved and their images condemned to bear the weight of a building for ever. The story is now regarded as a late aetiological construction rather than the actual origin of the motif, which 224

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I cornices on top of them, he will give the following explanation to those who ask him: The city of Caryae, in the Peloponnese, allied itself with the Persians, enemies of Greece. Subsequently, the Greeks, gloriously liberated by their victory in the war, declared war on the inhabitants of Caryae by common agreement. Therefore, having captured the city, killed the men, and razed the city, they led its matrons into servitude, not allowing them to remove their tunics or matronly ornaments, so that they would not be paraded only once in triumph, but rather, oppressed by grave affront and as an eternal example of servitude, they would seem to atone before posterity for the guilt of their city. For this reason, the architects of that time depicted their images in public buildings carrying a burden, so that the memory of the punishment for the crime of the women of Caryae would also reach future generations. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text This paragraph is one of Vitruvius' most famous and constitutes the legendary origin of the caryatids. Key points: 1. The Usefulness of History: The architect must not only know how to build, but also provide cultural and historical justification for the ornamental elements he employs. For Vitruvius, architecture is an eloquent art that “speaks” through its forms. 2. The caryatid narrative: Vitruvius gives an aetiological explanation for the architectural figure. He names Caryae in the Peloponnese, which must be distinguished from Caria in Asia Minor. His account presents the loadbearing women as an enduring image of the punishment and humiliation imposed on their city. The historical status of that account remains distinct from its symbolic function in the treatise. 3. Symbolic value: This passage illustrates how Roman (and Greek) architecture used figurative elements with a strong moral and commemorative content. M. Vitruvii Pollionis scholarship associates instead with archaic korai and the cult of Artemis Caryatis, whose ritual dances were performed by the girls of Caryae. 225

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I On architecture Book I, Chapter 1.6 Non minus Lacones, Pausania Agesilae filio duce, Plataico proelio pauca manu infinitum numerum exercitus Persarum cum superavissent, acto cum gloria triumpho spoliorum et praedae, porticum Persicam ex manubiis, laudis et virtutis civium indicem, victoriae posteris pro tropaeo constituerunt. Ibique captivorum simulacra barbarico vestis ornatu, superbia meritis contumeliis punita, sustinentia tectum conlocaverunt, uti et hostes horrescerent timore eorum fortitudinis effectus, et cives id exemplum virtutis aspicientes gloria erecti ad defendendam libertatem essent parati. Itaque ex eo multi statuas Persicas sustinentes epistylia et ornamenta eorum conlocaverunt, et ita ex eo argumento varietates egregias auxerunt operibus. Item sunt aliae eiusdem generis historiae, quarum notitiam architectos tenere oporteat. No less the Laconians, led by Pausanias, the son of Agesilaus, having defeated an immense Persian army with a small force in the battle of Plataea, having celebrated a glorious triumph of spoils and booty, erected a Persian portico from the proceeds of the spoils, a token of the praise and virtue of the citizens, and a trophy of victory for posterity. And there they placed the effigies of captives adorned with barbarian clothing, their pride punished with deserved insults, supporting a roof, so that both the enemies might shudder with fear at the effects of their fortitude, and the citizens, beholding that example of virtue, might be raised in glory and ready to defend their liberty. Therefore from it many placed Persian statues supporting their epistyles and ornaments, and thus from that argument they increased excellent varieties in their works. Likewise there are other stories of the same kind, of which architects should keep a knowledge. Critical Apparatus • Agesilae filio] Krohn retains “son of Agesilaus,” and the translation follows the adopted text. Historically, the commander at Plataea was Pausanias son of Cleombrotus (Herodotus 9.10). M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Key points: 1. Historical context: Vitruvius refers to the Greek victory at the Battle of Plataea (479 BCE), which ended the Persian Wars. The Spartans (Laconians), under the command of Pausanias, erected the Persian Stoa (Persike Stoa) in Sparta as a commemorative monument. 2. Symbolic function: The figures of captive Persians supporting the roof represent the triumph of Greek freedom over barbarian arrogance. They serve a dual purpose: • Intimidation of potential enemies. • Moral example and motivation for citizens. 3. Importance for architecture: These decorative elements are not mere ornaments, but bearers of historical and moral significance. The architect must know their origin in order to explain them and justify their use. This passage reinforces the central idea of the chapter: the architect must be a cultured man, capable of endowing his works with intellectual and symbolic content, and not just technical content. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Academic translation “Philosophy, for its part, perfects the architect in spirit, so that he is not arrogant, but rather gentle, fair, and loyal, and — most importantly — free from avarice. For no work can truly be accomplished without loyalty and integrity. Let him not be covetous or preoccupied with receiving gifts, but let him uphold his dignity with gravity, maintaining a good reputation. And this is precisely what philosophy prescribes.” Furthermore, philosophy explains the nature of things, what in Greek is called physiologia, a body of knowledge that must be mastered with special dedication, since it encompasses many and varied natural matters, as is also the case with water management. Indeed, the impulses, circulations, and pressures of natural air occur in very different ways depending on the differences in elevation and forced conduits; and no one will be able to solve their problems without knowing, thanks to philosophy, the principles of nature. Likewise, whoever reads the precepts written by Ctesibius, Archimedes, and other authors of the same kind will not be able to fully understand them unless they have been instructed in these matters by philosophers. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius explains the fundamental role of philosophy in the training of the architect, dividing it into two main aspects: 1. Moral (ethical) formation: Philosophy shapes the architect's character, instilling essential virtues such as humility, fairness, fidelity, and above all, the absence of greed. Vitruvius emphasizes that moral integrity (fides et castitas) is indispensable for practising the profession with dignity. 2. Scientific training (physics / physiology): Architects need knowledge of natural philosophy to understand complex physical phenomena, especially in hydraulics (aqueducts, water and air pressure). Without these principles, they would be unable to solve real-world technical problems. Vitruvius further links theory with practice by mentioning great Hellenistic engineers (Ctesibius and Archimedes), whose treatises can only be properly understood with a philosophical basis. This passage reinforces the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as a complete professional: not just a technician, but a cultured, ethical and scientifically trained man. 230

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Academic translation “Likewise, he must know music, in order to master canonical reason and mathematical notation, and to be able to correctly adjust the tensions of the ballistas, catapults and scorpions.” Indeed, in the capitals of these machines there are, on the right and left, holes for the hemitonia, through which twisted cords of sinew are tensioned by means of capstans and levers. These cords are not locked or permanently fixed until they produce, to the ear of the craftsman, an equal and uniform sound on both sides. For the arms that are inserted into these tensions, when extended, must deliver the blow equally and evenly. If they are not in the same pitch (homotonic), they will prevent the projectiles from being launched straight. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text (Academic Analysis) In this paragraph, Vitruvius justifies the need for the architect to master music (understood as harmonic and acoustic theory) for an eminently practical reason: the calibration of torsion war machines. Key points: 1. Connection between music and mechanics: Vitruvius establishes a direct relationship between musical theory (harmonic proportions, tones, intervals) and military engineering. The correct tension of the machine's strings is achieved by ear, applying acoustic principles (sonitus certos et aequales). 2. Key technical concept: Homoton (equal pitch/equal tension). If the two halves of the torsion engine are not perfectly balanced, the weapon will lose accuracy and the projectile will deviate from its trajectory. 3. vision of architecture: This example perfectly illustrates the Vitruvian thesis: the architect is not only a builder, but a technician -scientist who must apply knowledge from different disciplines (in this case, music) to concrete problems of design and execution. This passage is especially interesting because it shows how, in Antiquity, disciplines that we now consider separate (music and military art) were closely linked through mathematics and the theory of proportions. Arranged around the theater according to fourths, fifths, octaves and double octaves, they receive the actor’s voice and reinforce it by resonance, so that it reaches the spectators’ ears more clearly and pleasantly. Hydraulic organs and other similar instruments likewise cannot be constructed without knowledge of musical principles. Critical Apparatus • vasa aerea ] Corrected reading. Vessels and urns of bronze. • quae Graeci ἠχεῖα appellant] Ἠχεῖα (echeia) = acoustic resonators. • diatessaron et diapente et diapason ad disdiapason] Musical intervals: fourth, fifth, octave and double octave. • [in circinatione ] Adopted reading. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Explanatory note — Bk. 5.4–5.5 (the echea and theater acoustics). Vitruvius founds theater acoustics on the Harmonics of Aristoxenus of Tarentum: in 5.4 he sets out the three genera —enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic— and the division of the voice into tones, semitones, and tetrachords; in 5.5 he applies that theory to architecture through the echea (ἠχεῖα), bronze vessels —or clay ones, in modest theaters— tuned to the notes of the scale and set in niches under the seating to reinforce the actors' voices by resonance. The exact scheme of their positions (5.5.6) is lost in transmission. Vitruvius notes that wooden theaters need none, since the boarding itself resonates; masonry, stone, or marble theaters do. He admits he has seen none in Rome, citing as witness Lucius Mummius, who after destroying Corinth (146 BCE) brought the bronze echea of its theater to Rome and dedicated them at the temple of Luna. Archaeology has found almost no trace of them in ancient theaters; they reappear, however, in some two hundred medieval churches. Comparative note — Bk. 5.4–5.5 (echea). In the Budé, Book V is the work of Catherine Saliou (2009), whose commentary on the theater and its acoustics is standard. In the Cambridge commentary, Thomas N. Howe observes that Vitruvius here singles out an uncommon Greek technical feature, for which only between eight and sixteen possible sites are known. Granger (Loeb) preserves the Greek musical terminology (nete, paramese, mese, hypate); Corso– Romano and Tavernor–Schofield accompany the passage with diagrams of the scale. In 5.5 the manuscript tradition presents a crux (diatessaron for diapente in the series of intervals), discussed since Rose; this edition follows Rose's text and translates in its own voice. Nor could anyone build hydraulic machines or other instruments similar to these organs without knowing the principles of music. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius continues to justify the need for musical knowledge for the architect, now moving from the military field to the acoustic - architectural field. Key points: 1. Theater acoustics: Vitruvius describes one of the most sophisticated acoustic systems of Antiquity: the echeia, or bronze resonating vessels. These 234

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I were strategically placed under the seating tiers of theaters to amplify and enhance the sound quality of the actors. 2. Mathematical -musical foundation: The tuning of these vessels was carried out according to the Greek harmonic intervals (diatessaron = fourth, diapente = fifth, diapason = octave), demonstrating the practical application of Pythagorean musical theory in architecture. 3. Comprehensive vision: Music is not a cultural embellishment, but an indispensable technical tool. Without it, an architect could not properly design theaters or build complex instruments like the hydraulic organ. This passage is one of the most important sources we have on acoustics in ancient theaters and demonstrates the high degree of technical and scientific sophistication that Vitruvius demanded of the architect. Vitruvii Pollionis De architectura Book I, Chapter 1.10 Disciplinam vero medicinae novisse oportet propter inclinationem caeli, quae Graeci κλίματα dicunt, et aeris et locorum qui sunt salubres aut pestilentes, aquarumque usus. Sine his enim rationibus nulla salubris habitatio fieri potest. If a contract is 235

From astrology, however, one knows east, west, south, north, and also the system of the heavens, the equinox, the solstice, and the course of the stars. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I employer and the contractor can be protected. For if the contract is skilfully written, both will be mutually released without suffering any harm. Through astrology, one can know the east, the west, south, and north, as well as the arrangement of the sky, the equinoxes, the solstices, and the course of the stars. Explanation of the Meaning of the Text In this paragraph, Vitruvius concludes the enumeration of the disciplines that the architect must master, highlighting three areas of great practical importance: 1. Environmental Medicine / Hygiene: The architect must know how to choose healthy sites according to the climate (klimata), air quality, soil and water, anticipating health problems (a very Roman theme). 2. Law: Basic legal knowledge to avoid litigation related to construction (common walls, easements for light, water, rainwater runoff, sewers, etc.). Vitruvius emphasizes the architect's responsibility in preventing legal conflicts. 3. Astrology / Astronomy: Necessary for the correct orientation of buildings and, especially, for the design of sundials (horology). This chapter (I.1) presents the Vitruvian ideal of the architect as an encyclopedic professional, capable of integrating technical, scientific, humanistic, and juridical knowledge. None of these disciplines is accessory: they all respond to the concrete needs of his office. This, however, cannot be achieved in reality.”112 Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “12. Those unfamiliar with the subject (inperitis) may find it surprising that human nature can master and retain so many disciplines. Once they recognize the close connection and mutual exchange among all branches of knowledge, however, they will readily believe it possible. Encyclopedic education (encyclios disciplina) forms a single body composed of these members. Those trained in different fields from an early age therefore recognize the same features and the connections shared by all the disciplines, and so understand everything more readily. For this reason Pytheos, the distinguished architect of Minerva’s temple at Priene, states in his commentaries that an architect should be able to accomplish more in every art and discipline than specialists who, through sustained practice, have brought a single field to the highest distinction.” However, the latter is not feasible in reality. Exegetical Notes 1. The Encyclios Disciplina as a mystical body: Vitruvius uses a metaphor of Stoic and Platonic origin: education is a living organism (uti corpus unum), where geometry, music, and astronomy are not isolated sciences, but rather the "members" (membris) of a single being. This is fundamental: the architect does not accumulate knowledge in a fragmented way; the architect understands the common mathematical root that unites sound (music) with space (geometry) and time (astronomy). 2. The rectification of Pytheus (The tension between Idea and Matter): Pytheus (the great Hellenistic architect of the Temple of Priene and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus) was a radical in his theory; he asserted that the architect should know more about painting than a painter and more about sculpture than a sculptor. Vitruvius, with the Roman pragmatism that characterizes his framework, reins him in by closing the paragraph: Id autem re non expeditur. Vitruvius knows that human beings have physical limitations. 112Encyclios disciplina concerns an interconnected general education. The expression is related to Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία (enkyklios paideia); it is distinct from the later ecclesiastical use of “encyclical”. 240

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I The architect should not compete in manual dexterity with the specialist, but rather surpass them in the overall vision and geometric integration of the work. 3. The concept of Notes: The Carolingian text uses the word notes (characters, signs, marks). Vitruvius is saying that the wise person who studies from childhood discovers that the mathematical "marks" that govern a musical chord are the same "marks" that define the proportions of a column. Architecture is the science that knows how to read these universal notes and engrave them in stone. «13. In the other disciplines too, he need not excel individually, but must have some knowledge of them. No one can attain exceptional refinement in such a variety of subjects, since even understanding and grasping their theoretical principles is scarcely within human capacity.” Critical Translation “13. Indeed, the architect neither should nor can be a philologist or grammarian like Aristarchus, but that does not mean he should be illiterate (agrammatos); he should not be a musician like Aristoxenus, but neither should he be unfamiliar with music (amusos); he should not be a painter like Apelles, but he should be skilled in drawing (graphidos non inperitus); he should not be a sculptor of the stature of Myron or Polyclitus, but he should know the laws of plastic arts (rationis plasticae non ignarus); nor should he be a physician like Hippocrates, but that does not mean he should be ignorant of the principles of 241

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I medicine (aniatrologetos); finally, he is not required to excel in the other sciences, but he must have a knowledge of them that is not inexperienced (non inperitus).” In the midst of such a vast variety of subjects, no one can achieve singular mastery or refinement (elegantias singulares), since knowing and thoroughly assimilating its theoretical principles (ratiocinationes) is something that barely falls within the capabilities of the human intellect. Exegetical notes 1. The constellation of Hellenistic archetypes: Vitruvius here maps out the greatest sages of the classical world to define the boundaries of architecture. He cites Aristarchus (the great grammarian of Alexandria who standardized Homer's text), Aristoxenus (the great theorist of music and the harmonic scale), Apelles (Alexander the Great's favorite painter), Myron and Polyclitus (the fathers of the canon of Greek sculpture), and Hippocrates (the father of medicine). By contrasting the architect with these giants, Vitruvius demonstrates that architecture is an integrative discipline: the architect does not displace the specialist, but rather acts as the conductor who coordinates all these areas of knowledge within the realm of the building. 2. The structure of double negations (non agrammatos, non amusos): This philological subtlety is relevant. Vitruvius does not use Vulgar Latin; he resorts to negated Hellenisms to indicate a state of critical competence. The architect does not have to compose a symphony like Aristoxenus, but he cannot be amusos (deaf to harmony), because if he were, he would not know how to place the acoustic vessels in the theater (Book V). He does not have to sculpt the Doryphoros like Polyclitus, but he must understand ratio plastica so that the statues of the caryatids maintain the modular proportion with the entablature. It is an apologia for the knowledge of synthesis. 3. The Limit of Human Power: The paragraph's conclusion is a lesson in epistemological humility in the face of Pytheus’s abstract intellectualism. Vitruvius acknowledges that the absolute mastery of the singular refinements (elegantias singulares) of each science eludes the power (potestas) of human understanding. Architecture, therefore, is defined as the science of the possible and the harmonious: it prioritizes the balance of the whole over the hyper- 242

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I specialized obsession with the fragment. This aligns with the thesis on Sophia: the true sage is the one who unifies, not the one who atomizes. This fragment (I, 1, 14) masterfully concludes Vitruvius's syllogism on the nature of architectural knowledge. Vitruvius introduces an a fortiori argument (from lesser to greater): if specialists themselves — who dedicate their entire lives to a single discipline — rarely achieve universal acclaim, then demanding that the architect surpass them all in their respective fields is a logical contradiction. The architect's role is not competition, but technical coordination and selfsufficiency (ne quid indigeat). The transmitted text exhibits deficiencies in textual cohesion and decontextualized turns of phrase such as " in private the properties of the arts, " which is an erroneous translation of privatim proprietates tenent artium (which refers to " those who possess the exclusive mastery of a particular art "). Similarly, aevo perpetuo does not allude to " the nobility of the time," but to an " imperishable celebrity / immortal fame. " The Latin text, established on the review of Rose (confronted with Krohn), is presented below, with its critical translation and corresponding apparatus: Latin text «14. Nec tamen non tantum architecti non possunt in omnibus rebus habere summum effectum, sed etiam ipsi qui privatim proprietates tenent artium non efficiunt ut habeant omnes summum laudis principatum. Ergo si in singulis doctrinis singuli artifices neque omnes sed pauci aevo perpetuo nobilitatem vix sunt consecuti, quemadmodum potest architectus, qui pluribus artibus debet esse peritus, non id ipsum mirum et magnum facere ne quid ex his indigeat, sed etiam ut omnes artifices superet qui singulis doctrinis adsiduitatem cum industria summa praestiterunt.» “14. Not only are architects unable to achieve the highest accomplishment in every field; even specialists in individual arts do not all attain the highest distinction. If, in each discipline, only a few practitioners have scarcely won lasting renown, how can an architect, who must be skilled in many arts, be expected to surpass all the specialists who have devoted their utmost diligence and sustained effort to a single subject? Is it not already a remarkable achievement that he should lack none of the knowledge he needs?” 243

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “14. And yet, not only are architects unable to achieve supreme perfection (summum effectum) in all matters, but even those who possess exclusive mastery of a particular art (privatim proprietates tenent artium) do not, in their entirety, attain the highest principality of glory. Therefore, if in individual sciences particular artists — and of them not all, but only a few throughout the ages (aevo perpetuo) —have barely achieved renown, how is it possible that an architect, who must be skilled in multiple arts, accomplishes the prodigious and admirable feat not only of lacking none of the necessary knowledge in them (ne quid ex is indigeat), but of surpassing even all those artisans and specialists who have devoted absolute assiduity and the utmost industry to a single doctrine? ” Exegetical notes 1. Deconstructing the Myth of the Absolute Sage: This passage is a compelling argument for disassociating Vitruvius from the hyperbolic readings of the Renaissance. While the humanists of the Quattrocento sought to find in this chapter the justification for the absolute "universal man" (the unattainable polymath), Vitruvius's actual text is a lesson in Roman pragmatism and legal moderation. Vitruvius argues that the architect's goal is elemental selfsufficiency: "ne quid ex is indigeat " (that nothing should be foreign or lacking to him). The architect should not be a rival to the painter or the musician, but a valid interlocutor who understands the codes of each craft. 2. Specialized diligence versus spatial synthesis: Vitruvius contrasts adsiduitas (the specialist's obsessive and constant dedication to a single thing) with the architect's panoramic vision. The genius of architectural design lies not in fragmentary execution, but in symphonic coordination. The specialist works on the detail; the architect works on the relationship between the details. This distinction is fundamental to your theoretical framework, as it positions architecture as a second-order science or meta-discipline, whose object of study is not isolated matter, but the order that unifies the parts. 3. The Status of Nobility in the Arts: The use of the terms nobilitatem and laudis principatum reflects the Augustan mindset regarding the social status of the intellectual and the artisan. Vitruvius is attempting to elevate the profession of architecture above purely manual (fabrica) or servile labor. By demonstrating that the architect operates with the theory of all the arts, he 244

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I grants him a rank of intellectual nobility comparable to that of philosophers or high-ranking officials of the Empire, thus justifying why the treatise is dedicated directly to the Imperator. This passage (I, 1, 15) is the epistemological keystone of the entire Book I. Here Vitruvius definitively dismantles the error of Pytheus by introducing a binary Platonic-Aristotelian distinction: the opus the material, empirical and specialized execution and the ratiocinatio the theoretical, scientific and universal principle). Latin text «15. Igitur in hac re Pytheos errasse videtur quod non animadvertit ex duabus rebus singulas artes esse compositas, ex opere et eius ratiocinatione. Ex his autem unum proprium esse eorum qui singulis rebus sunt exercitati, id est operis effectus, alterum commune cum omnibus doctis, id est rationem, uti medicis et musicis et de venarum rythmo et pedum [motus], at si vulnus mederi aut aegrum eripere de periculo oportuerit, non accedet musicus, sed id opus proprium erit medici. Item in organo non medicus sed musicus modulabitur, ut aures suavem cantionibus recipiant iucunditatem.» «15. Therefore, in this matter Pythius seems to have erred because he did not observe that the individual arts are composed of two things, from work and its reasoning. Of these, however, one is proper to those who are trained in each thing, that is, the effect of the work, the other is common to all learned men, that is, reasoning, as is the case with physicians and musicians concerning the rhythm of the veins and the movement of the foot. But if it is necessary to heal a wound or rescue a patient from danger, the musician will not come, but that will be the proper work of the physician. Likewise, the organ will be played not by the physician but by the musician, so that the ears may receive pleasure from the songs. » Critical Translation “15. Consequently, at this point Pythius’s error is evident, for he failed to recognize that all the arts are composed of two factors: the material execution (opus) and the theory that underpins it (ratiocinatio). Of these two elements, the first — that is, the completion of the physical work (operis effectus) —is the exclusive domain of those who have practised a particular discipline; the second — the theory or rational principle (ratiocinatio) —is common to all men of 245

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I science (omnibus doctis). Thus, for example, both physicians and musicians share theoretical knowledge about the rhythm of blood pulses and its analogy with the movement of metric feet; however, if it is necessary to heal a wound or save a sick person from imminent danger, the musician will not come to the rescue, but such a task will be the proper and exclusive work of the physician. ” Likewise, it will not be the doctor, but the musician, who will play and perform on the organ, so that the ears may perceive the delight of its melodies. Exegetical notes 1. The Anatomy of Knowledge: Opus versus Ratiocinatio: Vitruvius here establishes a division that elevates architecture to the rank of a liberal science. Opus is blind; it is the mechanical repetition of the craftsman who knows how to move his hands but does not know why the structure works. Ratiocinatio is the logos, the mathematical matrix that governs the phenomenon physically and formally. The architect's value lies in the fact that, although he shares ratiocinatio with other scholars (commune cum omnibus doctis), he has the unique ability to project it onto the constructive opus. 2. The analogy of the pulse and the cosmic metronome (de venarum rhythmo et ad pedem motu) is an exceptional archaeological testimony of the Hellenistic medicine of Herophilus of Alexandria, who measured the body's pulse using water clocks and the metrical feet of Greek poetry and music. Vitruvius illustrates the thesis on Sophia: the physical universe is interconnected. Blood flows through the veins with the same numerical and harmonic law with which a musician composes a measure and with which an architect calculates the distances of the intercolumniations (modulatio) of a temple (Book III). 3. The delimitation of the professional field: At the end of the fragment, Vitruvius prioritizes common sense over theoretical utopia. The architect must possess the ratiocinatio of acoustics to design the theater (Book V), but when it comes to playing the instrument (organ), he takes a step back and yields the position to the practical musician. This distinction is methodologically important: architecture does not devour the other arts; it conceptually assimilates them to create the spatial container where these arts can coexist harmoniously. The physician heals bodies and the musician delights 246

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I souls, but it is the architect who builds the hospital and the theater where both operate. This passage (I, 1, 16) definitively closes the great epistemological introduction on the training of the architect in Book I. Vitruvius culminates here his defense of synthetic knowledge by linking astronomy, music and geometry through the laws of cosmic consonance and optics, and then decrees the real goal of the professional: to achieve a moderate but sufficient knowledge (mediocriter) that allows him to judge with technical authority without needing to be a manual craftsman. Latin text Brief context: Vitruvius criticizes Pythius, the architect of the Temple of Minerva at Priene, who had demanded that the architect have a perfect command of all the sciences. Vitruvius responds that this is impossible and unnecessary: the architect must know the theoretical aspects (ratiocinatio) of many disciplines, but the practical execution (opus) belongs to the specialists in each field. «16. Similiter cum astrologis et musicis est disputatio communis de sympathia stellarum et symphoniarum in quadratis et trigonis diatessaron et diapente, a geometris [divisus] qui graece λόγος ὀπτικός appellatur, ceterisque omnibus doctrinis multae res vel omnes communes sunt dumtaxat ad disputandum. Operum vero ingressus, qui manu aut tractationibus ad elegantiam perducuntur, ipsorum sunt qui proprie una arte ad faciendum sunt instituti. Ergo satis abunde videtur fecisse qui ex singulis doctrinis partes et rationes earum mediocriter habet notas eas quae necessariae sunt ad architecturam, uti si quid de his rebus et artibus iudicare et probare opus fuerit ne deficiatur.» “16. Similarly, astronomers and musicians share discussion of the correspondence between the stars and musical consonances, in squares and trines, and in the intervals of a fourth and a fifth; they share with geometers the theory of sight, which the Greeks call logos optikos. Many matters, or indeed all, are common to the disciplines at the level of theoretical discussion. The practical execution of works, however, brought to refinement by hand and skilled manipulation, belongs to those trained to practise a particular art. It is therefore amply sufficient for the architect to have a moderate knowledge of the parts and 247

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I principles of each discipline that are necessary for architecture, so that he is not found wanting when required to judge and approve matters concerning them.” Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “16. Similarly, there exists a common sphere of debate (disputatio communis) between astrologers and musicians regarding the cosmic sympathy of the stars and musical consonances, structured according to the relationships of squares and trigons, and the intervals of fourth (diatessaron) and fifth (diapente); likewise, the architect shares with geometers the science of vision, which in Greek is called λόγος ὀπτικός (logos optikos or perspective). In short, in all branches of knowledge, many subjects — if not all — are common to scholars exclusively on the level of theoretical argumentation (ad disputandum).” On the contrary, the practical execution of works (operum vero ingressus), which are brought to perfection and elegance by the hands and the skilled manipulation, belongs exclusively to those who have been properly trained and instructed in a single manual craft. Consequently, it is to be considered that an architect who possesses a moderate knowledge (mediocriter) of the principles and parts of each science—those strictly necessary for architecture—is more than adequately fulfilling (satis abunde) his duty, so that if it were necessary to issue a technical judgment or approve a project governed by these arts, his authority would not be deficient (ne deficiat). Exegetical notes 1. Astrology and Cosmic Aspects: This passage constitutes one of the most fascinating pieces of documentary evidence of Roman architectural Pythagoreanism. Vitruvius equates the musical intervals of a fourth (diatessaron, ratio 4:3) and a fifth (diapente, ratio 3:2) with the geometric configurations traced by the stars in the firmament when they form squares (square aspect, 90 °) and trines (trine aspect, 120 °). This fact confirms that Vitruvian architectural space is a resonant microcosm: temples and theaters are designed imitating the same metric proportions with which God tensions the strings of the heavens and the planets. 2. Logos optikos and architectural perception. The Greek expression λόγος ὀπτικός provides an important conceptual context for the optical adjustments discussed in Books III and IV. Greek geometric perspective taught that the human eye distorts the material line (making it 248

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I appear concave or convex). The architect, sharing this ratiocinatio with the geometers, does not design for the abstract plane of the paper, but for the retina of the viewer. Architecture intentionally alters the actual geometry (thickening the corner columns or curving the stylobate) so that the logos optikos of the eye perceives the building with perfect symmetry and visual stability. 3. The Canon of the Mean (Mediocriter notes): Vitruvius coined the definitive concept of the architect's professional training. The word mediocriter does not have the modern derogatory sense of "mediocre," but rather the classical sense of Aristotelian mediocritas: the golden mean, moderation, and temperance. The excellent architect does not fall into the error of excessive artisanal specialization (manu tractionibus); their domain is that of critical intellect. They must possess instrumental knowledge sharp enough to be an infallible judge of the work (iudicare et probare) and ensure that no contractor or specialist deceives the state administration. Architecture is, ultimately, the triumph of theoretical oversight over the brute force of the worker. 17. Quibus vero natura tantum tribuit sollertiae, acuminis, memoriae, ut possint geometriam, astrologiam, musicen ceterasque disciplinas penitus habere notas, praetereunt officia architectorum et efficiuntur mathematici. Itaque faciliter contra eas disciplinas disputare possunt, quod pluribus telis disciplinarum sunt armati. Hi autem inveniuntur raro, ut aliquando fuerunt Aristarchus Samius, Philolaus et Archytas Tarentini, Apollonius Pergaeus, Eratosthenes Cyrenaeus, Archimedes et Scopinas ab Syracusis, qui multas res ⟨mechanicas,⟩ organicas, gnomonicas numero naturalibusque rationibus inventas atque explicatas posteris reliquerunt. “17. Those whom nature has endowed with such skill, intellectual acuity and memory that they thoroughly master geometry, astronomy, music and the other disciplines go beyond the duties of architects and become mathematicians. They can readily discuss these disciplines, armed as they are with many intellectual weapons. Such people are rare: among them were Aristarchus113 of Samos, 113Aristarchus of Samos (Ἀρίσταρχος ὁ Σάμιος; c. 310–c. 230 BCE) was a Greek astronomer and mathematician. He is the earliest known proponent of a heliocentric model placing the Sun rather than the Earth at the center of the planetary system. See J. J. O’Connor and E. F. Robertson, ‘Aristarchus of Samos’, MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews. 249

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Philolaus114 and Archytas115 of Tarentum, Apollonius116 of Perga, Eratosthenes of Cyrene, and Archimedes and Scopinas of Syracuse. They left to posterity many mechanical and gnomonic inventions discovered and explained through calculation and the principles of nature.” Critical Translation and Hermeneutics “17. On the contrary, those beings whom nature has endowed with such skill (sollertiae), keenness of mind, and memory that they are capable of assimilating geometry, astronomy, music, and the other liberal arts in a profound and absolute way (penitus), surpass the limits and duties proper to architects (officia architectorum) to become pure mathematicians. For this reason, it is extremely easy for them to debate and challenge any of these disciplines, since they are equipped with the vastest arsenal of theoretical projectiles (pluribus telis disciplinarum). However, such men appear exceptionally in history, as Aristarchus of Samos, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, Apollonius of Perga, Eratosthenes of Cyrene, Archimedes, and Scopinas of Syracuse once were; colossi who bequeathed to posterity a vast quantity of mechanical devices (res organicas) and gnomonic instruments (gnomonicas), discovered and rigorously explained through numerical calculation and the physical laws of nature (numero naturalibusque rationibus). 114 Philolaus, also known as Philolaus of Tarentum or of Croton (Greek Φιλόλαος, Philolaos; c. 470–c. 380 BC), was a Greek Pythagorean and Presocratic philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, politician, music theorist and writer. He held that all matter consists of limiting and unlimited things joined by harmony, and that the universe is determined by numbers. He is credited with originating the hypothesis that the Earth was not the center of the universe, a theory included in the Pythagorean astronomical system. 115 Archytas of Tarentum (Greek Ἀρχύτας ὁ Ταραντίνος; c. 430–c. 360 BC) was a philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, statesman, general and contemporary of Plato. He worked in his native city, the Greek colony of Tarentum in Apulia, and belonged to the Pythagorean tradition. 116 Apollonius of Perga, also called Perge (Greek Ἀπολλώνιος; c. 262 BC–Alexandria, c. 190 BC), was a Greek mathematician and astronomer renowned for his work on conic sections. He gave the names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola to the curves now known by those terms. His study of conic sections informed later geometrical problem-solving; it should not be equated uncritically with the symbolic solution of general quadratic equations in modern algebra. 250

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Exegetical Notes 1. The ontological distinction: Architect versus Mathematician: Vitruvius defines the boundaries of the profession in relation to pure science. The architect needs theory to order physical matter, but his ultimate goal is the building, the structure. The mathematician, on the other hand, operates on a purely intellectual plane; he transcends the need to build because his mind masters the abstract laws that govern the universe. By placing mathematicians above the architect, Vitruvius demonstrates brilliant epistemological honesty: architecture is not the queen of the sciences because it is the most abstract, but because it synthesizes abstract thought for the benefit of civilization. 2. The pantheon of Hellenistic polymaths: The names cited constitute the canon of the Hellenistic scientific revolution analyzed here: ◦ Aristarchus of Samos: The first to propose the heliocentric model of the universe. ◦ Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum: Pythagorean philosophers; Archytas was the father of mathematical mechanics and a friend of Plato. ◦ Apollonius of Perga: The geometer who revolutionized the study of conic sections (ellipse, parabola and hyperbola). ◦ Eratosthenes of Cyrene: The sage who calculated the circumference of the Earth with astonishing accuracy by measuring the shadows at the solstice. ◦ Archimedes of Syracuse: The greatest mechanical and hydrostatic genius of antiquity, inventor of the burning mirrors and the claws that defended Syracuse. ◦ Scopinas of Syracuse: Famous inventor of complex sundials and linear gnomonic mechanisms. 3. The Duality of the Organic and the Gnonomic: Vitruvius closes the chapter by connecting this ending with the books that complete his treatise: the machines of Book X (res organicas) and the clocks of Book IX (gnomonicas). By pointing out that these inventions were explained by numero naturalibusque rationibus, Vitruvius offers us the interpretive key to his treatise: the machine and the clock are not products of chance or blind craftsmanship; they are the material crystallization of the mathematical laws of nature. The mathematician discovers them in the heavens, and the architect applies them on Earth. 251

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I [On Architecture 1.1.18] 18. Cum ergo talia ingenia ab naturali sollertia non passim cunctis gentibus sed paucis viris habere concedatur, officium vero architecti omnibus eruditionibus debeat esse exercitatum, et ratio propter amplitudinem rei permittat non iuxta necessitatem summas sed etiam mediocres scientias habere disciplinarum, peto, Caesar, et a te et ab îs, qui ea volumina sunt lecturi, ut, si quid parum ad regulam artis grammaticae fuerit explicatum, ignoscatur. Namque non uti summus philosophus nec rhetor disertus nec grammaticus summis rationibus artis exercitatus, sed ut architectus his litteris imbutus haec nisus sum scribere. De artis vero potestate quaeque insunt in ea ratiocinationes polliceor, uti spero, his voluminibus non modo aedificantibus sed etiam omnibus sapientibus cum maxima auctoritate me sine dubio praestaturum. 18. Since such gifts of natural ingenuity are granted only to a few people rather than to all peoples everywhere, and since an architect’s duties require training in all these branches of knowledge, the breadth of the subject reasonably permits a moderate rather than a supreme command of the disciplines needed for the work. I therefore ask you, Caesar, and those who will read these volumes to forgive anything expressed without strict observance of grammatical rules. I have attempted to write as an architect instructed in these studies, rather than as a great philosopher, an eloquent rhetorician or a grammarian thoroughly trained in the principles of the art. As for the powers of the art itself and the reasoning it involves, I undertake, as I hope, to establish my authority in these volumes beyond doubt, for the benefit of builders and of all learned readers. This passage (I, 1, 18) represents the absolute epilogue of the first chapter of Book I, an indispensable rhetorical capitulation. Here, Vitruvius executes the captatio benevolentiae (request for indulgence) before Octavian Augustus. Aware that his prose does not possess the refinement of a philosopher or a rhetorician, the author asserts his status as an enlightened architect (architectus his litteris inbutus) and appeals to imperial clemency regarding possible grammatical liberties, promising in return an unshakeable theoretical and technical competence. Lecturi means “those who will read”. The adopted text addresses Augustus and the future readers of the treatise. Roman volumina were commonly papyrus rolls, but their material form does not justify replacing lecturi with levaturi. 252

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Likewise, aedificantibus means “those engaged in building”, not “edifiers” in a moral sense. Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “18. Therefore, since the possession of such intellectual gifts and natural ingenuity is not granted indiscriminately to all nations but to a small number of exceptional men, and since the architect's craft must be practised within the full range of liberal arts, the very nature of the discipline — due to its colossal scope (propter amplitudinem rei) —allows for the possession not necessarily of the highest degree in these sciences, but rather a moderate knowledge (mediocres scientias) of them. For this reason, I beg you, Caesar, both you and all those who will read these volumes (volumina sunt lecturi), to forgive me if any passage has been explained in a manner that does not conform to the rules of grammatical composition.” I have endeavored to write these pages not in the style of an eminent philosopher, nor of an eloquent rhetorician, nor of a grammarian trained in the subtlest rules of his art, but rigorously like an architect steeped in literature. Nevertheless, with regard to the intrinsic power of the profession (artis potestate) and the rational principles that are integrated within it (ratiocinationes), I firmly commit myself — or so I hope — to offering in these volumes an unquestionable authority (maxima auctoritate), useful not only to builders (aedificantibus), but also to all scholars. Exegetical notes 1. The material form of reading. Roman volumina were commonly papyrus rolls rather than bound codices. This historical context helps explain the material act of reading, but the adopted wording is volumina sunt lecturi, “those who will read these volumes”. It neither prescribes a particular movement of the hands nor supports an emendation to levaturi. 2. The legitimization of technical prose: Vitruvius here constructs a manifesto in favor of specialized technical language. By contrasting his style with that of the summus philosophus or the rhetor disertus, the author argues that architecture possesses its own syntax. The beauty of his text does not lie in the ornamentation of words (political or literary rhetoric), but in the precision with which the words reflect the ratiocinatio of the building. It is a defense of scientific literature: the architect writes as he builds, with solidity (firmitas) and structural clarity, renouncing the artifices of sophistical eloquence. 253

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 3. The universal scope of the treatise (Omnibus sapientibus): The closing paragraph is the argument that unifies the thesis on Sophia. Vitruvius proudly proclaims that his work is not a mere catalog of constructions for masons or laborers (non modo aedificantibus). By including the sapientibus (the wise, the philosophers, the intellectual elite of the Empire), the treatise claims its place in the high culture of the Pax Romana. Vitruvius demonstrates that architecture is a knowledge of the State, a branch of applied philosophy indispensable for the ordering of the civilized world. The emperor governs men, the philosopher governs souls, and the architect builds the material space where both exercise their power. 254

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Chapter 2 Chapter 2 of Book I sets out the six principles of architectural composition. The enumeration at I.2.1 provides the conceptual framework for the definitions that follow. Latin text «[1.2.1] Architectura autem constat ex ordinatione, quae graece τάξις dicitur, et ex dispositione, hanc autem Graeci διάθεσιν vocitant, et eurythmia et symmetria et decore et distributione, quae graece οἰκονομία dicitur.» « [1.2.1] Architecture rests upon Order (ordinatio), which the Greeks call τάξις; Arrangement (dispositio), which they term διάθεσιν; and further upon Eurythmy, Symmetry, Propriety (decor), and Economy (distributio), which in Greek is called οἰκονομία. » Critical and Hermeneutic Translation Translation note — I.2.1. Vitruvius explicitly gives Greek equivalents for ordinatio (τάξις), dispositio (διάθεσις) and distributio (οἰκονομία). Eurythmia and symmetria are themselves Greek loans incorporated into technical Latin; the passage provides no Greek equivalent for decor here. All six Latin terms are therefore retained and explained in context, without presenting τὸ πρέπον as though it formed part of the text of I.2.1. Comparative apparatus — I.2.1. Fleury’s Budé edition confirms that I.2 forms the core of the general definitions in Book I. Ordinatio/τάξις, dispositio/διάθεσις and distributio/οἰκονομία are retained as technical pairs; eurythmia and symmetria remain technical terms of Greek origin. Decor is not automatically replaced by “decoration”: it expresses the suitability or propriety of the work’s appearance according to rule, custom and nature. Architectural and philological note — Dispositio. Ichnographia, orthographia and scaenographia are species dispositionis: graphic ways of conceiving and representing a project. Dispositio should not be reduced to the functional allocation of rooms, since the passage explicitly includes plan, elevation and perspective or scenographic representation. Comparative critical apparatus — I.2.1–2. The enumeration ordinatio/τάξις, dispositio/διάθεσις, eurythmia, symmetria, decor and distributio/οἰκονομία is stable in its general structure, but I.2.2 presents real differences in the 255

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I constitution of the text. The modern critical edition consulted marks [modica] and [commoditas] as doubtful, whereas other editions print them without reservation. The reconstruction of the definition of quantitas also varies: some critical texts introduce <membris>. These differences are not silently harmonized: the base text of the author’s manuscript is retained and the alternative recorded in the apparatus. Textual note — I.2.2. Krohn marks [modica] and [commoditas] as doubtful in the definition of ordinatio. This edition keeps them visibly marked wherever they occur in the adopted critical text and avoids building on them a doctrine dependent on their authenticity. Transmitted wording, editorial deletion, and supplementation are distinct philological categories and must be identified separately. Terminological note. Ordinatio cannot be equated without qualification with modern “order”, nor dispositio with ordinary “arrangement”. In this context, ordinatio concerns modulation and the correspondence of parts; dispositio concerns their concrete ordering and the modes of representing the project. The Greek terms τάξις, διάθεσις, ποσότης and ἰδέαι are retained because they contribute to Vitruvius’s conceptual precision. Exegesis Notes 1. The Ontology of Design: The Verb Constat: Vitruvius does not use the verbs habere (to have) or comprehendere (to understand). The use of constat ex implies that architecture emerges and subsists only when these six principles coexist simultaneously. If even one of them is missing, the constructed object ceases to be architecture (architecture) and degrades to a mere utilitarian building (fabrica). This nuance is important: the six principles are not optional tools, but rather the formal and efficient causes of sacred and civil space. 2. Vitruvius’s Greco-Roman biculturalism: It is highly significant that Vitruvius immediately translated his concepts into Greek (τάξις, διάθεσις, οἰκονομία). This demonstrates that the Latin of the 1st century BC still lacked an abstract vocabulary mature enough for the theory of art. By anchoring his treatise in Hellenistic terminology, Vitruvius sought to endow the new architecture of the Roman Empire with the same philosophical and scientific 256

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I dignity that the arts possessed in classical Greece. The Roman architect is not a mere builder; he is the heir to Hellenic paideia. 3. Preliminary conceptual map of the Six Axioms: For clarity of exposition, it is convenient to set out in synthetic form the order and hierarchy of these six concepts, which Vitruvius defines in the following paragraphs of the chapter: ◦ The Ordination (Ordinatio / τάξις): The establishment of the mathematical module and the general scale. ◦ The Arrangement (Dispositio / διάθεσις): The geometric and spatial representation on the plane through the plan, the elevation and the perspective. ◦ Eurythmy: The visual and harmonious beauty that the eye perceives in the proportions of the finished work. ◦ Symmetry (Symmetria): The regular metric correspondence between the parts and the whole based on a common unit of measurement (the module). ◦ The Decorum (Decor): The ethical, social and liturgical suitability of the building according to its function and the divinity to which it is consecrated. ◦ Distribution (Distributio / οἰκονομία): Economic management, administration of materials and adaptation of the work to the status of the owner. This fragment (I, 2, 2) is of colossal theoretical density, as it defines the first two axioms of architecture: Ordination (Ordinatio) and Arrangement (Dispositio). Furthermore, it introduces the celebrated triad of architectural representational forms (plan, elevation, and perspective), which constitutes the basis of Western technical drawing. Latin text «2. Ordinatio est modica membrorum operis commoditas separatim universeque proportionis ad symmetriam comparatio. Haec componitur ex quantitate, quae graece ποσότης dicitur. Quantitas autem est modulorum ex ipsius operis e singulisque membrorum partibus sumptio universi operis conveniens effectui. Dispositio autem est rerum apta conlocatio elegansque compositionibus effectus operis cum qualitate. Species dispositionis, quae graece dicuntur ἰδέαι, sunt hae: 257
