Ichnographia est circini regulaeque modice continens usus, e qua capiuntur formarum in solis arearum descriptiones. Orthographia autem est erecta frontis imago modiceque picta rationibus operis futuri figura. Item scaenographia est frontis et laterum abscedentium adumbratio ad circinique centrum omnium linearum responsus. Hae nascuntur ex cogitatione et inventione. Cogitatio est cura, studii plena et industriae vigilantiaeque, effectus propositi cum voluptate. Inventio autem est quaestionum obscurarum explicatio ratioque novae rei vigore mobili reperta. Hae sunt terminationes dispositionum.» « 2. Order is the balanced adjustment of the individual members of the work taken separately, and, for the work as a whole, the comparison of the proportion with a view to a symmetrical result. It is composed of quantity, which in Greek is called ποσότης. Quantity, in turn, consists in taking the modules from the members of the work itself and, from the several parts of those members, producing the harmonious and fitting effect of the work as a whole. Arrangement, for its part, is the apt placement of the elements and the elegant effect of the work that results from their combinations according to its character. The kinds of arrangement, which in Greek are called ἰδέαι, are these: the ground plan117(ichnographia), the elevation (orthographia), and the perspective (scaenographia). The ground plan is the measured use of compass and rule, by which the outlines of forms are set out upon the surfaces of the sites. The elevation is the upright image of the facade, drawn to scale as a figure of the work to come. Likewise, the perspective is the sketch of the facade together with its receding sides, with all the lines converging upon the center of a circle. These arise from reflection and invention. Reflection is the studious, industrious, and vigilant care devoted to the pleasurable accomplishment of a design. Invention, for its part, is the unravelling of obscure problems and the reasoned discovery of a new principle through a lively agility of mind. Such are the determinations of arrangement. Critical Translation and Hermeneutics “2. Order (ordinatio) consists of the just proportion (modica commoditas) of the members of a work taken separately, and in the comparison of the 117 F. Arq. Delineation of the floor of a building. 258

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I proportions of the whole with symmetry (symmetria). This is composed of quantity (quantitas), which in Greek is called ποσότης (posótes). Quantity, in turn, is the adoption of modules (modulorum sumptio) from the members of the work themselves, as well as the harmonious and convenient effect of the whole of the building derived from each of the parts of said members.” Arrangement (dispositio), for its part, is the appropriate placement of elements and the elegant effect of the work resulting from their combinations according to their quality. The forms or categories of arrangement, which in Greek are called ἰδέαι (idéai), are these three: ichnography (ichnographia or plan), orthography (orthographia or elevation), and scaenographia (perspective). • Ichnography (the ground plan) is the disciplined and continuous use of rule and compass, by which the outlines of the forms are set out upon the ground plane. • The orthography is the vertical representation of the facade and a figure drawn to scale in a moderate way, reflecting the proportions of the future work. • Scaenographia, the perspectival representation is the sketch of the facade and the sides that recede into the distance, with all vanishing lines converging towards the center of a circle. These categories arise from meditation (cogitation) and invention (invention). Meditation is attentive reflection, full of assiduity, industry, and vigilance, which pursues the effect of the devised purpose with intellectual delight. Invention, on the other hand, is the resolution of obscure problems and the discovery of a new constructive principle through agile and vigorous ingenuity. These are the delimitations of the dispositions. Exegetical Notes 1. Quantitas as the Birth of the Module: Vitruvius defines quantitas (ποσότης) not as an absolute metric dimension (meters or fixed feet), but as a relative and modular dimension (modulorum sumptio). The architect takes a part of the building — for example, the diameter of the column — and that part becomes the module M. All the rest of the temple (height, width of the forum, intercolumniations) will be a multiple or submultiple of that module. Ordering is the abstract order that reduces the complexity of matter to a single generating number. 259

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 2. The restoration of the three Ideas of drawing: Vitruvius uses the Platonic word ἰδέαι to refer to the plan, the elevation, and the perspective. This means that for the Roman, technical plans are not mere commercial illustrations; they are the mental forms or abstract archetypes that the architect projects onto paper before the building exists in material reality. ◦ The ichnographia (ground plan) is defined by the footprint on the ground (in solis arearum). ◦ The orthographia (elevation) is the rigorous orthogonal projection (erecta frontis imago). ◦ Scaenographia is a representation of the front and receding sides, with the lines answering to a center. Its precise geometric interpretation belongs to the history of the passage’s reception; the wording alone does not establish the complete system of Renaissance linear perspective. 3. The Psychology of Design: Cogitatio and Inventio: The closing of the paragraph connects technical drawing with the architect's mind. Vitruvius details that plans do not arise from nothing; they spring from cogitatio (the analytical, obsessive, and vigilant analysis of the site) and inventio (the creative spark, the vigore mobili, that elegantly resolves the technical problem). He emphasizes that meditation should result in an effect cum voluptate (with pleasure/delight). Architectural design is a joyful intellectual act: reason dominating the chaos of spatial limitations. This fragment (I, 2, 3) defines the third axiom of Vitruvius' treatise: Eurythmy. This principle shifts the theory of design from the purely numerical or abstract plane to the realm of visual perception and subjective aesthetics, establishing that architectural beauty is consummated in the gaze of the spectator (aspectus). To render the Latin as “all things correspond to their own magnitude” is a gross error. In Vitruvius, symmetria does not denote magnitude (absolute size) but rather modular proportionality—the internal metric correspondence between the parts. Latin text «3. Eurythmia est venusta species commodusque in compositionibus membrorum aspectus. Haec efficitur cum membra operis convenientis sunt 260

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I altitudinis ad latitudinem, latitudinis ad longitudinem, et ad summam omnia respondent suae symmetriae.» « 3. Eurythmy is a beautiful appearance and a graceful, becoming aspect in the composition of the members. This is achieved when the members of the work are of a height suited to their width, a width suited to their length, and, in sum, all correspond to their symmetry. »118 Critical Translation and Hermeneutics “3. Eurythmy is the beautiful appearance (venusta species) and the proportionate aspect (commodus aspectus) in the composition of the building's members. This is achieved when the members of the work maintain a suitable height in relation to their width, a suitable width in relation to their length, and, ultimately, when all the elements respond harmoniously to their own modular symmetry (suae symmetriae). ” Exegetical Notes 1. The Aesthetics of the Retina: The Weight of Aspectus: Unlike Ordinatio (which is a cold, mathematical calculation on papyrus), Eurythmy is defined exclusively through visual experience (aspectus and species). Vitruvius introduces here the psychological component of perception: the building must not only be geometrically exact, but it must also appear so to the human eye. Eurythmy is responsible for transforming the rigidity of number into visual grace (venusta), guaranteeing the aesthetic delight of the citizen who contemplates the work from street level. 2. modulation (X:Y:Z): Vitruvius defines eurhythmy as a system of proportional correspondences linked in the three dimensions of space. The text establishes a clear design principle: height must be related to width (H→W), width to length (W→L), and this dimensional trinity must ultimately be subject to the general rule of modular symmetry (suae symmetriae). This passage is vital to your conceptual framework, as it demonstrates that Roman classicism conceived of space in a volumetric and unitary way, preventing a façade from being designed independently of the depth of the building's body. 118 From the Latin eurythmia. Eurythmia refers to the act of moving in a harmonious way and seeking beauty. 261

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 3. The preamble to Optical Corrections: Vitruvius will detail these in Books III and IV (such as the entasis of columns or the inclination of pediments). Since the human eye distorts straight lines due to distance and perspective, the architect is obliged to apply the laws of eurhythmy to correct these illusions. Sometimes, for a temple to appear perfectly symmetrical, it is necessary to alter the actual measurements of its elements. Eurythmy, therefore, represents the triumph of optical design over the rigidity of pure geometric rules. This fragment (I, 2, 4) defines the fourth axiom of classical design: Symmetry (Symmetria). This concept, along with the module, is the absolute mathematical core of Roman architecture during the Augustan period. Latin text 4. Item symmetria est ex ipsius operis membris conveniens consensus ex partibusque separatis ad universae figurae speciem ratae partis responsus. Uti in hominis corpore e cubito, pede, palmo, digito ceterisque particulis symmetros est eurythmiae qualitas, sic est in operum perfectionibus. Et primum in aedibus sacris aut e columnarum crassitudinibus aut triglypho aut etiam embatere, ballista e foramine ⟨capituli⟩, quod Graeci περίτρητον vocitant, navibus interscalmio, quae διάπηγμα dicitur, item ceterorum operum e membris invenitur symmetriarum ratiocinatio. “4. Symmetria is the fitting correspondence among the members of a work and the relationship of its separate parts, measured by a determined unit, to the appearance of the whole. Just as the human body has commensurable relations among forearm, foot, palm, finger and other members, so do completed buildings. In sacred temples the measure is taken from the diameter of a column, a triglyph or an embater; in a ballista, from the opening of its capital, which the Greeks call peritreton; in ships, from the spacing between thole-pins, called dipegma. In other works too, the system of commensurability is derived from their members.” Critical and Hermeneutic Translation « 4. Likewise, symmetry (symmetria) consists in the convenient consonance (conveniens consensus) of the members of a work considered in themselves, and in the correspondence of the separate parts with respect to the appearance of the total configuration, taking as a basis a determined part as a module (rata pars). 262

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Just as the human body possesses the eurhythmic quality of symmetry, derived from the forearm, the foot, the palm, the finger, and other smaller parts, the same is true for the perfect execution of buildings. This is evident, first and foremost, in sacred temples, calculated either from the diameter or thickness of the columns (columnarum crassitudinibus), or from the triglyph (triglypho), or from the module (embater); similarly, it is found in military ballistics, derived from the diameter of the torsion opening in the capital (e foramine capituli), which the Greeks call περίτρητον (perítreton); and in ships, from the space between the oars, or interscalmus, called διάπηγμα (diapegma). Similarly, the analytical principle of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinatio) is discovered in any other type of work by examining its own members. Comparative critical apparatus — I.2.4. Embatere is adopted and the supplement <capituli> is made visible in ballista e foramine <capituli>, as in Krohn’s printed text (1912, 10, lines 18–20). The Greek terms require particular care: περίτρητον denotes the machine’s torsion opening. For the naval module associated with interscalmium, the Spanish edition’s running text has διάπηγμα, whereas its comparative note gives διπηχυια. Krohn’s printed text gives διπηχυαια and Rose (1899, 11, line 17) gives διάπηγμα. the authorial Spanish edition’s running reading is retained here, and the disagreement within the Spanish source is recorded rather than silently harmonized; the current Perseus transcription must not be assumed to reproduce every detail of Krohn’s Greek. Conceptual note — Symmetria. Here symmetria means commensurability or the modular correspondence of parts to a whole, rather than bilateral symmetry. The variety of examples—temple, ballista and ship—shows that Vitruvius formulates a principle of relative dimensioning applicable to different technical fields, rather than a single universal proportion. Exegetical Notes 1. Ancient symmetry does not mean the same as modern symmetry (a mirror image with respect to an axis). For Vitruvius, symmetry is the conveniens consensus (shared mathematical harmony). It is the proportional relationship that unites the parts with the whole. Its operational key is the rata pars (the aliquot or fixed part), which acts as the common metric divisor of the entire project. If the module (rata pars) measures 50 cm, the columns will measure 10×50 cm, the pediment 6×50 cm, and the forum 40×50 cm. 263

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 2. Anthropomorphic Metrological Canon: Vitruvius bases the validity of architectural symmetry on the human body. God or nature has designed the body in such a way that the finger is a fraction of the palm, the palm a fraction of the foot, and the foot a fraction of the cubit. Therefore, the classical metric system does not use impersonal abstractions, but organic and corporeal units. The building is a reflection of the biological order. 3. The Transdisciplinary Modular Unit: The recovered section confirms that the treatise unifies all engineering disciplines under a single scientific framework. Vitruvius demonstrates that the same mathematical thinking governs three seemingly unrelated fields: ◦ Sacred Architecture: Uses as a module the lower diameter of the column (crassitudo), the module of the Doric triglyph or the embatés (the space of the grid). ◦ Military Engineering (Siegecraft): The ballistae in Book X are not designed "by eye." Their full scale depends on the foramen (the hole through which the siege cords pass). The diameter of that hole is the rata pars, which determines the size of the entire siege machine. ◦ Engineering: Warships are designed based on the diapegma (the interscalm), the fixed distance that must exist between the seat of one rower and the next. For the High Empire, a temple, a war machine, and a naval vessel are, ontologically, the same geometric structure applied to different materials. The architect is the universal sage because he masters that symmetriarum ratiocinatio that unifies the world. This fragment (I, 2, 5) defines the fifth axiom of classical architecture: Decorum. This principle introduces the ethical, theological, and semiotic dimension into architectural design, decreeing that a building must not only be geometrically perfect and perceptually eurhythmic, but also politically correct and sacredly appropriate to its function and context. Latin text «5. Decor autem est emendatus operis aspectus probatis rebus compositi cum auctoritate. Is perficitur statione, quod graece θεματισμῷ dicitur, seu consuetudine aut natura. Statione, cum Iovi Fulguri et Caelo et Soli et Lunae 264

By prescription, when temples to Jupiter the Lightning-bringer, to the Heaven, the Sun, and the Moon are erected in the open air and unroofed (hypaethral); for of these gods we behold the semblance and the active power present before us in the open and resplendent sky. Decorum (decor) consists in the irreproachable aspect of a work (emendatus aspectus), constituted with authority from approved elements (probatis rebus). 119 Vitruvius preserves some of his associations in the section of his work On Architecture in which he describes how the design of a temple (aedes) should reflect the nature of the deity that will be housed in it: The character of the Corinthian order seems most appropriate for Venus, Flora, Proserpina and the nymphs [ Lymphae ] of the Fountains; for its slenderness, elegance and richness, and its ornamental leaves topped by volutes, seem to bear analogy to their dispositions. 265

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I This is achieved through ritual or institutional rules (statione), which in Greek are called θεματισμός (thematismós); through custom (consuetudo); or by the requirements of nature itself (natura)." • According to the ritual rule (statione): it is verified when temples are built for Jupiter Fulgurante, the Sky, the Sun and the Moon in the open air and without a roof (sub divo hypaethraque); for we see these gods present themselves, with their own image and active power, in a manifest, open and resplendent world. • Likewise, for Minerva, Mars and Hercules temples of the Doric order will be erected (aedes doricae); for these divinities, by virtue of their military strength and virile valour (virtutem), are decently entitled to sober buildings devoid of ornamental delights. • For Venus, Flora, Proserpina and the Nymphs of the Fountains (Fonti, Lumphis), temples erected in the Corinthian order (corinthio genere) will seem to possess the most appropriate qualities; for these deities, due to their delicacy (teneritatem), are given a fitting decorum by the use of more slender, flowery and ornamented works with leaves and volutes. • Ionic order (aedes ionicae) are built for Juno, Diana, Father Liber (Bacchus), and the other gods who share the same intermediate condition, the law of just and moderate proportion (ratio mediocritatis) will have been observed; since the establishment of their specific features will temper and mediate between the severe custom of the Dorics and the extreme delicacy of the Corinthians. Exegetical Notes 1. Philological note on probatis rebus. The transmitted text and modern critical editions read probatis rebus, “approved elements” or “recognized solutions”, within the definition of decor. No particular medieval corruption is asserted here without an identified manuscript witness. 2. Architecture as Theological and Semiotic Anthropomorphism: This passage constitutes the birth certificate of the theory of architectural genres or characters. Vitruvius demonstrates that the classical orders (Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian) are not mere decorative systems interchangeable at whim, but the tectonic transposition of the identity of the god who inhabits the cella: 266

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I ◦ The Doric order represents masculine Virtus: Devoid of superfluous ornamentation (sine deliciis), it embodies the robust musculature and severity of the soldier. It is the order of war and defensive wisdom (Mars, Minerva, Hercules). ◦ The Corinthian is the feminine Teneritas: Slender, ornamented with acanthus leaves and sinuous volutes, it represents the grace and fertility of the young woman (Venus, Flora). ◦ The Ionic order is the matronly Mediocritas: The just mean (ratio mediocritatis). It is neither as austere as the Doric nor as ornamental as the Corinthian; its volutes imitate the curly hair of the mother of the family or of deities who demand a solemn but balanced worship (Juno, Diana). 3. Hypaethra Architecture and the Cosmos as Temple: The rule of statio explained at the beginning demonstrates the indissoluble link between the gnomonics of Book IX and building typology. Building hypaethra (roofless) temples for the Sun, the Moon, or Jupiter is a cosmic imperative. It would be a theoretical affront to enclose, under an artificial wooden roof, the deities whose essence is infinite light and the ray of the firmament (in aperto mundo atque lucenti). Roman architecture submits to the laws of physics and the astronomy of the sky; the building breaks its own material boundary to merge with the celestial vault. This fragment (I, 2, 6) addresses the second dimension of decorum: Custom (Consuetudo). Vitruvius momentarily abandons theology to focus on the internal coherence of the building, formulating two universal laws of architecture: spatial congruence (the dignified correspondence between the exterior and the interior) and tectonic orthodoxy (strict respect for the rules of combining the orders). The Latin term consuetudinibus (meaning customs/traditions) and ordinis (meaning architectural order, not " order"). Likewise, epistyliis are not "epistles", but epistyles or architraves, and offendetur aspectus means that " the viewer's sight will be offended/the gaze will be scandalized ". Latin text «6. Ad consuetudinem autem decor sic exprimitur, cum aedificiis interioribus magnificis item vestibula convenientia et elegantia erunt facta. Si enim interiora prospectus habuerint elegantes, aditus autem humiles et inhonestos, non erunt 267

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I cum decore. Item si doricis epistyliis in coronis denticuli sculpentur aut in pulvinatis columnis ex ionicis epistyliis [capitulis] exprimentur triglyphi, translatis ex alia ratione proprietatibus in aliud genus operis offendetur aspectus, aliis ante ordinis consuetudinibus institutus.» “6. Propriety according to custom is achieved when magnificent interiors are accompanied by fitting and elegant vestibules. If the interiors offer elegant views but the entrances are low and undistinguished, the building will lack propriety. Likewise, if dentils are carved in the cornices of Doric entablatures, or triglyphs are introduced into Ionic entablatures with cushion-capital columns, the transfer of features from one system to another kind of work will offend the eye, because the established conventions of the orders are different.”120 Critical and Hermeneutic Translation “6. Furthermore, decorum is expressed according to custom (consuetudinem) in the following way: when magnificent residential interiors are accompanied by vestibules (vestibula) executed with identical propriety and elegance. Indeed, if the internal rooms offer elegant views but the entrances are low, meager, or indecorous (humiles et inhonestos), the work will lack decorum.” Similarly, if dentils (denticuli) were carved into the cornices of Doric entablatures, or if triglyphs were sculpted on Ionic architraves attached to columns with pulvinatis capitals, a grave offense would be committed. By transferring the specific features of one structural logic to another type of work, the viewer's sight would be seriously offended (offendetur aspectus), because the traditions and customs previously established for each architectural order (ordinis consuetudinibus) would have been violated. Exegetical Notes 1. The Sociology of Roman Space (The Dialectic of the Vestibulum): Vitruvius introduces a principle of distributive coherence linked to social status. In the Rome of the High Empire, the vestibule of the domus or palace is not a purely private space; it is the public stage where clients wait daily for the salutatio matutina. Designing a luxurious interior preceded by a squalid 120 A triglyph (Greek τρίγλυφος, from τρι-, “three”, and γλύφος, “carving” or “groove”) is a characteristic architectural ornament of the Doric frieze: a rectangular element in relief, taller than it is wide, with three vertical bands separated by two complete grooves and two half-grooves, one at each end. Sometimes only the central grooves occur. 268

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I entrance (inhonestos) is a political and aesthetic error. In the present author’s reading, the building may be likened to a Ciceronian rhetorical discourse: the exordium (the vestibule) must dignifiedly anticipate the grandeur of the body of the work. 2. Grammar and Syntax Errors: Vitruvius defines the architectural orders not as a collection of whimsical ornaments, but as languages with a grammar and syntax of their own (an interpretive analogy). ◦ The Doric order imitates the primitive structure of wooden beams: the triglyphs represent the ends of the crossbeams. Placing dentils (which belong to the Ionic tradition of light reed roofs) on a Doric cornice is an aberrant structural contradiction. ◦ Mixing Doric triglyphs with architraves and Ionic columns with pulvinated volute capitals (pulvinatis) destroys the veracity of the building. 3. Sight as Moral Judge (Offendetur aspectus): For the thesis on Sophia, the paragraph's conclusion is providential. Vitruvius points out that the spurious mixture of the orders produces an immediate visual offense: offendetur aspectus. This demonstrates that for the Romans, the eye of a cultivated spectator is not passive; it possesses an aesthetic education rooted in custom (consuetudo). Seeing a syntactic error in stone provokes the same intellectual rejection as hearing a serious grammatical mistake in a speech in the Forum. Architecture, therefore, is consolidated as a discipline regulated by cultural laws as strict as those of law or rhetoric. This fragment (I, 2, 7) defines the third and final dimension of decorum: Nature (Natura). With this passage, Vitruvius masterfully connects the theory of design with Galenic and Hippocratic medicine (ancient hygienism) and with astronomy applied to climatic orientation (bioclimatics). 1. Fana constituentur: Fanum in Latin means " sanctuary ", " sacred precinct " or " temple " (from which the word "profane" comes). 2. Aesculapio Saluti: They are not two separate deities called " Aesculapius Salutus ", but Asclepius (Aesculapius) and Salus (the goddess Hygieia of health). 3. Hibernaculis ab occidente hiberno: These are not " hibernations ", but the winter rooms of the Roman house, which must face southwest to take advantage of the afternoon heat. 269

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 4. Neque exclaratur neque obscuratur: This refers to the fact that the northern light " does not suffer glare or obscuration " from the passage of the sun. Latin text «7. Naturalis autem decor sic erit, si primum omnibus templis saluberrimae regiones aquarumque fontes in îs locis idonei eligentur in quibus fana constituantur, deinde maxime Aesculapio, Saluti, ut eorum deorum quorum plurimi medicinis aegri curari videntur. Propriety according to nature is achieved, first, by choosing the healthiest regions and suitable springs of water for the places where sanctuaries are established, especially those of Aesculapius and Salus, through whose healing arts many sick people appear to recover. When the sick are transferred from an unhealthy place to a healthy one and supplied with water from wholesome springs, they recover more quickly. The nature of the place thus enhances the deity’s reputation and dignity. Natural propriety also requires bedrooms and libraries to receive light from the east, baths and winter rooms from the winter sunset, and picture galleries and rooms needing steady light from the north, since that quarter is neither brightened nor darkened by the sun’s course but remains constant throughout the day.” Critical and Hermeneutic Translation 7. For its part, natural decorum (naturalis decor) will be manifested if, above all, the most healthy regions and suitable springs of water are chosen for the foundation of the sanctuaries (fana) in those locations where the temples are to be erected; this should be applied especially to Aesculapius and Salus, deities whose medical arts seem to heal a great number of sick people. Indeed, when bodies weakened by disease are moved from pestilent places to healthy environments, and are given access to water from wholesome springs, they 270

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I recover their health more quickly. In this way, through the influence of the very nature of the place (ex natura loci), the deity will receive increased worship and veneration invested with the highest dignity. Likewise, the decorum of nature will be respected if bedrooms (cubiculis) and libraries receive light from the east; bathrooms (balineis) and winter quarters (hibernaculis), from the winter west (west/southwest); and art galleries (pinacothecis), together with those rooms that require constant illumination, from the north, since that region of the firmament neither dazzles nor darkens with the course of the sun, but remains fixed, homogeneous, and immutable throughout the day (die perpetuo). Exegetical Notes 1. Hygienic Urbanism and Medical Theology: Vitruvius demonstrates that Roman sacred architecture is neither capricious nor purely aesthetic; it is subject to the biological laws of nature. Placing a sanctuary (fanum) dedicated to healing deities like Asclepius or Salus in an unhealthy swamp would destroy the god's credibility. If the sick person recovers thanks to the pure air and clean water of the place (ex natura loci), they will miraculously attribute their cure to divine intervention, increasing the dignity and political prestige of the state religion. Architecture here acts as a strategic ally of preventive medicine. 2. Bioclimatic Architecture and Solar Orientation: This paragraph constitutes the first manual of thermal orientation in Western history. Vitruvius distributes the program of needs of the domus following the movement of the sun and the needs of the mind and body: ◦ East: For bedrooms and libraries. The morning light prevents dampness in books and awakens the intellect early. ◦ Winter West (Southwest): For winter bathrooms and lounges (hibernaculis). By opening towards the west, these rooms capture the heat accumulated throughout the afternoon, warming the space precisely during the hours when they will be used during the cold months. 3. The North as the Space of Absolute Light (Die perpetuo): The recommendation to orient art galleries and studios towards the north (a 271

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I septentrione) is overwhelmingly scientifically sound. Since in the Northern Hemisphere the sun travels through the south, the light entering through northfacing windows is reflected, indirect, diffuse, and constant. Vitruvius points out that this illumination is neither clear nor obscured (it suffers neither the glare of midday nor the long shadows of sunset). It is an immutable light (certa immutabilis), ideal for painters to work and for viewers to contemplate the true colors of works of art without optical distortions. Latin text 8. Distributionis] Genitive of distributio: the passage introduces its second aspect, the arrangement of buildings for different uses. Aedificia apte disponentur] “Buildings will be suitably arranged”. Notes and Commentary • "alter gradus erit distributionis": Vitruvius presents distributio on two levels: the first economic and practical (1.2.8), and this second, sociological and functional according to the status of the owner. • "eloquentiae dignitatem": This refers to the dignity required by people of high social or political rank who need suitable spaces to exert their influence and receive visitors (clients, ambassadors, etc.). • "potentibus vero, quorum cogitationibus res publica gubernatur": Clear reference to the optimates or high-level Roman magistrates. It is one of the few passages where Vitruvius directly alludes to the Augustan political context. Comparative critical apparatus — I.2.5–9. In decor the critical tradition retains statione/θεματισμῷ, consuetudine and natura as three routes to propriety; the passage does not justify reducing decor to “ornament”. In distributio, οἰκονομία encompasses both the management of resources and costs and the suitability of a building to its owner’s use, means and rank. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Chapter 3 Latin text 1.3.1 Partes ipsius architecturae sunt tres: aedificatio, gnomonice, machinatio. Aedificatio autem divisa est bipertito, e quibus una est moenium et communium operum in publicis locis conlocatio, altera est privatorum aedificiorum explicatio. Publicorum autem distributiones sunt tres, e quibus est una defensionis, altera religionis, tertia opportunitatis. Defensionis est murorum turriumque et portarum ratio ad hostium impetus perpetuo repellendos excogitata; religionis deorum inmortalium fanorum aediumque sacrarum conlocatio; opportunitatis communium locorum ad usum publicum dispositio, uti portus, fora, porticus, balinea, theatra, ambulationes ceteraque quae isdem rationibus in publicis locis designantur. 1.3.1 The parts of architecture proper are three: construction, the making of sundials, and mechanics. Construction, in turn, is divided into two branches: the first is the laying-out of city walls and of works for common use in public places, the second the raising of private buildings. Public works admit of three classes: the first concerns defense, the second religion, and the third convenience. To defense belongs the design of walls, towers, and gates, devised to repel the assaults of enemies in perpetuity; to religion, the placing of shrines and sacred temples to the immortal gods; to convenience, the provision of common spaces for public use—such as harbors, fora, colonnades, baths, theaters, promenades, and the other works laid out on the same principles in public places. Academic translation 1.3.1 The parts of architecture proper are three: construction (aedificatio), gnomonics (gnomonice), and mechanics (machinatio). Construction, in turn, is divided into two sections: one consists of the erection of walls and common works in public spaces; the other is the arrangement of private buildings. For public works, there are three categories: the first is for defense; the second, for religion; the third, for convenience. Defense comprises the theory and design of walls, towers, and gates, conceived to perpetually repel enemy assaults; religion 277

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I encompasses the placement of sanctuaries and sacred temples of the immortal gods; Convenience consists in the organization of common places for public use, such as ports, forums, porticoes, baths, theaters, covered walkways and other constructions that are planned with similar criteria on public land. Philological and Exegetical Apparatus Textual note — I.3.1. The Latin text is checked against Rose and Krohn. This edition does not seek to establish a new recensio; its observations are therefore confined to problems affecting translation or interpretation and avoid unverified manuscript attributions. Terminological note — I.3.1. Aedificatio, gnomonice and machinatio are the three parts of architectura according to this chapter. Machinatio denotes the theory and practice of machines; gnomonice, astronomical and time measurement by shadows. Machinatio should not automatically be translated as “engineering”, nor gnomonice as “astronomy”, since both equivalents enlarge the scope of the ancient terms. 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.3.1. For the fixation of the Latin text, compare the archetypal edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 11-12; and the critical reading of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 12. • machinatio: The traditional translation of " engineering " is amended to " mechanical". In the context of the 1st century BC, machinatio strictly refers to the science of machines (both civil traction and military poliorctics), differentiating itself from the contemporary and institutionalized meaning of general engineering. • explicatio: The term is more precisely cast as "layout " or "deployment" of private buildings, surpassing the flat translation of "realization." Vitruvius alludes to the planned development of domestic and residential space. • Opportunitas: The Vitruvian concept of "opportunity" or "convenience" is restored in contrast to the modern utilitarianism implicit in "public utility. " Opportunitas is the suitability and functional benefit of space for the development of civic life and the leisure of citizens. • fanorum aediumque sacrarum: The translation precisely distinguishes between the two terms. Fanum designates the sacred enclosure or 278

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I consecrated area (sanctuary), while aedes sacra constitutes the building or structure of the temple itself. • Inambulations: This is technically translated as "covered walkways" (or ambulatories). These are not simple walks or strolls in the open air, but specific architectural typologies (such as freestanding porticoes or galleries) designed for exercise and social conversation protected from the weather. 1.3.1 The parts of architecture proper are three: construction, gnomonics, and mechanics. Construction is divided into two sections: public works and the arrangement of private buildings. Public works, in turn, have three distributions: defense, religion, and convenience (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.3.1). Latin text 2. Haec autem ita fieri debent, ut habeatur ratio firmitatis, utilitatis, venustatis. Firmitatis erit habita ratio, cum fuerit fundamentorum ad solidum depressio, quaque e materia, copiarum sine avaritia diligens electio; utilitatis autem, ⟨cum fuerit⟩ emendata et sine inpeditione usus locorum dispositio et ad regiones sui cuiusque generis apta et commoda distributio; venustatis vero, cum fuerit operis species grata et elegans membrorumque commensus iustas habeat symmetriarum ratiocinationes. Academic translation 1.3.2 These constructions must be achieved in such a way that solidity (firmitas), utility (utilitas), and beauty (venustas) are taken into account. Solidity will have been considered when the excavation of the foundations is deepened to firm ground (solidum) and when a diligent selection of materials is made from among those available, without sparing any expense (sine avaritia); utility, when the arrangement of the spaces is impeccable and presents no impediments to their use, and when the distribution of each type of building is suitable, comfortable, and properly oriented to its region; and beauty, when the appearance of the work is pleasing and elegant, and when the proportion of the members maintains a just calculation of symmetries (symmetriarum ratiocinationes). Comparative note — Bk. 1.3.2 (firmitas · utilitas · venustas). The canonical triad of a building's qualities. The major editions render it 279

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I with telling nuances: Granger (Loeb, 1931), 'durability, convenience, and beauty'; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999), 'soundness, utility, and attractiveness', stressing the functional sense; Gros (Budé) analyses its Hellenistic roots and its relation to the categories of technē; Corso & Romano (Einaudi) expand the historical commentary. In English, Sir Henry Wotton's paraphrase became famous: 'Commoditie, Firmenes, and Delight' (1624). This edition keeps the Latin terms in italics for their conceptual value. [Architectural-historical note: the triad epitomizes Roman building practice—firm foundation, useful distribution, proportionate ornament—and becomes, from Alberti onward, the theoretical framework of Western architecture.] Philological and Exegetical Apparatus Textual note — I.3.2. The text is checked against Rose and Krohn. The adopted reading retains emendata et sine inpeditione usus locorum dispositio and apta et commoda distributio. This edition reproduces minor variants only when they affect the translated meaning. 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.3.2. For the textual fixation, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 12; and the revision of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 12. • habeatur ratio: It is translated with greater academic precision as " take into account" or "attend to", maintaining the structure of the technical conditional of the treatise. • ad solidum depressio: the foundations are to be excavated down to firm bearing ground. Solidum denotes a sufficiently stable stratum; it does not require bedrock in every case. The passage concerns the support of the foundations, not the sinking of a finished building. • Diligent selection of resources without avarice. The Latin excludes avaricious parsimony in the procurement of resources.It alludes to the sources of resources or supplies of materials available in the area. The expression sine avaritia means literally "without stinginess" or "without parsimony", implying that a poorly understood economy harms the structure. 280

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I • emendata... sine impeditione: This is technically translated as " impeccable and without impediments". The term emendata suggests a plan that is corrected, refined, and free of design flaws. • ad regiones... distributio: Vitruvius refers not only to the "category " of the building, but also to its climatic and geographical orientation. The regions in this passage are the cardinal points and the zones of the sky (sun exposure and prevailing winds). • membrorumque commensus: This translates as "the proportion of the members" (or architectural elements). Commensus is the mutual metric correspondence between the parts and the whole. • symmetriarum ratiocinationes: The term symmetria in the classical world does not equate to the modern concept of bilateral mirror reflection. It means "modular relation". It is therefore translated as "the just calculation of symmetries ", that is, mathematical modulation based on a control member (the diameter of a column, for example). 1.3.2 These constructions must be achieved in such a way as to attend to solidity, utility, and beauty. Solidity will be ensured by deepening the foundations to the firm stratum and by diligently choosing the materials without sparing any expense; utility, when the arrangement of the spaces presents no impediment and their distribution is comfortable and suitable for each type of building; and beauty, when the appearance of the work is pleasing and the proportion of its members maintains a just calculation of symmetries (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.3.2). Comparative apparatus — I.3.1–2. Aedificatio, gnomonice and machinatio are operational divisions of the discipline; firmitas, utilitas and venustas are criteria Vitruvius requires of the works described. The triad is translated without turning it into a modern slogan: firmitas includes foundations and the choice of materials; utilitas, arrangement suited to use; venustas, a pleasing appearance and proportional relationships. Reception note — Firmitas, utilitas and venustas. The triad’s exceptional subsequent influence should not be projected back on to the lemma. In I.3.2 the three terms occur within a concrete explanation of how works should be executed; their canonisation as a universal formula belongs to the history of reception. 281

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Comparative critical apparatus — I.3.1–2. The text is compared with Krohn (1912) and Philippe Fleury’s Budé edition of Book I. The supplement <cum fuerit> before emendata in I.3.2 is explicitly marked in Krohn’s printed text (1912, 13, line 7), whose apparatus attributes its addition to Marini. Rose (1899, 14, line 9) prints cum emendata. The Spanish note’s claim that Krohn does not mark the supplement in the same way is corrected on this documentary basis. The celebrated triad firmitas–utilitas–venustas is retained in Latin in the commentary to prevent “solidity–function–beauty” from retrospectively becoming a modern theory of functionalism. Note on scope — I.3.2. Firmitas, utilitas and venustas are criteria Vitruvius formulates for these works within the argument of I.3. Their subsequent reception made them an emblematic triad of architectural theory. This edition avoids automatically extending them into an exhaustive definition of all architecture or assigning them a philosophical genealogy that the passage does not specify. 282

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Chapter 4 Latin text 1.4.1 In ipsis vero moenibus ea erunt principia. Primum electio loci saluberrimi. Is autem erit excelsus et non nebulosus, non pruinosus regionesque caeli spectans neque aestuosas neque frigidas sed temperatas, deinde si vitabitur palustris vicinitas. Cum enim aurae matutinae cum sole oriente ad oppidum pervenient et his ortae nebulae adiungentur spiritusque bestiarum palustrium venenatos cum nebula mixtos in habitatorum corpora flatu spargent, efficient locum pestilentem. First comes the choice of a thoroughly healthy site: one that is elevated, free from mist and frost, facing quarters of the sky that are neither sweltering nor cold but temperate, and, further, removed from the neighborhood of marshes. For when the morning breezes reach the town at sunrise, bringing with them the mists that have gathered and, mingled with those mists, the poisonous exhalations of the marsh creatures, and scatter them by their breath into the bodies of the inhabitants, they render the place pestilential. Likewise, walls set along the coast and facing south or west will be unhealthy; for in summer the southern sky grows warm at sunrise and burns at midday, while a westward aspect grows warm at sunrise, is hot at midday, and blazes in the evening. 121 Academic translation 1.4.1 As regards the configuration of the walls themselves, the fundamental principles will be the following. Likewise, the proximity of marshy lands should be avoided. For when the morning breezes reach the city at sunrise, bringing with them the fogs that rise from there, and the breath of 121 This explanation belongs to ancient environmental medicine: Vitruvius links mist, marshes, exhalations and disease. The note preserves that historical reasoning without recasting it as knowledge of microorganisms. 283

Similarly, if the walls are situated by the sea and face south or west, they will not be healthy; Since during the summer, the southern region of the sky heats up with the sunrise and burns at midday; meanwhile, the area facing west grows warm at dawn, heats up at midday and scorches at sunset. Critical Notes 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.4.1. For the fixation and variants of the Latin text, see the critical edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 12-13; and Fritz Krohn's edition, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 12-13. • Chapter 4: The old title is corrected to the modern standardized nomenclature 1.4.1 (Book I, Chapter 4, Paragraph 1) to ensure unified indexing in the reference apparatus. • moenibus: Although a literal version translates "in the walls themselves", in this context moenia does not refer only to the physical structure of the stone wall, but to the walled enclosure or the fortified urban perimeter that delimits the foundation of the city. • spiritusque bestiarum palustrium: "The spirits of the swamp beasts." Philologically, spiritus should be translated here as " breath, " "emanations," or "exhalations." Vitruvius operates under the ancient medical theory of miasmas (corrupt air currents that transmit diseases), so the allusion to bestiae refers to the harmful insects and microorganisms of stagnant waters. • Cum nebula mixtos. Nebula is adopted as the form transmitted in the reference critical text. The form neula is a modern transcription error and is not attributed to a medieval witness. • vespere fervet: The precision of Vitruvian thermal gradation is increased. The text describes a progressive increase in heat in the west orientation: tepescit (warms), calet (warms) and fervet (boils, or scorches). Translating fervet simply as "hot in the afternoon" distorts the author's emphasis on the suffocating effect of the west orientation. 1.4.1 Regarding the configuration of the walls, the first principle will be the choice of a highly healthy site: elevated, free from fog, and facing temperate regions, avoiding the proximity of marshes whose exhalations pollute the air. 284

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Likewise, walls situated by the sea should not face south or west, due to the excessive heat they suffer from midday until sunset (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.4.1). Latin text 1.4.2 Igitur mutationibus caloris et refrigerationis corpora quae in his locis sunt vitiantur. Hoc autem licet animadvertere etiam ex îs quae non sunt animalia. In cellis enim vinariis tectis lumina nemo capit a meridie nec ab occidente sed a septentrione, quod ea regio nullo tempore mutationes recipit sed est firma perpetuo et inmutabilis. Ideo etiam ea granaria quae ad solis cursum spectant bonitatem cito mutant, obsoniaque et poma quae non in ea parte caeli ponuntur quae est aversa a solis cursu, non diu servantur. 1.4.2 Therefore, the bodies that are in these places are spoiled by changes in heat and cooling. For in roofed wine cellars no one receives light from the south or from the west, but from the north, because that region at no time receives changes, but is permanently fixed and unchangeable. Therefore also those granaries that look towards the course of the sun quickly change their quality, and food and fruits that are not placed in that part of the sky that is turned away from the course of the sun are not preserved for long. Academic translation 1.4.2 Therefore, due to the variations of heat and cooling, bodies in these places suffer serious damage. This same principle can be observed even in inanimate objects. In covered wine cellars, for example, no one opens windows facing south or west, but rather north, since that region of the sky never experiences abrupt changes, but remains perpetually constant and unchanging. For this same reason, barns facing the sun's path quickly deteriorate the quality of their crops; and perishable foods and fruits do not keep for long unless placed in that part of the sky sheltered from the sun's path. Critical Interlineation Explanatory note: the στοιχεῖα and salubrity. In grounding the choice of site upon the balance of the elements, Vitruvius adopts the Greek doctrine of the στοιχεῖα —the “elements” or constituent principles of bodies—, which he enumerates in Latin as calor, umor, terra, and aer (heat, moisture, earth, and air). This conception derives from Greek natural philosophy (the four “roots” of Empedocles, later systematized by Aristotle) and is interwoven with Hippocratic medicine, particularly the treatise Airs, Waters, Places, which links climate and place to the health of the body. Vitruvius’s originality lies in making this physiology the foundation of urban site selection (salubritas): the architect must choose elevated, temperate sites far from marshes so that the elemental mixture (temperatura) of the inhabitants’ bodies remains in balance. Architecture is thereby bound to medicine—a connection Vitruvius himself claims when he requires the architect to know medicine propter inclinationes caeli (1.1.10). Textual note — I.4.5. The adopted text transmits στοιχεῖα, “elements” or “principles”. This edition retains the reading and confines its commentary to its role in Vitruvius’s argument, without reconstructing a history of manuscript corruption that has not been checked directly against the witnesses. 1.4.7 Sed si qui voluerit diligentius haec sensu percipere, animadvertat attendatque naturas avium et piscium et terrestrium animalium, et ita 292

Philological, historical and scientific analysis of passage 1.4.9, formally structured for its insertion as an exegetical apparatus in a critical edition or academic article. Exegetical Analysis of De architectura 1.4.9 1. The Legacy of Tradition: Mos Maiorum and Roman Pragmatism Vitruvius opens the passage with a forceful methodological statement: “Etiam atque etiam veterem revocandam censeo rationem ” (“I believe that the methodology of our ancestors must be recovered, again and again ”). This recourse is not merely nostalgic; it corresponds to the Roman concept of mos maiorum (the custom of the ancestors) as a legitimate source of technical and moral knowledge. In contrast to the abstract speculation of the Hellenistic philosophical schools, the author champions ancient ratio: a profoundly empirical criterion, based on continuous observation and accumulated success. For Vitruvius, the architect is a steward of public space and, as such, inherited tradition is a safety protocol tested by generations. Ritual Aruspicin to Empirical Health Control The core of the passage describes the examination of cattle entrails (inspicere iocinera), a practice formally identical to haruspicy, the ancient divinatory 298

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I discipline of Etruscan origin regulated by haruspices. However, Vitruvius performs a radical demythologization of the ritual: • Absence of the sacred: Livers are not examined to look for signs of the gods (such as caputiocineris or prophetic lines), but to check their objective physiological state (integram et solidam naturam). • Livestock as a bioindicator: Vitruvius understood that animals grazing in a fixed location act as a biological laboratory that metabolizes and concentrates the properties of the soil, the pastures (pabulum), and the water (aqua). If the liver shows necrosis or discoloration (livida et vitiosa), the ecosystem is corrupted. • The preliminary scientific method: The author describes a twostep verification protocol. If the first liver is damaged, more cattle are sacrificed (alia immolabant) to rule out an isolated pathology of the specimen (morbo) versus an endemic environmental poisoning (pabuli vitio). 3. The Theory of Miasma Contamination and Human Ecology The passage demonstrates the connection between Roman architecture and the medical theories of the Hippocratic school, specifically the treatise On Airs, Waters, and Places. Vitruvius establishes a direct correlation between animal and human health: the territory that destroys the organs of livestock will, sooner or later, destroy the constitution of the urban inhabitant (item humanis corporibus pestilentem futuram). The conclusion of the passage introduces a criterion for urban planning subordinated to ecology: if the environment is unhealthy, the solution is not constructive, but migratory (transmigrabant et mutabant regiones). Architecture cannot defeat nature; it must ally itself with its thermal and hydrological cycles. 4. Military Application: Castra Stativa The explicit mention of castra stativa (permanent camps or winter quarters) underscores the strategic importance of hygiene in Roman engineering. The Roman army could not afford epidemiological outbreaks in the legions stationed on the frontiers (limes). Analysis of the terrain using haruspicy (wisdom for livestock) was a mandatory step before the deployment of fixed defenses (munitiones), thus equating the rigor of military architecture with that of the founding of large civilian cities (oppida). 299

The lacuna in the adopted Latin and the uncertainty of modern botanical identification must remain visible. Latin text 10. Hoc autem fieri, uti pabulo ciboque salubres proprietates terrae videantur, licet animadvertere et cognoscere ex agris Cretensium, qui sunt circa Pothereum flumen, quod est Cretae inter duas civitates Gnoson et Gortynam. Dextra enim et sinistra eius fluminis pascuntur pecora; sed ex his quae pascuntur proxime Gnoson si * * * quae autem ex altera parte proxime Gortynam, non habent apparentem splenem. Unde etiam medici quaerentes de ea re invenerunt in his locis herbam, quam pecora rodendo inminuerunt lienes. Ita eam herbam colligendo curant lienosos hoc medicamento, quod etiam Cretenses ἄσπληνον vocitant. Ex eo licet scire cibo atque aqua proprietates locorum naturaliter pestilentes aut salubres esse. 1.4.10 The properties of the land as revealed through fodder and food may be observed in the Cretan fields around the river Pothereus, between Knossos and Gortyna. Cattle graze on both banks. Those near Knossos […] whereas those on the other side near Gortyna have no visible spleen. Investigating this, physicians found a local plant whose consumption by the cattle reduced their spleens. They therefore collected it to treat patients with diseases of the spleen; the Cretans call the remedy asplenon (ἄσπληνον). Food and water thus reveal whether a place’s natural properties are healthy or unhealthy. Textual note — I.4.10. The authorial Spanish base marks a lacuna after the cattle near Knossos, as does the adopted Krohn text. The electronic transcription of Rose supplies <lienosa> sunt, “have diseased spleens”, to complete the contrast with Gortyna. This is an editorial supplement, not a directly verified reading of Harley or Cotton. Asplenon (ἄσπληνον) is the plant name in the adopted text; its usual comparison with spleenwort belongs to botanical interpretation, not to the constitution of the damaged clause. Textual note — I.4.10. Krohn’s critical text retains a lacuna after proxime Gnoson; an unverified conjecture is therefore not introduced into the Latin as though it were transmitted text. Ἄσπληνον is the plant’s Greek name in the passage; this edition does not impose a single modern botanical identification. 300

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Academic translation 1.4.10 That this occurs — that is, that the salutary or harmful properties of the soil are manifested through fodder and food — can be observed and verified in the fields of Crete situated around the Potereus River, which flows between the cities of Knossos and Gortyna. Indeed, herds of cattle graze on both the right and left banks of this river; however, the cattle grazing on the bank closest to Knossos [in the supplemented interpretation] suffer from disorders of the spleen, while those feeding on the other bank, near Gortyna, do not have a noticeably enlarged spleen. For this reason, physicians, investigating the phenomenon, discovered in those areas a type of grass on which the cattle fed and which, when gnawed, reduced the size of their spleens. Thus, by harvesting this plant, they cure spleen ailments today with this medicine, which the Cretans call ásplenon (ἄσπληνον). From this fact, it can be inferred with certainty that, through food and water, the latent properties of the land naturally result in pestilent or healthy conditions. Critical Interlineation 1.4.11 Item si in paludibus moenia constituta erunt, quae paludes secundum mare fuerint, spectabuntque ad septentrionem aut inter septentrionem et orientem, eaeque paludes excelsiores fuerint quam litus marinum, ratione videbuntur esse constituta. Fossis enim ductis fit aquae exitus ad litus, et mare tempestatibus actum in paludes redundantia motionibus concitata marisque mixtionibus non patitur bestiarum palustrium genera ibi nasci, quaeque de superioribus locis natando proxime litus perveniunt, inconsueta salsitudine necantur. Exemplar autem huius rei Gallicae paludes possunt esse quae circum ⟨cingunt⟩ Altinum, Ravennam, Aquileiam aliaque quae in eiusmodi locis municipia sunt proxima paludibus, quod his rationibus habent incredibilem salubritatem. 1.4.11 Likewise, if walls are built in marshes, which marshes are next to the sea, and face north or between north and east, and those marshes are higher than the seashore, they will seem to have been built for a reason. For by digging ditches, the water is brought to the shore, and the sea, increased by storms, overflowing into the marshes, agitated by the movements and mixtures of the sea, does not allow the kinds of marsh animals to be born there, and those that swim from higher places to reach the shore are killed by the unusual salinity. An example of this can be the marshes of Gaul which are around Altinus, Ravenna, Aquileia 302

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I and others which are in such places towns close to the marshes, because for these reasons they have an incredible salubrious effect. 1. Gallicae paludes: A recurring historical error in literal translations that render it as "the marshes of France." In the geography of the 1st century BC, it strictly refers to the marshes of Cisalpine Gaul (the region of northern Italy, around the Po River delta and the Venetian Lagoon). — 2. Altinum, Ravenna, Aquileia: Strategic Roman cities on the northern Adriatic coast, famous for their complex system of canals and lagoons that combined commercial navigation with environmental health. Academic translation 1.4.11 Likewise, if a walled city is established on marshy land, provided that these marshes are located by the sea, facing north or between north and east, and are at a higher altitude than the seashore, its foundation will be considered to have been carried out according to sound architectural principles (ratione). Indeed, by opening ditches and canals, the drainage of stagnant water towards the coast is facilitated; moreover, when the sea rises due to storms, its overflows flow back into the marshes, whose waters, agitated by the waves and mixed with the sea flow, prevent the proliferation of the various species of marsh vermin; as for the microorganisms that swim down from the highlands towards the coast, they perish immediately upon being exposed to a salinity to which they are not accustomed. As an example of this phenomenon, one can cite the marshes of Cisalpine Gaul that surround Altino, Ravenna and Aquileia, as well as other municipalities that, being in similar places and adjacent to the marshes, enjoy extraordinary health thanks to these engineering principles. The technical expression ratione implies that the architectural project complies with the principles of constructive logic and physical science, being fully justified. 303

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I • marique mixtionibus: A literal version misinterpreted the text, translating it as "bitter mixtures" (probably confusing mare with the adjective amarus). Vitruvius is strictly referring to the mixture or combination of stagnant fresh water with salt water from the sea, a physical phenomenon that alters the ecosystem and prevents the water from rotting (putrefactio). • inconsueta salsitudine necantur: Vitruvius describes a biological principle of osmotic shock: freshwater organisms descending from the rivers of the highlands (de superioribus locis) die upon contact with the "unusual salinity" of the marine lagoon. • Incredible health: The paradox that marshy areas like Ravenna or Aquileia were " incredibly healthy" fascinated ancient authors. Vitruvius demonstrates that the constant movement of water (tidal dynamics and artificial canals) counteracts the miasma of stagnant water that was analyzed in the previous paragraphs. Translation and Commentary 1.4.11 Cities founded in marshy areas adjacent to the sea are viable if the marshes are located at a higher altitude than the coastline. The opening of channels (fossis) allows the waters to drain into the sea, while the tidal flow mixes the salt water with the fresh water, eradicating marsh vermin through osmotic shock. This principle of hydraulic engineering explains the extraordinary healthfulness of the municipalities of Cisalpine Gaul, such as Altino, Ravenna, and Aquileia (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.4.11). 4. Its inhabitants, afÒicted by illness every year, eventually appealed to Marcus Hostilius and obtained his agreement to seek a suitable site for moving the town. He acted without delay: after careful investigation he purchased land in a healthy place by the sea, obtained permission from the Roman Senate and people, built the walls, divided the building plots and conveyed each plot to a citizen for one sestertius. Located on such terrain, its inhabitants suffered from serious illnesses annually, so they formally petitioned Marcus Hostilius and publicly begged him to find and select a suitable site to relocate the city. Hostilius did not delay; After conducting a highly scientific investigation based on physical principles, he acquired a healthy plot of land by the sea and requested permission from the Roman Senate and people to relocate the city. Once granted, he erected new walls, divided the urban land into parcels, and granted legal ownership to each citizen for the symbolic price of one sestertius. For the fixation and variants of the Latin text of Salpia's move, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 16; and Fritz Krohn's review, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 16. • Pontine Marshes: The Pontine Marshes (Paludes Pomptinae), located south of Latium, represented the greatest challenge of unsanitary conditions and drainage in central Italy. Vitruvius cites them as the paradigmatic example of stagnant and incurable waters of his time. • stando putescunt: "standing up they rot." The verb stare here has the technical value of " to stagnate" (water that does not flow). Correctly translated it is: "when they stagnate, they spoil. " • serious humors: It does not refer to "heavy waters" in the liquid sense, but to "dense exhalations", miasmas or vapors laden with corrupted particles that floated on the air of the swamp affecting respiration. • M. Hostilium: the Marcus Hostilius named in Vitruvius’s account of the relocation of Salpia. The passage gives no office, cognomen, or precise date for his intervention. • areas divisit: "divided the territories". In Roman urban planning, areas are the "plots" or parcels of land designated for the construction of houses within the new orthogonal layout of the city. • nummo sestertio … mancipio dedit: Hostilius conveyed each building plot by mancipatio for a nominal sestertius. The legal formula denotes a formal transfer of ownership. The passage does not specify a beneficiary class or supply the full legal circumstances of the transaction. 1.4.12 Lands with stagnant, undrained water, such as the Pontine Marshes, become corrupted, emitting pestilent miasmas. This affected ancient Salpia in Apulia, where its citizens fell ill annually until Marcus Hostilius, through a rigorous technical study, moved the city to a healthy location by the sea. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I provide the municipality with a functional port (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.4.12). Comparative critical apparatus — I.4.1–12. The chapter has been compared with Krohn (1912) and Philippe Fleury’s Budé edition. The general structure is stable, but several points require caution: in I.4.1 moenia must be understood in relation to the urban enclosure, not merely the physical wall; spiritus bestiarum palustrium belongs to an ancient environmental explanation of disease and does not justify a microbiological reading; in I.4.2 lumina capere is architectural language for opening or arranging apertures for light; in I.4.5 στοιχεῖα denotes constituent principles or elements; and in I.4.10 the Cretan example contains a lacuna that should not be completed without editorial support. The notes consistently distinguish Latin reading, historical interpretation and modern reception. Historical and medical note — I.4. The chapter combines environmental observation, the theory of four principles, material analogies, animal feeding and sacrificial practices as criteria for a healthy site. Its historical value lies in showing how Vitruvius integrates the medicine, climatology and urban planning of his time; it should not be presented as anticipating contemporary epidemiology or environmental hygiene. Comparative apparatus — I.4. The siting of a city is organized around salubritas, exposure, moisture, marshes and climatic conditions. The critical text confirms “electio loci saluberrimi… excelsus et non nebulosus, non pruinosus… temperatas… palustris vicinitas”. The translation preserves this ancient environmental medicine without presenting it as contemporary epidemiology. Medical and historical note — Salubritas. Explanations of airs, bodies, humours and diseases belong to an ancient physiological framework. Where a topographical observation—drainage, moisture or insolation—can be compared with modern environmental criteria, that comparison is offered as technical reception, not as literal validation of Vitruvius’s aetiology. Textual note — Inspection of viscera. The use of sacrificed animals to assess the healthiness of pastures and waters is retained as an ancient practice described by Vitruvius. It is neither recast as a modern diagnostic method nor omitted because it lies outside present architectural practice. 307

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Chapter 5 Latin text 1.5.1 Cum ergo his rationibus erit salubritatis moenium conlocandorum explicatio regiones[que] electae fuerint fructibus ad alendam civitatem copiosae et viarum munitiones aut opportunitates fluminum seu per portus marinae subvectionis habuerit ad moenia comportationes expeditas, tunc turrium murorumque fundamenta sic sunt facienda uti fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videatur, crassitudine ampliore quam parietum qui supra terram sunt futuri, et ea impleantur quam solidissima structura. 1.5.1 When, therefore, the healthiness of the site for the walls has been secured on these principles, and a region has been chosen abounding in produce to feed the city, and the road network—or the advantage of a river, or the access of a sea-port—has provided ready means of transport to the walls, then the foundations of the towers and walls are to be laid in the following manner. Let them be dug down, if firm ground can be reached, to solid bottom and set within the solid, to a depth proportionate to the scale of the work, and made of a greater thickness than the walls that are to rise above the ground; and let the trenches be filled with the most solid masonry that can be laid. Academic translation 1.5.1 Once the sanitary viability of the site for the walls has been determined in accordance with these principles, and after choosing a territory abundant in crops to sustain the city; and provided that the road network, the advantages of the waterways, or maritime transport via ports offer expeditious routes for supplying the urban area, the construction of the foundations of the towers and walls will then proceed. These must be excavated — whenever possible — down to firm ground and embedded within it, penetrating to a depth that seems proportionate to the scale of the work; their thickness must be greater than that of the walls that will rise above ground level, and the trenches must be filled with a structure that is as solid and compact as possible. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I review of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 17-18. • Chapter 5: The old title is normalized to the contemporary scientific nomenclature 1.5.1 (Book I, Chapter 5, Paragraph 1) to give continuity to the critical apparatus of the manuscript. • fructibus ad alendam civitatem copiosae: The clause can be overlooked during transcription because of similar neighboring endings; any claim of a scribal omission must be established by collation. Vitruvius relates the healthfulness of the city’s location to the availability of fertile land and sufficient provisions for its inhabitants. • viarum munitiones / subvectiones expeditas: Second major omission from a literal version. It refers to transport infrastructure. Viarum munitiones does not mean defenses, but the "construction and paving of roads", while subvectiones refers to the logistical supply and import of goods via waterways or ports. • ad solidum et in solido: A fundamental technical term in Roman foundation engineering. Solidum designates the bedrock, the firm geological stratum, or the compact, non-clayey ground. Vitruvius requires two conditions: excavating until the firm stratum is reached (ad solidum) and laying the foundations within that stratum (in solido). A literal version incorrectly summarized this as "in the solid mass." • crassituine ampliare quam parietum: Classic structural principle. Underground foundations must have a greater thickness than the exterior walls (parietes) to correctly distribute axial loads and avoid collapses or differential settlements. 1.5.1 After ensuring the health of the site, agricultural supplies, and river, sea, or land communications, the foundations of towers and walls will be laid. Excavation must proceed down to solid rock (ad solidum) and deepen in proportion to the scale of the construction. The underground foundation will be thicker than the upper walls and will be filled with extremely compact masonry (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.1). 309

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Latin text 1.5.2 Item turres sunt proiciendae in exteriorem partem, uti cum ad murum hostis impetu velit adpropinquare, a turribus dextra ac sinistra lateribus apertis telis vulnerentur. Curandumque maxime videtur ut non facilis aditus sit ad oppugnandum murum, sed ita circumdandum ad loca praecipitia et excogitandum uti portarum itinera non sint directa sed scaeva. Namque cum ita factum fuerit, tum dextrum latus accedentibus quod scuto non erit tectum proximum erit muro. Conlocanda autem oppida sunt non quadrata nec procurrentibus angulis sed circinationibus, uti hostis ex pluribus locis conspiciatur. In quibus enim anguli procurrunt, difficiliter defenditur, quod angulus magis hostem tuetur quam civem. 1.5.2 Likewise, the towers must be projected beyond the outer face of the wall, so that when an enemy seeks to press an assault against it, he may be wounded by missiles from the towers on his right and left, his flanks lying exposed. Above all, care must be taken that there be no easy approach for storming the wall; rather, the ground about the towers should be so disposed that the way to the gates runs not straight but obliquely, bearing to the left. For when this is done, the right side of those advancing—the side not covered by the shield—will lie nearest the wall. Towns ought to be laid out not as a square, nor with projecting angles, but in a rounded circuit, so that the enemy may be observed from several points; for where angles project, defense is difficult, since the angle shields the enemy rather than the 123 townsman. Academic translation 1.5.2 Likewise, the towers should project outwards from the perimeter so that, when the enemy attempts to rush towards the wall, they are exposed on their left and right flanks and are wounded by projectiles launched from the towers. Similarly, every effort must be made to prevent easy access for assaulting the wall; on the contrary, the perimeter should be laid out taking advantage of steep terrain, and the access routes to the gates should be planned obliquely, not straight. When this is done, the right flank of the attackers — which is not 123 Scaeva describes an oblique or skewed approach. Vitruvius’s explanation presupposes a shield carried on the left arm: the attacker’s right side is more exposed as he approaches the wall. 310

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I covered by the shield — lies nearest the wall. Furthermore, the layout of cities should not be square or have sharp angles, but rather be arranged in continuous curved lines, so that the enemy can be spotted from multiple sides. In fact, where angles protrude, defense becomes extremely difficult, because the corner offers more protection to the attacker than to the citizen. Philological and Exegetical Apparatus 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.2. For the fixation of the tactical terms of Roman poliorcetics, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 18; and the philological review of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 18. • Lateribus apertis: In Roman military terminology, latera aperta refers to the "open" or unprotected flanks of a battle formation. The projecting arrangement of the towers allowed for a deadly crossfire that battered the flanks of the attacking troops. • itinera... non sint directa sed scaeva: A literal version erred in translating scaeva as "accident-ridden." Scaevus means "oblique," "deviated to the left," or "skewed." Vitruvius introduces here a classic rule of siege tactics: to force the enemy to approach by turning to the left. • erit tectum: A literal version suffered a notable lexical confusion by translating scuto (shield) as "roof" (tectum is here the participle of the verb tegere, to protect). Since Roman and Hellenistic soldiers carried the shield (scutum) on their left arm, the right flank was completely unprotected. If the route forced them to march with their right side exposed towards the wall, the defenders could easily shoot them with arrows. • circumitionibus: Not " Circles." Vitruvius does not demand perfectly circular cities, but rather layouts "in continuous curved lines" or organic shapes that follow the topography of the land, avoiding straight lines and corners that create blind spots. • angulus magis hostem tuetur quam civem: Geometric explanation of blind spots in fortifications. A salient angle (procurrentibus angulis) provides a sheltered space or " blind spot " where the attacker can take cover from projectiles falling from the top of adjacent walls. 311

Access routes to the gates should not be direct but oblique (scaeva), forcing attackers to expose their right flank, unprotected by a shield (scuto). Likewise, the city's layout should avoid projecting angles and adopt a continuous curved design (circumitionibus), preventing the enemy from exploiting blind spots at the corners for cover from the defenders (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.2). Latin text 1.5.3 Crassitudinem autem muri ita faciendam censeo uti armati homines supra obviam venientes alius alium sine inpeditione praeterire possint. dum in crassitudine perpetuae taleae oleagineae ustilatae quam creberrime instruantur, uti utraeque muri frontes inter se, quemadmodum fibulis, his taleis conligatae aeternam habeant firmitatem. Namque ei materiae nec caries nec tempestates nec vetustas potest nocere, sed ea et in terra obruta et in aqua conlocata permanet sine vitiis utilis sempiterno. Itaque non solum in muro sed etiam in substructionibus quique parietes murali crassitudine erunt faciundi hac ratione religati non cito vitiabuntur. 1.5.3 I hold that the thickness of the wall should be such that armed men meeting upon it can pass one another without hindrance; and within that thickness let continuous tie-beams of charred olive-wood be set as closely as possible, so that the two faces of the wall, bound together by these beams as if by clamps, may possess lasting strength. For no decay, no tempest, and no lapse of time can harm that material; rather, whether buried in the earth or set in water, it endures sound and serviceable for ever. And so, not only in the walls but also in the substructures, and in any partitions built to the thickness of a wall, whatever is bound together in this manner will not soon fall into decay. Indeed, this is a material that neither rot, nor inclement weather, nor the passage of time can damage; on the contrary, even when buried 312
