Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.3. For the textual fixation and readings of the manuscript regarding the compound term utilis sempiterno, see the critical edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 18-19; and Fritz Krohn's edition, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 18-19. • Armati homines... praeterire possint: Vitruvius defines the minimum thickness of the parapet or wall-walk not by means of abstract units of measurement (feet or cubits), but through a criterion of military logistical functionality. The ideal width must guarantee the free bidirectional and simultaneous flow of heavily armed sentries (armati) during a siege, avoiding tactical bottlenecks. • oleagineae ustilatae): The use of olive wood taleae (braces, crossbeams, or stakes) applied an empirical principle of structural strength. Vitruvius prescribed that the wood be singed or charred superficially (ustilatae). This thermal process removes the internal moisture from the wood and alters the organic compounds that attract wood-boring insects, acting as an ancient and effective method of waterproofing and biological preservation. • quemadmodum fibulis: In this context of construction engineering, the term fibula designates a clamp, connector, or locking key. Roman walls typically consisted of two outer faces of ashlar or masonry (frontes) filled internally with a core of loose stones and mortar (caementicium). Olive beams acted as transverse tensioners that tied both faces of the wall together, preventing the internal pressure of the fill from causing the structure to burst. • In earthly and underwater environments: Vitruvius praises the rot-resistant properties of olive wood treated with fire. Its resistance in underground and underwater environments made it ideal for substructures (retaining foundations or embankments), where constant humidity usually rotted other types of construction wood. 313

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I 1.5.3 The thickness of the parapet wall must allow the smooth passage of two armed soldiers. To ensure the cohesion of the structure, charred olive beams (taleae oleagineae ustilatae) must be inserted transversely to act as fasteners (fibulae) joining the two faces of the wall. Because fire-treated wood is immune to rot and moisture from the ground or water, this method of fastening guarantees the durability of both the defensive walls and the substructures (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.3). Critical Interlineation 1.5.4 Intervalla autem turrium ita sunt facienda ut ne longius sit alia ab alia sagittae missionis, uti si qua oppugnetur, tum a turribus quae erunt dextra sinistra scorpionibus reliquisque telorum missionibus hostes reiciantur. Etiamque contra interiores ⟨partes⟩ turrium dividendus est murus intervallis tam magnis quam erunt turres, ut itinera sint interioribus partibus turrium contignata, neque ea ferro fixa. Hostis enim si quam partem muri occupaverit, qui repugnabunt rescindent et si celeriter administraverint, non patientur reliquas partes turrium murique hostem penetrare, nisi se voluerit praecipitare. 1.5.4 The intervals between the towers should be so arranged that no one tower stands further from the next than a bowshot, so that if any point is besieged, the enemy may be driven off by scorpions and other missiles from the towers to right and left. Opposite the lower part of the towers the wall should likewise be interrupted by gaps as wide as the towers themselves, and the passages across these gaps, within the towers, should be floored with timber that is not fastened with iron. For should the enemy seize any part of the wall, the defenders will cut away these timbers; and if they act quickly, they will not suffer the enemy to penetrate the remaining towers and stretches of wall—unless he is willing to fling himself headlong. Academic translation 1.5.4 The intervals between the towers should be arranged so that the distance from one to another does not exceed the range of an arrow's shot; thus, if a section of the curtain wall is attacked, the enemy can be repelled from the towers to its right and left by the fire of scorpions and other ranged weapons. Likewise, the parapet of the wall, upon reaching the interior of the towers, should be interrupted by openings of a width equivalent to that of the towers themselves; 314

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I the passageways through these interior openings should be made of wooden platforms (contignata itinera) which should not be fixed with iron fittings. In this way, if the enemy manages to seize any section of the wall, the defenders can cut off the passage by quickly destroying the walkways; If they act swiftly, they will prevent the attacker from penetrating the remaining sections of the towers or the wall, unless he decides to throw himself into the void. Critical Notes 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.4. For the detailed study of the manuscript variants regarding ballistic machinery and Roman military carpentry (contignata), see Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 19; and Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 19. • Sagittae missionis / scorpionibus: Vitruvius subordinated the geometry of the urban perimeter to the effective range of Hellenistic and Roman torsion artillery. The scorpio (scorpion) was a light, precision catapult that launched iron bolts with a flat trajectory and lethal penetrating power. By spacing the towers closer than the range of a common arrow, it was ensured that any intermediate point along the curtain wall (curtina) was perfectly covered by the artillery flanks of the adjacent towers. • dividens est murus / intervallis tam magnis: The verb dividere here has the sense of "to interrupt" or "to fracture." Vitruvius prescribes a revolutionary structural solution for his time: the wall should not be a continuous passageway over which the enemy can run freely if they manage to scale a section. The wall walk should be physically interrupted at the internal access points that cross the towers. • itinera... contignata, neque ea ferro fixa: Demountable wooden walkways. Contignata refers to structures made of planks or formed by wooden beams joined in a simple way. The fundamental requirement that no nails or fastening hardware be used (neque ferro fixa) responds to a defensive tactic: to allow the planks to be removed or destroyed (rescindent) instantly. • qui repugnabunt rescindent: The verb rescindere implies a physical action of force: cutting, chopping, or dismantling. Vitruvius details the emergency protocol of the defending garrison (qui repugnabunt): by isolating the compromised section of wall through the removal of the timbers, the enemy 315

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I is trapped in a sealed sector, flanked by projectiles and with no other option than to retreat or jump into the ditch (nisi se voluerit praecipitare). 1.5.4 The distance between defensive towers should be defined according to the maximum range of an arrow, allowing light artillery or scorpions (scorpionibus) stationed on the flanks to repel the enemy. Furthermore, to prevent an attacker who has scaled the wall from progressing along the parapet, passage through the towers should be interrupted by movable wooden walkways without fixed fittings (neque ferro fixa). In case of assault, the defenders can quickly dismantle or destroy these planks (rescindent), isolating the enemy and halting their advance through the rest of the fortified complex (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.4). Latin text 1.5.5 Turres itaque rotundae aut polygonoe sunt faciendae. Quadratas enim machinae celerius dissipant, quod angulos arietes tundendo frangunt; in rotundationibus autem, uti cuneos ad centrum adigendo, laedere non possunt. Item munitiones muri turriumque aggeribus coniunctae maxime sunt tutiores, quod neque arietes neque suffossiones neque machinae ceterae eis valent nocere. 1.5.5 The towers, therefore, should be built round or polygonal; for siegeengines dismantle square towers the more readily, since the rams shatter the corners by their battering, whereas in rounded forms, driving the stones towards the center as if with wedges, they can do no harm. Likewise, fortifications of wall and towers joined with earthworks are by far the safest, since neither rams nor mining nor the other engines have power to injure them. 124 Academic translation 1.5.5 Consequently, towers should be built with a circular or polygonal plan. Indeed, siege engines destroy square towers more quickly because battering rams break the corners by repeatedly striking them; conversely, they fail to cause damage to circular structures, since the impacts are distributed towards the center of the curve in a manner similar to how voussoirs or wedges (cunei) act. Likewise, fortifications where the curtain walls and towers are reinforced by 124 The preference for circular or polygonal towers is explained within the siege technology known to Vitruvius, especially the impact of a battering ram on projecting corners. It is not a universal structural law. 316

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I earthworks (aggeres) are extremely secure, since neither battering rams, nor underground mining, nor any other siege engine can inflict any damage on them. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.5. For paleographic variants on the physical simile of the wedges (cuneos), see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 19; and the fixation of the text of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 19. • Vitruvius sets forth a fundamental rule of ancient siege warfare: the structural weakness of 90 ° angles against mechanical artillery and battering rams. A protruding corner concentrates the stresses of the impact and lacks adjacent lateral supports, which facilitates the collapse of squared masonry blocks. • uti cuneos ad centrum adigendo: An application of the physics of arches and vaults to vertical defense. Vitruvius argues that a cylindrical tower reacts to the impact of a battering ram like a horizontal relieving arch: striking the convex surface, the force is deflected and distributed radially towards the central axis (ad centrum), pressing the stones together like the voussoirs or wedges (cunei) of a vault, and so dissipating the kinetic energy of the enemy engine. • aggeribus coniunctae: The agger was a traditional defensive element of Roman military engineering, consisting of a massive earthen ramp or embankment supported against the inner face of the wall. By filling the interior space with compacted earth, the outer stone wall gained colossal inertia, absorbing the vibrations of battering ram blows without cracking. • Suffossiones: A technical term for underground mining or undermining work. It consisted of excavating tunnels beneath the foundations of the wall, temporarily shoring them up with wooden beams which were then set on fire to cause the wall to collapse under its own weight. The presence of a large earthen embankment (agger) discouraged these operations, as the massive weight of the structure caused the attackers' galleries to collapse before reaching the core of the fortification. 1.5.5 Fortified towers should have circular or polygonal plans, since square plans are vulnerable to battering rams that fracture their corners. In curved 317

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I structures, impacts dissipate radially towards the center of the construction in a manner identical to the pressure between the wedges (cunei) of an arch. The security of the perimeter is substantially increased if the walls are combined with earth embankments (aggeres), a hybrid system that neutralizes both artillery vibrations and underground mining tactics (suffossiones) (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.5). Critical Interlineation Explanatory note: round towers and the fracture of angles. Vitruvius’s preference for round or polygonal towers over square ones (1.5.5) rests on a structural and ballistic principle: the ram and the siege engines concentrate their blow upon the corners, where the masonry, lacking mass to distribute the impact, splinters and collapses quickly. On a curved surface, by contrast, the blocks are wedged towards the center and the blow is dispersed tangentially, so that the stone cannot easily be dislodged. The same reasoning—avoiding the weak point of the angle—recurs in the rounded circuit of the walls, which moreover removes the dead angles and allows the assailant to be watched from several flanks. 1.5.6 Sed non in omnibus locis est aggeris ratio facienda, nisi quibus extra murum ex alto loco plano pede accessus fuerit ad moenia oppugnanda. Itaque in eiusmodi locis primum fossae sunt faciendae latitudinibus et altitudinibus quam amplissimis, deinde fundamentum muri deprimendum est infra alveum fossae et id extruendum est ea crassitudine ut opus terrenum facile sustineatur. 1.5.6 A rampart, however, need not be raised in every place, but only where, outside the wall, there is level approach from higher ground for an assault upon it. In such places, first let ditches be dug as broad and deep as possible; then let the foundation of the wall be sunk within the bed of the ditch and built of such a thickness that it may readily bear the weight of the earthwork. Plano pede. “On level ground”, or “over accessible ground without a substantial change of level”. It describes the attacker’s access from outside; no precise topographical height relative to the wall top is established here. Academic translation 1.5.6 However, the use of the earthwork (agger) should not be implemented indiscriminately anywhere, but only in those locations where, outside the walls and from a rise in the terrain, access for assaulting the fortifications can be made 318

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I at ground level (plano pede). Therefore, in such locations, ditches should first be excavated with the greatest possible width and depth; next, the foundations of the wall should be deepened within the bed or channel of the ditch itself (intra alveum fossae), and the retaining wall should be erected with a thickness that is capable of easily counteracting the thrust of the mass of earth. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 2. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.6. For the fixation and interpretation of retaining wall engineering in antiquity, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 19-20; and Fritz Krohn's review, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 19-20. • Not in all places... except where: Vitruvius demonstrates his flexibility as an engineer by rejecting universal construction recipes. The internal embankment (agger) requires an enormous movement of earth and urban space; therefore, it is only justified if the external topography presents a plateau or hill that negates the advantage of the height of the wall itself. • plano pede: A Latin expression that literally means "on level ground" or "at ground level." It describes the tactical scenario in which an attacker, taking advantage of a natural elevation outside at the same level as the top of the wall, does not need to climb with ladders, but can charge in a straight horizontal line against the defenses. • Intra alveum fossae: The alveus is the channel, bed, or excavated bottom. Vitruvius prescribed that the foundations of the wall should not stop at the level of the surface of the ditch, but rather extend below the floor of the ditch itself. This prevented enemy sappers from undermining the base of the wall from inside the ditch by eroding the lower stones. • ut opus terrenum facile sustineatur: Vitruvius here formulates the primitive principles of earth retaining wall engineering. The inner face of the wall must act as a buttress capable of withstanding the active lateral thrust exerted by the large mass of earth accumulated in the agger, preventing failures due to overturning or sliding of the masonry. 1.5.6 The construction of an embankment (agger) is only necessary when the enemy has level access (plano pede) from an external elevation. In these vulnerable sectors, ditches of maximum dimensions must be excavated and the 319

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I foundations of the wall sunk directly below the bed of the ditch (intra alveum fossae). The thickness of this lower wall must be specifically dimensioned to resist the lateral thrust of the accumulated mass of earth (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.6). 3. Rowland and Howe, Vitruvius, 29. Latin text 1.5.7 Item interiore parte substructionis fundamentum distans ab exteriore introrsus amplo spatio, ita uti cohortes possint quemadmodum in acie instructae ad defendendum supra latitudinem aggeris consistere. Cum autem fundamenta ita distantia inter se fuerint constituta, tunc inter ea alia transversa, coniuncta exteriori et interiori fundamento, pectinatim disposita, quemadmodum serrae dentes solent esse, conlocentur. Cum enim sic erit factum, tunc ita oneris terreni magnitudo distributa in parvas partes neque universa pondere premens ⟨non⟩ poterit ulla ratione extrudere muri substructiones. 1.5.7 On the inner side of the substructure, likewise, let a further foundation be laid at a generous distance from the outer, so that cohorts may take their stand upon the breadth of the rampart, drawn up as if in line of battle to defend it. And when the two foundations have been set thus apart, let other foundations be laid between them, joining the outer to the inner and arranged comb-wise, after the manner of the teeth of a saw. For when this is done, the great mass of earth, distributed into small portions and no longer bearing down with its whole weight, will by no means be able to thrust out the substructures of the wall. Academic translation 1.5.7 Likewise, on the inner side of the substructure, a second foundation must be constructed, separated from the outer foundation towards the city center by a considerable distance, so that the military cohorts, deployed in battle formation (in acie instructae) for defense, can be stationed across the entire width of the embankment (agger). Once both foundations are in place at this distance from each other, other transverse walls must be interwoven between them to connect the outer and inner foundations, arranged in a comb-like pattern (pectinatim) resembling the teeth of a saw. When the work is carried out according to this design, the colossal magnitude of the earth pressure is fragmented and distributed in small sections; thus, by preventing the weight 320

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I from acting as a compact and uniform mass, the pressure will in no way be able to push outwards or destabilize the retaining walls of the rampart. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.7. For the geometric fixation of retaining walls with internal buttresses, see the critical edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 20; and Fritz Krohn's review, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 20. • cohorts... in acie instructae: Vitruvius links the geometric scale of the inner earthwork (agger) with the logistical needs of Roman military tactics. The width of the upper part of the structure is not calculated randomly, but to allow the operational deployment of entire cohorts in battle formation (acies). This ensured rapid maneuverability and rotation of fresh troops during a mass assault on the engaged sectors. • pectinatim disposita / serrae dentes: A famous passage from ancient structural engineering. Vitruvius describes the construction of internal transverse buttress walls arranged in parallel or "comb-like" (pectinatim), joining the exposed outer face of the wall with the internal retaining wall. The simile with the teeth of a saw (serrae dentes) visually illustrates how these perpendicular walls created independent structural cells or boxes. • Vitruvius empirically formulates the principle of the fragmentation of lateral earth pressures. By filling the spaces formed by the transverse walls with earth, the friction of the earth mass against the interior masonry walls reduces the overall active thrust. The mass no longer presses monolithically (neque universa pondere premens), but rather the weight is broken down and absorbed by the stone buttresses. • Extrudere muri substructiones: The verb extrudere denotes the action of pushing out, displacing, or bursting. In ancient soil mechanics, the main danger of large fills of clayey or humic soil was the failure of the retaining wall by overturning or basal sliding. The intricate network of double foundations and comb walls physically prevented this type of structural collapse. 1.5.7 To consolidate the embankment (agger), a second inner foundation will be erected at a distance that allows the tactical deployment of 321

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I military cohorts in battle formation (in acie instructae). Both foundations will be intertwined by perpendicular transverse walls in the shape of a comb (pectinatim), similar to the teeth of a saw. This structural solution fragments the active thrust of the earth fill into smaller sections, preventing the mass from exerting a hydrostatic or monolithic pressure capable of overturning or displacing (extrudere) the substructures of the fortification (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.7). Latin text 1.5.8 De ipso autem muro e qua materia struatur aut perficiatur, ideo non est praefiniendum, quod in omnibus locis quas optamus copias, eas non possumus habere. Sed ubi sunt saxa quadrata sive silex seu caementum aut coctus later sive crudus, his erit utendum. Non enim uti Babylone abundantes liquido bitumine pro calce et harena ex cocto latere factum habent murum, sic item possunt omnes regiones seu locorum proprietates habere tantas eiusdem generis utilitates, uti ex his comparationibus ad aeternitatem perfectus habeatur sine vitio murus. 1.5.8 As to the material of which the wall is to be built or finished, no fixed rule can be laid down, since we cannot everywhere command the resources we should wish. But wherever there are squared stones, or flint, or rubble, or fired or unfired brick, these are to be used. For not every region or locality can possess advantages of the same kind in such measure as Babylon, which, abounding in liquid bitumen in place of lime and sand, has its wall built of fired brick; yet from such resources as each affords, a wall may be made faultless and enduring for all time. Academic translation 1.5.8 As regards the material with which the wall itself is to be built and finished, it is not possible to establish a fixed rule, since we cannot always have the materials we would like available in every place. On the contrary, wherever there is regular ashlar (saxa quadrata), flint (silex), rubble (caementum), or brick — whether fired (coctus) or unfired (crudus) —they should be used. Indeed, not all regions or local ecosystems possess the extraordinary material advantages found, for example, in Babylon, where the abundance of liquid bitumen, used in place of lime and sand, made it possible to erect a wall of fired brick; therefore, it cannot be expected that by such analogies a perfect and imperishable wall can be achieved in every location. 322

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.5.8. For the textual tradition of the regional materials and the mention of the Babylonian walls, see Valentin Rose's edition, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 20; and Fritz Krohn's revision, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 20. • non est praefiniendum... copiae: Vitruvius here states the principle of material autarky or adaptation to the geological environment. The Roman architect and engineer should not impose an abstract theoretical design, but rather critically evaluate the resources of the quarry and the local deposits (copiae). The economy of transport in the ancient world made the large-scale importation of stone for perimeter fortifications unfeasible. • Saxa quadrata / flint / caementum: Typological classification of stone in Roman construction. Saxa quadrata are perfectly squared ashlar blocks with parallel faces, typical of monumental architecture. Flint refers to extremely hard stones, such as flint or basaltic volcanic rocks (frequently used in roads and foundations). Caementum designates rubble masonry, fragmented and irregular stones that were joined with mortar to form the core of the wall (opus caementicium). • coctus later sive crudus: Vitruvius equates the use of industrialized clay. Later crudus (adobe or sun-dried brick) remained common in domestic architecture and secondary walls of the Republican periphery, while later coctus (kiln-fired brick) represented maximum resistance to compression and humidity. • Babylon... liquid bitumen for lime: Historical mention of the Mesopotamian construction technique, also documented by Herodotus. Babylon lacked limestone quarries for making lime (calx) and suitable sand (harena), but it had natural outcrops of asphalt or bitumen from Hit. This viscous hydrocarbon acted as a fast-setting mortar and waterproofing agent with exceptional adhesion, fixing the courses of fired brick against river floods. Vitruvius classifies it as a fortunate geographical anomaly (locorum proprietates), inapplicable to the soil of the Italian peninsula. 1.5.8 It is not possible to prescribe a universal material for the construction of walls, since the suitable resources vary according to the region. The architect will 323

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I use the materials available in the surroundings, whether they be regular ashlar blocks (saxa quadrata), basalt or flint (silex), common masonry (caementum), or fired or unfired brick. The exceptional conditions of Babylon, where liquid bitumen (liquido bitumine) effectively replaced the traditional mixture of lime and sand, constitute a unique geographical advantage that cannot be demanded as a norm in other territories (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.5.8). Comparative critical apparatus — I.5. The chapter has been compared with Krohn and with the organization and commentary of Philippe Fleury’s Budé edition. In I.5.1 the modern critical text marks [erit] and [moenium conlocandorum explicatio] as problematic, and prints marinae subvectionis habuerit where other traditions and normalizations offer marinae subvectiones habuerint. In I.5.2 the readings scaeva and circumdandum/circundandum belong to the transmission and should not be reduced to mere spelling variants. In I.5.7 the simile pectinatim, quemadmodum serrae dentes describes the transverse bonding of the substructures: the comparison explains a constructional arrangement rather than a decorative motif. Architectural and military note — I.5. The prescriptions for projecting towers, oblique approaches, wall thicknesses, earthworks and cross-walls follow an ancient defensive logic. The edition avoids making them universal rules of fortification: Vitruvius reasons in terms of rams, missiles, shields, scorpions and the siege techniques of his historical setting. Comparative apparatus — I.5. Fortification requires foundations on firm ground, proportionate thicknesses, projecting towers and layouts that hinder a frontal assault. Agger, fossa, murus, turris, intervallum and emplecton are checked according to their constructional functions. The military recommendations are discussed historically rather than as contemporary instructions. Construction note — Walls and towers. The explanation for architects distinguishes foundations, wall mass, transverse bonding and tower position. Claims about the durability of materials are retained in their Roman context, rather than converted without evidence into present structural prescriptions. 324

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Chapter 6 Latin text 1.6.1 Moenibus circumdatis sequuntur intra murum arearum divisiones platearumque et angiportûm ad caeli regionem directiones. Dirigentur haec autem recte, si exclusi erunt ex angiportis venti prudenter. Qui si frigidi sunt, laedunt; si calidi, vitiant; si umidi, nocent. Quare vitandum videtur hoc vitium et avertendum ne fiat quod in multis civitatibus usu solet venire. Quemadmodum in insula Lesbo oppidum Mytilenae magnificenter est aedificatum et eleganter, sed positum non prudenter. In qua civitate Auster cum flat, homines aegrotant; cum Corus, tussiunt; cum Septentrio, restituuntur in salubritatem, sed in angiportis et plateis non possunt consistere propter vehementiam frigoris. 1.6.1 Once the walls have been built, there follow, within them, the apportionment of the building plots and the laying-out of the streets and lanes according to the quarters of the sky. These will be rightly directed if the winds are prudently excluded from the lanes; for if they are cold they are hurtful, if hot they enervate, if damp they are noxious. This fault, then, must be avoided, and care taken lest there befall what commonly happens in many cities. At Mytilene, for instance, in the island of Lesbos, the town is built with magnificence and elegance, but sited without prudence: in that city, when the south wind blows the people fall ill; when the north-west wind blows they cough; and when the north wind blows they are restored to health, yet cannot linger in the lanes and streets because of the sharpness of the cold. Critical textual note — I.6.1. This edition uses the normalized spelling sequuntur. Krohn (1912, 20, line 7) prints sequuntur in his text; Rose (1899, 22, line 5) prints secuntur. Both apparatuses report secuntur for H, identified as Harley MS 2767 in their lists of sigla. The Spanish note’s statement that Krohn prints secuntur in the running text is therefore corrected. The forms belong to sequor, third-person plural, and the difference is orthographic. The attribution to H is reported from these printed apparatuses, not from a new direct collation of the manuscript. Academic translation 1.6.1 Once the perimeter of the walls is completed, the parcelling of building plots (areae) and the alignment of the main streets (plateae) and alleyways (angiporta) within the enclosure will proceed according to the celestial 325

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I directions. This street layout will be correctly oriented only if the entry of winds into the alleyways is prevented by prudent design. Indeed, if the winds are cold, they cause illness; if they are warm, they pollute the atmosphere; and if they are humid, they are harmful. Therefore, this defect must be avoided, and care must be taken to prevent what often happens in many cities, such as Mytilene, a town on the island of Lesbos, which was built with magnificence and elegance but situated without foresight. In that city, when the Auster (south wind) blows, the inhabitants fall ill; When the Corus (north-west wind) blows, they suffer from coughs; and when the Septentrion (north wind) blows, they regain their health, although it is impossible for them to remain in the streets and alleys due to the vehemence of the cold. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.6.1. For the fixation of the spelling variants and the medical description of the climate in Lesvos, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 20-21; and Fritz Krohn's review, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 20-21. • Arearum divisiones platearumque et angiportorum: Vitruvius establishes the hierarchy of Roman urban planning (spatial units). The areae are the plots intended for dwellings or public buildings; the plateae are the main avenues, wide and for general traffic; the angiporta are the secondary alleys or narrower passages. The author subordinates the geometry of the entire urban network to a climatic factor: the aerodynamics of the wind. • ad caeli regionem directiones: The road layout is not drawn randomly or solely according to aesthetic criteria. It must be aligned with the "celestial regions" (the cardinal points and the solar paths), a principle that united surveying and astronomy to regulate lighting and air currents within the orthogonal grid. • Auster / Corus / Septentrio: Vitruvius applies the theory of classical medical winds. The Auster is the humid and warm south wind, associated in Hippocratic medicine with the dispersion of dense humours and fevers; the Corus (northwest wind) is dry and violent, causing inflammatory respiratory conditions (tussiunt); the Septentrio (north wind) purified the air of cities by 326

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I expelling miasmas, promoting health, but required architectural protection due to its extreme temperatures. • Mytilene... sed positum non prudenter: Vitruvius uses Mytilene (capital of Lesbos) as a technical counterexample. He acknowledges its formal and constructive values (magnificer... et eleganter), but criticizes its bioclimatic design flaw. By aligning the alleyways directly with the prevailing winds, the streets acted as wind tunnels or funnels that amplified the harshness of the local climate, harming health and the use of public space (non possunt constantere). 1.6.1 Once the walls were completed, the division of building plots (areae) and the layout of avenues (plateae) and alleyways (angiporta) should be oriented according to the regions of the sky to block the prevailing winds. Vitruvius warns about the physiological effects of the climate: hot winds corrupt and humid ones damage. Formally beautiful cities like Mytilene erred in aligning their streets with the winds, causing the South Wind (Auster) to cause illness and the north-west wind (Corus) respiratory ailments, demonstrating that urban aesthetics must be subordinated to environmental hygiene (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.6.1). Temperature in Vitruvian Latin is not the modern quantitative measurement, but the notion of climatic equilibrium and proportion. If the urban fabric slows down air currents, a protected microclimate is generated that optimizes bodily homeostasis. • Gravedo, arteriace...: Ancient symptomatology of respiratory ailments. Gravedo defines heavy nasal congestion or coryza; arteriace is a medical Hellenism that designates the inflammation of the arteria aspera (the trachea and bronchi, not the blood arteries); phthisis represents obstructive pulmonary consumption or tuberculosis; and sanguinis eectio is the expulsion of blood through the respiratory tract (hemoptysis). • Non detractionibus sed adiectionibus: A fundamental therapeutic concept of Galenic and Hippocratic medicine. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I ailments due to excess (plethora) or deficiency. Diseases requiring detractions (evacuations, bloodletting, or purges) were those caused by excess humours. In contrast, chronic pulmonary pathologies generated malnutrition and physical deterioration, thus requiring adiectiones: therapies of reconstitution, rest, warmth, and nutrition. • aer agitatus... detrahit sucum: Vitruvius offers a microclimatic explanation based on physical evaporation. The air agitated by the wind becomes thinner or more subtle (extenuatur) and acts by increasing the rate of perspiration and drying of the patient's mucous membranes. By stripping away the sucus (the bodily juices or fluids that maintained the flexibility and defense of the tissues), the wind accelerates the emaciation or malnutrition (exiliora) of the patients. • lenis et crassus aer: The paradox of "thick or dense air." While modern urban planning prioritizes constant ventilation, ancient science considered that still, warm, and dense (crassus) air inside sheltered alleyways acted as a physical balm for damaged lungs. Lacking turbulence (perflatus), this stable air provided an environmental rest that allowed the body to absorb nutrients and recover lost energy. 1.6.3 The exclusion of winds in urban design generates optimal thermal stability (temperature) for the recovery from chronic respiratory pathologies, such as catarrh (gravedo), bronchitis (arteriace), tuberculosis (phthisis), and hemoptysis. Since these diseases require restorative therapies (adictiones) rather than evacuation therapies, dynamic and agitated air is detrimental because it accelerates dehydration and loss of vital fluids (sucum) in the patient. Archaeological note — Bk. 1.6 (the winds and the Tower of the Winds). The layout of the city, Vitruvius says, must orient the streets by the winds: along the lines dividing the eight winds —Solanus (E), Auster (S), Favonius (W), Septentrio (N) and, at the corners, Eurus (SE), Africus (SW), Caurus or Corus (NW), and Aquilo (NE)— so that no street channels the wind against the houses. Against those who counted only four winds, Vitruvius praises those who recognized eight, and cites as a living witness Andronicus of Cyrrhus, who raised at Athens an octagonal marble tower with a figure of each wind on its face and, at the apex, a bronze Triton turning to point to the quarter from which the wind blew. This is the Tower of the Winds (Horologion) in the Roman Agora of Athens (c. 50 BCE), of Pentelic marble, with nine sundials and a water-clock within: one of the very few buildings of classical antiquity to survive almost intact —and one that links this chapter to the gnomonics of Book IX. Archaeological note — I.6.4. Vitruvius contrasts a division into four winds with one into eight, citing the octagonal tower of Andronicus of Cyrrhus at Athens, decorated with personifications of the winds and crowned, according to his description, by a bronze Triton that turned with the wind. The surviving monument confirms the octagonal plan and wind reliefs; the bronze weathervane does not survive. 1.6.4 Some have held that there are four winds: Solanus from the equinoctial east, Auster from the south, Favonius from the equinoctial west and Septentrio from the north. Those who investigated more carefully, however, stated that there are eight, notably Andronicus126 of Cyrrhus. As an example he erected an octagonal marble tower at Athens, with an image of each wind carved on the face corresponding to the direction from which it blows. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I • East/West Equinoctiali: Vitruvius uses Roman astronomical terminology to pinpoint the exact cardinal directions. The orient aequinoctiali (equinoctial east) and octenoctiali (equinoctial west) refer to the points on the horizon where the sun rises and sets during the spring and autumn equinoxes, as distinct from the solstitial points (summer and winter). The associated primordial winds are the Solanus (east wind) and the Favonius (the Greek zephyr, west wind). • Andronicus Cyrrestes: Andronicus of Cyrrhus (Syrian by origin), astronomer and mathematician of the 1st century BC. His tower in the Roman Agora of Athens combined a multiple sundial, an internal water clock (clepsydra) for cloudy days and the weathervane system described by Vitruvius, constituting a compendium of the sciences of astronomy and gnomonics of the time. • Imagines excalptas contra suos flatus: The eight friezes sculpted in bas-relief at the top of the tower are still preserved. Each wind deity is represented anthropomorphically and flying, carrying specific climatic attributes and oriented exactly towards the geographical direction from which its wind originates (e.g., Boreas in the north, Notus in the south). • metam marmoream: The meta refers to the conical or pyramidal shape that crowns the roof of the tower, constructed with interlocking Pentelic marble slabs. Its design imitated the meta of Roman circuses, serving as a solid and elevated base for the automaton's axis. • Tritonem aereum... indicem virgam: The description of this bronze Triton represents the first historical record of an automated anemoscope or weathervane. The mythological marine figure functioned under simple static and aerodynamic principles: as the air current acted upon the Triton's tail or folds, it rotated on a central pivot until it offered the least resistance to the wind, aligning its torso and the indicator rod (virga) towards the exact quadrant from which the wind originated, pointing to the sculpted deity that generated it. 1.6.4 In contrast to the traditional theory of the four cardinal winds, Vitruvius adopted the scientific system of eight winds proposed by Andronicus of Cyrrhus. As empirical proof, Andronicus erected an octagonal marble tower in Athens with the effigies of the Aeolian deities sculpted on its respective faces. The monument was crowned by a bronze Triton (Tritonem aereum) which, 334

(of inclination), since any difference in level would distort the symmetry of the solar shadows, distorting the geometric calculation of the north-south axis. • Gnomon / Skiatheras: A gnomon is a rigid vertical rod or stylus perpendicular to the horizontal plane. Vitruvius introduces the specialized term from Alexandrian science, skiatheras ("the one who catches the shadow"), highlighting the gnomon's status as an analog device for capturing astronomical and spatial data. • Antemeridiana circiter hora quinta: Vitruvius prescribes a specific time window for taking the first measurement. Since the Roman day was divided into 12 variable hours from sunrise to sunset, the fifth hour of the morning corresponds to the period immediately before noon (the solar zenith occurs exactly at the end of the sixth hour). During this time, the shadow of the gnomon is long and sharp enough to be indexed accurately, and its speed of movement allows for clear marking. • Circinus diductus / linea rotundationis: The method of concentric circles or equal shadows. By drawing a circle taking as the exact radius the length of the shadow of the fifth hour of the morning, Vitruvius generates a geometric control arc based on the astronomical principle that the 338

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I sun occupies symmetrical positions with respect to the local meridian before and after noon. Gnomon / σκιαθήρας. The gnomon is the vertical element that casts the shadow. Vitruvius explains its function through σκιαθήρας, “shadow tracker” or “shadow observer”. The note does not assign the term to a particular “Alexandrian science” without an additional source. Parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam. The procedure uses two shadows of equal length, one before and one after midday, to establish a reference line. The note avoids attributing to the text a trigonometrical formulation that Vitruvius does not express. • parem antemeridianae umbrae postmeridianam: The implicit trigonometric basis of the method. Throughout the day, the shadow of the gnomon describes a hyperbolic curve decreasing towards midday and increasing towards sunset. By intersecting the afternoon shadow with the morning circle, two vectors of equal length are obtained. The bisector of the angle formed by these two fixed points of shadow will invariably indicate the exact axis of midday (the true north-south line or astronomical meridian). 1.6.6 The layout of the road requires precisely leveling a horizontal surface (amussium) and installing a bronze stylus or gnomon (skiatheras) in its center. Around the fifth hour of the morning, the end of the shadow is marked with a point, and a circle is drawn using that distance as the radius. In the afternoon, when the shadow grows longer again and exactly intersects the drawn circle, a second point is marked, geometrically equating both solar longitudes (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.6.6). 3. Reliquae partes dextra ac sinistra tres et tres aequales his distribuendae sunt in tota rotundatione, ut aequales divisiones octo ventorum designatae sint in descriptione. Tum per angulos inter duas ventorum regiones et platearum et angiportorum videntur deberi dirigi descriptiones. 1.6.7 From the two shadow-marks draw intersecting arcs with the compasses. Through their intersection and the center draw a line to the circumference, establishing south and north. Take one-sixteenth of the entire circumference and, with the compasses centered where the meridian meets it, mark that distance on either side at both the southern and northern ends. Critical Notes (Explanation of the Vitruvius Text) • Eratosthenes of Cyrene... rationibus mathematicis: Vitruvius testifies to the geodetic method of Eratosthenes (c. 276 – 194 BCE). This consisted of simultaneously measuring the difference in the inclination of the sun's rays at midday during the summer solstice in two cities located on the same meridian: Syene (Aswan), where the sun reached its zenith and cast no shadow on the bottom of a well, and Alexandria, where, using the shadow of a gnomon (or scaphe), he determined an angle of inclination equivalent to 7.2 ° (one fiftieth of the total circumference of 360 °). Multiplying the physical distance between the two cities by 50, he obtained the global dimension of the planet. • ducentorum quinquaginta duum milium stadium: The figure of 252 000 stadia adopted by Vitruvius represents the practical correction attributed to Eratosthenes (or his successors) to make the number perfectly divisible by 360 ° from the division of the circle, assigning exactly 700 stades per geographical degree. Depending on the stadium module used (probably the Egyptian stadium of ≈ 157.5 m), the calculation yields a circumference of about 39 690 km, a value astonishingly close to modern satellite measurement (≈ 40 075 km). • quae fiunt passuum CCCXV milia: Conversion to the official metrological system of the Roman Empire. A double Roman step (passus) is equivalent to 5 feet (≈ 1.48 m). Since a standard stadium contained 125 double 346

The letters A–F serve solely to identify points in the graphic construction described by Vitruvius. A is the center; B and C are the ends of two equal shadows; D is the intersection of arcs drawn from B and C; E and F are the ends of the meridian line. The note does not project the cardo maximus, the groma or modern descriptive geometry on to the procedure. ◦ A: It is the origin of the system, the central vertex of the horizontal plane where the vertical gnomon is erected. ◦ B: Represents the shadow vector at the fifth hour of the morning. The distance AB defines the radius (r) of the control circle. ◦ C: This is the afternoon control point. The astronomical equality states that when the evening shadow measures exactly the same as the radius r, it intersects the perimeter at C. The segment BC delimits the chord of an arc symmetric with respect to midday. ◦ D: It is the point of the perpendicular bisector. By drawing two arcs with the compass of equal radius from B and C, their intersection (decussatio) generates the intermediate control point D. ◦ EF: This is the definitive meridian axis. By drawing the straight line that joins D with the center A and extending it to the perimeter, the diameter EF is obtained. The letter E will designate the South (Auster) and the letter F will indicate the North (Sepcentrio). This diameter is the mathematical basis upon which the Roman surveyor will lay out the groma to structure the cardo maximus of the new city. 1.6.12 Vitruvius concludes the urban planning guidelines by referring to two geometric diagrams (schemata) located at the end of the scroll (in extremo volumine), designed to illustrate the compass rose and the protective deviation of the streets. Item in septentrionali parte centrum circini ponendum in rotundationis et septentrionali linea, ubi est littera F, et signandum dextra ac sinistra, ubi sunt litterae I et K, et ab G ad K et ab H ad I per centrum lineae perducendae. Ita quod erit spatium ab G ad H, erit spatium venti austri et partis meridianae; item quod erit spatium ab I ad K, erit septentrionis. Reliquae partes dextra ter ac sinistra ter dividendae sunt aequaliter, quae sunt ad orientem, in quibus litterae L M, et ab occidente, in quibus sunt litterae N et O. Ab M ad O et ab L ad N perducendae sunt lineae decusatim. Et ita erunt aequaliter ventorum octo spatia in circumitione. Quae cum ita descripta erunt, in singulis angulis octagoni, cum a meridie incipiemus, inter eurum et austrum in angulo erit littera G, inter austrum et africum H, inter africum et favonium N, inter favonium et caurum O, inter caurum et septentrionem K, inter septentrionem et aquilonem I, inter aquilonem et solanum L, inter solanum et eurum M. Ita his confectis inter angulos octagoni gnomon ponatur, et ita dirigantur angiportorum divisiones. 1.6.13 Next, a sixteenth part of the whole circumference is to be taken with the compasses. Setting the compass-point on the meridian line where it meets the circle at the southern end, marked with the letter E, make two marks to right and left, where the letters G and H shall be placed; likewise, at the northern end, marked with the letter F, set the compass-point and make marks to right and left, where the letters I and K shall fall; then draw lines through the center, from G to K and from H to I. Thus the space from G to H will be the sector of the South wind (Auster) and the meridian quarter, and the space from I to K that of the North wind (Septentrio). The remaining parts—three on the right and three on the left—are to be divided equally: to the east, where the letters L and M stand; and to the west, where the letters N and O stand. From M to O and from L to N let lines be drawn through the center. Thus there will be eight equal spaces for the winds around the circumference. When the diagram is so drawn, 354

Rose (1899, 29–30) and Krohn (1912, 25–26) print G–H in the southern sector and I–K in the northern sector; both retain lineae decussatim for M–O and L–N, and the final phrase gnomon ponatur. Academic translation 1.6.13 Next, a measurement equal to one sixteenth of the total perimeter of the circumference will be taken with the compass. Placing the point of the compass on the meridian line, just where it intersects the circle at the southern end — marked with the letter E —, two marks will be made to the right and left, where the letters G and H will be placed respectively. Similarly, at the northernmost point — marked with the letter F — the compass point will be placed, and marks will be made to the right and left where the letters I and K will be located. Following this, straight lines will be drawn passing through the center: one from G to K and another from H to I. In this way, the space between G and H will constitute the sector assigned to the Austro (South) wind, and the space between I and K will correspond to the Septentrio (North). The remaining areas — three to the right and three to the left — will be divided into equal parts: to the east, the points with the letters L and M will be marked, and to the west, the letters N and O. Then, straight lines will be drawn crossing the center from M to O and from L to N. Thus, the circumference will be divided symmetrically into the eight spaces corresponding to the winds. Once this diagram is drawn, if we start from the south, the vertices of the regular octagon will be defined as follows: the letter G will be at the angle between the Euro and the Austro; the letter H between the Austro and the Africo; the letter N between the Africo and 355

Methodological note — Winds and street layout. The chapter does not provide a modern meteorological wind rose. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Chapter 7 1.7.1 Divisis angiportis et plateis constitutis arearum electio ad opportunitatem et usum communem civitatis est explicanda aedibus sacris, foro reliquisque locis communibus. Et si erunt moenia secundum mare, area ubi forum constituatur eligenda proxime portum, sin autem mediterraneo, in oppido medio. Aedibus vero sacris, quorum deorum maxime in tutela civitas videtur esse, et Iovi et Iunoni et Minervae in excelsissimo loco unde moenium maxima pars conspiciatur areae distribuantur. Mercurio autem in foro, aut etiam ut Isidi et Serapi in emporio, Apollini Patrique Libero secundum theatrum, Herculi in quibus civitatibus non sunt gymnasia neque amphitheatra ad circum, Marti extra urbem sed ad campum, itemque Veneri ad portum. Id autem etiam Etruscis haruspicibus disciplinarum scripturis ita est dedicatum: extra murum Veneris, Volcani, Martis fana ideo conlocari uti non insuescat in urbe adulescentibus seu matribus familiarum veneria libido, Volcanique vi e moenibus religionibus et sacrificiis evocata ab timore incendiorum aedificia videantur liberari. Martis vero divinitas cum sit extra moenia dedicata, non erit inter cives armigera dissensio, sed ab hostibus ea defensa belli periculo conservabit. 1.7.1 Once the lanes and streets have been laid out, sites must be chosen for sacred temples, the forum and other public places, with regard to the city’s convenience and common use. In a coastal town the forum should be near the harbour; in an inland town, at its center. Temples of the gods under whose special protection the city stands, such as Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, should occupy the highest place, from which most of the walls can be seen. Mercury’s temple belongs in the forum or trading center, as do those of Isis and Serapis; Apollo’s and Father Liber’s near the theater; Hercules’s near the circus in towns without gymnasia or amphitheatres; Mars’s outside the city beside the exercise ground; and Venus’s likewise near the harbour. Etruscan haruspical writings prescribe that the shrines of Venus, Vulcan and Mars stand outside the walls, so that erotic passion does not become habitual among the young and the matrons, and so that Vulcan’s power, summoned beyond the walls through rites and sacrifices, appears to free buildings from fear of fire. Mars’s divinity, consecrated 359

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I outside the walls, is to prevent armed discord among the citizens and defend the city from its enemies.131 1. haruspicibus disciplinarum scripturis: Refers to the Etruscan Disciplina, the set of ritual and sacred books (such as the Libri Rituales and Acherontici) that regulated the founding of cities (ritus etruscus) and which the Romans adopted as a pillar of their sacred urbanism. Academic translation 1.7.1 Once the alleyways have been divided and the main avenues established, the allocation of building plots (areae) intended for the convenience and common use of the citizenry must proceed: the sacred temples, the forum, and the remaining public spaces. If the walls are situated by the sea, the plot for the forum should be chosen in the vicinity of the port; if, on the contrary, the city is located inland, the forum will be situated in the very center of the urban area. For the sacred temples of those gods under whose principal protection the city appears to be placed — such as Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva — plots will be distributed in the highest place (in excelsissimo loco), from where most of the perimeter of the walls can be seen. In contrast, the temple of Mercury was located in the forum or the market (emporium), as were those of Isis and Serapis; the temple of Apollo and that of Father Liberus (Bacchus), next to the theater; the temple of Hercules, in those cities lacking gymnasiums or amphitheaters, in the vicinity of the circus; the temple of Mars, outside the city but next to the training ground (campus); and likewise the temple of Venus, near the port. This arrangement is similarly prescribed in the texts containing the discipline of the Etruscan haruspices: the sanctuaries (fana) of Venus, Vulcan, and Mars must be erected outside the city walls so that neither young men nor mothers become accustomed to sexual lust within the city. Likewise, by banishing Vulcan's destructive power from the city walls through rituals and sacrifices, public buildings appear to be freed from the fear of fire. Finally, by consecrating the divinity of Mars outside the walls, armed conflicts among the citizens are prevented, protecting the community and preserving it from the dangers of war against external enemies. 131 Vitruvius presents the reasons for placing the temples of Venus, Vulcan and Mars outside the walls as prescriptions of the discipline of the Etruscan haruspices. They should be read as ancient religious rationalizations rather than secular zoning criteria. 360

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 2. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.7.1. For the study of zoning and the analysis of the ritus etruscus in the foundation of Roman settlements, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 26-28; and Fritz Krohn's review, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 26-28. • electio arearum / foro... proxime portum: Vitruvius applies a functional and typological criterion for the distribution of space (areae). The forum (forum) is the economic, legal, and political center. In a maritime colony, its position must correspond to the logistics of overseas trade (proxime portum), connecting the port with the road axis. In continental cities (mediterranea), the geometry of the military model is applied: the forum occupies the intersection of the cardo and the decumanus, in the geographical heart of the settlement (ino oppido medio). • Iovi et Iunoni et Minervae in excelsissimo loco: This is the urbanistic translation of the model of the Capitoline Triad of Rome. The main temple, dedicated to the state cult, must preside over the city from the acropolis or the highest topographical point (excelsissimus locus). This position not only corresponds to a theological hierarchy, but also to a defensive-visual function: the gods act as sentinels guarding the curtain of the walls (moenium maxima pars conspiciatur). • Theological - Functional Zoning: Vitruvius details a sacred geography where the function of the god coincides with the socio-economic nature of the neighborhood: ◦ Mercury, Isis and Serapis: Gods of commerce and navigation, located where money and merchandise flow (in foro aut in emporio). ◦ Apollo and Father Liberus: Deities linked to the lyric arts, music, drama and wine, assigned to the leisure district, adjacent to the theater structure. ◦ Hercules: Patron of physical strength and athletic effort, linked to the circus due to a lack of traditional Greek infrastructure (gymnasia). • Etruscis haruspicibus... extra murum: Vitruvius justifies zoning restrictions through Etruscan tradition, the legal and religious framework that conditioned Roman urban planning. The haruspices segregated three specific 361

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I deities from the inner sacred space (the pomerium) for reasons of social hygiene, civil security, and collective psychology. • Veneris, Volcani, Martis fana: ◦ Venus: By placing her cult outside the walls (generally linked to the port or marginal areas), the State sought to mitigate prostitution and preserve the morality of young people and matrons (matres familiarum), containing erotic passions on the periphery. ◦ Vulcan: A pragmatic risk prevention measure. By ritually expelling the power of destructive fire (Volcani vi) from the high-density construction of the timber and masonry neighborhoods, the city was protected from catastrophic fires (timore incendiorum). ◦ Mars: The god of war must reside in the Campus Martius, the outdoor military training ground. Keeping the worship of weapons outside the domestic walls psychologically avoided internal violence, civil war, or coups d'état (armigera dissensio), projecting martial aggression exclusively towards the foreign enemy (ab hostibus ea defensa). 1.7.1 Once the road network was delimited, Vitruvius established the zoning of public plots (areae), combining commercial functionality with the Etruscan sacred tradition. While the forum was located at the port or the city center according to its geography, the Capitoline Triad (Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva) had to crown the highest point of the terrain for purposes of representation and surveillance. The sanctuaries of Mercury, Apollo, and Hercules were integrated into their respective economic and leisure districts. Conversely, following the writings of the haruspices, the temples of Venus, Vulcan, and Mars were segregated outside the city walls; This territorial planning policy sought to safeguard public morality, avert the danger of urban fires, and channel military force exclusively towards external defense against the enemy (Vitruvius, De architectura 1.7.1). 3. Item Cereri extra urbem loco, quo ⟨non quolibet⟩ nomine semper homines nisi per sacrificium necesse habeant adire; cum religione, caste sanctisque moribus is locus debet tueri. Ceterisque diis ad sacrificiorum rationes aptae templis areae sunt distribuendae. De ipsis autem aedibus sacris faciundis et de earum symmetriis in tertio et quarto volumine reddam rationes, quia in secundo visum est mihi primum de materiae copiis, quae in aedificiis sunt parandae, quibus sint virtutibus et quem habeant usum, exponere, ⟨deinde⟩ commensus aedificiorum et ordines et genera singula symmetriarum peragere et in singulis voluminibus explicare. 1.7.2 Likewise, Ceres is to have a site outside the city, in a place to which people need not go for any ordinary reason, but only for sacrifice. That place must be maintained with religion, chastity and holy customs. Suitable sites for the temples of the other gods are to be assigned according to the requirements of their sacrifices. I shall explain the construction of the sacred temples themselves and their systems of symmetria in the third and fourth volumes. In the second, I have thought it appropriate first to set out the supplies of materials to be prepared for building, their qualities and their uses; afterwards I shall examine the commensurations of buildings, the orders and each type of symmetria, explaining them in their respective volumes. Primum / deinde] These adverbs articulate the program: materials are treated first in Book II, followed by dimensions and orders in Books III and IV. The Spanish edition and Krohn mark <deinde> as an editorial supplement. The reading imum is not attributed to a particular manuscript without documentary support. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 1.7.2. For the text and its program of materials, temple building and symmetria, compare Rose (1899), 30, and Krohn (1912), 26. The passage itself does not identify particular agrarian mysteries as the reason for the sanctuary’s location. • Cereri extra urbem loco… Vitruvius prescribes a sanctuary outside the walls and requires the place to be maintained religiously, with purity and holy customs. The text does not mention the Eleusinian Mysteries, the 363

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER I Thesmophoria or an explicit requirement of ritual secrecy here; those associations are not presented as the direct cause of its location. • Ad sacrificiorum rationes. Sites for the other temples must suit the requirements of their sacrifices. Vitruvius does not develop here a typology automatically assigning chthonic deities to pits, celestial deities to heights, or large-scale sacrifices to broad open spaces. • De materiae copiis... quibus sint virtutibus: Justification of the plan of the work. Before addressing the aesthetics of the architectural orders, Vitruvius adopts a strictly constructive and engineering approach. He maintains that it is useless to design ideal beauty if the architect is ignorant of the physics, resistance, and behavior of the raw materials. Book II will therefore become a treatise on the science of materials (analysis of sand, lime, stone, pozzolanic cement, and wood). • commensus... et genera singula symmetriarum: Introduction to the architectural theory of the following books. The term commensus translates the Greek concept of proportional symmetry (the modular metric correspondence between individual elements and the whole of the work). Vitruvius anticipates the structure of Books III and IV, dedicated entirely to the typology of religious temples and the codification of the classical orders (Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian), thereby closing the general introductory framework of the discipline. 1.7.2 Vitruvius concludes the arrangement of sacred sites by placing the sanctuary of Ceres outside the city and requiring its place to be preserved religiously, with purity and holy customs. The passage does not state that secrecy in the mysteries is the reason for the site. Other temple plots must suit their sacrificial requirements. Finally, the author sets out the treatise’s program: materials and their properties are treated first in Book II; the dimensions, orders and different systems of symmetria follow in Books III and IV. Textual note — I.7.2. Krohn’s text (1912) is followed: quo ⟨non quolibet⟩ nomine semper homines…; cum religione…; and de earum symmetriis, with ⟨deinde⟩ as an editorial supplement. Rose (1899) prints a different text here— quo non omnes semper homines…; cum religiose…. The difference is recorded because it affects the wording, although it does not alter the passage’s general meaning. 364

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER I 4. Rowland and Howe, Vitruvius, 32. Comparative critical apparatus — I.7. Krohn prints sin autem mediterraneo in I.7.1, while other critical texts give mediterranea; both reflect an unstable area of transmission. In I.7.2 the difference is more substantial: Krohn reconstructs quo <non quolibet> nomine semper… cum religione…, whereas Rose and other texts print quo non omnes semper homines… cum religiose…. This edition keeps the difference visible because it affects the syntax of the prescription concerning Ceres. <Deinde> is also retained as an editorial supplement in the final program for the following books. Historical and religious note — I.7. The distribution of sanctuaries should not be confused with a modern zoning ordinance. Vitruvius combines civic convenience, visibility, proximity to particular public spaces and religious rationalizations attributed to the Etruscan discipline. The commentary distinguishes the text’s assertions from later reconstructions of Roman religious urbanism. Comparative apparatus — I.7. Forum, portus, aedes sacrae and loci communes are distributed according to the city’s position and use. The locations assigned to Venus, Vulcan, Mars, Jupiter, Juno and Minerva are retained as religious and urban rationalizations transmitted by Vitruvius; they are not universalised as rules of Roman urban planning. Synthesis for architects — Book I. The sequence moves from the education of the architectus to the definition of the discipline and then to the urban scale: choice of site, fortification, street orientation and the distribution of public and religious spaces. Modern technical interpretation is offered as comparison, never as a substitute for the ancient reasoning. The Preface to Book Two (II.Pr.1), one of the most famous literary and anecdotal passages in Vitruvius's work. It recounts the audacious stratagem of the Macedonian architect Dinocrates to attract the attention of Alexander the Great, by presenting himself before the royal court disguised as the mythological hero Hercules. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II ARGUMENTUM LIBRI II — On the origin of architecture and civil life, and on building materials: brick, sand, lime, pozzolana, quarry stone, wall patterns (reticulatum, incertum, isódomon, pseudisódomon, émplecton) and woods, with their virtues and defects according to the proportion of natural elements. Notice. — Book II turns from theory to matter. After an anthropological preface on the origins of building — the primitive hut, society born around fire — it treats the materials of construction: brick, sand, lime, the volcanic pozzolana that sets under water, stone and quarries, the methods of walling (opus reticulatum, incertum, the Greek emplekton) and timber. It is the foundational ancient source for Roman building technology, and modern materials science has confirmed much of its account of lime and pozzolanic mortar. II.Pr.1 Dinocrates architectus cogitationibus et sollertia fretus, cum Alexander rerum potiretur, profectus est e Macedonia ad exercitum regiae cupidus commendationis. Is e patria a propinquis et amicis tulit ad primos ordines et purpuratos litteras ut aditus haberet faciliores, ab eisque exceptus humane petît uti quamprimum ad Alexandrum perduceretur. Cum polliciti essent, tardiores fuerunt idoneum tempus expectantes. Itaque Dinocrates ab his se existimans ludi ab se petît praesidium. Fuerat enim amplissima statura, facie grata, forma dignitateque summa. His igitur naturae muneribus confisus vestimenta posuit in hospitio et oleo corpus perunxit caputque coronavit populea fronde, laevum umerum pelle leonina texit, dextraque clavam tenens incessit contra tribunal regis ius dicentis. 366

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II II.Pr.1 Dinocrates132 the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly, and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they promised to do so, they delayed while waiting for a suitable occasion. Thinking that they were making a fool of him, Dinocrates sought a resource within himself. He was very tall, with a pleasing face and an impressive, dignified physique. Trusting in these natural gifts, he left his clothes at the inn, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, draped a lion’s skin over his left shoulder and, holding a club in his right hand, advanced towards the tribunal where the king was administering justice. 1. Dinocrates: Name of the celebrated Hellenistic architect and urban planner of the late 4th century BC, the architect of Alexandria's urban plan. In other ancient sources (such as Plutarch or Strabo) his name appears spelled with phonetic variants such as Deinocrates, Stasicrates, or Cheiromocrates. — 2. purpuratos: Technical term from the Macedonian court and the Hellenistic kingdoms (philoi or diadochos) that designated the high dignitaries, ministers, and generals of the king's utmost confidence, who possessed the privilege of wearing robes dyed royal purple. The popular medieval translation confused the adjective with "purple-colored letters." — 3. ab se: Philological emendation of the main manuscript tradition. The expression indicates that Dinocrates, seeing the mediation of the courtiers thwarted, decided to rely on his own means and initiative, resorting to his own person as his only shield or "protection " (praesidium). 132 Dinocrates (Δεινοκράτης; transmitted forms Dinocrates and Deinochares) was a Greek architect contemporary with Alexander the Great. Vitruvius devotes the preface to Book II (2.pref.1–4) to him, recounting how he presented himself to the king and proposed carving Mount Athos into a colossal statue, with a city in its left hand and, in its right, a basin collecting the mountain’s waters and discharging them into the sea. Alexander rejected the project after asking about land capable of feeding the city, but retained its author. Tradition attributes to Dinocrates the plan of Alexandria, founded in 331 BC, and its orthogonal Hippodamian layout. His identification with the Chirocrates mentioned by Strabo remains disputed, as do the attribution of Hephaestion’s funeral pyre at Babylon and of work on the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. In Vitruvius the episode serves an argumentative purpose: it contrasts princely favor with professional competence alone and introduces the author’s vindication of his own position. 367

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II Academic translation II.Pr.1 The architect Dinocrates, fully confident in his ideas and skill, set out from Macedonia for the army's military camp in the days when Alexander had gained absolute dominion over the world, eager to obtain royal patronage and recommendation. From his homeland, he brought letters of recommendation signed by his relatives and friends, addressed to the leading officers and high court dignitaries (purpurati), in order to facilitate his access to the sovereign. Having been received by them courteously, he begged them to present him to Alexander as soon as possible; however, although they promised to do so, they were indolent and dilatory, waiting for a moment they deemed opportune. Therefore, Dinocrates, suspecting that these officers were making a mockery of him, decided to take matters into his own hands. Since he possessed an imposing stature, a graceful face, and a presence of extraordinary beauty and dignity, trusting in these gifts of nature, he stripped off his clothes at the inn, anointed his entire body with oil, crowned his head with poplar fronds, covered his left shoulder with a lion skin, and, wielding a mace in his right hand, advanced with a firm step directly to the tribunal where the king dispensed justice. For the philological study of biographical anecdotes in Hellenistic and Roman technical literature, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 29; and the textual fixation of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 29. • cum Alexander rerum potiretur: Historical and political setting. The expression rerum potiri (to exercise absolute power) places the action at the height of Alexander the Great's campaigns in the East (c. 332–331 BCE). Vitruvius uses this prologue not only as an entertaining element, but as a metaphor for patronage and the relationship between absolute political power and the design of state architecture. • primos ordines et purpuratos / ludi: An indirect Vitruvian critique of court bureaucracy. The text describes the subtle mechanisms of exclusion at the Macedonian court, where ordinary diplomatic channels (letters of recommendation from the purpurati) often stalled in empty promises. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II that he was being manipulated (ludi), Dinocrates breaks official protocol with a visually striking action. • naturae muneribus confisus / oleo corpus perunxit: Vitruvius highlights the athletic physique of the Macedonian architect. By anointing himself with oil (oleo perunxit), Dinocrates adopts the aesthetic and heroic practices of the athletes of the Greek gymnasiums, highlighting his musculature under the sunlight to impress the audience and Alexander himself, who was a fervent admirer of classical physical beauty. • populea fronde / pelle leonina / clavam tenens: Analysis of the iconographic staging (Theatrical Performance). Dinocrates does not disguise himself arbitrarily; he executes a careful visual assimilation with Hercules (Heracles), the quintessential civilizing hero. The elements are unequivocal sacred attributes: the Nemean lion skin (pelle leonina) used as a cloak, the club (clava), and the crown of white poplar leaves (populea frons), a tree consecrated to Hercules after his descent into the Underworld. • Contra tribunal regis ius dicentis: The climax of political audacity. Dinocrates interrupts the monarch's most sacred and solemn public act: the administration of justice (ius dicere). By bursting into the forum or military camp with the appearance of a living mythological hero, he unsettles the royal security and inevitably forces Alexander's direct attention, breaking through the filter of secretaries and generals. II.Pr.1 Vitruvius opens his second book with the famous image of Dinocrates of Macedon, an architect who, faced with the indolence and delaying tactics of the royal courtiers (purpurati) in presenting him to Alexander the Great, opted for a bold strategy of visual self-promotion. Using his imposing physique, Dinocrates burst into the public court where the monarch dispensed justice (ius dicentis), naked, anointed with oil, and adorned with Herculean attributes — the lion skin, the mace, and the poplar crown — breaking court protocol to force the conqueror's direct patronage (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.Pr.1). 5. The term novitas (the eccentricity or strangeness of the spectacle) breaks the monotony of the royal court. In Greco-Roman culture, attracting the attention of the crowd (populus) was the indispensable first step to capture the interest of the monarch, who operated under the gaze of the public. • Cogitationes et formas: Vitruvius employs a key conceptual binomial in his own architectural theory. Cogitationes represent the theoretical ideas or mental conception of the design, while forms refer to the models, plans, or tangible perspective representations that the architect brought with him to visually persuade the king. • Athon montem in statuae virilis figuram: The Mount Athos project constitutes the first major documented example of anthropomorphic architecture on a territorial scale, or land art, in antiquity. Dinocrates proposed sculpting a mountain over 2000 meters high to mold the figure of Alexander himself (implicitly assimilated to Hercules, reinforcing the disguise with which he presented himself). • manu laeva moenia... dextra pateram: The iconographic distribution of the macrostatue follows the conventions of Greek divine and heroic statuary: ◦ Left hand (The city): Holds the walls of a great city (civitatis amplissimae moenia). This image symbolizes the sovereign as ecumenical founder, protector and physical container of civilization over untamed nature. ◦ Right hand (The patera): Holds a ceremonial bowl or libation dish (patera). The technical function of this piece is to act as a gigantic dam or collection vessel that unifies the mountain's hydrographic basins (omnium fluminum... aquam). By channeling the water and artistically directing it towards the sea, the monarch is presented not only as a conqueror of peoples, but as an organizer of the forces of nature and the hydrological cycle. 371
