THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II (subvectiones) exposed a Hellenistic city to disaster in the event of naval blockades during wars, seasonal storms, or crop failures in exporting regions. This logistical vulnerability renders the site unsuitable (locum inprobandum), however dazzling the architectural proposal. • Ut enim natus infans sine nutricis lacte...: Analysis of the Physiological - Urban Metaphor. Vitruvius resorts to a medical and biological analogy of Aristotelian origin: the city as a living organism. The agricultural territory (agri) is equivalent to the nurse (nutrix), and the food that flows into the interior of the walls (fructibus in moenibus afÒuentibus) is the mother's milk (lac). Without this constant vital flow, the organic development of the city comes to a sudden halt, preventing the population from growing (frequently habere). • formationem probandam... teque volo esse mecum: The lucidity of Alexander's patronage. The king demonstrates the ability to separate the architect's technical talent from the geographical infeasibility of his initial project. By retaining Dinocrates in his service (quod tua opera sum usurus), Alexander secures for his court a brilliant designer with large-scale thinking, to whom he will later entrust a task where formal genius and ideal geographical conditions will coincide: the founding of Alexandria in Egypt. II.Pr.3 The outcome of the meeting between the monarch and the architect offers a lesson in economic geography and territorial pragmatism. Despite being fascinated by the aesthetics of the colossus of Mount Athos, Alexander the Great rejected the project due to the absence of a peripheral agricultural territory capable of guaranteeing the sustenance of the population (frumentaria ratio). Through an organicist metaphor that compares dependence on external grain to an infant deprived of its nurse's nourishment, the sovereign sanctions the unviability of colonies exclusively dependent on unstable maritime supply lines (transmarinis subvectionibus), although he does incorporate Dinocrates into his entourage of state engineers (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.Pr.3). There, when Alexander had observed a naturally safe harbor, an excellent emporium, corn fields around the whole of Egypt, and the great benefits of the immense river Nile, he ordered him to found the city of Alexandria in his own name. Thus Dinocrates, commended by his face and dignity of body, attained that nobility. But to me, emperor, nature has not given stature, age has disfigured my face, and illness has sapped my strength. Therefore, since I am deserted by these protections, I hope to attain commendation through the aids of science and writings. 1. Alexandriam constituere: Refers to the founding of Alexandria in the Nile Delta (c. 331 BCE). Historiography confirms that Dinocrates of Macedon acted as the director of the urban layout and chief engineer (architectus) of the new city, applying a rigorous orthogonal or Hippodamian plan. — 2. imperator: Political vocative addressed directly to Caesar Augustus. Vitruvius uses this military and civil title to appeal directly to the axis of imperial power in Rome, establishing an implicit parallel between the Alexander - Dinocrates and Augustus-Vitruvius relationship. — 3. praesidiis: Military metaphor. Vitruvius defines physical attributes (beauty, youth, strength) as bodily "defenses" or "protections" that open doors at court. Finding himself deprived of them by the passage of time, he transfers the concept of praesidium to the realm of intellectual and scientific production. Academic translation II.Pr.4 From that meeting onward, Dinocrates never left the monarch's side and accompanied him on his expedition to Egypt. There, when Alexander observed a port protected by nature itself, a commercial center (emporium) with unbeatable conditions, cultivated plains that extended throughout Egypt capable of ensuring the supply of wheat, and the immense logistical advantages offered by the mighty Nile River, he ordered him to found and lay out the city 376

It was in this way that Dinocrates, having won royal favor thanks to the grace of his face and the imposing dignity of his physical presence, achieved such high renown and noble esteem. As for me, Emperor, nature did not endow me with great stature; Old age has disfigured my face, and illness has diminished my physical strength. Consequently, finding myself without those physical credentials, I trust that I can gain your recognition and recommendation by relying on the aid of science and my architectural writings. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 4. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 2.Pr.4. For the study of the urban planning of Alexandria in Egypt and the author's self-representation strategies in relation to Augustus, see Valentin Rose's edition, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 30-31; and Fritz Krohn's fixation of the Latin text, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 30- 31. • portum naturaliter tutum / emporium egregium: Vitruvius summarizes the geostrategic reasons that made Alexandria the metropolis of the eastern Mediterranean. Unlike the unfeasible project of Mount Athos (analyzed in II.Pr.3), the Egyptian site met the optimal conditions of urban science: natural naval protection against the island of Pharos, commercial connectivity (emporium) and an inexhaustible agricultural basin fed by the silt of the Nile. • Fields... grain fields / Nile great utilities: The Nile Delta represented the great granary of the ancient world. By combining unlimited agricultural production with the Nile's river infrastructure (which allowed grain to be transported from the interior of Egypt to the ships in the port), Alexander solved the equation he had posed to Dinocrates: the perfect reconciliation between frumentaria ratio (food sovereignty) and the monumental projection of political power. • a facie dignitateque corporis: Vitruvius closes the Hellenistic anecdote by insisting that the trigger for Dinocrates' success was not initially his technical portfolio, but his spectacular physical stature and his mastery of political theatricality. This observation serves as a springboard to introduce his personal manifesto. 377

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II • Mihi autem... faciem deformavit aetas, valetudo detraxit vires: The Autobiographical Turn and the Rhetoric of Physical Decline. Vitruvius presents himself to Augustus as the exact opposite of Dinocrates: an old man (aetas), marked by illness (valetudo) and devoid of visual appeal or athletic prowess. This confession does not seek compassion, but rather operates under a classical literary convention: the devaluation of the body to extol the imperishable value of the intellect. • Per auxilia scientiae scriptaque: The thesis of Vitruvius's treatise. The author proposes to Emperor Augustus a new model of patronage based not on the immediate visual appeal of megalomaniacal projects, but on the solidity of scientific knowledge and the written codification of the laws of architecture. His ten books are, therefore, his own "lion's skin" and his "club": the intellectual instruments with which he aspires to earn immortality and the commendation (commendatio) of the sovereign of Rome. II.Pr.4 The prologue concludes by linking Dinocrates' definitive success with the founding of Alexandria, a site that, unlike Mount Athos, combined a safe natural harbour with the agricultural and logistical potential of the Nile River. Vitruvius takes advantage of this historical resolution to articulate a sharp autobiographical contrast directed at Augustus (imperator); acknowledging his lack of the youth, stature, and physical presence that elevated the Macedonian master, the Roman writer claims state patronage based strictly on the rigor of technical knowledge (scientia) and the enduring value of his written work as his sole title of architectural nobility (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.Pr.4). 5. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II Chapter 1 2.1.1 Homines vetere more ut ferae in silvis et speluncis et nemoribus nascebantur ciboque agresti vescendo vitam exigebant. Interea quodam in loco ab tempestatibus et ventis densae crebritatibus arbores agitatae et inter se terentes ramos ignem excitaverunt, et eius flamma vehementi perterriti qui circa eum locum fuerunt sunt fugati. postea re quieta propius accedentes cum animadvertissent commoditatem esse magnam corporibus ignis teporem, ligna adicientes et îs conservantes alios adducebant et nutu monstrantes ostendebant quas haberent ex eo utilitates. In eo hominum congressu cum profundebantur aliter ⟨atque aliter⟩ e spiritu voces, cotidiana consuetudine vocabula ut obtigerant constituerunt, deinde significando res saepius in usu ex eventu fari fortuito coeperunt et ita sermones inter se procreaverunt. 2.1.1 In the earliest ages of the world, men were born like the wild beasts in forests, caves, and groves, and passed their lives feeding upon wild fare. Meanwhile, in a certain place, trees densely crowded and tossed by storms and winds, and rubbing their branches one against another, kindled fire; and those who were about that place, terrified by the fierce flame, were put to flight. Afterwards, when it had grown quiet, drawing nearer they perceived that the warmth of the fire was of great comfort to their bodies; and, adding wood and so keeping it alive, they brought others to it, and by signs made plain what advantages they had from it. In that gathering of men, as their voices were uttered in differing ways with the breath, they established by daily use words as chance had brought them; then, signifying the things in more frequent use, they came by chance to speak, and thus speech was born among them. 135 1. 1. densae crebritatibus: A typically Vitruvian -style phrase describing the high density, thickness, and physical proximity of tree masses in primeval forests. This compact arrangement of the forests is the indispensable mechanical condition for the natural friction generated by the wind to produce the outbreak of fire. — 2. hominum congressu: A technical term from ancient 135 The origin of fire and language belongs to an ancient genealogy of civilisation. Parallels with Lucretius or other intellectual traditions are comparative; Vitruvius does not declare any precise doctrinal dependence here. 381

It represents the foundational milestone in the transition from the untamed state of nature to civilized society. — 3. sermones: A concept that in this context does not define mere solemn speeches, but rather articulated language, interactive conversation, and the social communicative faculty that crystallizes after the fixation of arbitrary words. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 4. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 2.1.1. For the study of ancient theories on anthropogenesis and the development of language, see the critical edition of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 31-32; and the apparatus of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 31-32. • veteri more ut ferae: Vitruvius adopts a strictly materialist and historical perspective on human evolution, radically opposed to Hesiod's providentialist theological myth of the "Golden Age. " The first humans are described as being in a state of wild animality, nomadic, scattered, and lacking the basic tools of civilization. Here, the author aligns himself with the philosophical tradition of Democritus, Epicurus, and, fundamentally, with the doctrine expounded by the Roman poet Lucretius in Book V of his work De rerum natura. • demystification of fire. In contrast to the Greek myth of Prometheus (who steals fire from the gods to give it to humanity), Vitruvius offers a naturalistic and mechanical explanation of the phenomenon: the accidental friction of tree branches caused by the wind. The driving force of cultural change is not divine intervention, but a physical and fortuitous meteorological phenomenon. • ignis teporem / utilitates: Fire acts as the ultimate social catalyst. Upon discovering the physical advantage of heat (commoditatem ad ignis teporem), humans overcome their initial fear and learn to domesticate the element by gathering firewood (ligna adicientes). Maintaining the hearth requires temporary sedentary behavior and cooperation, forcing isolated individuals to gather in a common place (hominum congressus). 382

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II • vocabula ut obtigerant / sermones procreaverunt: Analysis of the Cratilian-Epicurean Theory of Language. Vitruvius explains how the birth of civil society is inseparable from the birth of language. Linguistic genesis consists of three well-defined phases: 1. Primary cries: Modulations of the voice caused by spontaneous physical or emotional impulses (profundebantur aliter spiritu voces). 2. Arbitrariness and convention: The random assignment of names to objects according to the chance of daily encounters (vocabula ut obtigerant constituerunt), consolidated by collective habit (cotiedad consuetudine). 3. articulation: The pragmatic repetition oriented towards utility that gives rise to rational dialogue and language itself (sermones inter se procreaverunt). 2.1.1 Vitruvius opens the main body of his second book by presenting a materialist and evolutionist theory on the origin of humanity, in line with atomist and Lucretian schools of thought. The passage describes the fundamental transition from a wild and disconnected existence to social cohesion, identifying the accidental domestication of fire — caused by the friction of forest vegetation — and the subsequent gathering of human communities around hearths (hominum congressus) as the driving force behind this change. This shared space forced the abandonment of instinctive cries in favor of the conventional establishment of arbitrary linguistic signs, giving rise to the simultaneous birth of society and articulated language (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.1.1). 5. Rowland and Howe, Vitruvius, 34, 146–147. 2.1.2. This paragraph is one of the most famous texts in Western architectural theory, as it sets out the anatomical and evolutionary conditions that differentiate humans from animals and describes the birth of architecture through the imitation of nature and social competition, giving rise to the theoretical concept of the primitive hut. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II ambularent mundique et astrorum magnificentiam aspicerent, item manibus et articulis quam vellent rem faciliter tractarent, coeperunt in eo coetu alii de fronde facere tecta, alii speluncas fodere sub montibus, nonnulli hirundinum nidos et aedificationes earum imitantes de luto et virgulis facere loca quae subirent. Tunc observantes aliena tecta et adicientes suis cogitationibus res novas, efficiebant in dies meliora genera casarum. 2.1.2 The discovery of fire thus first gave rise to gatherings, deliberation and communal life, and brought more people together in one place. Nature had given them an advantage over the other animals: they walked upright rather than bent towards the ground, could contemplate the magnificence of the world and stars, and could handle whatever they wished with their hands and fingers. In that gathering some began to make shelters from foliage, others to dig caves beneath hills, and others, imitating swallows and their nests, to build places of mud and twigs in which to shelter. By observing one another’s dwellings and adding new ideas of their own, they made better kinds of huts each day.136 Note — II.1.2. Vitruvius continues the account by connecting human assembly with upright posture, manual ability and the observation of constructional solutions. He describes roofs of foliage, caves and shelters of mud and branches inspired, among other models, by swallows’ nests. 1. concilium et convictus: A literal translation of the tradition that read convictus as a participle ("they were convinced"). This is a substantive legal and sociological triad of Vitruvius (conventus, concilium, convictus): the physical assembly, common deliberation, and cohabitation or shared life under the same roof. — 2. non proni sed erecti: An expression of philosophical and histological origin that describes bipedalism. Vitruvius treats the upright posture not only as a physical trait, but as an ontological dignity bestowed by nature (naturae praemium). — 3. manibus et articulis: Manual dexterity and digital articulation. Vitruvius brilliantly identifies bipedalism and the freeing of the hands as the two biological and engineering preconditions indispensable for the birth of technology and toolmaking. 136 Upright posture and manual skill form part of the ancient anthropology through which Vitruvius explains the origins of civic life (2.1.2). 384

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II Academic translation 2.1.2 Therefore, when, because of the discovery of fire, a first congregation (conventus), communal deliberation (concilium), and shared life (convictus) originated among human beings, and when a large number of individuals gathered in one place — favored by a gift of nature that differentiated them from other animals, namely: not walking bent forward (proni), but upright (erecti), which allowed them to contemplate the magnificence of the universe and the stars, as well as to manipulate any object with absolute ease through their hands and joints—, within that community, some began to weave roofs with foliage, others to excavate caves at the foot of the mountains, and some, imitating the constructive skill and nests of swallows, to make enclosures of mud and branches where they could take shelter. Later, by observing the roofs of their neighbors and adding new innovations to their own ideas (cogitationes), they perfected the different types of huts day by day with better workmanship. Notes (Explanation of Vitruvius's Text) 4. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 2.1.2. For the analysis of physical anthropology in the Roman world and the typological evolution of primitive housing, see the edition of Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899), 32; and the fixation of the Latin text of Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 32. • naturae praemium / non proni sed erecti: The anatomical foundation of culture. Vitruvius aligns himself with the Stoic and Ciceronian tradition (cf. Cicero, De natura deorum II.150) in arguing that the erect posture has a dual function: a cognitive/spiritual one (to gaze upon the cosmos and the stars, elevating thought) and a pragmatic /mechanical one (to free the upper limbs). Animals, being proni (looking towards the ground), are determined by their immediate biological needs; human beings, being erectus, possess the visual and physical distance necessary to design their environment. • manibus et articulis... facilitater tractarent: The hand as a tool of tools. Vitruvius anticipates modern theses of technical anthropology on hominization. The human hand, endowed with versatile joints and digital opposition, allows for tractatio (the skilful manipulation of raw materials). Without this anatomical advantage, human intelligence could not have materialized in physical culture or architecture. 385

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II • Hirundinum nests... imitators: The concept of Constructive Mimesis. The origin of architecture does not stem from divine revelation, but from careful observation and imitation of zoology. Primitive humans imitate the technique of swallows (hirundines), which mix flexible organic elements (branches, straw) with moist binders (mud, clay). This is the zero degree of masonry: the transition from the simple appropriation of natural space (the cave) to the manufacture of an artificial habitat through the combination of materials. • observantes aliena tecta / adicientes suis cogitationibus: The engine of technical progress is social emulation and cognitive development. Architecture evolves thanks to two interconnected factors: 1. Observing others: Community contact within the coetus fosters competition and learning through imitation. Human beings copy the successes of their neighbors. 2. Mental optimization: The design process (cogitation) allows for projecting variations and improvements on what is observed, which generates a constant morphological evolution (efficiebant in dies meliora genera casarum), transforming the rough branch hut into a functional architectural typology. 2.1.2 Vitruvius defines the origin of architecture as stemming from a concatenation of anatomical determinants and dynamics of social emulation. Thanks to the evolutionary advantages of bipedalism (non proni sed erecti) and the consequent motor versatility of the hands (manibus et articulis), primitive humans managed to overcome the stage of gathering and become agents of transformation of matter. The text places the genesis of building in zoological imitation — particularly of swallows' nests through the amalgamation of mud and reeds —, a primordial process that was accelerated thanks to social coexistence, where the visual exchange of technical solutions and the accumulation of individual cognitive experiences drove the progressive improvement of the hut (meliora genera casarum) as a basic typology of human habitat (Vitruvius, De architectura 2.1.2). But since they were of an imitative and teachable nature, daily glorying in their inventions, they pointed out to one another the results of their building; and thus, sharpening their wits in rivalry, they grew day by day of sounder judgment. At first, with forked stakes set up and twigs laid between, they wove their walls with mud. Others built walls of lumps of dried clay, binding them together with timber, and, to keep off the rains and the heat, they covered them with reeds and leaves. Academic translation 2.1.3 Since human beings possess a nature suited to imitation and learning, each day, proud of their inventions, they showed each other the results of their constructions. Thus, exercising their ingenuity through competition, they achieved more refined judgments day after day. At first, they erected forked posts (wooden poles), interlaced branches, and covered the walls with mud. Others built walls by piling up sun-dried clods of mud, lining them with plant materials, and covering them with reeds and foliage for protection from the rain and heat. However, upon discovering that during winter storms these roofs could not withstand the rain, they began to build gabled structures (fastigia), covering them with mud and installing sloping roofs (stillicidia) so that rainwater could be drained away. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II • Competition as a catalyst: Vitruvius emphasizes that progress is not only individual, but social; by competing with each other (exercentes ingenia certationibus), individuals constantly raised their standards of constructive quality. • Material evolution: ◦ Framework system: The first step was the use of vertical posts (furcis) and horizontal support elements (virgulis) covered with clay. ◦ Earth walls: The second stage consisted of the use of blocks or lumps of dry clay (luteas glaebas). • Tectonic evolution: The need to drain water was the direct cause of the invention of the pitched roof (proclinatis tectis). When flat roofs failed during the winter, humans understood the need to create slopes (fastigia) to channel water away, thus preventing seepage and protecting the mud structure from erosion. From what has been said above we may see that these things were originally established as has been described, since to this day the buildings of foreign nations are made of such materials: in Gaul, Spain, Lusitania, and Aquitaine, roofed with oak shingles or with thatch. Among the Colchians in Pontus, where forests abound, whole trees are laid flat upon the ground to right and to left, a space being left between them as wide as the length of the trees allows; and upon the outer ends of these, others are laid across, so enclosing the dwelling-space within. Then, binding together the four corners with beams laid alternately, and raising the walls of tree-trunks set plumb above the lower ones, they carry up towers to a height; and the gaps that are left, by reason of the thickness of the timber, they stop with chips and mud. The roofs, drawing in by degrees from the extreme angles, they raise pyramid-fashion; and these they cover with foliage and mud, thus fashioning, after the barbarian manner, the testudinate (covered) roofs of their towers. Academic translation " We can observe that these constructions originated in the manner described above, since to this day foreign peoples build their dwellings with these same materials; for example, in Gaul, Hispania, Lusitania, and Aquitania, they use sturdy wooden planks or straw. Among the Colchian people in Pontus, due to the abundance of forests, they place whole trees flat on the ground to the right and left, leaving a space between them proportional to the length of the trunks; on the ends of these they place transverse beams that enclose the central space of the dwelling. Then, overlapping alternating beams on the four sides, they join the corners, and in this way, raising the walls of trees plumb from the base, they erect towers; the gaps left by the thickness of the wood are filled with wood chips and mud." Likewise, as for the roofs, they place transverse beams that recede from the ends, gradually contracting them, and thus raise a pyramidal structure on all four sides towards the center, which, when covered with foliage and mud, creates vaulted roofs in the barbarian style. Critical and Technical Analysis • Ethnography as evidence: Vitruvius uses the observation of " barbarian " peoples (Gauls, Iberians, Colchians) not as a curiosity, but as 389

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II empirical evidence for his evolutionary theory. By observing that these cultures still used thatched roofs or log structures, he confirms that these were the formative stages of human architecture. • Colchid technique: The description details a construction system using interlocking logs (log cabin construction). Whole trees are placed horizontally and locked at the corners to form a self-supporting structure. • Space management: The use of schidiae (wood chips or wedges) and mud to fill the gaps (intervalla) between cylindrical logs is a necessary technical solution to guarantee thermal insulation and watertightness of the walls. • Evolution of the roof: The description of the roof describes a truncated pyramidal covering (metas). By setting back the beams (gradatim contrahentes), they manage to create a dome or sloping roof which, once sealed with mud and foliage, acquires a "testudina-like" shape (similar to the shape of a turtle's shell), characteristic of barbarian defensive or storage constructions. Over them they set a framework of logs tied together, which they cover with reeds and brushwood, and heap great mounds of earth above their dwellings. Thus they make their houses very warm in winter and very cool in summer. Some build their huts of marsh sedge. They cut these mounds in half with a trench and, when excavating paths, widened the spaces as much as the terrain allowed. Critical Apparatus and Footnotes • tumulos naturales... distinguentes: Vitruvius describes here the creation of semi-buried or excavated dwellings in mounds (tumuli), a logical adaptation to climates where the lack of wood prevents the construction of elevated structures. • metas: The term refers to the conical or pyramidal shape, similar to a circus goal, which allows for an optimal distribution of the earth load on the wooden structure. 391

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II • ulva palustri: Refers to an aquatic plant (marsh rushes or grasses) traditionally used as a roofing material due to its impermeability and lightness. • Massiliae... subacta cum paleis terra: Vitruvius cites Marseille as a case where the technique of rammed earth with straw (adobe or rudimentary rammed earth) is used as an alternative to fired clay tiles. • Romuli casa: The hut of Romulus (casa Romuli) was a sacred site in Rome deliberately preserved in its primitive appearance — straw and wood — to commemorate the austere foundation of the city in contrast to the opulence of the imperial era. References: Vitruvius, De architectura, 2.1.5. (Reference edition: Krohn, F., 1912). De architectura 2.1.6. Vitruvius synthesizes the definitive step from instinctive need to technique (ars) and human civilization. Latin text Ita his signis de antiquis inventionibus aedificiorum sic ea fuisse ratiocinantes possumus iudicare. Cum autem cotidie faciendo tritiores manus ad aedificandum perfecissent et sollertia ingenia exercendo per consuetudinem ad artes pervenissent, tum etiam industria in animis eorum adiecta perfecit ut qui fuerunt in his studiosiores fabros esse se profiterentur. Cum ergo haec ita fuerint primo constituta et natura non solum sensibus ornavisset gentes quemadmodum reliqua animalia, sed etiam cogitationibus et consiliis armavisset mentes et subiecisset cetera animalia sub potestate, tunc vero ex fabricationibus aedificiorum gradatim progressi ad ceteras artes et disciplinas, e fera agrestique vita ad mansuetam perduxerunt humanitatem. From these tokens, then, we may judge that the building-inventions of the ancients were of this kind, and so reason concerning them. And as, by daily practice, men’s hands grew more skilled in building, and as by exercising their wits they attained through habit to the arts, then industry, added to their minds, brought it about that those who were the more diligent in such things should claim to be craftsmen. Since, therefore, these things were thus first established, and since nature had not only endowed mankind with the senses, as it had the other animals, but had also armed their minds with thought and judgment, and had set the other animals beneath their dominion, they advanced by degrees 392

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II from the building of houses to the other arts and disciplines, and led humanity from a wild and rustic life to a gentler civilization. Academic translation " Thus, we can judge from this evidence that the ancient inventions of architecture were like this. Now, as daily practice in the exercise of construction granted greater dexterity to their hands, and by exercising their ingenuity through habit, they attained mastery of the arts, it then happened that the application of their industry to such minds caused the most studious among them to proclaim themselves artisans (fabri). Once these principles were thus established, and considering that nature not only endowed people with senses — as it did with other animals — but also armed their minds with thought and reflection, subjecting other creatures to its power, it was then that, after gradually progressing from building to the rest of the arts and disciplines, they managed to transform their wild and rustic existence into a civilized and peaceful humanity." Critical Apparatus and Notes • tritiores manus: The term tritiores (from terere, to rub or wear down) refers to the constant practice that softens or refines movements. It refers to the transition from brute physical effort to refined manual technique. • studiosiores fabros: Vitruvius marks the birth of the specialized craft. The architect or builder is no longer just any individual, but one who, through study and practice (studiosiores), elevates his activity to the level of a recognized profession. • cogitationibus et consiliis: Vitruvius establishes here a hierarchical distinction between animal nature (endowed with senses) and human nature (endowed with reflective reason and strategic planning). • mansuetam humanitatem: This term defines the final stage of civilization: humanitas as a state of gentleness (mansueta) that arises from social life, the exchange of knowledge and the creation of a built environment. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II De architectura 2.1.7. It closes the first chapter of the second book, serving as an epilogue to the history of the development of architecture and a technical prologue to the following chapters dedicated to materials. Latin text Tum autem struentes animose et aevo prospicientes maioribus cogitationibus ex varietate artium natis, non casas sed etiam domos fundatas et latericiis parietibus aut e lapide structas materiaque et tegula tectas perficere coeperunt; deinde observationibus studiorum e vagantibus iudiciis et incertis ad certas symmetriarum perduxerunt rationes. Posteaquam animadverterunt profusos esse partus naturae et abundantem materiae copiam ad aedificationes ab ea comparatam, tractando nutrierunt et auctam per artes ornaverunt voluptatibus elegantiam vitae. Igitur de his rebus, quae sunt in aedificiis ad usum idoneae, quibusque sunt qualitatibus et quas habeant virtutes, ut potuero, dicam. Then, schooling their minds and looking forward to greater conceptions born of the variety of the arts, they began to build, not huts, but houses with foundations, with walls of brick or stone, and roofed with timber and tiles; and next, by careful observation, they were led from wavering and uncertain notions to fixed rules of symmetry. When they perceived that nature had brought forth her materials in abundance, and had furnished a plentiful store for building, they tended these with care, and, enlarging them through the arts, adorned the elegance of life with its pleasures. I shall therefore speak, as best I can, of those things which are fit for use in building, with what properties they are endowed, and how they possess their excellences. Academic translation “Later, as they became more intellectually inclined and projected more ambitious thoughts born from the variety of the arts, they began to build not only huts, but also houses with foundations, raised with brick or stone walls, and covered with beams and tiles. Then, through observation and study, they managed to move from vague and uncertain judgments to precise systems of symmetry. After noticing that nature offers a profusion of materials and that from it comes the abundance of resources for construction, they cultivated them through technical treatment and, having augmented them through the arts, embellished them to increase the elegance of life. Therefore, I will explain 394

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II as best I can which elements used in buildings are suitable for use, what qualities they possess, and what properties (virtutes) they offer. ” Critical Apparatus and Notes • prospicientes maioribus cogitationibus: The transition from the rural to the urban requires a new scale of thought: the architect no longer improvises, but projects (prospicientes) with a long-term goal. • Foundation domes: Vitruvius marks a fundamental technical milestone: the introduction of foundations (fundata). Civilized architecture begins when construction becomes permanent, stable, and technologically complex (use of stone and brick). • e vagantibus iudiciis... ad certas symmetriarum rationes: This is the core of Vitruvian philosophy: the transition from empirical and uncertain trial and error to a normative system (symmetria). Architecture reaches its maturity when it is codified in mathematical rules and exact proportions. • voluptatibus elegantiam vitae: Vitruvius concludes that the ultimate goal of construction technique is human well-being (voluptas), elevating the mere need for shelter to the category of elegance and vital refinement. • Virtues: In Vitruvian lexicon, the virtues of materials are not moral qualities, but physical properties (resistance, durability, flexibility, load capacity). VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II et e quibus rebus esset nata dicere. ergo in primo de artis officio itemque quid oporteat esse in architecto, ibi pronuntiavi., in hoc de naturalibus materiae rebus, quem habeant usum, disputabo. Namque hic liber non profitetur unde architectura nascatur, sed unde origines aedificiorum sunt institutae et quibus rationibus enutritae et progressae sint gradatim ad hanc finitionem. But should anyone wish to dispute the order of this book, thinking that it ought to have been placed first, lest he suppose that I have erred, I will render my reason thus. When I was writing the body of architecture, I thought in the first volume to set forth with what branches of learning and disciplines it is adorned, to define its departments, and to say from what things it has sprung; and there I declared what an architect ought to be. In the first, therefore, I treat of the duty of the art; in this, of the natural properties of materials, and what use they have. For this book does not profess to show whence architecture is born, but whence the origins of building were established, and by what means they were fostered and advanced by degrees to their present condition. Academic translation “But if anyone wishes to argue about the order of this book, thinking that it should have been structured differently, lest they believe I have erred, I will give my reason here: in writing the body of architecture, I considered that in the first volume I should explain with what knowledge and disciplines it should be adorned, define the limits of its different categories, and explain from what elements it has arisen. Therefore, I declared there what qualities the architect should possess. Thus, in the first I spoke about the duties of art; in this, I will discuss the nature of materials and their uses. For this book does not intend to explain where architecture originates, but rather where the origins of buildings were established, and by what means they were nurtured and gradually progressed to their present form. ” Critical Apparatus and Notes • Reddam rationem: Vitruvius uses legal and rhetorical language when apologizing for his structure: he is " giving an account" to the reader for his editorial decision. • Corpus architecturae: He defines his work not as a collection of notes, but as a "body" or organic and complete system. 396

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II • Eruditionibus et disciplinis: This refers to the catalog of knowledge (mathematics, music, geometry, etc.) that Vitruvius required in Book I for the comprehensive training of the architect. • Thematic difference: Vitruvius clarifies the distinction between Book I (the architect and the theoretical framework of the profession) and Book II (the empirical study of the subject and the evolutionary history of construction), emphasizing that his current objective is the technical genealogy of the building. Bibliographic references: • Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 2.1.8. • Fritz Krohn, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912). • Valentin Rose, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1899). For paragraph 2.1.8, which functions as a methodological epilogue where Vitruvius justifies the structural order of his corpus: Academic Footnote 1. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, De architectura 2.1.8. In this passage, the author makes a conscious defense of architecture as a systematic discipline (corpus architecturae). The justification of the order — where Book I establishes the intellectual training of the professional (eruditionibus et disciplinis) and Book II addresses the material and historical genesis of building — underscores the Vitruvian transition from abstract theory to the physics of materials. For an analysis of the treatise's editorial structure and the contrast between the architect's officium and the nature of materiae, see Fritz Krohn's critical edition, Vitruvii De architectura libri decem (Leipzig: Teubner, 1912), 34; as well as the commentary by Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas Noble Howe, Vitruvius: 'Ten Books on Architecture' (New York: Cambridge University Press, 1999), 147. Analysis of the components: • Justification: The note highlights that Vitruvius does not organize his work randomly, but with a clear didactic intention: first the subject (the architect) and then the object (the construction and its materials). 397

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II • Technical Terminology: Emphasis is placed on the distinction between the "disciplines" (educational background) and the "nature of things" (naturales materiae rebus), which is the guiding principle of his method. • References: The note integrates both the standard philological fixation (Krohn) and the most authoritative modern reference in English (Rowland and Howe), guaranteeing the required academic rigor. De architectura 2.1.9. It concludes the introduction to Book II and establishes the epistemological framework of the physics of materials. Latin text Ergo ita suo ordine et loco huius erit voluminis constitutio. Nunc revertar ad propositum et de copiis, quae aptae sunt aedificiorum perfectionibus, quemadmodum videantur esse ab natura rerum procreatae quibusque mixtionibus principiorum congressus temperentur, ne obscura sed perspicua legentibus sint, ratiocinabor. Namque nulla materiarum genera neque corpora neque res sine principiorum coetu nasci neque subici intellectui possunt, neque aliter natura rerum praeceptis physicorum veras patitur habere explicationes, nisi causae, quae insunt in his rebus, quemadmodum et quid ita sint, subtilibus rationibus habeant demonstrationes. This volume, then, will have its constitution in its own order and place. Now I shall return to my purpose and reason concerning the materials suitable for the perfecting of buildings: how they appear to have been brought forth by the nature of things, and by what minglings of their first principles their combinations are tempered; and I shall make this not obscure but clear to my readers. For no kinds of matter, no bodies, no things can come into being without a concurrence of first principles, nor be brought within the understanding; nor, otherwise, can the precepts of the physicists touching the nature of things have true explanations, unless the causes inherent in these things—how and why they are as they are—be demonstrated by subtle reasoning. Academic translation “Thus, this volume will have its constitution according to its proper order and place. Now I will return to my purpose and reason about the resources that are suitable for the perfection of constructions, about how they seem to have been brought forth by the nature of things, and by what mixtures of principles the 398

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II combinations of their elements are moderated, so that they are not obscure, but clear to the readers. For no kind of matter, body, or object can come into being or be subjected to understanding without the union of its principles; nor does nature allow explanations about reality to gain validity according to the precepts of physics, unless the causes present in such things — the how and the why they are as they are — possess demonstrations based on subtle reasoning. ” Critical Apparatus and Notes • Constitutio: In this context, it refers to the logical and organizational structure of the treatise. • Principiorum coetu. Vitruvius here uses the vocabulary of the physical principles that he immediately develops by summarizing several Greek doctrines. Coetus and congressus denote the coming together or combination of those principles. The passage should not be reduced to a single atomist doctrine, since the chapter juxtaposes explanations from Thales, Heraclitus, Democritus/Epicurus and the Pythagorean tradition. • Praeceptis physicorum: Vitruvius demands for architecture the scientific rigor of ancient physics. It is not enough to know the use of materials, but it is essential to demonstrate their underlying causes through "subtle reasoning" (subtilibus rationibus). • Methodology: The author emphasizes that his exposition must be "clear to the readers" (perspicua legentibus), avoiding academic obscurity in favor of a rational explanation of the physical properties. Comparative critical apparatus — II.1. The account of fire, human assembly, language and the first buildings is retained as a Vitruvian genealogy, although it admits comparison with Lucretius and other ancient traditions. Densae crebritatibus is an awkward construction that should not be regularized merely for elegance. Nutu and sermones mark the transition from gesture and voice to shared communication; tritiores manus, studiosiores fabri and certas symmetriarum rationes articulate practice, specialization and proportional rules. Historical and architectural note — II.1. The primitive dwellings attributed to different peoples are literary ethnographic testimonies, not a demonstrated archaeological sequence. Their argumentative function is to show 399

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II constructional diversity produced by imitation, experience, available resources and cumulative improvement. Comparative apparatus — II.1. “Homines veteri more ut ferae…” introduces a conjectural history of the origins of social life and building: fire, conventus, concilium, convictus, language, imitation and the progressive improvement of shelters. It is presented as ancient architectural anthropology, not modern prehistoric archaeology. Architectural and hermeneutic note — The origins of building. Vitruvius connects primitive architecture with observation and imitation: branches, forked supports, mud, reeds, trunks and roofs precede progressively regularized forms. Comparison with vernacular techniques may be illustrative, but does not prove a universal historical sequence. References: 400

Heraclitus137 of Ephesus, whom the Greeks called skoteinos (σκοτεινός) because of the obscurity of his writings, held fire to be that principle. Democritus and his follower Epicurus proposed atoms, which some Latin writers call indivisible bodies and others individual particles. The Pythagorean school added air and earth to water and fire. Democritus, although he did not name the substances individually but proposed indivisible bodies, seems to have held that these bodies, being separate, cannot be damaged, destroyed or divided by cutting, but retain an inexhaustible solidity throughout eternity.138 Academic translation “Thales was the first to consider water as the principle of all things. Heraclitus of Ephesus, whom the Greeks called 'the obscure' (σκοτεινός) because of the obscurity of his writings, pointed to fire. Democritus, and his successor Epicurus, postulated atoms, which our people called indivisible bodies and, equally, individuals. The doctrine of the Pythagoreans, for its part, added air and earth to water and fire. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II because, being separate, they suffer no harm, are not destroyed, and are not divided by cuts, but retain within themselves an infinite solidity for all eternity. ” Critical Apparatus and Notes • σκοτεινός (skoteinos), “dark” or “obscure,” is the traditional epithet of Heraclitus, referring to the difficulty of his expression. The string ζθνηεηλνο is a modern graphic corruption, not an independently identified manuscript reading. • Principium: Vitruvius identifies the pre-Socratic concept of arche (fundamental principle) as the basis on which the physics of materials is built. • Atomism: The mention of Democritus and Epicurus underscores Vitruvius's interest in the corpuscular theory. The idea of matter composed of solid and unalterable "individuals" (atoms) is what explains the strength and durability of building materials. • Pythagoreanism: By adding air and earth, Vitruvius completes the tetralogy of natural elements, which will become the axis of his explanation of why some materials are more suitable than others to bear loads or withstand the weather. Bibliographic references: • Krohn, F., ed. Vitruvii De architectura libri decem. Leipzig: Teubner, 1912. • Rose, V., ed. Vitruvii De architectura libri decem. Leipzig: Teubner, 1899. De architectura 2.2.2. Vitruvius justifies the need to understand the nature of materials in order to avoid errors in building practice. Latin text Ex his ergo congruentibus, cum res omnes coire nascique videantur, et hae in infinitis generibus rerum naturae sint disparatae, putavi oportere de varietatibus et discriminibus usus earum, quasque haberent in aedificiis qualitates, exponere; uti, cum fuerint notae, non habeant qui aedificare cogitant errorem, sed aptas ad usum copias aedificiis comparent. 402

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II Since all things appear to arise from combinations of these principles, yet occur in infinitely different forms in nature, I thought it necessary to explain the varieties of materials, the differences in their uses and their qualities in buildings. With that knowledge, those planning to build can avoid error and obtain materials suited to the work. Academic translation " Therefore, since all things seem to be born and formed from the concordance of these principles, and given that in the nature of things they appear differentiated into an infinity of kinds, I judged it necessary to expound their varieties, the differences in their use, and the qualities they possess within buildings; so that, once known, those who plan to build will not fall into error, but will select the resources (copiae) most suitable for the utility of their constructions. " Critical Apparatus and Notes • Congruentibus: Vitruvius refers here to the combination or harmony of the elements (atoms or physical principles) mentioned in the previous paragraph, the basis of the material constitution of the universe. • Varietatibus et discriminibus: The author emphasizes the importance of empirical classification; for the architect, it is not enough to know that the material exists, but he must understand its specific differences in order to assign to each material its appropriate technical function in the work. • Aptas ad usum copias: The ultimate purpose of materials theory is the correct choice (aptas), thus avoiding improvisation and ensuring that the resources used are suitable to guarantee the stability and functionality of the building. References: • Krohn, F., ed. Vitruvii De architectura libri decem. Leipzig: Teubner, 1912. • Rose, V., ed. Vitruvii De architectura libri decem. Leipzig: Teubner, 1899. Comparative critical apparatus — II.2.1–2. The sequence Thales–Heraclitus– Democritus/Epicurus–Pythagoreans brings distinct physical doctrines together around the problem of principia. Insecabilia corpora and individua explain atomoi and should not be modernised as contemporary atomic physics. 403

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II Congruentibus and the mixtiones principiorum provide the transition to the technical classification of materiae. Philosophical and technical note — Principia. Vitruvius uses ancient physics to argue that the observable properties of materials depend on their constitution. The edition separates that historical explanation from modern materials science. Comparative apparatus — II.2. The doctrines of Thales, Heraclitus, Democritus/Epicurus and Pythagoras are presented as ancient opinions about the principia rerum. Aqua, ignis, atomi/insecabilia corpora and the doctrine of four elements form the cosmological framework Vitruvius uses before discussing materials. The commentary separates philosophical doxography from materials science. Textual and philosophical note — Terminology. Σκοτεινός is retained as the Greek epithet of Heraclitus; atomos is explained alongside insecabilia corpora and individua. “Atom” is not translated as though the ancient concept were identical to the entity of modern physics. 404

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II Chapter 3 De architectura 2.3.1. Vitruvius begins his technical description of brickmaking (lateres). Latin text Itaque primum de lateribus, qua de terra duci eos oporteat, dicam. Non enim de harenoso neque calculoso luto neque sabulone soluto sunt ducendi, quod ex his generibus cum sint ducti primum fiunt graves, deinde cum ab imbribus in parietibus sparguntur, dilabuntur et dissolvuntur, paleaeque in his non cohaerescunt propter asperitatem. Faciendi autem sunt ex terra albida cretosa sive de rubrica aut etiam masculo sabulone. Haec enim genera propter levitatem habent firmitatem et non sunt in opere ponderosa et faciliter aggerantur. I shall first discuss bricks and the earth from which they should be molded. They should not be made from sandy or gravelly clay or loose sand: bricks of these materials are heavy, break up and dissolve when rain strikes the walls, and do not bind well with straw because of their roughness. They should instead be made from whitish clayey earth, red earth or coarse, firm sand. These materials combine lightness with strength, add little weight to the work and are readily laid up. Academic translation " Therefore, I will speak first of bricks, explaining from what kind of earth they should be made. They should not be made of sandy, stony, or loose sand, because, when made from these materials, they are heavy, and, moreover, when they are battered by rain in the walls, they crumble and dissolve, and straw does not adhere to them because of their roughness. Instead, they should be made of white clay (chalk), red clay (rubrica), or even firm, coarse sand (masculo sabulone). For these types, due to their lightness, possess stability, are not heavy in the construction, and are easy to lift. " Critical Apparatus and Notes • duci eos] The adopted text uses the passive infinitive duci with lateres, “bricks”, as the subject of the dependent statement. A gerundive referring to lateres would be ducendi, not ducenda. • Suitable materials: Vitruvius advises against sandy soils (harenous) or calcareous soils with gravel (calculous), as they lack plastic cohesion. He proposes, instead, white clay soils (chalk) or ferruginous soils (rubric), which 405

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II offer the necessary structure for the straw, added as a reinforcing element, to fulfill its binding function. • masculo sabulone] Firm, coarse sand in the adopted authorial explanation. The ancient qualitative description should not be replaced without evidence by an exact modern granulometric specification. Bibliographic references: In De architectura 2.3.2, Vitruvius details the seasonal and curing conditions necessary to guarantee the technical quality of the bricks. Latin text Ducendi autem sunt per vernum tempus et autumnale, ut uno tenore siccescant. Qui enim per solstitium parantur, ideo vitiosi fiunt, quod summum corium sol acriter cum praecoquit, efficit ut videatur aridum, interior autem sit non siccus. Et cum postea siccescendo se contrahit, perrumpit ea quae erant arida. Ita rimosi facti efficiuntur inbecilli. Maxime autem utiliores erunt, si ante biennium fuerint ducti; namque non ante possunt penitus siccescere. Itaque cum recentes et non aridi sunt structi, tectorio inducto rigidoque obsolidate, permanente ipsi sidentes non possunt eandem altitudinem, qua est tectorium, tenere, contractioneque moti non haerent cum eo, sed ab coniunctione eius disparantur. Igitur tectoria ab structura seiuncta, propter tenuitatem per se stare non possunt, sed franguntur, ipsique parietes fortuito sidentes vitiantur. Ideo etiam Uticenses laterem, si sit aridus et ante quinquennium ductus, cum arbitrio magistratus fuerit ita probatus, tunc utuntur in parietum structuris. Bricks should be molded in spring or autumn so that they dry evenly. Those made at midsummer are defective because the sun rapidly bakes their outer skin, making it appear dry while the interior remains moist. As the interior later contracts in drying, it breaks through the dry surface, leaving the bricks cracked and weak. Bricks are most useful if molded two years before use, since they cannot dry thoroughly sooner. If fresh, undried bricks are built into a wall and coated with plaster that then sets hard, the bricks continue to settle and cannot retain the plaster’s height. Their shrinkage separates them from it; the plaster, detached from the masonry and too thin to support itself, breaks, while the settling walls are also damaged. For this reason the people of Utica use bricks in walls only after they have dried for five years and have been approved by a magistrate’s inspection. 406

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II Academic translation " They must be made (ducendi) during the spring and autumn, so that they dry evenly. Those prepared during the solstice are defective because, when the sun violently bakes their outer layer, it makes them appear dry, even though the interior is not. Then, as they contract during the final drying, the already dry crust breaks, leaving the bricks cracked and weakened. They are much more useful, however, if they have been made two years in advance, since they cannot dry completely before then. Therefore, if they are used when they are still fresh and not well dried, when the coating (tectorio) is applied and hardened, the bricks settle and cannot maintain the same height as the coating; as they move due to contraction, they do not adhere to it and separate from their joint." Thus, the facing, being separated from the structure, cannot support itself due to its thinness and cracks, deteriorating the walls themselves as they settle unevenly. For this reason, the inhabitants of Utica only allow the use of bricks in their structures if they are thoroughly dried, have been manufactured five years prior, and have the approval of the magistrate. Critical Apparatus and Notes • Ducendi (to be made): Vitruvius uses the verb ducere (to lead/form) to refer to the technical process of molding clay. • Solstice (solstitium): Excessive summer heat is discouraged because it causes uneven drying: the outer surface becomes brittle while the core retains moisture, which generates cracks (rimosi) as the material contracts. • Settlement (sidentes): The author warns about the physical contraction of fresh brick. If the facing (tectorio) hardens on damp bricks, the subsequent shrinkage of these bricks causes a separation between the supporting structure and the finishing layer, resulting in cracks. • The Utica model (Uticenses): Vitruvius praises the technical legislation of the city of Utica (in North Africa), which established a mandatory five-year drying period and quality control supervised by magistrates, guaranteeing structural safety. Now there are three kinds of bricks. One which is called Lydian in Greek, that is, which our people use, is a foot and a half long and a foot wide. With the other two Greek buildings are built. Of these one is called pentadoron, the other tetradoron. But the Greeks call doron a palm, because the giving of gifts is called doron in Greek, and this is always done with the palm of the hand. The Lydian brick used by our people is a foot and a half long and one foot wide. The two other kinds are used in Greek buildings: pentadoron and tetradoron. The Greeks call the palm doron, associating it with the giving of gifts, which is done with the palm of the hand. A square brick of five palms on each side is pentadoron; one of four palms is tetradoron. Modern metric equivalents depend on the standard adopted and must be identified as editorial conversions. 140 Both Vitruvius and Pliny mention three types of brick: Lydian, tetradoron and pentadoron (Adam 1996, 64; Cairoli 2004, 152; Vitruvius 1995, 103). THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II utilitates, quod neque in aedificationibus sunt onerosi, et cum non patiantur penetrare in corpus umidam potestatem, a tempestatibus non dissolvuntur. 4. Half-bricks are made along with these bricks. In laying them, courses of full bricks are placed on one face and half-bricks on the other. With both faces built to the line and the courses alternating, the walls are bonded: the middle of a brick lies over the joint below, giving both strength and an attractive appearance on each face. At Maxilua and Callet in Further Spain, and at Pitane in Asia, bricks, once molded and dried, float when thrown into water. This appears to be because the earth from which they are made is pumice-like: light and consolidated with air, it neither admits nor absorbs water. Being naturally light and porous, yet resistant to moisture entering their substance, such bricks are supported by water like pumice, whatever their total weight. They have great advantages: they do not burden buildings, and storms do not dissolve them. Along with these bricks, half-bricks are manufactured (semi-bricks); when the wall is built, whole bricks are placed in one row and half-bricks in the other. Thus, when they are laid plumb on both faces, the walls are bonded in alternating courses, and the centers of the bricks, placed over the joints, give the wall firmness and a pleasing appearance on both sides. At Maxilua and Callet in Further Spain, and at Pitane in Asia, bricks that have been molded and dried float when thrown into water. The earth used is pumice-like: light and consolidated with air, it neither admits nor absorbs water. Its light, porous substance prevents moisture from entering, so that water supports the bricks as it supports pumice, whatever their total weight. They therefore have great advantages: they add little load to buildings and are not dissolved by storms. Comparative apparatus — II.3. Later here denotes the molded, air-dried brick described by Vitruvius. The selection of earth, seasonal drying and three genera laterum are checked. Lydium measures sesquipede by pede; πεντάδωρον and τετράδωρον are retained as Greek metrological names and explained without being silently replaced by centimeters. 409

The reason why lime, on receiving water and sand, strengthens masonry appears to be that stones, like other bodies, are compounded from the elements. Those containing more air are soft; those containing more water are pliant through moisture; those containing more earth are hard; those containing more fire are more brittle. If such stones, before firing, are finely crushed, mixed with sand and put into masonry, they do not set and cannot hold it together. When placed in a kiln and seized by the violent heat of the fire, however, they lose the strength of their original solidity: their powers are burned out and exhausted, leaving open pores and voids. 415

Editorial note. — Chapter 6 is the most celebrated passage on Roman concrete. Vitruvius describes the powder (pulvis) of the country round Baiae and the slopes of Vesuvius — pozzolana, a volcanic ash — which, mixed with lime and rubble, sets into a mass so hard that it withstands not only the weather but the waves of the sea, hardening even under water. He accounts for its action by the latent fire, sulphur and alum of the volcanic ground. This hydraulic mortar (with the pulvis Puteolanus of 5.12) is the technical foundation of the great vaulted and maritime architecture of imperial Rome, and modern chemistry has confirmed the reactive volcanic silica that he intuited. Structurarum genera sunt haec, reticulatum quo nunc omnes utuntur, et antiquum quod incertum dicitur. ex his venustius est reticulatum, sed ad rimas faciendas ideo paratum quod in omnes partes dissoluta habet cubilia et coagmenta. incerta vero caementa alia super alia sedentia inter seque imbricata non speciosam sed firmiorem quam reticulata praestant structuram. Archaeological note — II.8, masonry bonds. Vitruvius contrasts two arrangements of wall facing: reticulatum, customary in his time, and the older incertum. He considers the former more elegant (venustius), though more prone to cracking because of the arrangement of beds and joints; the latter he judges less handsome but stronger. Vitruvian terminology has decisively influenced modern archaeological nomenclature, although that classification should not be projected without qualification on to every phase of Roman construction. Opus incertum uses irregular pieces visible in the facing; opus reticulatum arranges cubilia with their faces forming a diagonal network. Later or combined techniques, such as brick facings and so-called opus mixtum, belong to developments beyond the passage’s immediate description. Vitruvius subsequently compares these fabrics with Greek procedures, including emplekton and the use of transverse elements (διάτονοι). 1. There are two kinds of masonry facing: the reticulatum now commonly used, and the older kind called incertum. The reticulatum is more attractive but is liable to crack because its bedding surfaces and joints are discontinuous in every direction. In the incertum, irregular rubble stones rest upon and overlap one another, producing masonry that is less handsome but stronger than the reticulatum. The types of masonry (structurae) are these: the reticulated (reticulatum), which everyone uses now, and the ancient one, which is called incertum. Of these, the most elegant is the reticulated, but it is prone to cracking because its beds and joints settle in all directions. In contrast, the uncertain, with its stones (camenta) interlocked course upon course, although less showy, is more solid than the reticulated. 2. utraque autem ex minutissimis sunt instruenda, uti materia ex calce et harena crebriter parietes satiati diutius contineantur. molli enim et rara potestate cum sint, exsiccant sugendo e materia sucum. cum autem superarit et abundarit copia 429

Both kinds should be built with very small stones, so that abundant mortar of lime and sand saturates the walls and holds them together longer. Soft, porous stones dry out by drawing moisture from the mortar. If lime and sand are plentiful, the wall retains more moisture and does not quickly weaken. But once the pores of the stones have absorbed the mortar’s moisture, the lime separates from the sand and disintegrates; the rubble can no longer adhere, and the walls become ruinous with age. Both are to be built with small stones, so that the walls, saturated by the frequent joints of lime and sand, may hold more firmly. For since the stones are rough and porous by nature, as they dry they absorb the water of the mortar and consume it to excess; but when there is an abundance of lime and sand, the wall, having more mortar, does not soon lose its cohesion but keeps the stones bound together. 3. id autem licet animadvertere etiam de nonnullis monumentis, quae circa urbem facta sunt e marmore seu lapidibus quadratis intrinsecusque medio calcata structuris, vetustate evanida facta materia caementorumque exsucta raritate, proruunt et coagmentorum ab ruina dissolutis iuncturis dissipantur. 3. It is falsely believed that this spring causes an effeminate condition in those who drink from it. I shall explain how that mistaken report spread. Its water cannot produce the softness and immodesty alleged: it is clear and excellent to taste. When Melas and Arevanias brought a joint colony from Argos and Troezen, they expelled the local Carians and Leleges. Driven into the mountains, these people gathered in bands, raided the settlers and devastated the district. One colonist later built a tavern beside the spring, attracted by the water’s quality, and by conducting his business drew the local people to it. Coming first singly and then in groups, they gradually exchanged their harsh customs for the gentler ways of the Greeks. Editorial note. — Chapter 8 is the principal ancient source on wall construction. Vitruvius contrasts the fashionable reticulate facing (opus reticulatum), elegant but prone to cracking, with the older random facing (opus incertum), less handsome but sounder; both, set in lime-and-sand mortar over a rubble core, are weakened if the core is coarse. He commends Greek practice: the squared, mortarless ashlar laid as isodomon (courses of equal height) or pseudisodomon (unequal courses), and the emplekton (ἔμπλεκτον), faced on both sides with bonding-stones (diatoni) tying the two leaves together — the weakness of the Roman two-leaf wall being precisely the want of such ties. The terms 444

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II reticulatum, incertum, isodomon, pseudisodomon and emplekton are retained, with glosses, in the Glossarium. Comparative critical apparatus — II.8. The terminological core requires retaining opus reticulatum, opus incertum, isodomum, pseudisodomum and ἔμπλεκτον as technical terms. In II.8.5–7 the critical text also transmits διατόνους for the pieces that pass through and bond the wall’s thickness. Isodomum denotes courses of equal height; pseudisodomum, unequal courses. Greek ἔμπλεκτον is explained by the relation between facings, lengthwise pieces and bonding through the thickness, not simply as “infill”. Architectural note — II.8. Vitruvius compares masonry systems with simultaneous attention to appearance, joints, beds, moisture absorption, transverse bonding and speed of execution. A constructional reading must preserve the distinctions between facing, core, cubilia, coagmenta and diatonoi; reducing everything to modern categories of “masonry” or “concrete” erases essential distinctions in the passage. Textual and constructional note — II.8. The description of bonds distinguishes transmitted terminology from graphic reconstruction. Ἰσόδομον, ψευδισόδομον, ἔμπλεκτον and διάτονοι are retained as Greek technical terms accompanied by a functional explanation. Equivalence with modern archaeological categories is offered only where secure and is not used to alter the Latin. Synthesis for architects — II.8. The central problem is not merely the appearance of the facing: Vitruvius considers cubilia, coagmenta, continuity of joints, transverse ties and the behavior of the core. The comparative apparatus avoids equating opus reticulatum and incertum without qualification with any visually similar modern construction. 445

I have described each class, the properties with which they seem to be endowed by nature, and the way in which they grow. Comparative critical apparatus — II.9. The chapter on timber retains the ancient physiological explanation in terms of moisture, heat, air and an earthy component. Favonius remains a seasonal reference, and the properties of abies, quercus, ulmus, populus, cupressus, pinus, alnus and larix are not translated into modern mechanical equivalents not formulated in the Latin. Recommendations for felling, seasoning and use are presented as ancient building technology, distinguishing empirical observation from causal explanation. Technical note — Materies. Here materies may mean construction timber rather than “matter” in the abstract. The sequence of species relates their imagined internal structure to behavior under load or in moisture and to specific architectural uses. Philological and constructional note — II.9. Materies is translated according to context as construction timber, not merely “matter”. The explanation of seasonal felling and seasoning is retained within its ancient physiological framework. Abies, quercus, aesculus, robur, ulmus, populus, salix, tilia, vitex, cupressus, pinus, alnus and larix are checked as names of timbers or species, avoiding excessively confident botanical equivalents where ancient identification is disputed. The first foothills of the Apennines rise from the Tyrrhenian Sea between the Alps and the outer regions of Etruria. The ridge curves through Italy, approaches the Adriatic coast in its central bend and continues towards the strait. Its nearer slope, facing Etruria and Campania, lies in sunlight and remains exposed to the sun’s course. The farther slope, facing the upper sea, looks north and is continually shaded. Trees growing there, nourished by moisture, become very large, and their veins swell with abundant sap. Once felled and hewn, they lose their vital force; as the veins stiffen and dry, their porous substance becomes weak and insubstantial. Such timber therefore lacks durability in buildings. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER II As far as I have been able to reason, I have explained the necessary building materials, the proportions of the natural elements that compose them, and the virtues and defects of each, so that these may not be unknown to those who are to build. Thus, those who can follow these precepts will be more prudent and will be able to choose, among the various types, the use of each in their works. The edition retains Vitruvius’s taxonomy without converting it into a modern botanical classification. Where transmission or geographical identification does not allow a secure equivalent, the Latin term is retained and explained in a note. Synthesis note for architects — Book II. The book constructs a coherent argumentative sequence: origins of building → constitution of matter → selection of brick, sand, lime, pozzolana and stone → masonry bonds → timber. This technical logic can be summarized for the contemporary reader without attributing later scientific categories to Vitruvius. Comparative apparatus — II.10. For the architect, the book constitutes an ancient theory of materials and their use in construction: selection, preparation, ageing, bonding, provenance and suitability for use. The edition preserves this technological logic without attributing chemistry, petrography, strength of materials or botany in modern formulation to Vitruvius. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI III — On temples: proportion and symmetry taken from the well-formed human body (homo ad circulum et quadratum), perfect numbers, the five species of temples according to the intercolumniation (pycnostyle, systyle, diastyle, areostyle, eustyle) and the rules of the Ionic order, with its bases, columns and capitals. 461

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER II Editorial note. — Book III opens the discussion of temples with the relation between symmetria, proportio and ἀναλογία. Comparison with the human body provides Vitruvius with a model of commensurability between parts and whole. The celebrated geometrical construction of the man in relation to the circle and square belongs to the text of 3.1.3; modern expressions such as “Vitruvian Man” or homo ad circulum et quadratum are used solely as historiographical designations, not as literal formulas from the treatise. Textual note — Book II. The Latin is checked against Krohn (1912). Material names, construction procedures, ancient units and the distinction between Vitruvius’s physical explanation and modern materials science are retained. Orthographical variation, editorial supplementation and substantive readings are treated separately; the antiquity of a practice does not establish the precise date of a surviving archaeological example. 462

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Preface 1. Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus. Is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum. Utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset! Si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, ⟨qui, etiam⟩si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur. Igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare. The Delphic Apollo150, through the responses of the Pythia, proclaimed Socrates the wisest of all men. Socrates is remembered as having said, with prudence and great learning, that men’s breasts ought to have been fitted with windows and left open, so that their thoughts would not remain hidden but be exposed to examination. Would that nature had followed his judgment and made them manifest and visible! Then not only would the merits or faults of minds be seen at a glance, but the knowledge of the various disciplines, placed before the eyes for examination, would not be exposed to uncertain judgments. The learned and knowledgeable would receive firm and lasting authority, and craftsmen themselves would attract confidence through their understanding: even if they were not wealthy, known through the long standing of their workshops, or furnished with favor in the forum and eloquence, their 150 The Temple of Apollo, also known as the Apollonion (Greek: Ἀπολλώνιον, Romanized: Apollṓnion), was an important part of the pan-Hellenic religious sanctuary located in central Greece at Delphi. The temple and the sanctuary in general were dedicated to one of the major Greek deities, Apollo, the god of archery, music, light, prophecy, the arts, and healing. 463

Since things are constituted otherwise, as nature willed, and men’s talents remain concealed within their breasts, people cannot judge the knowledge peculiar to each art, which lies deeply hidden. Note — Bk. 3, pref. 1. The image of a breast fitted with 'windows' to reveal one's thoughts goes back to the fable of Momus (cf. Lucian, Hermotimus 20); Vitruvius adapts the topos to protest that technical merit, hidden from view, is left at the mercy of favor and forensic eloquence rather than of true judgment. 2. This can be seen above all in the sculptors and painters of old. Those who enjoyed marks of distinction and the favor of recommendation remain in everlasting memory among posterity—Myron, Polyclitus151, Phidias152, 151 Polyclitus (Greek: Πολύκλειτος), called " the Elder " to distinguish him from Polyclitus the Younger, was a 5th-century BC Greek bronze sculptor born in Argos or Sicyon. Along with the famous Phidias, Myron, and Cresilas, he is one of the most important sculptors of classical antiquity. The 4th-century BC catalog attributed to Xenocrates (" Xenocratic Catalog "), which served as Pliny's guide to art, placed Polyclitus between Phidias and Myron. Polyclitus was most famous for his bronze statues of gods and athletes, apart from the enormous statue of the goddess Hera, intended for worship in the Heraion of Argos.
