THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III Lysippus153 and the others who won renown through their art. They achieved it because they made works for great cities, kings or noble citizens. Others, with no less zeal, talent and skill, made works no less admirably finished for citizens both noble and of modest means, yet obtained no remembrance: they were forsaken not by diligence or artistic skill, but by good fortune. Such were Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium and many more. Likewise among painters there were Aristomenes of Thasos, Polycles and Androcydes of Cyzicus, Theon of Magnesia and the others, who lacked neither diligence, artistic commitment nor skill, but whose standing was obstructed by a small patrimony, adverse fortune or the superiority of rivals in the competition for distinction. Editorial comparison — III, preface 1–3. The running Latin and translation follow the authorial Spanish constitution, agreeing here with Krohn (1912, 56 –58). In preface 1, Krohn transposes and reconstructs the clause about craftsmen within the hypothetical account of visible merit; Rose (1899, 62) retains a differently constituted negative clause after iudicare. In preface 2, Krohn prints Hegias and Androcydes <Cyzice>ni, whereas Rose (1899, 62) prints Teleas and <Andron Ephesii>. These are identified editorial differences, not new direct readings of Harley or Cotton. In preface 3, the previously truncated sentence potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione is restored in accordance with the authorial Spanish edition and Krohn. 3. Nec tamen est admirandum, si propter ignotitiam artis virtutes obscurantur, sed maxime indignandum, cum etiam saepe eblandiatur gratia conviviorum a veris iudiciis falsam probationem. Ergo, uti Socrati placuit, si ita sensus et sententiae scientiaeque disciplinis auctae perspicuae et perlucidae fuissent, non gratia neque ambitio valeret, sed si qui veris certisque laboribus doctrinarum pervenissent ad scientiam summam, eis ultro opera traderentur. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III ea non sunt inlustria neque apparentia in aspectu, ut putamus oportuisse, et animadverto potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione, potius his praeceptis editis ostendam nostrae scientiae virtutem. It is no wonder that merit is obscured through ignorance of the art; but it is especially a cause for indignation when favor won at banquets often coaxes a false approval from true judgment. As Socrates wished, had perceptions, opinions and knowledge enriched by the disciplines been clear and transparent, neither favor nor ambition would prevail: works would be entrusted spontaneously to those who had attained the highest knowledge through genuine and sound scholarly labor. Since these things are neither manifest nor visible, as we think they ought to be, and I observe that the unlearned more often surpass the learned through favor, I judge that I should not compete with the unlearned in ambition. I shall instead show the worth of our knowledge by publishing these precepts. 4. Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum exposui, et subieci causas quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi. deinde quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus <regionibus> singuli spirant deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui. item in secundo de materia quas habeat in operibus utilitates et quibus virtutibus e natura rerum est comparata peregi. nunc in tertio de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris dicam et uti oportet perscriptas exponam. Accordingly, Emperor, in the first book I set forth for you what the art is, what virtues it possesses, and in what disciplines the architect ought to be trained; I added the reasons why he must be skilled in them, distributed the whole of architecture by a division, and defined it by definitions. Then, treating what was first and most necessary, I explained by reasoned argument how, in laying out city walls, to choose healthy sites; I showed by linear diagrams which the winds are and from what regions each blows; I taught how the streets and lanes within the walls may be correctly laid out, and so brought the first book to 466

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III a close. In the second I dealt with materials—what advantages they afford in works, and with what qualities Nature has endowed them. Now, in the third, I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and set them forth, as is fitting, in full detail. Methodological note — Comparative apparatus. Rose, Krohn and Budé are used as comparable editorial layers, not as interchangeable authorities. A difference between editions is recorded only when it affects the constitution of the text, a technical term, numeral, proportion or architectural interpretation; simple modernizations of spelling are not inflated into variants. Comparative critical apparatus — III, preface. The preface is compared with Rose, Krohn and Pierre Gros’s Budé edition of Book III. The Socratic image of pectora fenestrata supplies a rhetorical framework for the visibility of professional merit. Vitruvius contrasts fame and social favor with scientia, doctrina and scripta; the edition avoids turning this authorial complaint into demonstrated biographical information. Names of artists and architects are retained according to the Latin text and distinguished from identifications or chronologies proposed by modern scholarship. Hermeneutic note — III, preface. The preface is not an independent digression: it prepares Book III through reflection on judgment, authority and knowledge. The transition from visible reputation to invisible technical knowledge anticipates the need for verifiable rules of symmetria and proportio in sacred architecture. 467

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Chapter 1 1. Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent. ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur. proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum. namque non potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis, nisi uti hominis bene figurati <> membrorum habuerit exactam rationem. The composition of temples depends on symmetria, whose principles architects must observe with the greatest care. Symmetria arises from proportion, which the Greeks call analogia (ἀναλογία). Proportion is the commensuration of the members and the whole of a work with a determined part as their common measure; from it the system of commensurability is established. No temple can have a coherent composition without symmetria and proportion, unless its members stand in an exact relationship comparable to that of a well-formed human body. 2. Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, ⟨a medio pectore⟩ ad summum verticem quartae. Ipsius autem oris altitudinis tertia est pars ab imo mento ad imas nares, nasum ab imis naribus ad finem mediûm superciliorum tantundem, ab ea fine ad imas radices capilli frons efficitur item tertiae partis. Pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae. Reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti. For nature has so composed the human body that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead at the roots of the hair, is a tenth part of the stature; the outstretched hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, as much again. The head, from the chin to the crown, is an eighth part; from the top of the breast, including the neck, to the roots of the hair, a sixth; and from the middle of the breast to the crown, a fourth. Of the height of the face itself, a third runs from the base of the chin to the underside of the nose; the nose, from its base to the line of the brows, as much again; and thence to the roots of the 468

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III hair the forehead is formed, likewise a third. The foot is a sixth part of the body's height; the forearm a fourth; and the breast likewise a fourth. The other members too have their proportions of commensurability, of which the ancient painters and the celebrated sculptors availed themselves to win great and boundless praise. 3. similiter vero sacrarum aedium membra ad universam totius magnitudinis summam ex partibus singulis convenientissimum debent habere commensus responsum. item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus. namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus manibus et pedibus pansis circinique conlocatum centrum in umbilico eius, circumagendo rotundationem utrarumque manuum et pedum digiti linea tangentur. non minus quemadmodum schema rotundationis in corpore efficitur, item quadrata designatio in eo invenietur. nam si a pedibus imis ad summum caput mensum erit eaque mensura relata fuerit ad manus pansas, invenietur eadem latitudo uti altitudo, quemadmodum areae quae ad normam sunt quadratae. Similarly, each part of a temple must bear a most fitting correspondence of commensurability to the total magnitude of the whole. The body’s natural central point is the navel. If a man lies on his back with his hands and feet outstretched, and the center of a pair of compasses is placed at his navel, the circle described will touch the fingers of both hands and the toes of both feet. A square figure can be found in the body just as a circle can: if the distance from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head is measured and transferred to the outstretched hands, the breadth will equal the height, as in surfaces squared with a set square.154 In the same way, the members of sacred temples must maintain a perfectly adjusted correspondence of commensurability, each in relation to the others and all in relation to the total magnitude. Likewise, the natural center of the body is the navel. For if a man be laid on his back, with his hands and feet outstretched, and the point of a compass be placed 154Ad normam means ‘to the square’. The norma (γνώμων) is the builder’s square; the term recurs technically at 7.3.5. The relation between bodily height and the span of the outstretched arms underlies the discussion of the homo quadratus and temple proportion. 469

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III upon his navel, the circle thereby described will touch the tips of the fingers of both hands and of the toes. And just as the body yields a circular outline, so too a square figure may be found within it: for if the distance from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head be measured, and that measure be applied to the outstretched hands, the breadth will be found equal to the height, as in a perfect square.155 The state of the interpretive question. The passage of the human body inscribed in the circle and the square (3.1.3) is the root of a long modern interpretive tradition, with which this edition engages without uncritical adherence. Rudolf Wittkower (Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism, 1949) read in Vitruvius the foundation of the humanist system of harmonic proportions binding man, building, and universe. Joseph Rykwert (The Dancing Column, 1996) explored the anthropomorphic root of the orders and the 'bodily' meaning of the column. Alberto Pérez-Gómez (Architecture and the Crisis of Modern Science, 1983) showed that Vitruvian sciographia is not modern linear perspective but a perception of the building's totality in depth. Indra Kagis McEwen (Vitruvius: Writing the Body of Architecture, 2003) set the treatise within the political-religious framework of Augustus and the body-architecture analogy. And Pierre Gros, editor of the Budé, has established the textual criticism and Vitruvius's relation to the tradition of the Greek treatises. This edition takes these contributions as its framework, distinguishes the datum of the text from its symbolic reading, and marks as 'the author's personal hermeneutic proposal' whatever exceeds what the text asserts. Recent secondary bibliography (post-2010). To the classic studies there have been added, in the last decade, contributions that renew the reading of Vitruvius and that this edition takes into account: Marden Fitzpatrick Nichols, Author and Audience in Vitruvius' De architectura (Cambridge, 2017), the first study in English to treat the De architectura as a literary work and to examine the authorial persona and the rhetoric of decor (Books VI–VII); Mireille 155 The classic passage on inscribing the human body in geometrical figures (homo ad circulum et ad quadratum). This passage and the preceding one (3.1.2) gave rise to Leonardo da Vinci’s celebrated drawing (c. 1490, Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice). Leonardo, however, does not inscribe the two figures concentrically, as is often assumed, but moves the center of the square to the pubis, departing from the letter of Vitruvius’s text. Compare 3.1.2–3 and Pliny, Natural History 7.77, on the body’s commensurability. 470

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III Courrént, Vitruve auctor: L'œuvre littéraire de Vitruve et sa réception dans la littérature (Ausonius, 2019); and John Oksanish, Vitruvian Man: Rome under Construction (Oxford, 2019), which sets the treatise within the ideological construction of Augustan Rome. On the technical-archaeometric side, the ROMACONS project (J. P. Oleson et al., Building for Eternity, 2014) experimentally verified the hydraulic concrete. These works, together with the Budé volumes directed by Pierre Gros, constitute the current state of the question. Critical note — III.1.3. The adopted text reads item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus, followed by namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus. These words describe the navel as the center of the circle traced around the outstretched body. No specific reading of Harley MS 2767 is established by this note. The relation to Leonardo’s drawing, made around 1490 and now in the Gallerie dell’Accademia in Venice, belongs to the history of the passage’s reception. Possible routes through the printed edition associated with Sulpicius or through Francesco di Giorgio Martini require separate historical documentation. See Vitruvius, De architectura 3.1.3; Martin Kemp, Leonardo da Vinci: The Marvellous Works of Nature and Man (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006), 96–99. Critical note — III.1.3. Krohn’s text gives “item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus. namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus…”. There is therefore no basis for treating namque as a corruption or dittography. The passage describes, successively, the relation of the body to a circumference centered on the navel and the equality between bodily height and arm-span that permits comparison with a square. Renaissance reception, above all Leonardo da Vinci’s drawing now known as Vitruvian Man, belongs to the history of reception and must be distinguished from establishing the Latin text. Comparative note — Bk. 3.1.2–3 (homo ad circulum et quadratum). The treatise's most celebrated passage: the well-proportioned body, laid out with limbs extended, inscribed—with its center at the navel (umbilicus)—in the circle drawn with a compass (circinus) and, at once, in the square. Text and commentary should be distinguished: the adopted text speaks of a «homo bene figuratus», without the formula «ad circulum et quadratum», which is a fixture of the editorial tradition (see the critical note to 3.1.3). The reference editions 471

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III agree in rendering circinus as «compass» and in keeping the navel as the circle's center, but differ in commentary: Granger (Loeb, 1931) translates the geometric procedure literally; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) specify the construction and its architectural import; Gros (Budé) sets the figure within the tradition of micro-macrocosmic analogy and proportion; Corso and Romano (Einaudi) expand the historical commentary. The present edition offers its own translation, close to the adopted Latin and to the authorial Spanish translation, adopting no external version. [Historical-architectural note] The image founded a long posterity: Cesare Cesariano's homo ad quadratum (1521), Leonardo da Vinci's drawing (ca. 1490), which shifted the center to the pubis to reconcile circle and square, and, in the twentieth century, Le Corbusier's Modulor. Comparative note — III.1.2–3. Vitruvius takes the homo bene figuratus as a comparison for architectural commensurability. The Latin text does not contain the formula homo ad circulum et quadratum: this is a later historiographical designation. Nor does it state that circle and square must share the same geometrical center. The navel is the center of the circumference described by the outstretched limbs; comparison with the square, by contrast, proceeds from the equality of height and arm-span. Architectural and philological note — Homo bene figuratus. The human body serves as an analogy of commensurability: each member has a ratio to the whole. The text does not prescribe that temples should literally reproduce a human figure, nor does it contain the modern expression “Vitruvian Man”. Graphic reconstructions of circle and square belong to the history of reception and must be labeled accordingly. 4. ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem. igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, <> maxime in aedibus deorum, <⟨quod eorum⟩> operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere. Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members answer proportionally to the whole figure, the ancients seem to have established with good reason that in the execution of works too each of the members should keep 472

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III an exact commensurability with the aspect of the whole figure. And so, though they handed down orders of proportion for works of every kind, they did so above all in the temples of the gods, whose merits and faults are wont to endure for ever. Note — Bk. 3.1.2–3. The canon of bodily proportions (face 1/10, head 1/8, foot 1/6…) and the double inscription of the well-formed man in the circle—its center at the navel—and in the square ground the analogy between the human body and the temple. On its afterlife, from Leonardo to Le Corbusier, see the introductory study 'Vitruvius Today.' 5. Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt. Perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero [ab palmo pes] est inventus. Si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex ⟨X⟩ singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis. Simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri. They also derived from the members of the body the units of measure required in every work—the finger, palm, foot and cubit—and distributed them according to the perfect number, which the Greeks call teleion (τέλειον). The ancients established ten as the perfect number, for it was discovered from the number of fingers on the hands. Since the fingers articulated in both hands amount by nature to ten, Plato too considered ten perfect because the decad is completed from ten single units, called monades (μονάδες) by the Greeks. Once eleven or twelve is reached, however, the excess cannot be perfect until the second decad is attained; single units are particles of that number. 6. Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex. Cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; 473

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα. The mathematicians, arguing the contrary, called six the perfect number because its constituent divisions correspond to it: a sixth is one, a third two and a half three; two-thirds, called dimoiron (δίμοιρον), are four; five-sixths, called pentamoiron (πεντάμοιρον), are five; and the complete number is six. In the progression beyond six, adding one produces seven, the ephekton (ἔφεκτον); adding a third produces eight, the epitritos (ἐπίτριτος); adding a half produces nine, the sesquialter or hemiolios (ἡμιόλιος); adding two-thirds produces ten, the epidimoiron (ἐπιδίμοιρον); adding five produces eleven, the epipempton (ἐπίπεμπτον); and twelve, made from two complete sixes, is diplasion (διπλάσιον), the double. Critical note — III.1.5–6. The discussion of six, ten and their proportional fractions is retained in full according to the authorial Spanish edition and Krohn (1912, 60–61). Krohn marks ab palmo pes for deletion in III.1.5 and supplies ⟨X⟩ before singularibus rebus; Rose (1899, 65) prints ab palmo pes without those deletion brackets. In III.1.6 Rose (1899, 66) prints a bracketed section from bessem through διπλάσιον, and his apparatus describes it as an interpolation from an ancient mathematical book. Krohn does not enclose the corresponding numerical excursus in those brackets. Rose’s assessment is thus documented as his editorial judgment; it is not evidence of an independently inspected manuscript omission. Latin fractional terminology and Greek names of ratios are retained, since the two systems must not be collapsed into an unsupported modern equivalence. Critical note — III.1.6. The excursus on six and numerical ratios is retained in Krohn’s text. This edition will not call it an interpolation or a spurious passage without expressly documenting a decision in the critical apparatus of the edition cited. The terminology combines Latin fractions with Greek proportional vocabulary; the Greek terms are therefore retained where a single modern equivalent would be reductive. 474

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III 7. Non minus etiam, quod pes hominis altitudinis sextam habet partem, (ita etiam, ex eo quod perficitur pedum numero corporis ⟨altitudo, veteribus columnis basis scapi elata⟩ sexies altitudines terminavit) eum perfectum constituerunt, cubitumque animadverterunt ex sex palmis constare digitisque XXIIII. Ex eo etiam videntur civitates Graecorum fecisse, quemadmodum cubitus est sex palmorum, in drachma, qua nummo uterentur, aereos signatos uti asses ex aequo sex, quos obolos appellant, quadrantesque obolorum, quae alii dichalca, nonnulli trichalca dicunt, pro digitis viginti quattuor in drachma constituisse. They also regarded six as perfect because the human foot is a sixth of the body’s height (the body’s height is completed by six foot-lengths; likewise, in ancient columns, the height of the shaft with its base was determined as sixfold). They observed that the cubit comprises six palms and twenty-four fingers. The Greek cities appear to have followed the same pattern: just as the cubit contains six palms, they established six equally valued bronze pieces, like asses, in the drachma which they used as currency, calling them obols; quarter-obols, called dichalca by some and trichalca by others, numbered twenty-four to the drachma, corresponding to the fingers. This is also confirmed by the foot’s being a sixth of human height: since the body’s stature is determined by six foot-lengths, they considered that number perfect. They observed that the cubit consists of six palms, or twenty-four fingers. The Greek cities appear to have acted accordingly: just as the cubit contains six palms, they struck six bronze coins of the as type, called obols, to the drachma which they used as currency. The quarter-obols, called dichalca by some and trichalca by others, corresponded to the twenty-four fingers of the drachma. 8. Nostri autem primo fecerunt ⟨perfectum⟩ antiquum numerum et in denario denos aeris constituerunt, et ea re compositio nominis ad hodiernum diem denarium retinet. Etiamque quarta pars quod efficiebatur ex duobus assibus et tertio semisse, sestertium vocitaverunt. Postea autem quam animadverterunt utrosque numeros esse perfectos, et sex et decem, utrosque in unum coiecerunt et fecerunt perfectissimum decusis sexis. Huius autem rei auctorem invenerunt pedem. E cubito enim cum dempti sunt palmi duo, relinquitur pes quattuor 475

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III palmorum, palmus autem habet quattuor digitos. Ita efficitur, ut habeat pes sedecim digitos et totidem asses aeracius denarius. Our own people, on the other hand, first adopted the ancient perfect number and fixed ten bronze asses to the denarius; and hence the composition of the name preserves to this day the 'denarius.' And the quarter part, which was made up of two asses and a semis, they called the sestertius. But afterwards, observing that both numbers were perfect—six and ten—they combined them into one and formed the most perfect number, sixteen. Of this they found the foot to be the author: for, when two palms are taken from the cubit, there remains the foot of four palms, and the palm has four fingers; so it comes about that the foot has sixteen fingers, and the denarius as many bronze asses. Note — Bk. 3.1.7–8. Vitruvius derives the measures from the body: the foot (16 digits = 4 palms), the cubit (24 digits = 6 palms), and relates them to the monetary systems—the Greek drachma divided into six obols, the Roman denarius of sixteen asses. The commensurability of these units underpins the doctrine of symmetria. 9. Ergo si convenit ex articulis hominis numerum inventum esse et ex membris separatis ad universam corporis speciem ratae partis commensus fieri responsum, relinquitur ut suspiciamus eos qui etiam aedes deorum inmortalium constituentes ita membra operum ordinaverunt ut proportionibus et symmetriis separatae atque universae convenientes efficerentur eorum distributiones. Therefore, if it is agreed that number was found from the joints of the human body, and that between the several members and the whole aspect of the body there is a correspondence of commensurability according to a determined part, it remains for us to admire those who, in building the temples of the immortal gods also, so ordered the members of their works that, taken severally and together, they might be made concordant in their proportions and symmetries throughout the distribution of the whole edifice. Editorial note. — Chapter 1 contains the most famous proposition of the whole treatise: that the design of a temple rests on symmetria (commensurability), and that the model for it is the proportion of the well-formed human body (homo bene figuratus). Vitruvius lists the canonical ratios — the face a tenth of the height, the head an eighth, the foot a sixth — and observes that a man lying with limbs outstretched can be inscribed in both a circle (centered on the navel) and 476

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III a square. This is the textual canon that Leonardo would later draw; it is not itself the “Vitruvian Man” (see Glossarium, homo bene figuratus, and the Theses, no. 4). The chapter also reports the ancient debate over the perfect numbers — six (the foot-module) and ten (the count of the fingers) — and their reconciliation in sixteen, anticipating the Renaissance theory of proportion. Textual apparatus — III.1. The homo bene figuratus passage is checked fraction by fraction: facies, palma, pes, cubitus, pectus and total height. Equality between height and arm-span, and the constructions of circle and square, are maintained in accordance with what the text explicitly states. Any additional geometrical system is identified as a reconstruction. Philological note — Symmetria, proportio and analogia. In this chapter, “proportion” must not absorb symmetria. The functional distinction between the relationship of a part, the commensurability of members and a common ratio is preserved. The Spanish version avoids arbitrarily alternating “symmetry”, “proportion” and “modulation” when the Latin changes its term. Comparative critical apparatus — III.1.1–9. Symmetria, proportio, commodulatio and ἀναλογία are not reduced to modern synonyms. Proportio denotes a measurable relationship of parts; symmetria, the ordered commensurability of members with one another and with the whole; commodulatio emphasizes their common reference to a module. In III.1.3 the transmitted text places the bodily circle’s center at the navel, whereas the relation to the square is constructed from equality between height and arm-span. The edition preserves the sequence of six and ten as an ancient history of number and measure, without attributing to it a universal mathematical theory foreign to the passage. 477

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Chapter 2 1. Aedium autem principia sunt e quibus constat figurarum aspectus. ea primum in antis, quod graece ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν dicitur, deinde prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, <dipteros,> hypaethros. horum exprimuntur formationes his rationibus. Archaeological note — III.2, temple types. Vitruvius classifies temples by the arrangement of their columns: in antis (naos en parastasin), prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral, pseudodipteral, dipteral and hypaethral. Archaeology illustrates each type: Vitruvius himself exemplifies the in antis temple, with two columns between the antae, by the “Three Fortunes” near Rome’s Colline Gate; the peripteral scheme, with six columns at the front and eleven on each side, is that of the canonical Greek temple; the pseudodipteral arrangement, octastyle with a single row where a double row could stand, is exemplified by the temple of Diana at Magnesia, by Hermogenes of Alabanda, and that of Apollo, by Menesthes; the dipteral, with its double colonnade, and the hypaethral, decastyle and open to the sky, complete the sequence. The pseudoperipteral type—columns engaged in the cella wall to simulate a peripteral arrangement, defined by Vitruvius in 4.8—was the most widespread in the Roman world. Its best-preserved examples are the temple of Portunus in the Forum Boarium, Ionic and dating to the late second century BC, and above all the Maison Carrée at Nîmes, a Corinthian hexastyle prostyle temple of around AD 2, the world’s best-preserved Roman temple. The principles of temples, on which the aspect of their forms depends, are these: first the in antis, which in Greek is called ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν (a temple between antae); then the prostyle, the amphiprostyle, the peripteral, the pseudodipteral, the dipteral, and the hypaethral. Their configurations are expressed by the following rules. 2. in antis erit aedes, cum habebit in fronte antas parietum qui cellam circumcludunt, et inter antas in medio columnas duas, supraque fastigium symmetria ea conlocatum quae in hoc libro fuerit perscripta. huius autem exemplar erit ad tres Fortunas ex tribus quod est proxime portam Collinam. A temple is in antis when the front has the antae of the walls enclosing the cella, with two columns between them and a pediment above, arranged 478

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III according to the symmetria prescribed in this book. Of the three temples at the Three Fortunes, the one nearest the Colline Gate provides an example. A temple is in antis when its facade presents the antae of the walls enclosing the cella, with two columns between them and, above, a pediment arranged according to the relations of symmetria prescribed in this book. At the Three Fortunes, the temple nearest the Colline Gate is an example of this type. 3. prostylos omnia habet quemadmodum in antis, columnas autem contra antas angulares duas, supraque epistylia quemadmodum et in antis, et dextra ac sinistra in versuris singula. huius exemplar est in insula Tiberina in aede Iovis et Fauni. The prostyle has all the features of the in antis temple, but with two corner columns opposite the antae and architraves above, as in the in antis, with a single architrave return on each side, right and left. An example stands on Tiber Island, in the temple of Jupiter and Faunus. Architectural and textual note — III.2.3. The phrase et dextra ac sinistra in versuris singula continues the description of the epistylia, the architraves: singula is neuter plural. the Spanish edition’s translation adds “one column on each side” in this clause; the Latin supplies no additional noun for columns there. The English keeps the architrave returns explicit instead of adding a further pair of columns. This is a correction of the grammatical and architectural reference, not an emendation of the Latin printed by Krohn (1912, 63) and Rose (1899, 68). 4. amphiprostylos omnia habet ea quae prostylos, praetereaque habet in postico ad eundem modum columnas et fastigium. The amphiprostyle has all that the prostyle has, and besides, at the rear, columns and a pediment arranged in the same way. The amphiprostyle has everything that the prostyle has, together with columns and a pediment at the rear, arranged in the same way. 5. Peripteros autem erit, quae habebit in fronte et postico senas columnas, in lateribus cum angularibus undenas. Ita autem sint hae columnae conlocatae, ut intercolumnii latitudinis intervallum sit a parietibus circum ad extremos ordines columnarum, habeatque ambulationem circa cellam aedis, 479

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III quemadmodum est sine postico in porticu Metelli Iovis Statoris Hermodori et Mariana Honoris et Virtutis a Mucio facta. A peripteral temple has six columns at the front and rear, and eleven on each side including the corner columns. Arrange them so that a space equal to one intercolumniation separates the walls from the outer rows of columns all around, providing a walk around the cella. The examples, without a rear part in the adopted wording, are the temple of Jupiter Stator by Hermodorus in the Portico of Metellus and Marius’s temple of Honor and Virtue, built by Mucius. 6. Pseudodipteros autem sic conlocatur, ut in fronte et postico sint columnae octonae, in lateribus cum angularibus quinae denae. Sint autem parietes cellae contra quaternas columnas medianas in fronte et postico. Ita duorum intercolumniorum et imae crassitudinis columnae spatium erit ab parietibus circa ad extremos ordines columnarum. Huius exemplar Romae non est, sed Magnesiae Dianae Hermogenis Alabandei et Apollinis a Menesthe facta. The pseudodipteral is arranged with eight columns at the front and rear, and fifteen on each side including the corner columns. The cella walls stand opposite the four central columns at the front and rear. A space of two intercolumniations plus the lower column diameter thus lies between the walls and the outer rows of columns all around. There is no example at Rome, but there is the temple of Diana at Magnesia, the work of Hermogenes of Alabanda, and that of Apollo, built by Menesthes. Textual note — III.2.5–6. Krohn (1912, 63), followed by the authorial Spanish edition, transposes sine postico before the examples beginning in porticu Metelli; Rose (1899, 68) places it after Honoris et Virtutis. The different scope is preserved in the adopted translation rather than silently settled by an archaeological identification. In III.2.6 Krohn prints Hermogenis Alabandei, identifying Hermogenes as Alabandean; Rose prints Hermogenis, Alabandis etiam Apollinis, locating the temple of Apollo at Alabanda. The Spanish edition follows Krohn. Menesthes is the named architect of Apollo’s temple, not Hermogenes. These are differences in editorial constitution and punctuation, not newly collated manuscript readings. 7. dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a Chersiphrone constituta. 480

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III The dipteral is octastyle both in the pronaos and at the rear, but about the temple it has double rows of columns—as is the temple of Quirinus, of the Doric order, and that of Diana at Ephesus, of the Ionic order, built by Chersiphron. 8. hypaethros vero decastylos est in pronao et postico. reliqua omnia eadem habet quae dipteros, sed interiore parte columnas in altitudine duplices, remotas a parietibus ad circumitionem ut porticus peristyliorum. medium autem sub divo est sine tecto. Aditus valvarum ex utraque parte in pronao et postico. huius item exemplar Romae non est, sed Athenis octastylos ex templo Olympio. The hypaethral temple is decastyle in the pronaos and at the rear. In all other respects it resembles the dipteral, but inside it has columns in two tiers, set away from the walls to provide a circuit like the porticoes of peristyles. The center is open to the sky and unroofed. There are doorways at both ends, in the pronaos and at the rear. There is no example at Rome; at Athens the text gives the octastyle temple of Olympian Zeus. Note — Bk. 3.2. The typology (in antis, prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral, pseudodipteral, dipteral, hypaethral) derives from Greek theory. The examples range from Rome—the three Fortunes, the Tiber Island, the portico of Metellus —to Asia Minor, where Hermogenes of Priene (2nd c. BC) fixed the symmetries of the Ionic pseudodipteral, a recurring authority in this book. Archaeological note — III.2. Vitruvius’s classification here rests on the arrangement of the colonnade in relation to the cella and its fronts. The ancient technical terms—in antis, prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros—should be retained, and each form explained from the text’s own definition, without projecting later archaeological taxonomies on to Vitruvius. Krohn includes dipteros in the sequence; hypaethros is defined subsequently by its particular arrangement and must not be confused with a supposed “dipteral-epipteral” type. Note — III.2. Vitruvian typology distinguishes in antis, prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros according to the arrangement of columns and cella. The examples combine Roman and Greek buildings. Modern archaeological identifications and the chronology of each monument must remain separate from the typological definition provided by the Latin text. 481

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Architectural note — III.2. The types in antis, prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros classify the relation of the cella to its fronts and surrounding colonnades. The categories of III.3 instead classify the spacing of columns. The two taxonomies are complementary and must not be confused. Modern archaeological identifications and dates remain separate from the definitions in the Latin text. Textual apparatus — III.2. The typological sequence is retained with its Greek or Latinised terms. The supplement <dipteros>, wherever it forms part of the adopted critical text, must remain typographically visible in the apparatus. The number of columns on each front and flank is checked against the verbal description before any diagram is validated. Note on figures — Temples. Figures of in antis, prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros and hypaethros temples are not used circularly to “correct” the text. The reading is established first; only then is the graphic reconstruction checked for compatibility. Comparative critical apparatus — III.2. The sequence in antis/ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν, prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, <dipteros> and hypaethros is retained as a technical taxonomy. <Dipteros> in the opening enumeration must be marked as an editorial supplement wherever the text is constituted in that way, although the type is developed immediately afterwards. Column numbers and monumental examples are reviewed as part of the typological argument; later archaeological identifications are presented separately. 482

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III Chapter 3 1. Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos intervallorum iusta distributione. There are five kinds of temples, whose names are these: pycnostyle, with closely set columns; systyle, with somewhat greater spacing; diastyle, with the columns farther apart than is fitting; araeostyle, with wide and sparse intercolumniations; and eustyle, with a just distribution of the intervals. Vitruvius distinguishes five kinds of temples by their intercolumniations: pycnostyle (pycnostylos), with very closely set columns; systyle (systylos), with somewhat more generous intervals; diastyle (diastylos), with wider separations; araeostyle (araeostylos), with columns farther apart than is fitting; and eustyle (eustylos), characterized by a proportionate distribution of the intervals. Textual note — III.3.1, 5 and 9. The two Spanish formulations in the Spanish edition do not distribute the qualification “farther apart than is fitting” in the same way. Its running Latin and first translation follow Krohn (1912, 64), attaching amplius quam oportet inter se diductis to diastylos. Rose (1899, 69) instead attaches rarius quam oportet inter se diductis to araeostylos; the Spanish edition’s explanatory parallel follows this latter distribution. The English preserves both authorial paragraphs separately and records the difference, rather than merging the two editorial constitutions. The varicae restored in III.3.5 follows Krohn (1912, 65), whose apparatus attributes the reading to Turnebus; ⟨improviso⟩ in III.3.9 is marked as Krohn’s supplement (1912, 66). Both belong to the authorial Spanish edition’s adopted constitution and are not presented as newly verified manuscript words. 2. ergo pycnostylos est cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae. item systylos est in qua duarum columnarum crassitudo in intercolumnio poterit conlocari, et spirarum plinthides aeque magnae sint ei spatio quod fuerit inter duas plinthides, quemadmodum est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae. 483

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Thus the pycnostyle is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be inserted, as in the temple of the Divine Julius, that of Venus in Caesar's forum, and any others composed in this way. The systyle, in turn, is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of two columns can be placed, and in which the plinths of the bases are as large as the space that lies between two plinths, as in the temple of Fortuna Equestris, near the stone theater, and the rest composed on the same principles. 3. haec utraque genera vitiosum habent usum. matres enim familiarum cum ad supplicationem gradibus ascendunt, non possunt per intercolumnia amplexae adire nisi ordines fecerint, item valvarum aspectus abstruditur columnarum crebritate ipsaque signa obscurantur, item circa aedem propter angustias inpediuntur ambulationes. Both these kinds have a faulty use. For the matrons, when they mount the steps in supplication, cannot pass through the intercolumniations arm in arm, but only in single file; moreover, the view of the doors is obstructed by the crowding of the columns, and the statues themselves are darkened; and likewise, owing to the narrowness, the walks around the temple are impeded. 4. diastyli autem haec erit compositio, cum trium columnarum crassitudinem intercolumnio interponere possumus, tamquam est Apollinis et Dianae aedis. haec dispositio hanc habet difficultatem quod epistylia propter intervallorum magnitudinem franguntur. The arrangement of the diastyle will be this: when we can interpose in the intercolumniation the thickness of three columns, as in the temple of Apollo and Diana. This disposition has the drawback that the architraves break on account of the great width of the intervals. 5. In araeostylis autem nec lapideis nec marmoreis epistyliis uti datur, sed inponendae de materia trabes perpetuae. Et ipsarum aedium species sunt varicae, barycephalae, humiles, latae, ornanturque signis fictilibus aut aereis inauratis earum fastigia tuscanico more, uti est ad Circum Maximum Cereris et Herculis Pompeiani, item Capitolii. In araeostyles it is not possible to use architraves of stone or marble; instead, continuous timber beams must be laid on. The very aspect of such temples is splayed, top-heavy, low and broad, and their pediments are adorned with figures of terracotta or gilded bronze, in the Tuscan manner—as in the 484

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III temple of Ceres near the Circus Maximus, that of Hercules Pompeianus, and the Capitol. In araeostyle temples, stone or marble architraves cannot be used: continuous timber beams must be placed on the columns. According to Vitruvius, these temples have a barycephala appearance—a visually heavy upper part—and are low and broad. Their pediments are adorned in the Tuscan manner with figures of terracotta or gilded bronze. He cites as examples the temple of Ceres beside the Circus Maximus, that of Hercules Pompeianus and the Capitol. Note — Bk. 3.3 (araeostyle). The araeostyle—low, broad, and 'top-heavy,' with wooden architraves and terracotta or gilt-bronze ornament 'in the Tuscan manner' (tuscanico more)—is associated in the passage with the Tuscan manner of building; the Republican Capitol is its chief example. Cf. Vitr. IV.7, where the Tuscan temple is set out in detail. Note — III.3.5. The Latin adjective transliterated from Greek, barycephala, here describes the formal effect of low, broad buildings with a visually heavy roof or crowning element. The passage should not become a general definition of the “archaic Etruscan temple”: Vitruvius establishes a formal connection with tuscanico more and supplies concrete examples; the historical and archaeological category is later. 6. Reddenda nunc est eustyli ratio, quae maxime probabilis et ad usum et ad speciem et ad firmitatem rationes habet explicatas. namque facienda sunt in intervallis spatia duarum columnarum et quartae partis columnae crassitudinis, mediumque intercolumnium unum quod erit in fronte, alterum quod in postico, trium columnarum crassitudine. sic enim habebit et figurationis aspectum venustum et aditus usum sine inpeditionibus et circa cellam ambulatio auctoritatem. It now remains to set forth the method of the eustyle, which is the most commendable and has the principles of use, appearance, and stability fully worked out. For in the intervals there must be made spaces of two and a quarter column-thicknesses, and a single central intercolumniation—one at the front and one at the rear—of three column-thicknesses. For thus it will have at once a graceful aspect in its figure, a convenient and unhindered approach, and a dignity in the walk about the cella. 485

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III 7. huius autem rei ratio explicabitur sic. frons loci quae in aede constituta fuerit, si tetrastylos facienda fuerit, dividatur in partes XI S praeter crepidines et proiecturas spirarum, si sex erit columnarum, in partes XVIII. si octastylos constituetur, dividatur in XXIV et semissem. item ex his partibus sive tetrastyli sive hexastyli sive octastyli una pars sumatur eaque erit modulus. cuius moduli unus erit crassitudinis columnarum. intercolumnia singula, praeter media, modulorum duorum et moduli quartae partis. mediana in fronte et postico singula ternûm modulorum. ipsarum columnarum altitudo modulorum VIIII et dimidiae moduli partis. ita ex ea divisione intercolumnia altitudinesque columnarum habebunt iustam rationem. The method of this will be explained as follows. The front of the site laid out for the temple, if it is to be tetrastyle, let it be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the crepidines (steps or platform margins) and the projections of the column bases; if it is of six columns, into 18 parts; if octastyle is to be set out, into 24½. Then, from these parts—whether of a tetrastyle, a hexastyle, or an octastyle—let one be taken, and that will be the module. The thickness of the columns will be one module. The intercolumniations, except the central ones, will each be two and a quarter modules; the central ones, at front and rear, three modules each. The height of the columns themselves will be nine and a half modules. Thus, by this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will keep a just proportion. 8. huius exemplar Romae nullum habemus, sed in Asia Teo hexastylon Liberi Patris. Eas autem symmetrias constituit Hermogenes, qui etiam primus invenit octastylon pseudodipterive rationem. ex dipteri enim aedis symmetria distulit interiores ordines columnarum XXXIV eaque ratione sumptus operasque compendii fecit. is in medio ambulationi laxamentum egregie circa cellam fecit, de aspectuque nihil inminuit sed sine desiderio supervacuorum conservavit auctoritatem totius operis distributione. Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia the hexastyle of Father Liber at Teos. These symmetries were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the method of the octastyle pseudodipteral. For from the symmetry of the dipteral temple he removed the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by this means he saved expense and labor. In the middle he made an admirable open ambulatory about the cella, and in no way 486

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III diminished the appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous, he preserved the dignity of the whole work in its distribution. Note — Bk. 3.3. Of the five kinds of intercolumniation Vitruvius prefers the eustyle, whose modular system (front divided into equal parts; column = 1 module; intercolumniations of 2¼ and 3 modules) he attributes to Hermogenes, whom he also credits with inventing the octastyle pseudodipteral, saving thirtyfour columns over the dipteral. Textual note — III.3.8. the Spanish edition’s running Latin and Krohn’s printed text (1912, 66, line 4) give XXXIV, thirty-four; Rose’s printed text (1899, 71, line 13) gives XXXVIII, thirty-eight. Krohn’s apparatus explicitly records “xxxiv Phil: xxxviii x”, identifying thirty-four as the editorial reading associated with Philander and distinguishing it from the reading labeled x. This confirms the choice of thirty-four in the authorial base and corrects the Spanish comparative note’s attribution of thirty-eight to the current Perseus text of Krohn. Neither H nor Cotton is independently assigned a reading here. Hermogenes’s association with the pseudodipteral scheme belongs to Vitruvius’s own account. 9. Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo est inventa, ut aspectus propter asperitatem intercolumniorum habeat auctoritatem, praeterea, si ex ⟨improviso⟩ imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum laxamento liberam moram. Haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris aedium dispositionibus! Quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum Hermogenes fecisse reliquisseque fontes, unde posteri possent haurire disciplinarum rationes. For the principle of the pteroma and the arrangement of columns about the temple was devised so that the appearance might have dignity through the relief created by the intercolumniations, and further, that if a sudden downpour of rain should overtake and shut in a throng of people, they might have within the temple and about the cella an ample and free place to wait. All this is worked out thus in the arrangements of pseudodipteral temples. Wherefore Hermogenes seems to have acted with keen and great sagacity in the execution of his works, and to have left springs from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines. 487

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III 10. Aedibus araeostylis columnae sic sunt faciendae uti crassitudines earum sint partis octavae ad altitudines. item in diastylo dimetienda est altitudo columnae in partes octo et dimidiam et unius partis columnae crassitudo conlocetur. in systylo altitudo dividatur in novem et dimidiam partem et ex eis una ad crassitudinem columnae detur. item in pycnostylo dividenda est altitudo in ⟨partes⟩ decem et eius una pars facienda est columnae crassitudo. eustyli autem aedis columnae, uti systyli, in novem partes altitudo dividatur et dimidiam partem et eius una pars constituatur in crassitudine imi scapi. ita habebitur pro rata parte intercolumniorum ratio. In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thickness is an eighth part of their height. Likewise in the diastyle, let the height of the column be divided into eight and a half parts, and let the thickness of the column be one part. In the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column. Likewise in the pycnostyle, the height is to be divided into ten, and one part of it made the thickness of the column. In the eustyle temple, as in the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one of them be fixed as the thickness of the lower shaft. Thus the proportion will be had according to the kind of intercolumniation. In araeostyle temples the columns must be made with a diameter equal to oneeighth of their height. In the diastyle, divide the column height into eight and a half parts and give one part to the diameter. In the systyle, divide the height into nine and a half parts and give one to the diameter. In the pycnostyle, divide the height into ten and give one part to the column diameter. In the eustyle, as in the systyle, divide the height into nine and a half parts and assign one part to the diameter at the bottom of the shaft. The proportion will thus correspond to the class of intercolumniation. 11. quemadmodum enim crescunt spatia inter columnas, proportionibus adaugendae sunt crassitudines scaporum. namque si in araeostylo nona aut decima pars crassitudinis fuerit, tenuis et exilis apparebit, ideo quod per latitudinem intercolumniorum aer consumit et inminuit aspectu scaporum crassitudinem; contra vero pycnostylis, si octava pars crassitudinis fuerit, propter crebritatem et angustias intercolumniorum tumidam et invenustam efficiet speciem. itaque generis operis oportet persequi symmetrias. etiamque angulares 488

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III columnae crassiores faciendae sunt ex sua diametro quinquagesima parte, quod eae ab aere circumciduntur et graciliores videntur esse aspicientibus. ergo quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum. For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be enlarged in proportion. For if in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and slender, because through the width of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the diameter of their thickness to the view. Contrariwise, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, on account of the frequency and narrowness of the intercolumniations it will produce a swollen and graceless appearance. One must therefore pursue the symmetries proper to each kind of work. Moreover, the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their diameter, because they are cut round by the air and appear more slender to those who behold them. Therefore what the eye deceives must be redressed by calculation. Note — Bk. 3.3 (optical corrections). Vitruvius states here a cardinal principle of his aesthetics: 'what the eye deceives must be redressed by calculation' (quod oculus fallit ratiocinatione est exaequandum). From it derive the thickening of the corner columns by 1/50 of their diameter and the adjustment of thickness according to the width of the intercolumniation. Note — III.3.11. Quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum formulates Vitruvius’s principle of visual compensation with particular clarity: perception may require measurable adjustments to abstract geometrical regularity. Optical correction or compensation is the appropriate description, without attributing to the passage a modern theory of perception that it does not develop. 12. contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae videntur uti si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur. item quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et semissem dividatur earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo columnae fiat. item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus dividatur in partes septem earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur. quae autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes septem et dimidiam, ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae 489

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III rationem. quae erunt ab quadraginta pedibus ad quinquaginta, item dividendae sunt in octo partes et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo contrahantur. item si quae altiores erunt, eadem ratione pro rata constituantur contracturae. The diminution at the tops of columns, in the hypotrachelia, should be made as follows. For a column up to fifteen feet high, divide the lower diameter into six parts and make the upper diameter five of them. For a column from fifteen to twenty feet, divide the lower shaft into six and a half parts and make the upper diameter five and a half. For columns from twenty to thirty feet, divide the lower shaft into seven parts and complete the upper diminution with six. For a column from thirty to forty feet high, divide the lower diameter into seven and a half parts and give the top six and a half. For columns from forty to fifty feet, divide the lower diameter into eight parts and diminish the top of the shaft, below the capital, to seven. For taller columns, establish the diminution proportionally by the same principle. The diminution of the diameter at the upper hypotrachelium is determined by the column’s height. For a column up to fifteen feet, divide the lower diameter into six parts and give the upper diameter five. Between fifteen and twenty feet, divide it into six and a half and give the upper diameter five and a half. Between twenty and thirty feet, divide it into seven and give the top six. Between thirty and forty feet, divide it into seven and a half and give the top six and a half. Between forty and fifty feet, divide it into eight and give the top seven. For greater heights, establish the diminution proportionally by the same principle. The contractions at the tops of the columns, at the necks, are to be made thus: if the column is up to fifteen feet, let the lower thickness be divided into six parts, and let the top be made of five of them. Likewise for one from fifteen feet to twenty, let the lower shaft be divided into six and a half parts, and let the upper thickness of the column be made of five and a half. Likewise for one from twenty to thirty feet, let the lower shaft be divided into seven parts, and let the contraction at the top be completed with six of them. One that is from thirty to forty feet high, let the lower part be divided into seven and a half parts, and of these let it have six and a half at the top by the rule of contraction. Those from forty to fifty feet are likewise to be divided into eight parts, and 490

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III seven of them contracted at the top of the shaft beneath the capital. Likewise, if any are higher, let their contractions be fixed proportionally by the same rule. 13. haec autem propter altitudinis intervallum, scandentis oculi species, adiciuntur crassitudinibus temperaturae. venustates enim persequitur visus, cuius si non blandimur voluptati proportione et modulorum adiectionibus, uti quod fallitur temperatione adaugeatur, vastus et invenustus conspicientibus remittetur aspectus. de adiectione quae adicitur in mediis columnis, quae apud Graecos ἔντασις appellatur, in extremo libro erit forma et ratio eius quemadmodum mollis et conveniens efficiatur subscripta. These compensating adjustments are added to the thicknesses on account of the interval of height, as the eye ascends. For sight pursues beauty, and if we do not flatter its pleasure by proportion and by additions of modules— so that what deceives may be augmented by compensation—the aspect will be rendered coarse and graceless to beholders. As for the addition made in the middle of the columns, which among the Greeks is called entasis (ἔντασις), at the end of the book its form and method will be set down, showing how it is made soft and fitting. Comparative note — Bk. 3.3.13 (entasis). The entasis (ἔντασις)—the slight swelling or adiectio of the shaft that corrects the optical illusion of concavity—is, with the contractions and the inclination of the members, one of the system's optical «temperings». Vitruvius defers its drawing to a plate «at the end of the book» (in extremo libro), lost in the manuscript tradition, which has made the exact profile an open problem since the Renaissance (Fra Giocondo, Alberti, the practice of the curves). The editions reflect this: Rose (Teubner, 1899) fixes the text without restoring the figure; Granger (Loeb, 1931) renders adiectio as the «increase» of the shaft; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) discuss the geometric reconstruction of the curve; the Budé (dir. Gros) reviews the hypotheses of the profile (parabola, arc of a circle). The present edition keeps the term and translates in its own words, adopting no external version. [Historical-architectural note] The entasis is the most celebrated of the Greek optical corrections; the Parthenon combines it with the curvature of the stylobate (see scamilli impares, 3.4.5). 491

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Critical note — III.3.13. Ἔντασις denotes the addition to or modification of the shaft’s profile in its middle region. The surviving text refers to a forma et ratio at the end of the book; the loss or incomplete transmission of the figures prevents turning that reference into a single geometrical reconstruction. The edition therefore retains the Greek term and distinguishes textual testimony from the various reconstructions proposed since the Renaissance. Technical note — Rhythm and module. The eustyle is not merely the “ideal type”: Vitruvius presents it as a solution balancing usus, species and firmitas through ordinary intercolumniations of two and a quarter diameters and a wider axial intercolumniation. A comparative table must show intercolumniation, diameter-to-height ratio and examples separately, avoiding confusion between measurements expressed in diameters and Roman feet. Metrological note — Doron. Vitruvius explains doron by reference to the palm and relates pentadoron/tetradoron to five/four palms. Any modern metric equivalent is given as an approximation dependent on the standard adopted; the ancient dimensions retain priority in the text. Construction note — Semilateria and joints. The alternation of lateres and semilateria is interpreted as a strategy for bonding facings and joints. Modern explanation of the bond is kept separate from Vitruvius’s exact words and does not turn a reasonable reconstruction into a textual reading. Textual and metrological apparatus — III.3. Pycnostylos, systylos, diastylos, araeostylos and eustylos depend on numerical relationships between diameter, height and intercolumniation. Each fraction must be retained in ancient notation in the base commentary before conversion to a decimal in auxiliary tables. Architectural note — Entasis and optical corrections. Ἔντασις and the thickening of corner columns are presented as devices described by Vitruvius. No universal formula is attributed to these adjustments where the text refers to a figure or leaves variables dependent on scale. Comparative critical apparatus — III.3.1–13. The chapter is compared with Krohn and with the Budé edition of Book III established, translated and annotated by Pierre Gros. Pycnostylos, systylos, diastylos, araeostylos and eustylos are categories defined by colonnade rhythm and must remain technical terms. In III.3.10 the diameter-to-height ratio varies with the width of the 492

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III intercolumniation; in III.3.11 nona aut decima pars is restored against the copying error “non aut decima” in an unidentified transcription. Quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum grounds the optical compensations; it does not, however, authorize attributing to Vitruvius every visual correction known to later architecture. 493

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Chapter 4 1. Fundationes eorum operum fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videbitur, extruaturque structura totum solum quam solidissima. Supraque terram parietes extruantur sub columnas dimidio crassiores quam columnae sunt futurae, uti firmiora sint inferiora superioribus; quae stereobates appellantur, nam excipiunt onera. Spirarumque proiecturae non procedant extra solidum; item supra parietis ad eundem modum crassitudo servanda est. Intervalla autem concamaranda aut solidanda festucationibus, uti distineantur. The foundations of these works must be dug, if solid ground can be found, down to and into it, to a depth proportionate to the magnitude of the work; the whole foundation area must be built up with masonry as solid as possible. Above ground, raise walls beneath the columns one-half thicker than the columns are to be, so that the lower parts are stronger than the upper. These are called stereobates, since they receive the loads. The projections of the bases must not extend beyond the solid support; the wall thickness must likewise be maintained above. The spaces between must be vaulted or consolidated by ramming, so that they are held apart. The foundations of these works are to be dug, if it can be found, from solid ground and down to the solid, to whatever depth seems fitting in proportion to the magnitude of the work, and the whole substructure is to be built up as solidly as possible. Above the ground, let walls be raised beneath the columns, thicker by a half than the columns that are to stand upon them, so that the lower parts may be firmer than the upper; these are called stereobates, for they receive the loads. Let the projections of the bases not extend beyond the solid. Likewise, the same thickness of wall is to be kept above. The intervening spaces are to be vaulted or consolidated by ramming, so that they are well braced. Textual note — III.4.1. The Spanish edition follows Krohn (1912, 68) in reading ad solidum et in solido, “down to firm ground and into it”; Rose (1899, 73) prints ab solido et in solidum. The Spanish edition’s first rendering follows the former construction, while its parallel rendering begins “from firm ground and down to the firm”. Both authorial renderings are presented separately in English, with their different formulations visible. The adopted Latin follows the 494

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III authorial Spanish edition/Krohn; this is a documented editorial constitution, not a new manuscript attribution. Note — Bk. 3.4 (foundations). The stereobates (stereobatae, 'the loadbearers') are the foundation walls, thicker than the columns they carry; for unstable or marshy ground Vitruvius prescribes machine-driven piles of alder, olive, or oak—a technique confirmed by the archaeology of Roman foundations on wet terrain. 2. sin autem solidum non invenietur, sed locus erit congesticius ad imum aut paluster, tunc is locus fodiatur exinaniaturque et palis alneis aut oleagineis aut robusteis ustilatis configatur, sublicaque machinis adigatur quam creberrime, carbonibusque expleantur intervalla palorum et tunc structuris solidissimis fundamenta impleantur. extructis autem fundamentis ad libramentum stylobatae sunt conlocandi. If solid ground cannot be found, and the site consists of fill down to the bottom or is marshy, dig out and empty the place. Drive in charred stakes of alder, olive or oak, using machines to set the piles as closely together as possible; fill the spaces between them with charcoal, then fill the foundations with exceptionally solid masonry. Once the foundations have been constructed, set the stylobates level. If no solid ground is found and the site consists of deep fill or marsh, it must be excavated and emptied. Charred piles of alder, olive or oak are then driven by machines as densely as possible. Fill the spaces between the piles with charcoal and construct very solid masonry foundations above them. Once the foundations have been built and leveled, place the stylobates. But if solid ground is not found, and the site is made up of fill to the bottom, or marshy, then let that place be dug out and emptied, and secured with charred piles of alder, olive, or oak; let the piles be driven in by machines as close together as possible, and let the intervals between them be filled with charcoal; and then let the foundations be filled with the most solid masonry. When the foundations have been raised to the level, let the stylobates be set in place. 3. supra stylobatas columnae disponendae quemadmodum supra scriptum est, sive in pycnostylo quemadmodum pycnostyla, sive systylo aut diastylo aut eustylo quemadmodum supra scripta sunt et constituta. in araeostylis enim libertas est quantum cuique libet constituendi. sed ita columnae in peripteris conlocentur 495

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III uti quot intercolumnia sunt in fronte, totidem bis intercolumnia fiant in lateribus. ita enim erit duplex longitudo operis ad latitudinem. namque qui columnarum duplicationes fecerunt erravisse videntur, quod unum intercolumnium in longitudine plus quam oporteat procurrere videtur. On the stylobates arrange the columns as prescribed above for the pycnostyle, systyle, diastyle or eustyle. In araeostyles there is freedom to establish whatever spacing one wishes. In peripteral temples, however, arrange the columns so that the sides have twice as many intercolumniations as the front; the length of the work will thus be twice its breadth. Those who doubled the number of columns appear to have erred, because the length extends one intercolumniation farther than it should. Columns are arranged on the stylobates according to the rules already established for the pycnostyle, systyle, diastyle or eustyle. In araeostyles there is greater freedom of arrangement. In peripteral temples, however, the number of intercolumniations on the sides must be twice the number on the facade, making the building twice as long as it is wide. Vitruvius considers it an error simply to double the number of columns, since this makes the length exceed the required dimension by one intercolumniation. Upon the stylobates the columns are to be arranged as written above— whether in the pycnostyle as for pycnostyles, or in the systyle, diastyle, or eustyle as prescribed and established above. In araeostyles there is freedom to set them out as each pleases. But let the columns in peripteral temples be so placed that, however many intercolumniations there are at the front, twice as many are made on the sides; for thus the length of the work will be double its breadth. Those who doubled the number of columns seem to have erred, because one intercolumniation too many makes the length run out farther than it should. 4. Gradus in fronte constituendi ita sunt, uti sint semper inpares; namque cum dextro pede primus gradus ascendatur, item in summo templo primus erit ponendus. Crassitudines autem eorum graduum ita finiendas censeo, ut neque crassiores dextante nec tenuiores dodrante sint conlocatae; sic enim durus non erit ascensus. Retractiones autem graduum nec minus quam sesquipedales nec plus quam bipedales faciendae videntur. Item si circa aedem gradus futuri sunt, ad eundem modum fieri debent. 496

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III The steps at the front must always be odd in number: since the first step is mounted with the right foot, the same foot must be placed first at the top of the temple. I consider that the risers should be no higher than a dextans and no lower than a dodrans, that is, five-sixths and three-quarters of a foot respectively, so that the ascent is not difficult. The treads should be no less than one and a half feet and no more than two feet. Steps around the temple must be made in the same way. The steps at the front are to be so arranged that they are always odd in number; for since the first step is mounted with the right foot, the right foot must likewise be set first upon the top of the temple. As for the thickness of these steps, I judge it should be so fixed that they be laid neither thicker than a dextans (⁵⁄₆ of a foot) nor thinner than a dodrans (³⁄₄ of a foot); for thus the ascent will not be steep. The treads should be made not less than a foot and a half nor more than two feet. Likewise, if there are to be steps around the temple, they should be made in the same way. Metrological note — III.4.4. The Spanish edition’s first rendering gives the risers as nine to ten fingers, whereas its parallel rendering correctly gives dodrans and dextans as three-quarters and five-sixths of a foot. Krohn (1912, 69) and Rose (1899, 74–75) print dodrante and dextante. These are fractions of a foot, not nine and ten of the sixteen digits in a foot. Both English renderings therefore retain the checked fractions; the Spanish discrepancy is recorded here rather than reproduced as a second, incompatible prescription. Comparative note — III.4.4–5. The requirement for an odd number of steps, so that the ascent begins and ends with the right foot, and the riser limits of a dodrans and a dextans (¾ and ⅚ of a Roman foot) belong to III.4.4. They must be distinguished from scamilli impares in III.4.5. The latter phrase is associated with a central rise of the stylobate and an optical appearance of hollowing if it is set strictly level. Its precise material interpretation remains disputed; supports, offsets and unequal leveling elements are among the reconstructions proposed. The figure promised at the end of the book is not supplied by the surviving wording. Granger, Rowland and Howe, Gros, and Corso and Romano are relevant points of comparison for the reception of the problem; their individual solutions require direct consultation. The association with 497

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III the curvature of Greek stylobates, including the Parthenon, belongs to architectural comparison and does not resolve the Latin expression by itself. Note — III.4.4–5. The prescription of an odd number of steps belongs to the text itself and is explicitly connected with beginning and ending the ascent with the right foot. It must be distinguished from scamilli impares in the following paragraph, one of the treatise’s most disputed technical passages. 5. sin autem circa aedem ex tribus lateribus podium faciendum erit, id constituatur uti quadrae spirae trunci coronae lysis ad ipsum stylobatam qui erit sub columnarum spiris conveniant. stylobatam ita oportet exaequari uti habeat per medium adiectionem per scamillos inpares. si enim ad libellam dirigetur, alveolatum oculo videbitur. hoc autem ut scamilli ad id convenientes fiant, item in extremo libro forma et demonstratio erit descripta. If a podium is to be built around three sides of the temple, its plinths, bases, dado blocks, cornices and lysis molding must correspond to the stylobate beneath the column bases. The stylobate should be leveled with a rise at its center by means of scamilli impares; if it is set strictly level, it will appear hollow to the eye. A figure and demonstration of how the scamilli are to be adapted for this purpose will likewise be drawn at the end of the book. Critical note — Scamilli impares. The passage’s connection with the curvature or leveling of the stylobate and with optical corrections is plausible and forms part of its technical reception, but the exact material form of the scamilli has received divergent interpretations. Transmitted text, editorial conjecture and graphic reconstruction must remain typographically distinct. Comparative textual apparatus — III.4. The chapter combines foundations, stereobatae, stylobata, steps and podium with one of the most difficult passages of the technical tradition: “scamillos inpares”. The edition preserves the Latin phrase as a textual and architectural problem; it does not silently adopt a Renaissance or modern reconstruction as though it were the only possible reading. Metrological note — Steps and podium. Numbers of steps, heights and modular relationships are retained first in their ancient formulation. Any modern decimal or metric conversion is reserved for auxiliary tables; if a figure 498

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III conflicts with a reconstruction, the textual tradition is reviewed first rather than emended for geometrical convenience. Comparative critical apparatus — III.4. The chapter articulates foundations, stereobatae, stylobata, steps and podium. The prescription for alder, olive or oak piles charred on the surface belongs to the text itself for made ground or marshy sites. In III.4.4 the odd number of steps is explained by beginning and ending the ascent with the right foot. This rule must not be confused with the scamilli impares of III.4.5, a technical expression whose interpretation has a long editorial and architectural history. The edition keeps that distinction visible and avoids resolving the second problem by false etymology or a single reconstruction. Architectural and textual note — Scamilli impares. The expression in III.4.5 is one of Book III’s most disputed passages.
