It must be retained in Latin in the commentary and explained cautiously: it is connected with the stylobate’s leveling or curvature and with perceptual corrections, but the material reconstructions proposed since the Renaissance are not equivalent to the textual evidence. 499

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Chapter 5 1. His perfectis in suis locis spirae conlocentur, eaeque ad symmetriam sic perficiantur, uti crassitudo cum plintho sit columnae ex dimidia crassitudine proiecturamque, quam Graeci ἐκφοράν vocitant, habeant S extantem: ita tum lata et longa erit columnae crassitudinis unius et dimidiae. When these parts are complete, set the column bases in position and proportion them so that their height, including the plinth, is half the column’s diameter. They are to have the projection called ekphora (ἐκφορά) in Greek of […]; their overall width and length will thus be one and a half column diameters. Once these parts are complete, the bases (spirae) are set in position and executed according to these symmetriae: their height, including the plinth, equals half the column diameter; their projection, called ἐκφορά (ekphora) by the Greeks, is a quarter of a diameter. The total width and length of the base thus reach one and a half column diameters. Textual and proportional note — III.5.1. The Spanish edition and Krohn’s printed text (1912, 69, line 29) give S extantem; Krohn’s apparatus explains S as semisse and distinguishes this editorial reading from sextantem. Rose’s printed text (1899, 75) gives aeque tantam. The first authorial Spanish translation marks the quantity as […]; the parallel architectural explanation derives a quarterdiameter projection on each side from an overall width of one and a half diameters. Both renderings are retained here and their different functions made explicit. The quarter diameter is a proportional interpretation, not a manuscript reading or a silent resolution of S extantem. 2. altitudo eius si atticurges erit, ita dividatur ut superior pars tertia parte sit crassitudinis columnae, reliquum plintho relinquatur. dempta plintho reliquum dividatur in partes quattuor fiatque superior torus quartae, reliquae tres aequaliter dividantur et una sit inferior torus, altera pars cum suis quadris scotia, quam Graeci τροχίλον dicunt. If the base is Attic, divide its height so that the upper part is one-third of the column diameter, leaving the remainder for the plinth. Excluding the plinth, divide what remains into four parts and make the upper torus one part. Divide the other three equally between the lower torus and the scotia with its fillets, which the Greeks call trochilus (τροχίλος). 500

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III If the base is Attic, divide its height so that the part above the plinth is one-third of the column’s diameter, leaving the remainder for the plinth. Excluding the plinth, divide the remaining height into four parts: one part forms the upper torus. Divide the other three parts into two equal portions, one for the lower torus and the other for the scotia and its fillets, which the Greeks call trochilus. 3. sin autem ionicae erunt faciendae, symmetriae earum sic erunt constituendae uti latitudo spirae quoqueversus sit columnae crassitudinis adiecta ⟨e⟩ crassitudine quarta et octava, altitudo ita uti atticurges, item et eius plinthos, reliquumque praeter plinthum, quod erit tertia pars crassitudinis columnae, dividatur in partes septem. inde trium partium torus qui est in summo, reliquae quattuor partes dividendae sunt aequaliter et una pars fiat cum suis astragalis et supercilio superior trochilus, altera pars inferiori trochilo relinquatur, sed inferior maior apparebit ideo quod habebit ad extremam plinthum proiecturam. astragali faciendi sunt octavae partis trochili. proiectura erit spirae pars octava et sexta decuma pars crassitudinis columnae. Of these, three for the torus that is at the top; let the remaining four be divided equally, and let one part, with its astragals and its fillet, be made the upper trochilus, and the other part left for the lower trochilus. Its height and plinth are as in the Attic base. Apart from the plinth, divide the remainder, which is one-third of the column diameter, into seven parts. The lower will appear larger, 501

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III since its projection reaches the edge of the plinth. Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam. When the bases have been completed and set in place, position the central columns of the pronaos and the rear part plumb through their central axes. The corner columns and those aligned with them along the temple’s right and left sides must have their inner faces, towards the cella walls, set vertically, while their outer faces †show their diminution†. In this way the forms of the temple’s composition will be adjusted according to such a principle of diminution. The corner columns and those aligned with them on the temple’s right and left sides are arranged so that their inner faces, towards the cella walls, remain vertical; the diminution prescribed earlier is applied to their outer faces. Scapis columnarum statutis capitulorum ratio ⟨sic est habenda.⟩ si pulvinata erunt, his symmetriis conformabuntur, uti, quam crassus imus scapus fuerit addita octava decuma parte scapi, abacus habeat longitudinem et latitudinem; crassitudinem cum volutis eius dimidiam. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III abaco in interiorem partem frontibus volutarum parte duodevicensima et eius dimidia. Tunc crassitudo dividenda est in partes novem et dimidiam, et secundum abacum in quattuor partibus volutarum secundum extremi abaci quadram lineae demittendae, quae cathetoe dicuntur. Tunc ex novem partibus et dimidia una pars et dimidia abaci crassitudo relinquatur, reliquae octo volutis constituantur. Once the column shafts have been erected, the capitals are proportioned as follows. If they are cushion capitals, the abacus must have a length and breadth equal to the lower shaft diameter plus one-eighteenth of that diameter, and its height including the volutes must be half that measure. The fronts of the volutes must be set back inwards from the edge of the abacus by one-eighteenth and half of that part. Divide the height into nine and a half parts and, in the four positions of the volutes, drop the lines called cathetoe along the outer square of the abacus. Of the nine and a half parts, reserve one and a half for the abacus’s thickness and assign the remaining eight to the volutes. The shafts of the columns being set up, the rule of the capitals will be this. If they are of the cushioned kind (pulvinata), they will be shaped by these symmetries: that the abacus have in length and breadth as much as the thickness of the lower shaft plus an eighteenth part of the shaft; its thickness, with the volutes, half of that. One must draw back from the outer edge of the abacus inward, at the fronts of the volutes, an eighteenth part and its half. Then let the thickness be divided into nine and a half parts, and, along the abacus, in the four parts of the volutes, according to the square of the abacus's edge, let the lines be dropped which are called cathetuses (κάθετοι). Of the nine and a half parts, let one and a half be reserved for the thickness of the abacus, and the remaining eight be assigned to the volutes. Textual and numerical note — III.5.4–6. The running Latin follows the authorial Spanish edition and Krohn (1912, 70–71), retaining the crux †uti dicant se earum contracturam and the supplements ⟨sic est habenda⟩, ⟨conlocetur⟩ and ⟨schema volutae⟩. The literal English keeps the difficulty of III.5.4 distinct from the author’s architectural paraphrase. In III.5.5 the authorial Spanish translation’s first rendering says “a 503

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III nineteenth part and a half”, but both printed Latin editions have duodevicensima, eighteenth, and the authorial Spanish edition’s parallel explanation likewise gives eighteenth. The English therefore uses an eighteenth part plus half of that part, while recording the source’s discrepancy here. No new manuscript reading is asserted. 6. Tunc ab linea, quae secundum abaci extremam partem demissa erit, in interiorem partem ⟨alia⟩ recedat unius et dimidiatae partis latitudine. Let these lines then be divided so that four and a half parts remain beneath the abacus. Then, at the point that divides the four and a half from the three and a half, let the center of the eye (oculus) be placed, and from that center let a circle be described whose diameter equals one of the eight parts: that will be the size of the eye, and in it let a diameter be drawn answering to the cathetus. Then, beginning at the top, beneath the abacus, let half the space of the eye be diminished in each of the quarter-turns, until one comes back to the same quadrant that is beneath the abacus. From the vertical line drawn beside the abacus’s outer edge, take another line inwards at a distance of one and a half parts. Divide these lines so that four and a half parts remain beneath the abacus. At the point separating those four and a half parts from the remaining three and a half, establish the center of the eye (oculus). From it draw a circle with a diameter equal to one of the eight parts assigned to the volute. This is the eye’s size; through its center draw the diameter coinciding with the cathetus. Beginning at the upper zone beneath the abacus, reduce the volute’s construction by half the eye’s diameter in each quarter-turn, until returning to the quadrant beneath the abacus. 504

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER III In this book I have set forth, as clearly as I could, the arrangements of Ionic temples. What the proportions of the Doric and Corinthian may be, I shall explain in the following book. Comparative note — Book III. The English translation derives from Diego Kurilo’s original Spanish text. Krohn’s Latin text and the electronic transcription of Rose provide independent controls for the passages discussed in this apparatus. The Book III edition established and translated by Pierre Gros (Budé, 1990) is an essential reference, but a complete independent collation of its critical apparatus is not claimed here. No individual manuscript reading or editorial decision is attributed to Gros, Rose, Krohn or Granger without identifiable documentary support. Greek ἀναλογία in III.1.1 is the adopted technical term; a damaged electronic transcription does not by itself demonstrate corruption in the manuscript tradition. Critical and comparative note — Conclusion of Book III. This edition’s checks distinguish three levels: (1) the adopted Latin text and its transmission problems; (2) the translation, which seeks to preserve technical terminology and argumentative syntax without introducing explanations foreign to the original; and (3) the historical and architectural commentary, where modern interpretations are recorded. The Latin has been systematically compared with Krohn (Teubner, 1912) in the passages reviewed. The Budé edition of Book III, established, translated and annotated by Pierre Gros (CUF, 1990), serves as a standard of philological and archaeological rigor and, wherever a particular reading or interpretation can be documented, as an explicit point of comparison. No decisions are attributed to Gros, Rose, Krohn or other editors without verification in the relevant source. Comparative apparatus — III.5. The Ionic order is treated as a continuous proportional sequence: spirae, column shafts, cushion capitals, volutes, epistylia, zophorus, denticuli, corona and sima. Plinths, tori, scotiae, astragals, the echinus, abacus, canalis and balteus retain their technical functions and dependence on the stated module. Supplements in the critical text remain typographically distinguishable. Discrepancies affecting height, projection, division or module take priority over merely graphic variants; conversion to modern units must not silently replace the ancient ratios. 511

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER III Comparative critical apparatus — III.5. The chapter on the Ionic order is reviewed as a continuous sequence: spirae/bases → shafts → cushion capitals → volutes → epistylia → zophorus → denticuli → corona and sima. Ἐκφορά, cathetus, oculus, canalis, echinus and other terms whose modern equivalent may be only approximate are retained as technical vocabulary. Supplements marked by the critical edition—for example <sic erit> and other restored elements in the geometrical description—must remain typographically distinct from transmitted text. Proportions are checked against the lower-diameter module and are not silently converted into metric units. Philological and graphic note — The Ionic volute. The volute’s construction depends on a chain of divisions, centers and radii whose intelligibility requires text and diagram. A modern figure must reproduce the described sequence exactly and distinguish the Latin evidence from the graphic solutions proposed by editors. A numeral must not be corrected because it “looks better” in the drawing: the critical reading is determined first and the figure constructed afterwards. Technical synthesis for architects — Book III. The book proceeds from the building’s general commensurability to temple typology, from the rhythm of columns to foundations, and finally to the complete detail of the Ionic order. The common principle is that each local dimension acquires meaning through its measurable relation to the whole, but Vitruvius also introduces optical compensations: the system is not a rigid numerical grid, but a proportional discipline adjusted to construction and perception. Comparative apparatus — III.5. The construction of the Ionic order is checked as a proportional chain: spira, columna, capitulum, epistylium, zophorus, corona and sima. The dimensions of plinth, tori, scotiae, astragals, volutes, echinus and abacus must remain dependent on the diameter or module specified by Vitruvius. Architectural and philological note — The Ionic capital. Voluta, echinus, abacus, canal/canalis and balteus are retained as technical vocabulary. The geometrical instructions for volutes are explained step by step, but any modern diagram is identified as an editorial reconstruction rather than an autograph figure by Vitruvius. 512

The comparative apparatus therefore prioritizes discrepancies that alter a member’s module, height, projection or division; purely graphic or orthographic variants are not needlessly multiplied. Synthesis for architects — Book III. Vitruvius articulates the temple through relations between whole, members and module. The book’s contemporary value lies in understanding a historical system of dimensional coordination and visual correction, not in turning its proportions into universal standards. 513

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV ARGUMENTUM LIBRI IV — On the orders: the origin of the Corinthian capital (Callimachus), the rules of the Doric order and of the triglyphs and metopes, the arrangement of temples according to their orientation, the classes of temples according to their plan and the altars of the gods. Notice. — Book IV completes the orders. It gives the aetiology of the three genera — the Doric drawn from the male body, the Ionic from the matronly, the Corinthian capital invented by Callimachus from an acanthus grown about a votive basket — and the rules of the Doric, with the famous problem of the corner triglyph. It then treats the parts of temples (cellae, doorways, the Tuscan and round temples) and closes with the orientation of altars. With Book III it forms the most influential ancient account of the classical orders. Preface 1. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV When these cities had expelled the Carians and Leleges, they called that region of the earth Ionia, after their leader Ion, and, setting up there temples to the immortal gods, began to build shrines. And they built first a temple to Apollo Panionios, as they had seen in Achaea, and called it Doric, because they had seen it first made in that order in the cities of the Dorians. 6. in ea aede cum voluissent columnas conlocare, non habentes symmetrias earum et quaerentes quibus rationibus efficere possent uti et ad onus ferendum essent idoneae et in aspectu probatam haberent venustatem, dimensi sunt virilis pedis vestigium et id retulerunt in altitudinem. cum invenissent pedem sextam partem esse altitudinis in homine, item in columnam transtulerunt et qua crassitudine fecerunt basim scapi, tantas sex cum capitulo in altitudinem extulerunt. ita dorica columna virilis corporis proportionem et firmitatem et venustatem in aedificiis praestare coepit. When they wished to set columns in that temple, not knowing their symmetries and seeking by what rules they might make them at once fit to bear the load and of approved beauty to the sight, they measured the print of a man's foot and referred it to the height. Finding that the foot is a sixth part of a man's height, they carried the same over to the column, and, with the thickness they gave to the base of the shaft, raised it six times that measure in height, including the capital. Thus the Doric column began to furnish in buildings the proportion, firmness, and beauty of the male body. 7. Item postea Dianae ⟨cum cogitarent⟩ constituere aedem quaerentes novi generis speciem, isdem vestigiis ad muliebrem transtulerunt gracilitatem, et fecerunt primum columnae crassitudinem altitudinis octava parte, ut haberet speciem excelsiorem. basi spiram supposuerunt pro calceo, capitulo volutas uti capillamento concrispatos cincinnos praependentes dextra ac sinistra conlocaverunt et cymatiis et encarpis pro crinibus dispositis frontes ornaverunt truncoque toto strias uti stolarum rugas matronali more demiserunt. ita duobus discriminibus columnarum inventionem, unam virili sine ornatu nuda specie, alteram muliebri subtilitate et ornatu symmetriaque sunt mutuati. Afterwards, wishing to raise a temple to Diana in the aspect of a new order, they turned by the same footprints to feminine slenderness, and first made the thickness of the column an eighth part of its height, that it might have 518

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV a loftier look. Beneath the base they set a base-molding (spira) in place of a shoe; on the capital they placed volutes hanging to right and left like curled ringlets of hair, and adorned the fronts with cymatia and festoons (encarpi) arranged like locks; and down the whole shaft they let flutes fall like the folds of matrons' robes. Thus by two distinct criteria they took the invention of columns: one of male aspect, bare and without ornament; the other of feminine delicacy, ornament, and symmetry. 8. posteri vero elegantia subtilitateque iudiciorum progressi et gracilioribus modulis delectati septem crassitudinis diametros in altitudinem columnae doricae, ionicae novem constituerunt. id autem <genus>, quod Iones fecerunt primo, Ionicum est nominatum. Tertium vero, quod Corinthium dicitur, virginalis habet gracilitatis imitationem, quod virginis propter aetatis teneritatem gracilioribus membris figuratae effectus recipiunt ornatus venustiores. The later architects, advancing in the elegance and subtlety of their judgment and delighting in more slender modules, fixed the height of the Doric column at seven diameters of the thickness, and that of the Ionic at nine. And the order which the Ionians first made was called Ionic. The third, which is called Corinthian, imitates the slender grace of a maiden; for maidens, by reason of the tenderness of their age, figured with more slender members, receive in ornament more graceful effects. Note — Bk. 4.1. The anthropomorphic aetiology of the orders—Doric with the proportion and firmness of the male body (foot = 1/6 of the height), Ionic with matronly slenderness and dress (volute as ringlets, flutes as the folds of the stola), Corinthian with maidenly grace—is the most influential formulation of the bond between body and architecture. On its mythic frame (Dorus, son of Hellen; Ion, son of Xuthus) see the introductory study. 9. eius autem capituli prima inventio sic memoratur esse facta. virgo civis Corinthia iam matura nuptiis inplicata morbo decessit. post sepulturam eius, quibus ea virgo viva pupulis delectabatur, nutrix collecta et composita in calatho pertulit ad monumentum et in summo conlocavit et, uti ea permanerent diutius subdiu, tegula texit. is calathus fortuito supra acanthi radicem fuerat conlocatus. interim pondere pressa radix acanthi media folia et cauliculos circum vernum tempus profudit, cuius cauliculi secundum calathi latera crescentes et ab 519

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV angulis tegulae ponderis necessitate expressi flexuras in extremas partes volutarum facere sunt coacti. The first invention of this capital is recorded to have come about thus. A maiden, a citizen of Corinth, already of marriageable age, was carried off by illness. After her burial, her nurse gathered the little cups in which the girl had delighted while alive, arranged them in a basket (calathus), carried it to the tomb, and set it on top; and, that they might last longer in the open air, she covered it with a tile. The basket had by chance been placed over the root of an acanthus. 10. tunc Callimachus, qui propter elegantiam et subtilitatem artis marmoreae ab Atheniensibus κατατηξίτεχνος () fuerat nominatus, praeteriens hoc monumentum animadvertit eum calathum et circa foliorum nascentem teneritatem, delectatusque genere et formae novitate ad id exemplar columnas apud Corinthios fecit symmetriasque constituit, et ex eo in operis perfectionibus Corinthii generis distribuit rationes. Meanwhile the acanthus root, pressed down by the weight, put forth about springtime leaves and little stalks through the middle; and its stalks, growing up along the sides of the basket and forced by the weight of the tile's corners, were constrained to form volutes at their ends. Then Callimachus, whom the Athenians had named katatexitechnos (κατατηξίτεχνος, 'one who refines art to the point of consuming it') for the elegance and subtlety of his work in marble, passing by this monument, noticed the basket and the tender foliage growing about it; and, delighted by the novelty of the kind and form, he made columns after that model among the Corinthians and established their symmetries, and thenceforth distributed the rules of the Corinthian order in the execution of works. Note — Bk. 4.1.9–10. The legend of the basket (calathus) on the Corinthian maiden's tomb, wreathed by the acanthus, and of Callimachus— katatexitechnos, 'the refiner of art'—is aetiological, not historical: the Corinthian capital is attested archaeologically before Callimachus (5th c. BC), e.g. at Bassae. Vitruvius transmits the received Attic tradition. Cf. Pliny, Nat. 34.92. 11. eius autem capituli symmetria sic est facienda uti quanta fuerit crassitudo imae columnae, tanta sit altitudo capituli cum abaco. abaci latitudo ita habeat rationem ut quanta fuerit altitudo, tanta duo sint diagonia ab angulo ad 520

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV angulum spatia. ita enim iustas habebunt frontes quoquoversus latitudines. frontes sinuentur introrsus ab extremis angulis abaci suae frontis latitudinis nona. imum capituli tantam habeat crassitudinem, quantam habet summa columna praeter apothesim et astragalum. abaci crassitudo septima capituli altitudinis. The symmetry of this capital is to be made so that its height, including the abacus, equals the thickness of the lower part of the column. Let the width of the abacus be in such proportion that its two diagonals, from angle to angle, are twice the height; for thus the fronts will have, on every side, the just width. Let the fronts be curved inward, from the outer angles of the abacus, by a ninth part of the width of their front. At its lower part let the capital have as much thickness as the upper part of the column, apart from the apothesis and the astragal. The thickness of the abacus is a seventh part of the capital's height. 12. dempta abaci crassitudine, dividatur reliqua pars in partes tres, e quibus una imo folio detur. secundum folium mediam altitudinem teneat. coliculi eandem habeant altitudinem, e quibus folia nascuntur proiecta uti excipiant quae ex coliculis natae procurrunt ad extremos angulos volutae, minoresque helices infra sinum medium qui est in abaco ⟨sub⟩ flores subiecti scalpantur. flores in quattuor partibus quanta erit abaci crassitudo tam magni formentur. ita his symmetriis corinthia capitula suas habebunt exactiones. Sunt autem quae isdem columnis inponuntur capitulorum genera variis vocabulis nominata, quorum nec proprietates symmetriarum nec columnarum genus aliud nominare possumus, sed ipsorum vocabula traducta et commutata ex corinthiis et pulvinatis et doricis videmus, quorum symmetriae sunt in novarum scalpturarum translatae subtilitatem. The thickness of the abacus being subtracted, let the remaining part be divided into three parts, of which one is given to the lower leaf; let the second leaf occupy the middle height; let the stalks (cauliculi) have the same height, from which the projecting leaves spring that receive the volutes which, born of the stalks, run out to the extreme angles, while the smaller helices are carved within their middle—that which is on the abacus—beneath the flower. Let the flowers, on the four sides, be made as large as the thickness of the abacus. Thus, by these symmetries, the Corinthian capitals will have their due proportions. 521

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV There are also, set upon these same columns, kinds of capitals named by various terms, whose properties of symmetry we cannot set out, nor assign them to any other kind of column; but we see that their very names are borrowed and adapted from the Corinthian, the cushioned (Ionic) and the Doric, whose symmetries have been carried over into the refinement of new carvings. Editorial note. — Chapter 1 gives the famous account of the origin of the orders and, in particular, the aetiology of the Corinthian capital. Vitruvius reads the orders anthropomorphically: the Doric drawn from the proportions of a man’s body (at first six, later seven diameters high), the Ionic from a matron’s slenderness — its volutes for the hair, its flutes for the folds of the robe — and the Corinthian from the slight grace of a maiden. The capital itself he ascribes to Callimachus, nicknamed by the Athenians κατατηξίτεχνος (“the refiner of his art”), who, passing the grave of a Corinthian maiden, saw an acanthus grown about a votive basket weighted by a roof-tile, its leaves curling into volutes, and made of it the new capital. The tale is legend, not history; but it embodies the Vitruvian principle that architectural form is an imitation of nature (cf. 2.1 and 4.2 on the timber origins of the stone members). Critical and historical note — IV.1. The Corinthian column shares the Ionic column’s proportions except for its capital; its upper members may follow Doric or Ionic arrangements. A rigid modern definition of a complete Corinthian order should therefore not be imposed on the passage. Dorus, Ion, the masculine and feminine analogies, and the story of the maiden’s basket and acanthus belong to Vitruvius’s aetiological account. Prima inventio … memoratur presents the Callimachus story as a tradition of invention rather than independently demonstrated biography. 522

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV Chapter 2 1. Quoniam autem de generibus columnarum origines et inventiones supra sunt scriptae, non alienum mihi videtur isdem rationibus de ornamentis eorum quemadmodum sunt prognata et quibus principiis et originibus inventa dicere. in aedificiis omnibus insuper conlocatur materiatio variis vocabulis nominata. ea autem uti in nominationibus, ita in re varias habet utilitates. trabes enim supra columnas et parastaticas et antas ponuntur, in contignationibus tigna et axes. sub tectis, si maiora spatia sunt, et transtra et capreoli, si commoda, columen et cantherii prominentes ad extremam suggrundationem. supra cantherios templa, deinde insuper sub tegulas asseres ita prominentes uti parietes proiecturis eorum tegantur. But since the origins and inventions of the kinds of columns have been set out above, it does not seem out of place to treat in the same way of their ornaments: how they arose and from what principles and origins they derive. In every building there is set, above, a framework of timber called by various names; and this framework, just as it varies in its names, so too it varies in its uses. For the beams (trabes) rest upon the columns, the pilasters (parastaticae) and the antae; in the floor-framing are placed the joists (tigna) and boards; under the roofs, where the spans are larger, the cross-beams (transtra) and the braces (capreoli); where they are moderate, the ridge-beam (columen) and the rafters (cantherii) that project to the edge of the eaves (suggrundatio); over the rafters, the purlins (templa); and then, above, beneath the tiles, the laths (asseres) projecting so that the walls are covered by their overhang. 2. ita unaquaeque res et locum et genus et ordinem proprium tuetur. e quibus rebus et a materiatura fabrili in lapideis et marmoreis aedium sacrarum aedificationibus artifices dispositiones eorum scalpturis sunt imitati et eas inventiones persequendas putaverunt. ideo quod antiqui fabri quodam in loco aedificantes, cum ita ab interioribus parietibus ad extremas partes tigna prominentia habuissent conlocata, inter tigna struxerunt supraque coronas et fastigia venustiore specie fabrilibus operibus ornaverunt, tum proiecturas tignorum quantum eminebant ad lineam et perpendiculum parietum praesecuerunt, quae species cum invenusta îs visa esset tabellas ita formatas uti nunc fiunt triglyphi contra tignorum praecisiones in fronte fixerunt et eas cera caerulea depinxerunt ut praecisiones tignorum tectae non offenderent visum. ita 523

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV divisiones triglyphorum et ⟨met⟩oparum tignorum dispositione et intertigniûm habere in doricis operibus coeperunt. Thus each thing keeps its own place, kind, and order. Hence, taking their model from timber carpentry, the craftsmen imitated in their carvings—in the stone and marble construction of temples—the arrangement of those members, and judged that such discoveries should be followed. For the ancient carpenters, building in a certain place, once they had set the beams (tigna) projecting from the inner walls out to the outermost parts, raised their structure between the beams and, above, adorned the cornices and pediments with carpentry of more graceful aspect; then they cut back the projections of the beams, as far as they jutted out, to the line and the vertical of the walls. And since that aspect seemed to them ungraceful, they fixed on the front, against the cut ends of the beams, small tablets shaped as triglyphs are now made, and painted them with blue wax, so that the cut ends of the beams, thus covered, should not offend the eye. So, imitating the divisions of the beams, they began to have in Doric works the arrangement of triglyphs and, between beam and beam, the metopes. 3. postea alii in aliis operibus ad perpendiculum triglyphorum cantherios prominentes proiecerunt eorumque proiecturas simaverunt. ex eo uti tignorum dispositionibus triglyphi, ita e cantheriorum proiecturis mutulorum sub coronis ratio est inventa. ita fere in operibus lapideis et marmoreis mutuli inclinatis scalpturis deformantur, quod imitatio est cantheriorum. etenim necessario propter stillicidia proclinati conlocantur. ergo et triglyphorum et mutulorum in doricis operibus ratio ex ea imitatione inventa est. Afterwards others, in other works, carried the projecting rafters out to the vertical of the triglyphs and gave their projections a cyma (sima) profile. Hence, just as the triglyphs arose from the arrangement of the joists, so from the projections of the rafters the principle of the mutules (mutuli) beneath the cornices was found. Thus, generally, in works of stone and marble the mutules are carved with an inward slope, since they are an imitation of the rafters; for these are necessarily set sloping on account of the rain-drip (stillicidia). Therefore the principle of both the triglyphs and the mutules in Doric works was discovered from that imitation. 4. Non enim quemadmodum nonnulli errantes dixerunt fenestrarum imagines esse triglyphos ita potest esse, quod in angulis contraque tetrantes columnarum 524

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV triglyphi constituuntur, quibus in locis omnino non patitur res fenestras fieri. dissolvuntur enim angulorum in aedificiis iuncturae, si in îs fenestrarum fuerint lumina relicta. etiamque ubi nunc triglyphi constituuntur si ibi luminum spatia fuisse iudicabuntur, isdem rationibus denticuli in ionicis fenestrarum occupavisse loca videbuntur. utraque enim et inter denticulos et inter triglyphos quae sunt intervalla metopae nominantur. ὀπαι enim Graeci tignorum cubicula et asserum appellant, uti nostri ea cava columbaria. ita quod inter duas opas est intertignium, id μετόπη est apud eos nominata Ita. For it cannot be, as some have said in error, that triglyphs are images of windows; because triglyphs are set at the corners and opposite the quarter-points (tetrantes) of the columns—places where it is by no means possible to make windows. For the joints at the corners of buildings would be broken apart if window-openings were left in them. And further, if it were judged that, where triglyphs now stand, there had once been openings for light, then by the same reasoning the dentils in the Ionic would be supposed to have occupied the place of windows. For in both cases the intervals—both those between the dentils and those between the triglyphs—are called metopes. For the Greeks call the sockets (cubilia) of the beams and of the laths ὀπαί, just as ours call those hollows columbaria. Thus what lies between two ὀπαί, the inter-beam space, they name μετόπη. Comparative note — Bk. 4.2 (structural truth). Here Vitruvius states one of the most influential doctrines of architectural theory: stone ornaments are the translation—petrification—of timber roofing (triglyphs from beam-ends, mutules from rafters, dentils from laths), so that they must not represent what cannot exist in constructional reality (quod non potest in veritate fieri… non… certam rationem habere). Hence his rejection of dentils beneath mutules. The editions fix the passage without major divergence (Rose, Teubner 1899; Budé, dir. Gros); Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress its scope as a principle of «constructional truth». [Historical-architectural note] It is the ancient root of modern structural rationalism: Laugier's «primitive hut» (Essai sur l'architecture, 1753), Viollet-le-Duc's rationalism, and, in the twentieth century, «truth to materials» and «form follows function». Cf. the note on the angular triglyph (4.3.1–2). 525

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV 5. Uti autem in doricis triglyphorum et mutulorum est inventa ratio, item in ionicis denticulorum constitutio propriam in operibus habet rationem, et quemadmodum mutuli cantheriorum proiecturae ferunt imaginem, sic in ionicis denticuli ex proiecturis asserum habent imitationem. itaque in graecis operibus nemo sub mutulo denticulos constituit. non enim possunt subtus cantherios asseres esse. quod ergo supra cantherios et templa in veritate debet esse conlocatum, id in imaginibus si infra constitutum fuerit mendosam habebit operis rationem. etiam quod antiqui non probaverunt neque instituerunt in fastigiis <mutulos aut> denticulos fieri sed puras coronas, ideo quod nec cantherii nec asseres contra fastigiorum frontes distribuuntur nec possunt prominere, sed ad stillicidia proclinati conlocantur. ita quod non potest in veritate fieri, id non putaverunt in imaginibus factum posse certam rationem habere. And just as in the Doric the principle of triglyphs and mutules was found, so in the Ionic the disposition of the dentils has its own basis in the works; and just as the mutules reproduce the image of the projections of the rafters, so in the Ionic the dentils imitate the projections of the laths (asseres). For this reason, in Greek works no one sets dentils beneath mutules, since laths cannot lie beneath rafters. So what in reality must be set above the rafters and the purlin, if in the images it is placed below, will give the work a faulty design. The ancients, moreover, did not approve or establish the making of ⟨mutules or⟩ dentils on the pediments, but only plain cornices, because neither the rafters nor the laths are distributed against the fronts of the pediments, nor can they project, but are set sloping towards the drip. Thus, what cannot be done in reality, they judged could have no sound design when done in the images. 6. omnia enim certa proprietate et a veris naturae deducta moribus transduxerunt in operum perfectiones, et ea probaverunt quorum explicationes in disputationibus rationem possunt habere veritatis. itaque ex eis originibus symmetrias et proportiones uniuscuiusque generis constitutas reliquerunt. quorum ingressus persecutus de ionicis et corinthiis institutionibus supra dixi, nunc vero doricam rationem summamque eius speciem breviter exponam. For they carried over all things into the perfection of their works with sure propriety and drawn from the true laws of nature, and they approved only those things whose explanations can uphold, in debate, the principle of truth. And so, from those origins, they left the symmetries and proportions of each kind 526

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV established. Having traced their development, I have spoken above of the Ionic and Corinthian rules; now, however, I shall briefly set out the Doric system and the general character of its appearance. Critical and architectural note — IV.2. The sequence tigna–triglyphi, cantherii –mutuli and asseres–denticuli explains stone ornament through an ancient theory of translation from timber construction. Opas, tignorum cubicula, intertignium and metopa form a technical chain which must not be reduced to generic decoration. Vitruvius explicitly rejects the explanation of triglyphs as images of windows. His relation between veritas and imago is historically influential, but neither its aetiology nor his proposed Greek derivations independently prove the archaeological origin of every member. The supplement ⟨met⟩oparum retains its editorial status. 527

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV Chapter 3 1. Nonnulli antiqui architecti negaverunt dorico genere aedes sacras oportere fieri, quod mendosae et disconvenientes in his symmetriae conficiebantur. itaque negavit Arcesius, item Pytheos, non minus Hermogenes. nam is cum paratam habuisset marmoris copiam in doricae aedis perfectionem, <> commutavit ex eadem copia et eam ionicam Libero Patri fecit. sed tamen non quod invenusta est species aut genus aut formae dignitas, sed quod inpedita est distributio et incommoda in opere triglyphorum et lacunariorum [distributione]. Critical note — Bk. 4.3.1–2. The 'angular triglyph conflict' is the chief objection to the Doric in temples: the triglyph must fall at once over the column's axis and at the corner of the frieze—incompatible demands that force either the narrowing of the end intercolumniation or the distortion of the metope. Hence Arcesius, Pytheos, and Hermogenes rejected it. Vitruvius nonetheless sets out the corrected system. It is one of the classic problems of Greek architecture. Some ancient architects denied that sacred buildings should be built in the Doric style, because they created false and inappropriate symmetries. And so Arcesius denied it, Pythius as well, and Hermogenes no less. For when he had prepared a supply of marble for the completion of the Doric building, he changed it from the same supply and made it Ionic for the Free Father. However, it is not that the species or genus or dignity of the form are unattractive, but rather that the distribution is complicated and inconvenient in the arrangement of the triglyphs and ceiling work. 2. namque necesse est triglyphos constitui contra medios tetrantes columnarum, metopasque quae inter triglyphos fient aeque longas esse quam altas. contraque in angulares columnas triglyphi in extremis partibus constituuntur et non contra medios tetrantes. ita metopae, quae proximae ad angulares triglyphos fiunt, non exeunt quadratae sed oblongiores triglyphi dimidia latitudine. at qui metopas aequales volunt facere, intercolumnia extrema contrahunt triglyphi dimidia latitudine. hoc autem sive metoparum longitudinibus sive intercolumniorum contractionibus efficietur, est mendosum. quapropter antiqui vitare visi sunt in aedibus sacris doricae symmetriae rationem. For the triglyphs must be set opposite the middle quarter-points (tetrantes) of the columns, and the metopes between the triglyphs must be as long as they are 528

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV high. But at the corner columns the triglyphs are placed at the ends, not opposite the middle points; and so the metopes nearest the corner triglyphs come out not square but oblong, broader by half the width of a triglyph. Those who wish to make the metopes equal contract the outermost intercolumniations by half the width of a triglyph. But this—whether done by lengthening the metopes or by narrowing the intercolumniations—is faulty. For this reason the ancients seem to have avoided the scheme of Doric symmetry in their temples. Explanatory note — Bk. 4.3 (the angular-triglyph problem). This is one of the most famous passages in the treatise. Vitruvius sets out the structural contradiction of the Doric order: the rule requires each triglyph to be centered on the axis of its column and every metope to be square; yet at the corners the triglyph must occupy the end of the frieze, so that the adjoining metope becomes wider —by half a triglyph's width— and ceases to be square. The two ancient remedies —widening the corner metope or contracting the outermost intercolumniation— Vitruvius calls mendosum, 'faulty.' For this awkwardness, he says, the ancients avoided the Doric order in temples; and he recalls that Hermogenes, having already prepared the marble for a Doric temple, converted it into an Ionic one dedicated to Father Bacchus (Liber Pater). The Roman solution —leaving a half-metope at the corner— allowed columns and triglyphs to be aligned once more. Collation confirms the transmitted Latin (namque necesse est triglyphos constitui contra medios tetrantes columnarum… est mendosum), with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 4.3 (angular triglyph). On the angular-triglyph problem, Gros's Budé (1992) devotes an extended commentary to the 'errors' that exegetes charge against Vitruvius, seeking to understand the logic of his choices rather than to correct them, and sets the passage within Vitruvius's polemic against the partisans of the Ionic order. Granger (Loeb) renders mendosum literally; Rowland and Howe explain the Roman half-metope solution with diagrams; Corso-Romano detail the terminology of tetrantes and metopae. This edition keeps the transmitted Latin (namque necesse est… est mendosum) unemended and translates in its own voice. The testimony of H and of the codices collated by Gros offers no variant here that alters the sense: the difficulty is doctrinal, not textual. 529

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV 3. Nos autem exponimus, uti ordo postulat, quemadmodum a praeceptoribus accepimus, uti si qui voluerit his rationibus attendens ita ingredi, habeat proportiones explicatas, quibus emendatas et sine vitiis efficere possit aedium sacrarum dorico more perfectiones. frons aedis doricae in loco quo columnae constituuntur dividatur, si tetrastylos erit, in partes XXVII, si hexastylos, XXXXII. ex his pars una erit modulus, qui graece ἐμβάτης dicitur, cuius moduli constitutione ratiocinationibus efficiuntur omnis operis distributiones. We, however, set it forth as the order of treatment requires, just as we received it from our teachers, so that anyone who wishes to proceed with attention to these rules may have the proportions laid out by which he can achieve, corrected and free of faults, the perfection of sacred buildings in the Doric manner. The front of a Doric temple, at the place where the columns are set, is divided—if it is tetrastyle—into twenty-seven parts; if hexastyle, into forty-two. One of these parts will be the module, which in Greek is called ἐμβάτης (embátes), by whose establishment all the distributions of the work are determined by calculation. 4. Crassitudo columnarum erit duorum modulorum, altitudo cum capitulo XIIII. capituli crassitudo unius moduli, latitudo duorum et moduli sextae partis. crassitudo capituli dividatur in partes tres, e quibus una plinthus cum cymatio fiat, altera echinus cum anulis, tertia hypotrachelion. contrahatur columna ita uti in tertio libro de ionicis est scriptum. epistylii altitudo unius moduli cum taenia et guttis, taenia moduli septima, guttarum longitudo sub taenia contra triglyphos alta cum regula parte sexta moduli praependeat. item epistylii latitudo ima respondeat hypotrachelio summae columnae. supra epistylium conlocandi sunt triglyphi cum suis metopis, alti unius et dimidiati moduli, lati in fronte unius moduli, ita divisi ut in angularibus columnis et in mediis contra tetrantes medios sint conlocati, et intercolumniis reliquis bini, in mediis pronao et postico terni. ita relaxatis mediis intervallis, sine inpeditionibus aditus accedentibus erit ad deorum simulacra. The thickness of the columns will be two modules, and their height, including the capital, fourteen. The thickness of the capital is one module, and its width two and one-sixth modules. The thickness of the capital is divided into three parts: one forms the plinth with the cymatium; the second, the echinus with its annulets; the third, the hypotrachelion. The column is diminished as is written, for the Ionic, in the third book. The height of the architrave (epistylium) is one 530

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV module, with the taenia and the guttae; the taenia a seventh of the module; the length of the guttae, beneath the taenia and in line with the triglyphs, hangs down to the line of the taenia, and their width is a sixth of the module. Likewise the lower face of the architrave should answer to the hypotrachelion at the top of the column. Above the architrave the triglyphs are set with their metopes, one and a half modules high and one module wide at the front, so arranged that at the corner columns and the middle ones they stand opposite the middle quarterpoints (tetrantes), with two in the remaining intercolumniations and three in the middle of the pronaos and the rear portico. Thus, with the central intervals left open, there will be unimpeded access for those approaching the images of the gods. 5. triglyphorum latitudo dividatur in partes sex, ex quibus partibus quinque in medio, duae dimidiae dextra ac sinistra designentur regula. una in medio deformetur femur, quod graece μηρός dicitur. secundum eam canaliculi ad normae cacumen inprimantur. ex ordine eorum dextra ac sinistra altera femina constituantur. in extremis partibus semicanaliculi intervertantur. triglyphis ita conlocatis, metopae quae sunt inter triglyphos aeque altae sint quam longae, item in extremis angulis hemimetopia sint inpressa dimidia moduli latitudine. ita enim erit ut omnia vitia et metoparum et intercolumniorum et lacunariorum, quod aequales divisiones factae erunt, emendentur. The width of the triglyphs is divided into six parts, of which five are marked out in the middle, and two halves, right and left, by the rule. In the middle one thigh (femur) is shaped, which in Greek is called μηρός; along it the channels are cut to the point of the set-square (norma); on either side of them, right and left, the other thighs (femina) are formed; at the outer edges the half-channels are turned in. With the triglyphs thus placed, the metopes between the triglyphs should be as high as they are long; likewise at the outermost corners half-metopes are impressed, half a module wide. For thus it will come about that all the faults—of the metopes, of the intercolumniations, and of the coffers—are corrected, since the divisions will have been made equal. 6. triglyphi capitula sexta parte moduli sunt faciunda. supra triglyphorum capitula corona est conlocanda in proiectura dimidiae et sextae partis habens cymatium doricum in imo, alterum in summo. item cum cymatiis corona crassa ex dimidia moduli. dividendae autem sunt in corona ima ad perpendiculum 531

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV triglyphorum et medias metopas viarum directiones et guttarum distributiones, ita uti guttae sex in longitudinem, tres in latitudinem pateant. reliqua spatia, quod latiores sunt metopae quam triglyphi, pura relinquantur aut flumina scalpantur, ad ipsumque mentum coronae incidatur linea quae scotia dicitur. reliqua omnia, tympana simae coronae, quemadmodum supra scriptum est in ionicis, ita perficiantur. The capitals of the triglyphs are made one-sixth of a module. Above the triglyph capitals a cornice (corona) is to be set, with a projection of one-half and onesixth, having a Doric cymatium below and another above. With the cornice, then, and the cymatia, the whole cornice is to be made half a module thick. On the front of the cornice, above the triglyphs and the metopes, are distributed— plumb with the triglyphs and the centers of the metopes—the channels (viae) and the arrangement of the guttae, so that six guttae appear lengthwise and three across. The remaining spaces, since the metopes are wider than the triglyphs, are left plain or carved with small figures of gods. And on the very underside (mentum) of the cornice a line is cut which in Greek is called σκωτία (scotia). Everything else—the capitals of the columns, the architraves, the cornices—is finished as written above for the Ionic. 7. Haec ratio in operibus diastylis erit constituta. si vero systylon et monotriglyphon opus erit faciundum, frons aedis, si tetrastylos erit, dividatur in partes XVIIII S, si hexastylos erit, dividatur in partes XXVIIII S. ex his pars una erit modulus, ad quem uti supra scriptum est dividantur. This scheme will be established for diastyle works. But if a systyle and monotriglyph work is to be made, the front of the temple, if tetrastyle, is divided into nineteen and a half parts; if hexastyle, into twenty-nine and a half. Of these, one part will be the module, by which everything is divided as written above. 8. ita supra singula epistylia et metopae et triglyphi bini erunt conlocandi, in angularibus hoc amplius dimidiatus et quantum est spatium hemitriglyphi id accedit. in mediano contra fastigium trium triglyphorum et trium metoparum spatium distabit, quo latius medium intercolumnium accedentibus ad aedem habeat laxamentum et adversus simulacra deorum aspectus dignitatem. Thus, above each architrave side, metopes and triglyphs will be placed in pairs; at the corners, this goes further, so much so that the space of the hemiglyph is reduced by half. In the middle, against the pediment, there will be 532

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV a space of three triglyphs and three metopes, so that the wider middle of the intercolumniations will have a relief for those approaching the house and a dignity of appearance in front of the images of the gods. 9. Columnas autem striari XX striis oportet. quae si planae erunt, angulos habeant XX designatos. sin autem excavabuntur, sic est forma facienda ita uti quam magnum est intervallum striae, tam magnis striaturae paribus lateribus quadratum describatur, in medio autem quadrato circini centrum conlocetur et agatur linea rotundationis, quae quadrationis angulos tangat, et quantum erit curvaturae inter rotundationem et quadratam descriptionem, tantum ad formam excaventur. ita dorica columna sui generis striaturae habebit perfectionem. But the columns must be fluted with 20 flutes. If they are flat, let them have 20 designated angles. But if they are to be excavated, the form will be made so that the greater the interval of the fluting, the greater the equal sides of the fluting will be, describing the square; and in the middle of the square of the circle the center is placed, and a rounding line is drawn, which touches the angles of the square, and the extension of the curvature between the rounding and the description of the square should only be excavated for the form. Thus the Doric column will have the perfection of its type of fluting. 10. de adiectione eius qua media adaugetur, uti in tertio volumine de ionicis est perscripta, ita et in his transferatur. Quoniam exterior species symmetriarum et corinthiorum et doricorum et ionicorum est perscripta, necesse est etiam interiores cellarum pronaique distributiones explicare. As for the addition to it, whereby half is added, as is recorded in the third volume on Ionic matters, so too it is carried over in these. Since the external appearance of the symmetrical, Corinthian, Doric and Ionic cells has been recorded, it is also necessary to explain the internal distribution of the cells and their inclinations. Editorial note. — Chapter 3 sets out the Doric order, which, Vitruvius reports, some earlier architects had judged unfit for temples on account of its “faulty” symmetries. The difficulty is the celebrated corner-triglyph problem: each triglyph must stand over the axis of its column, yet the frieze must also close with a triglyph at the angle — two demands that cannot both be met without contracting the end intercolumniation or widening the corner metopes. 533

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV Vitruvius gives the rules (the module system, the triglyph divided into six parts, the half-metope at the corner) by which the conflict is managed; it would exercise theorists from the Hellenistic age to the Renaissance. The Doric shaft is fluted with twenty flutes, and the whole order, like the Ionic dentils, is read as the stone image of an earlier timber construction (cf. 4.2). Critical and metrological note — IV.3. The Doric difficulty concerns the distribution of triglyphs, metopes and intercolumniations: the corner triglyph, column axis and square metope cannot all be reconciled without adjustment. Femur and μηρός here denote the vertical bands of the triglyph; a problematic form such as femina must not yield an incoherent translation as ‘women’. Modulus, tetrantes, hemitriglyphium and the series XIX S / XXIX S remain ancient dimensional expressions. The twenty flutes and the arrangement of guttae require control against the particular reconstruction, rather than decimal normalization in the Latin. 534

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV Chapter 4 1. distribuitur autem longitudo aedis uti latitudo sit longitudinis dimidiae partis, ipsaque cella parte quarta longior sit, quam est latitudo, cum pariete, qui paries valvarum habuerit conlocationem. reliquae tres partes pronai ad antas parietum procurrant, quae antae columnarum crassitudinem habere debent. et si aedes erit latitudine maior quam pedes XX, duae columnae inter duas antas interponantur, quae disiungant pteromatos et pronai spatium. item intercolumnia tria, quae erunt inter antas et columnas, pluteis marmoreis sive ex intestino opere factis intercludantur ita uti fores habeant, per quas itinera pronao fiant. The length of the temple is distributed so that the width is half the length, and the cella itself is one quarter longer than it is wide, including the wall in which the doors are set. The remaining three parts run forward, for the pronaos, to the antae of the walls; these antae should have the thickness of the columns. And if the temple is more than twenty feet wide, let two columns be set between the two antae, separating the space of the surrounding colonnade (pteroma) from that of the pronaos. Likewise, let the three intercolumniations between the antae and the columns be closed with marble screens or panels of joinery, leaving doors in them by which one may enter the pronaos. 2. item si maior erit latitudo quam pedes XL, columnae contra regiones columnarum, quae inter antas sunt, introrsus conlocentur. et hae altitudinem habeant aeque quam quae sunt in fronte, crassitudines autem earum extenuentur his rationibus uti si octava parte erunt quae sunt in fronte, hae fiant X parte, sin autem VIIII aut decima, pro rata parte. in concluso enim aere si quae extenuatae erunt, non discernentur. sin autem videbuntur graciliores, cum exterioribus fuerint striae <XX aut> XXIIII, in his faciendae erunt XXVIII aut XXXII. ita quod detrahitur de corpore scapi, striarum numero adiecto adaugebitur ratione quo minus videatur, et ita exaequabitur dispari ratione columnarum crassitudo. 2. If the temple is more than forty feet wide, place interior columns opposite those standing between the antae. Their height should equal that of the front columns, but their diameters should be reduced: where the front columns have a diameter one-eighth of their height, the interior ones should have one-tenth; where the front proportion is one-ninth or one-tenth, reduce 535

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV the interior diameters proportionately. In an enclosed space the reduction will be less apparent. If they nevertheless seem too slender, give the interior columns twenty-eight or thirty-two flutes where the exterior columns have ⟨twenty or⟩ twenty-four. The greater number of flutes compensates visually for the reduction in the shaft, allowing columns of unequal diameters to appear equivalent. 3. hoc autem efficit ea ratio quod oculus plura et crebriora signa tangendo maiore visus circumitione pervagatur. namque si duae columnae aeque crassae lineis circummetientur, e quibus una sit non striata altera striata, et circa striglium cava et angulos striarum linea corpora tangat, tametsi columnae aeque crassae fuerint, lineae quae circumdatae erunt <non erunt> aequales, quod striarum et striglium circuitus maiorem efficit lineae longitudinem. sin autem hoc ita videbitur, non est alienum in angustis locis et in concluso spatio graciliores columnarum symmetrias in opere constituere, cum habeamus adiutricem striarum temperaturam. This comes about because the eye, touching more numerous and frequent marks, ranges over a wider compass of vision. For if two equally thick columns are measured round with lines, one unfluted and the other fluted, and the line follows the bodies along the hollows of the flutes and the edges (striglium) between them, then, even though the columns are equally thick, the lines drawn around them will not be equal, because the circuit of the flutes and their channels gives the line a greater length. And if this is so, it is not out of place, in narrow places and enclosed spaces, to employ more slender proportions in the columns, since we have the tempering of the fluting to help us. 4. ipsius autem cellae parietum crassitudinem pro rata parte magnitudinis fieri oportet, dum antae eorum crassitudinibus columnarum sint aequales. et si ex structis futuri sunt, quam minutissimis caementis struantur, sin autem quadrato saxo aut marmore, maxime modicis paribusque videtur esse faciundum, quod media coagmenta medii lapides continentes firmiorem facient omnis operis perfectionem, item circum coagmenta et cubilia eminentes expressiones graphicoteran efficient in aspectu delectationem. The thickness of the walls of the cella itself should be made in proportion to its size, provided that its antae are equal to the thickness of the columns. And if they are to be of rubble-work, let them be built with the smallest possible 536

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV aggregate; but if of squared stone or marble, it is best to use modest and equal pieces, since the middle stones, binding the central joints, will make the whole work firmer in its finish; and moreover the projecting reliefs around the joints and the beds will produce a more elegant delight to the eye. Architectural note — IV.4. Pronaos and cella denote distinct parts of the temple and remain terminologically separate. Their proportions, the disposition of antae and columns, and the treatment of wall surfaces must be read as interdependent instructions rather than as a list of isolated modern dimensions. 537

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV Chapter 5 1. 1. Regiones autem, quas debent spectare aedes sacrae deorum inmortalium, sic erunt constituendae, uti, si nulla ratio inpedierit liberaque fuerit potestas, aedis signumque, quod erit in cella conlocatum, spectet ad vespertinam caeli regionem, uti, qui adierint ad aram immolantes aut sacrificia facientes, spectent ad partem caeli orientis et simulacrum, quod erit in aede, et ita vota suscipientes contueantur aedem et orientem caelum ipsaque simulacra videantur exaudientia contueri supplicantes et sacrificantes, quod aras omnes deorum necesse esse videatur ad orientem spectare. The directions faced by the temples of the immortal gods should be established as follows. If nothing prevents it and the choice is free, let the temple and the image within its cella face the western part of the sky, so that those approaching the altar to sacrifice look towards the east and the image in the temple. In taking their vows they will thus behold both the temple and the rising sky, while the images appear to listen to those praying and sacrificing. For the altars of all the gods should, it seems, face east. 2. sin autem loci natura interpellaverit, tunc convertendae sunt earum regionum constitutiones, uti quam plurima pars moenium e templis earum conspiciatur. item si secundum flumina aedis sacra fiet, ita uti Aegypto circa Nilum, ad fluminis ripas videntur spectare debere. similiter si circum vias publicas erunt aedificia deorum, ita constituantur uti praetereuntes possint respicere et in conspectu salutationes facere. But if the nature of the site interferes, then the orientation of those regions must be changed, so that as much of the city as possible may be seen from the temples of the gods. Likewise, if sacred temples are built beside rivers—as in Egypt, around the Nile—they ought to face the river’s banks. And similarly, if the buildings of the gods stand along the public roads, let them be so arranged that passers-by may see them from the front and make their salutations in full view. Historical and ritual note — IV.5. The orientation rule is conditional. Where the site permits, the cult image and cella are arranged so that the worshipper looking towards the deity also faces east. Topography, the city, rivers and public roads can require exceptions. The orientation of the building, the image and the observer must therefore be distinguished. Archaeological diversity may 538
THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV illuminate the rule’s reception without turning the literary prescription into a universal account of Greek and Roman sanctuaries. 539

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV Chapter 6 1. 1. Ostiorum autem et eorum antepagmentorum in aedibus hae sunt rationes, uti primum constituatur, quot genera sint [futurae]. Genera sunt enim thyromaton haec: doricum, ionicum, atticurges. Horum ⟨dorici generis⟩ symmetriae conspiciuntur his rationibus, uti corona summa, quae supra antepagmentum superius inponitur, aeque librata sit capitulis summis columnarum, quae in pronao fuerint. Lumen autem thyretri constituatur sic, uti quae altitudo aedis a pavimento ad lacunaria fuerit, dividatur in partes tres semis et ex eis duae partes ⟨semis⟩ lumini valvarum altitudine constituantur. Haec autem dividatur in partes XII et ex eis quinque et dimidia latitudo luminis fiat in imo. Et in summo contrahatur, si erit lumen ab imo ad sedecim pedes, antepagmenti III parte; ⟨si⟩ XVI pedum ad XXV, superior pars luminis contrahatur antepagmenti parte IIII; si ab pedibus XXV ad XXX, summa pars contrahatur antepagmenti parte VIII. Reliqua, quo altiora erunt, ad perpendiculum videntur oportere conlocari. 1. The rules for temple doors and their frames are as follows. First, the different kinds must be distinguished: Doric, Ionic and Attic. The Doric proportions follow these principles. The upper cornice above the lintel should be level with the tops of the column capitals in the pronaos. Establish the clear opening by dividing the height of the temple, from pavement to coffering, into three and a half parts, and assigning two and a half to the height of the doorway. Divide this height into twelve parts and make the lower width of the opening five and a half of them. If the opening is no more than sixteen feet high, contract it at the top by one-third of the jamb; from sixteen to twenty-five feet, by onequarter; and from twenty-five to thirty feet, by one-eighth. Taller openings should, it seems, have vertical sides. The symmetries of the Doric are set out thus: let the upper cornice, which rests on the top jamb, be level with the tops of the capitals of the columns in the pronaos. Let the door-opening (lumen) be fixed so that the height of the temple, from the pavement to the coffered ceiling, is divided into three parts and a half, and of these two and a half make the height of the opening for the leaves. Let this height be divided into twelve parts, and of these let five and a half form the width of the opening at the bottom; and at the top let it be drawn in: if the opening is up to sixteen feet, by a third part of the jamb; if from sixteen to 540

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV twenty-five feet, by a fourth part; if from twenty-five to thirty feet, by a seventh part. The rest, the higher they are, should be set plumb. 2. ipsa autem antepagmenta contrahantur in summo suae crassitudinis XIIII parte. supercilii crassitudo quanta antepagmentorum in summa parte erit crassitudo. cymatium faciundum est antepagmenti parte sexta, proiectura autem quanta est eius crassitudo. sculpendum est cymatium lesbium cum astragalo. supra cymatium quod erit in supercilio, conlocandum est hyperthyrum crassitudine supercilii, et in eo scalpendum est cymatium doricum, astragalum lesbium. sima scalptura corona plana cum cymatio, proiectura autem eius erit quanta altitudo. supercilii quod supra antepagmenta inponitur, dextra atque sinistra proiecturae sic sunt faciundae uti crepidines excurrant et in unguem ipso cymatio coniungantur. Let the jambs themselves be drawn in at the top by a fourteenth part of their thickness. Let the thickness of the lintel (supercilium) equal that of the jambs at their upper part. The cyma is made a sixth part of the jamb, and its projection equal to its thickness; a Lesbian cyma with an astragal is to be carved. Above the cyma that crowns the lintel is placed the hyperthyrum, of the thickness of the lintel, and on it a Doric cyma and a Lesbian astragal are carved. At the very top a plain cornice with its cyma is carved, its projection equal to its height. Of the lintel that rests upon the jambs, the projections to right and left are so made that the fillets run out and join in a mitre with the cyma itself. 3. Sin autem ionico genere futura erunt, lumen altum ad eundem modum quemadmodum in doricis fieri videtur. latitudo constituatur ut altitudo dividatur in partes duas et dimidiam, eiusque partis unius ima luminis fiat latitudo. contracturae ita uti in doricis. crassitudo antepagmentorum ⟨ex⟩ altitudine luminis in fronte XIIII parte, cymatium huius crassitudinis sexta. reliqua pars praeter cymatium dividatur in partes XII. harum trium prima corsa fiat cum astragalo, secunda quattuor, tertia quinque, et eae aeque corsae cum astragalis circumcurrant. 3. For Ionic doors, the height of the clear opening should be determined as for Doric doors. Establish the width by dividing the height into two and a half parts and making the lower width one of them. The contractions follow the Doric rules. The face of the frame should be one-fourteenth of the opening’s height, and its cyma one-sixth of that thickness. Divide the remainder, 541

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IV excluding the cyma, into twelve parts: assign three to the first fascia with its astragal, four to the second and five to the third. These fasciae and their astragals should continue around the opening. 4. Hyperthyra autem ad eundem modum componantur quemadmodum in doricis. Pro crepidinibus ancones, sive parotides vocantur, excalptae dextra ac sinistra praependeant ad imi supercilii libramentum, praeter folium. Eae habeant in fronte crassitudinem ex antepagmenti tribus partibus, imo quarta parte graciliore quam superiora. Fores ita compingantur, uti scapi cardinales sint ex latitudine luminis totius XII parte. Inter duos scapos tympana ex XII partibus habeant ternas partes. The hyperthyra are composed in the same way as in the Doric, in proportional parts. The consoles (ancones)—or parotides, as they are also called —carved to right and left, hang down to the level of the lower lintel, save for the acanthus leaf. Let them have, at the front, a thickness of two of the three parts of the jamb, and at the bottom be a fourth part more slender than above. Let the leaves (fores) be framed so that the hinge-stiles (scapi cardinales) are a twelfth part of the whole width of the opening. Between the two stiles let the panels (tympana) have three of the twelve parts. 5. inpagibus distributiones ita fient uti divisis altitudinibus in partes V duae superiori, tres inferiori designentur. super medium medii inpages conlocentur, ex reliquis alii in summo alii in imo compingantur. altitudo inpagis fiat tympani tertia parte, cymatium sexta parte inpagis. scaporum latitudines inpagis dimidia parte, item replum de inpage dimidia et sexta parte. scapi qui sunt secundum antepagmentum, dimidium inpagis constituantur. sin autem valvatae erunt, altitudines ita manebunt, in latitudinem adiciatur amplius foris latitudo. si quadriforis futura est, altitudo adiciatur. The rails (impages) are distributed by dividing the height into five parts: two are assigned to the upper, three to the lower. Over the middle let the middle rails be set; of the rest, some are framed at the top, others at the bottom. Let the height of the rail be a third part of the panel, and its cyma a sixth of the rail. Let the width of the stiles be half the rail; the meeting-stile (replum), half plus a sixth of the rail. The stiles next to the jambs are made half the rail. But if the doors are to be folding (valvatae), the heights remain the same, and to the width is added that of another leaf; if it is to be four-leaved, height is added. 542

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV 6. Atticurge autem isdem rationibus perficiuntur quibus dorica. praeterea corsae sub cymatiis in antepagmentis circumdantur, quae ita distribui debent uti antepagmenti praeter cymatium ex partibus VII habeant duas partes. ipsaque non fiunt clathrata neque bifora sed valvata, et aperturas habent in exteriores partes. Quas rationes aedium sacrarum in formationibus oporteat fieri <doricis> ionicis corinthiisque operibus, quoad potui attingere, veluti legitimis moribus exposui. nunc de tuscanicis dispositionibus quemadmodum institui oporteat dicam. Attic doors are executed by the same rules as the Doric. Moreover, beneath the cymas, bands (corsae) are set round the jambs, which are to be so distributed that, of the seven parts of the jamb—apart from the cyma—they occupy two parts. And these doors are made neither latticed nor folding, but with leaves (valvatae), and they open outward. I have set forth, as far as I have been able, according to established usage, what rules should be followed in designing sacred temples in Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian works. Now I shall speak of how the Tuscan arrangements ought to be set out. Note — Bk. 4.6. This chapter is the only systematic ancient source on the design of classical monumental doors. It distinguishes three kinds—Doric, Ionic, and Attic—and fixes their proportions and joinery: jambs (antepagmenta), lintel (supercilium), hyperthyron, consoles (ancones), hingestiles, panels (tympana), rails (impages), and leaves (valvae). A fundamental reference for reconstructing ancient doors. I have explained, as far as I have been able, which aspects of sacred buildings should be carried out in Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian works, according to legitimate usage. I shall now speak of the Tuscan arrangements as they ought to be established. Critical and terminological note — IV.6. Temple doors form a chain of proportions linking temple height, lumen, frame, supercilium and moldings. Antepagmenta, hyperthyrum, corsae, ancones/parotides, scapi cardinales, tympana, impages and replum are retained where a single modern joinery term would claim excessive precision. Supplements such as ⟨dorici generis⟩ remain editorial interventions. The contractions of the opening and frame are proportional data, not a modern system of graphic perspective. 543

Historical explanations of the orders are attributed to Vitruvius and distinguished from modern archaeological reconstruction. 1. Altars should face east and always stand below the cult images within the temple, so that those who pray and sacrifice look upward towards the deity. Their heights should vary according to the decor appropriate to each god. For Jupiter and all the celestial gods, make the altars as high as possible; for Vesta, Earth and the Mother, set them low. These principles yield altar forms appropriate in their proportions. Explanatory note — Bk. 4.9 (orientation of altars). The brief closing chapter of Book IV fixes the decorum of altars: they should face east and stand lower than the image of the god, so that the worshipper looks upward to the divinity. Vitruvius grades their height by the celestial hierarchy —very high for Jupiter and the gods of heaven; low for Vesta, Earth, and Sea (the chthonic and hearth deities)— applying to ritual the principle of decor that governs the whole treatise. The eastward orientation links the sacrifice to sunrise, a convention of Roman cult confirmed by archaeology at many sanctuaries. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. 552

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IV Having explained the composition of temples in this book, I shall give the rules for the arrangement of public works in the next. It sustains the contrast between the high altars of Jupiter and the celestial gods and low altars associated with terrestrial powers. Marique in another printed constitution must be recorded as an alternative reading, not silently combined with Matrique. The prescription belongs to Vitruvius’s ritual decor and does not describe every altar documented archaeologically. 553

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V ARGUMENTUM LIBRI V — ON public buildings: the forum and the basilica, the treasury, the curia and the prison; the Greek and Latin theater, its acoustics and the resonant bronze vessels; musical scales according to the theory of Aristoxenus; the porticoes, the palaestras, the ports and the shipyards. Notice. — Book V concerns the public buildings of the forum. It describes the forum and basilica — including the one Vitruvius himself built at Fanum Fortunae, his only documented work — the treasury, prison and senate-house, then the theater, with its harmonic theory and the bronze sounding-vessels (echea) tuned to the Greek genera. Baths, the palaestra and gymnasium, and harbors with their underwater concrete complete the book. It is a primary source for Roman urbanism, acoustics and hydraulic engineering. Preface 1.
