Since this is the pattern of growth, the upper members are appropriately reduced in both height and thickness. 4. Basilicarum loca adiuncta foris quam calidissimis partibus oportet constitui, ut per hiemem sine molestia tempestatium se conferre in eas negotiatores possint. Earumque latitudines ne minus quam ex tertia, ne plus ex dimidia longitudinis constituantur, nisi si loci natura inpedierit et aliter coegerit symmetriam commutari. Sin autem locus erit amplior in longitudine, chalcidica in extremis constituantur, uti sunt in Iulia Aquiliana. The sites of the basilicas, adjoined to the fora, should be established on the warmest sides, so that in winter the merchants may resort to them without the annoyance of storms. Their widths should be set at no less than a third and no more than half of their length, unless the nature of the site prevents it and compels the symmetry to be otherwise altered. But if the site is more ample in length, let chalcidica be placed at the ends, as they are in the Julia Aquiliana. 5. Columnae basilicarum tam altae, quam porticus latae fuerint, faciendae videntur; porticus, quam medium spatium futurum est, ex tertia finiatur. Columnae superiores minores quam inferiores, uti supra scriptum est, constituantur. Pluteum, quod fuerit inter superiores et inferiores columnas, item quarta parte minus, quam superiores columnae fuerint, oportere fieri videtur, uti supra basilicae contignationem ambulantes ab negotiatoribus ne conspiciantur. Epistylia, zophora, coronae ex symmetriis columnarum, uti in tertio libro diximus, explicentur. The columns of the basilicas appear to be as tall as the width of the portico; the gallery, which will be the space in between, should be completed from the third level. The upper columns should be smaller than the lower ones, as described above. The shelf, which was between the upper and lower columns, also a quarter shorter than the upper columns, seems to have been necessary so as not to be seen by the merchants walking on the basilica floor. The architraves 560

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V (epistylia), friezes (zophora), and cornices are set out according to the symmetries of the columns, as we said in the third book. 6. Non minus summam dignitatem et venustatem possunt habere comparationes basilicarum quo genere Coloniae Iuliae Fanestri conlocavi curavique faciendam, cuius proportiones et symmetriae sic sunt constitutae. mediana testudo inter columnas est longa pedes CXX, lata pedes LX. porticus eius circa testudinem inter parietes et columnas lata pedes XX. columnae altitudinibus perpetuis cum capitulis pedes L, crassitudinibus quinûm, habentes post se parastaticas altas pedes XX, latas pedes II S, crassas I S, quae sustinent trabes in quibus invehuntur porticuum contignationes. supraque eas aliae parastaticae pedum XVIII, latae binûm, crassae pedem, quae excipiunt item trabes sustinentes cantherium et porticûm, quae sunt summissa infra testudinem, tecta. 6. No less can comparisons of the basilicas of the kind I have placed and taken care to build in the Colonia Julia Fanestri, the proportions and symmetries of which are thus established. The central hall (testudo) between the columns is 120 feet long, 60 feet wide. Its portico around the dome between the walls and columns is 20 feet wide. The columns are of continuous heights with capitals of 50 feet, five feet thick, having behind them parastatics 20 feet high, 25 feet wide, and 15 feet thick, which support the beams on which the floors of the porticoes are carried. And above them other parastatics 18 feet, two feet wide, and a foot thick, which also accommodate the beams supporting the cantherium and the roofs of the porticoes, which are lowered below the dome. Designs of no less dignity and beauty can be achieved in basilicas — of which kind I myself designed and supervised the building (conlocavi curavique) at the Colonia Iulia Fanestris, whose proportions and symmetries were established as follows. The central vaulted nave (testudo), between the columns, is one hundred and twenty feet long and sixty wide. Its surrounding portico, between the walls and the columns, is twenty feet wide. The columns, in continuous height including their capitals, are fifty feet, with a thickness of five; behind them stand pilasters (parastaticae) twenty feet high, two and a half wide and one and a half thick, which support the beams that carry the floors of the porticoes. And above these are other pilasters eighteen feet high, two wide and 561

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V one thick, which in turn receive the beams that bear the rafters (cantherium) and the roofs of the porticoes, set below the level of the central nave. 7. reliqua spatia inter parastaticarum et columnarum trabes per intercolumnia luminibus sunt relicta. columnae sunt in latitudine testudinis cum angularibus dextra ac sinistra quaternae, in longitudine quae est foro proxima cum isdem angularibus octo, ex altera parte cum angularibus VI, ideo quod mediae duae in ea parte non sunt positae ne inpediant aspectus pronai aedis Augusti, quae est in medio latere parietis basilicae conlocata spectans medium forum et aedem Iovis, The remaining spaces, between the beams of the pilasters and those of the columns, are left open through the intercolumniations to admit light. Across the width of the nave (testudo) the columns are four on each side, counting the corner ones, right and left; along the long side nearest the forum, eight with the same corner columns; and on the other side, six, because the two central columns were not set on that side, so as not to block the view of the pronaos of the temple of Augustus, which stands in the middle of the basilica’s side wall, facing the center of the forum and the temple of Jupiter. 8. item tribunal quod est in ea aede hemicycli schematis minoris curvatura formatum. eius autem hemicycli in fronte est intervallum pedes XLVI, introrsus curvatura pedes XV, uti qui apud magistratus starent negotiantes in basilica ne inpedirent. supra columnas ex tribus tignis bipedalibus compactis trabes sunt circa conlocatae. eaeque ab tertiis columnis quae sunt in interiore parte revertuntur ad antas quae a pronao procurrunt dextraque et sinistra hemicyclium tangunt. Likewise, the tribunal in that hall is formed with the curvature of a hemicycle of a lesser segment. The front of this hemicycle is forty-six feet across, and its curvature inward fifteen feet, so that those who stood before the magistrates might not obstruct those doing business in the basilica. Above the columns, beams made of three two-foot timbers joined together are placed around; and these, from the third columns which are on the inner side, return to the antae that run forward from the pronaos and touch the hemicycle on the right and left. Likewise, the tribunal (tribunal) in that same hall is shaped as a hemicycle: its front spans forty-six feet and its inward curve fifteen, so that those appearing 562

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V before the magistrates would not impede those doing business in the basilica. Above the columns, on the inner side, beams made of three two-foot timbers joined together turn back towards the antae that project from the pronaos and meet the hemicycle on the right and left. 9. supra trabes contra capitula ex fulmentis dispositae pilae sunt conlocatae altae pedes III, latae quoqueversus quaternis. supra eas ex duobus tignis bipedalibus trabes everganeae circa sunt conlocatae. quibus insuper transtra cum capreolis columnarum contra corpora et antas et parietes pronai conlocata sustinent unum culmen perpetuae basilicae, alterum a medio supra pronaum aedis. Above the beams, opposite the capitals and set upon brackets, piers (pilae) are placed, three feet high and four feet wide each way. Upon these, made of two two-foot timbers, beams are laid running round about. And upon these, the cross-beams with the struts (capreoli) of the columns, set against the shafts, the antae and the walls of the pronaos, support two ridge-beams: one running the whole length of the basilica, the other rising from the center over the pronaos of the temple. 10. ita fastigiorum duplex pectinata dispositio extrinsecus tecti et interioris altae testudinis praestat speciem venustam. item sublata epistyliorum ornamenta et pluteorum columnarumque superiorum distributio operosam detrahit molestiam sumptusque inminuit ex magna parte summam. ipsae vero columnae in altitudine perpetua sub trabes testudinis perductae et magnificentiam inpensae et auctoritatem operi adaugere videntur. Thus the double arrangement of the roof-pediments, so produced, presents a beautiful appearance both on the exterior of the roof and within the high vaulted nave (testudo). Moreover, the omission of the ornaments of the architraves (epistylia), together with the arrangement of the parapets (plutei) and the upper columns, removes laborious work and greatly reduces the total cost. And the columns themselves, carried up in continuous height to the beams of the vault, seem to add magnificence to the outlay and authority to the work. Critical note — Bk. 5.1.6–10 (Basilica at Fano). This is the only building Vitruvius declares he himself designed and superintended (conlocavi curavique), in the Colonia Iulia Fanestris (Fano). The passage was corrupt and is here restored after Rose: in 5.1.10, 'tecti nata dispositio' (not 'T uti notae'); in 563

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V 5.1.8 two phrases lost by haplography are restored, 'hemicycli schematis minoris curvatura formatum. eius autem hemicycli' and 'circa conlocatae. eaeque ab tertiis columnis quae sunt'. The reading 'in the shape of a T', current in modern translations, derives from that corruption, though it aptly describes the actual plan (nave + transverse temple of Augustus). The archaeological discovery at Fano (2026) allows the Vitruvian measurements (testudo 120×60 feet; columns of 50 feet) to be checked for the first time; see Appendix S. Comparative note — Bk. 5.1.6–10 (Basilica at Fano). In the Budé series, Book V is the work of Catherine Saliou (Les Belles Lettres, 2009), the volume that completes the collection and argues each difficult reading, weighing the alternatives before deciding; her commentary on the forensic basilica is fundamental. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) transmit the 'T-shaped' description which, as the critical note observes, derives from the corruption T uti notae; Tavernor and Schofield (Penguin, 2009) accompany their version with reconstructions. This edition restores the text after Rose and translates in its own voice. What is new with respect to the whole editorial tradition is the comparison with the archaeological discovery at Fano (2026), treated as preliminary evidence: for the first time the Vitruvian measurements (a testudo of 120×60 feet, columns of 50 feet) can be checked against material remains; see Appendix S. Editorial note. — In 5.1.6–10 Vitruvius describes the basilica he himself designed and supervised at the Colonia Iulia Fanestris (modern Fano) — the one building he explicitly claims as his own work (conlocavi curavique). He departs from the usual plan: the columns rise the full height of the hall (testudo), the aisle running round them; the tribunal is set in a hemicycle forty-six feet across; and a double arrangement of pediments crowns roof and interior. The passage is therefore doubly valuable — as the only first-hand account of a Vitruvian design and as a control on his theory put into practice. On the proposed identification with the 2026 excavations in Piazza Andrea Costa, treated as provisional, see the Theses (no. 7). Critical and metrological note — V.1. The forum is distinguished from the Greek agora, and the basilica’s placement is related to seasonal use. At Fanum Fortunae, conlocavi curavique faciendam states Vitruvius’s responsibility for design and supervision. The central space of 120 × 60 Roman feet, the twenty- 564

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V foot portico and columns fifty feet high and five in diameter remain primary textual data. Testudo, porticus and parastaticae require explanatory translation. Excavation may inform a reconstruction, but neither a compatible ground plan nor institutional identification replaces the textual apparatus or establishes every architectural detail. 565

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V Chapter 2 1. Aerarium, carcer, curia foro sunt coniungenda, sed ita uti magnitudo ⟨ac⟩ symmetriae eorum foro respondeant. maxime quidem curia in primis est facienda ad dignitatem municipii sive civitatis. et si quadrata erit, quantum habuerit latitudinis dimidia addita constituatur altitudo, sin autem oblonga fuerit, longitudo et latitudo componatur et summae compositae, eius dimidia pars sub lacunariis altitudini detur. The treasury, the prison, and the senate-house (curia) should adjoin the forum, but so that the magnitude of their symmetry answers to the forum. Above all the curia is to be built in keeping with the dignity of the municipality or city. If it is square, let its height be established by adding to its width the half of that width; but if it is oblong, let its length and width be added together, and of that total sum let the half be given to the height, up to the coffered ceiling. 2. praeterea praecingendi sunt parietes medii coronis ex intestino opere aut albario ad dimidiam partem altitudinis. quae si non erunt, vox ibi disputantium elata in altitudinem intellectui non poterit esse audientibus. cum autem coronis praecincti parietes erunt, vox ab imis, morata priusquam in aera elata dissipabitur, auribus erit intellecta. Furthermore, the walls are to be girded at mid-height by cornices of joinery (intestinum opus) or of stucco (albarium). For if these are lacking, the voice of those debating, rising into the height, cannot be understood by the listeners. But when the walls are girded with cornices, the voice, held back from below before it rises into the air and is dissipated, will be understood by the ears. Critical and acoustic note — V.2. Aerarium, carcer and curia are related to the forum through dimensional correspondence. The curia’s height depends on whether its plan is square or oblong. Intestinum opus and albarium distinguish interior finishing or joinery from stucco work. The continuous cornice at mid-height is explained by Vitruvius as restraining the upward dispersal of the voice. Modern concepts of reflection, absorption or reverberation may assist comparison, but are not quantities measured in the ancient text. 566

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V Chapter 3 1. Cum forum constitutum fuerit, tum deorum inmortalium diebus festis ludorum spectationibus eligendus est locus theatro quam saluberrimus, uti in primo libro de salubritatibus in moenium conlocationibus est scriptum. per ludos enim cum coniugibus et liberis persedentes delectationibus detinentur et corpora propter voluptatem inmota patentes habent venas, in quas insidunt aurarum flatus, qui si a regionibus palustribus aut aliis regionibus vitiosis advenient, nocentes spiritus corporibus infundent. itaque si curiosius eligetur locus theatro, vitabuntur vitia. Once the forum was established, then, in anticipation of the festivals of the immortal gods, a place as wholesome as possible should be chosen for the theater, as is written in the first book concerning the healthfulness of settlements within the walls. For during the games, those who sit with their wives and children are seized by pleasure, and their bodies are immobile because of it, and their veins are open, through which gusts of wind enter, which, if they come from marshy or other vicious regions, infuse their bodies with harmful spirits. Therefore, if the place for the theater is chosen with greater care, defects will be avoided. 2. etiamque providendum est ne impetus habeat a meridie. sol enim cum implet eius rotunditatem, aer conclusus curvatura neque habens potestatem vagandi versando confervescit et candens adurit excoquitque et inminuit e corporibus umores. ideo maxime vitandae sunt his rebus vitiosae regiones et eligendae salubres. Care must also be taken that the hall does not receive the southern exposure. For when the sun fills the chamber with its heat, the air enclosed in the vault, having no way to circulate, boils and consumes with its vapor the sturdy parts of the bodies. 3. fundamentorum autem, si in montibus fuerint, facilior erit ratio, sed si necessitas coegerit in plano aut palustri loco ea constitui, solidationes substructionesque ita erunt faciendae, quemadmodum de fundationibus aedium sacrarum in tertio libro est scriptum. insuper fundamenta lapideis et marmoreis copiis gradationes ab substructione fieri debent. 567

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V But the arrangement of the foundations, if they are in the mountains, will be easier; but if necessity compels them to be established on a plain or in a marshy place, the consolidations and substructures will be made in the same way as is written about the foundations of the sacred buildings in the third book. Moreover, the foundations must be of stone and the steps of marble for the substructure. 4. praecinctiones ad altitudines theatrorum pro rata parte faciendae videntur, neque altiores quam quanta praecinctionis itineris sit latitudo. si enim excelsiores fuerint, repellent et eicient e superiore parte vocem nec patientur in sedibus suis, quae sunt supra praecinctiones, verborum casus certa significatione ad aures pervenire. et ad summam ita est gubernandum uti linea cum ad imum gradum et ad summum extenta fuerit, omnia cacumina graduum angulosque tangat. ita vox non inpedietur. The praecinctiones (belts) should be made in proportion to the height of the theaters, and no higher than the width of the passage of the praecinctio; for if they were too high, they would drive the voice upward and would not let the endings of words reach with clarity the ears of those seated above the praecinctiones. In sum, it must be so governed that, when a line is drawn from the lowest step to the highest, it touches all the summits and angles of the steps: thus the voice will not be hindered. 5. aditus complures et spatiosos oportet disponere, nec coniunctos superiores inferioribus sed ex omnibus locis perpetuos et directos sine inversuris faciendos, uti cum populus dimittatur de spectaculis, ne comprimatur, sed habeat ex omnibus locis exitus separatos sine inpeditione. Etiam diligenter est animadvertendum ne sit locus surdus, sed ut in eo vox quam clarissime vagari possit. hoc vero fieri ita poterit, si locus electus fuerit ubi non inpediatur resonantia. It is necessary to provide several spacious entrances, and not to connect the upper and lower ones, but to make them continuous and direct from all areas without any obstacles, so that when people leave the performances, they should not be cramped, but have separate exits from all areas without obstruction. Care must also be taken to ensure that it is not a soundproof space, but that the voice can travel through it as clearly as possible. This can only be achieved if a location has been chosen where echoes are not lingering. 568

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 6. vox autem est spiritus fluens aeris, e tactu sensibilis auditu. ea movetur circulorum rotundationibus infinitis, uti si in stantem aquam lapide inmisso nascantur innumerabiles undarum circuli crescentes, a centro quam latissime possint et vagantes, nisi angustia loci interpellaverit aut aliqua offensio quae non patitur designationes earum undarum ad exitus pervenire. itaque cum interpellentur offensionibus, primae redundantes insequentium disturbant designationes. But the voice is like a flowing breath of air, and it is truly perceptible to the ear. It moves through the endless roar of the circles, as if a stone were thrown into stagnant water; countless circles of waves are born, growing from the center as wide as they can, and wandering, unless the narrowness of the place interrupts them or some offense prevents the designs of these waves from reaching their outlet. And so, when they are interrupted by offenses, the first overflow of the following ones disturbs their designs. 7. eadem ratione vox item ad circinum efficit motiones, sed in aqua circuli planitiae in latitudine moventur, vox et in latitudine progreditur et altitudinem gradatim scandit. igitur ut in aqua undarum designationibus, item in voce cum offensio nulla primam undam interpellaverit, non disturbat secundam nec insequentes, sed omnes sine resonantia perveniunt ad imorum et ad summorum aures. In the same way, the voice makes its movements as if traced by a compass (ad circinum). But whereas in water the circles move in breadth over the flat surface, the voice advances at once in breadth and ascends gradually in height. Therefore, as with the waves on the surface of water, so with the voice: when the first wave meets no obstacle, it does not impede the second or the third, but all reach, without resonance, the ears of those below and those above. 8. ergo veteres architecti naturae vestigia persecuti indagationibus vocis scandentis theatrorum perfecerunt gradationes, et quaesierunt per canonicam mathematicorum et musicam rationem ut quaecumque vox esset in scaena, clarior et suavior ad spectatorum perveniret aures. uti enim organa aeneis lamminis aut corneis ἠχεῖα ad chordarum sonitûm claritatem perficiuntur, sic theatrorum per harmonicen ad augendam vocem ratiocinationes ab antiquis sunt constitutae. 569

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V Therefore, the ancient architects, following the steps of nature, investigating the rising sound of theaters, completed the gradations, and sought, through the canonical method of mathematics and music, that whatever voice was on the stage, it should reach the ears of the spectators in a clear and sweet manner. For just as organs are made of brass plates or ox horns for the clarity of the heart's sound, so the ancients established the reasoning of theaters to augment the voice through harmonics. Critical note — V.3. The theater’s healthy site, avoidance of southern exposure and cavea slope belong to Vitruvius’s environmental and medical framework. He distinguishes the horizontal and upward propagation of vox and seeks to avoid obstructions that impair intelligibility. A modern account of waves or the acoustic field remains commentary rather than a replacement for his ancient explanation. 570

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V Chapter 4 1. Harmonice autem est musica litteratura obscura et difficilis, maxime quidem quibus graecae litterae non sunt notae. quam si volumus explicare, necesse est etiam graecis verbis uti, quod nonnulla eorum latinas non habent appellationes. itaque ut potuero quam apertissime ex Aristoxeni scripturis interpretabor et eius diagramma subscribam finitionesque sonituum designabo, uti qui diligentius attenderit facilius percipere possit. Harmonic theory is a difficult and obscure branch of learning, especially for those unfamiliar with Greek. To explain it, we must use Greek terms, since some have no Latin equivalents. I shall therefore interpret the writings of Aristoxenus as clearly as I can and set out his diagram and the limits of the notes, so that attentive readers may understand them more readily. 2. vox enim mutationibus cum flectitur alias fit acuta alias gravis, duobusque modis movetur, e quibus unus effectus habet continuatos, alter distantes. continuata vox neque in finitionibus consistit neque in loco ullo, efficitque terminationes non apparentes, intervalla autem media apparentia, uti sermone cum dicamus sol lux flos vox. nunc enim nec unde incipit nec ubi desinit intellegitur, sed quod ex acuta facta est gravis et ex gravi acuta, apparet auribus. per distantiam autem e contrario. namque cum flectitur inmutatione vox statuit se in alicuius sonitus finitione, deinde in alterius, et id ultro citro crebre faciendo ⟨non⟩ constans apparet sensibus, uti in cantionibus cum flectentes vocem varietatem facimus modulationis. itaque intervallis ea cum versatur, et unde initium fecit et ubi desiit apparet in sonorum patentibus finitionibus, medianis autem patentia intervallis obscurantur. As the voice changes inflection, it becomes high or low and moves in two ways: continuously or by distinct intervals. Continuous movement settles at no fixed pitch; its boundaries are imperceptible, although the intervening movement is audible, as when we say sol, lux, flos, vox in ordinary speech. We do not identify its precise starting and stopping points, but the ear hears the change from high to low and from low to high. Movement by intervals is different. The voice settles at one definite pitch, then another, and repeatedly passes between them, as in singing when changes of pitch produce melodic variety. The beginnings and endings are then perceptible at the clearly defined notes, while the intervening passage is obscured by the intervals. 571

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V 3. Genera vero sunt modulationum tria, primum quod Graeci nominant ἁρμονίην, secundum χρῶμα, tertium διάτονον. est autem harmoniae modulatio ab arte concepta, et ea re cantio eius maxime gravem et egregiam habet auctoritatem. chroma subtili sollertia ac crebritate modulorum suaviorem habet delectationem. diatoni vero quod naturalis est, facilior est intervallorum distantia. in his tribus generibus dissimiles sunt tetrachordorum dispositiones, quod harmonia [tetrachordorum] et tonos et dihesis habet binas. dihesis autem est toni pars quarta, ita in hemitonio duae diheses sunt conlocatae. chromati duo hemitonia in ordine sunt composita, tertium trium hemitoniorum est intervallum; dia⟨tono⟩ toni duo sunt continuati, tertium hemitonium finit tetrachordi magnitudinem. ita in tribus generibus tetrachorda ex duobus tonis et hemitonio sunt peraequata, sed ipsa cum separatim uniuscuiusque generis finibus considerantur, dissimilem habent intervallorum designationem. There are three genera of melody: the first, called harmonia by the Greeks, is the enharmonic; the second is chroma, the chromatic; and the third is the diatonic. The enharmonic is an artistic construction whose melody has a particularly grave and distinguished character. The chromatic offers a gentler pleasure through the subtle skill and closeness of its steps. The diatonic is natural and its intervals are easier to grasp. The tetrachords are divided differently in the three genera. The enharmonic contains two whole tones and two dieses; a diesis is one-quarter of a tone, so two dieses make a semitone. The chromatic has two successive semitones and a third interval of three semitones. The diatonic has two successive whole tones, with a final semitone completing the tetrachord. Each genus therefore spans two tones and a semitone, although the division of that span differs. 4. igitur intervalla tonorum et hemitoniorum et ⟨diheseon⟩ tetrachordorum in voce divisit natura finîtque terminationes eorum mensuris intervallorum quantitate, modisque certis distantibus constituit qualitates, quibus etiam artifices qui organa fabricant ex natura constitutis utendo comparant ad concentus convenientes eorum perfectiones. Nature has divided the voice into the intervals of tones, semitones and dieses within the tetrachords, fixing their limits by the size of the intervals and establishing distinct qualities at definite distances. Instrument makers use these natural divisions to bring their finished instruments into consonance. 572

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 5. Sonitus, qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur, in unoquoque genere sunt X et VIII, e quibus VIII sunt in tribus generibus perpetui et stantes, reliqui X cum communiter modulantur sunt vagantes. stantes autem sunt qui inter mobiles [sunt] interpositi, continent tetrachordi coniunctionem et e generum discriminibus suis finibus sunt permanentes, appellantur autem sic, proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon, nete hyperbolaeon. mobiles autem sunt qui in tetrachordo inter inmotos dispositi in generibus ex locis loca mutant, vocabula autem habent haec, parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, <paranete synhemmenon,> trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon, paranete hyperbolaeon. The notes, called phthongoi (φθόγγοι) in Greek, number eighteen in each genus. Eight remain fixed in all three genera; the other ten are movable when the genera are considered together. The fixed notes, interposed among the movable ones, maintain the connection of the tetrachords and retain their positions as the genera change. Their names are proslambanomenos, hypate hypaton, hypate meson, mese, nete synhemmenon, paramese, nete diezeugmenon and nete hyperbolaeon. The movable notes occupy positions between the fixed notes within a tetrachord and change their places with the genus. They are parhypate hypaton, lichanos hypaton, parhypate meson, lichanos meson, trite synhemmenon, ⟨paranete synhemmenon⟩, trite diezeugmenon, paranete diezeugmenon, trite hyperbolaeon and paranete hyperbolaeon. 6. ei autem qua moventur, recipiunt virtutes alias, intervalla enim et distantias habent crescentes. itaque parhypate, quae in harmonia distat ab hypate <dimidium> hemitonium, in chroma transmutata habet hemitonium. quae lichanos in harmonia dicitur, ab hypate distat hemitonium, in chroma translata progreditur duo hemitonia, in diatono distat ab hypate tria hemitonia. ita X sonitus propter translationes in generibus efficiunt triplicem modulationum varietatem. The movable notes acquire different properties as their intervals and distances increase. Thus parhypate, which in the enharmonic lies half a semitone above hypate, lies a semitone above it in the chromatic. Lichanos is a semitone above hypate in the enharmonic, two semitones above it in the chromatic, and three 573

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V in the diatonic. Through their changes of position in the genera, these ten notes produce three different arrangements of melody. 7. Tetrachorda autem sunt quinque: primum gravissimum, quod graece dicitur ὕπατον, secundum medianum, quod appellatur μέσον, tertium coniunctum, quod συνημμένον dicitur, quartum disiunctum, quod διεζευγμένον nominatur, quintum, quod est acutissimum, graece ὑπερβόλαιον dicitur. Concentus, quos natura hominis modulari potest, graece quae συμφωνίαι dicuntur, sunt sex: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, et disdiatessaron, et disdiapente, et disdiapason. There are five tetrachords: the lowest, called hypaton (ὕπατον); the middle, meson (μέσον); the conjunct, synhemmenon (συνημμένον); the disjunct, diezeugmenon (διεζευγμένον); and the highest, hyperbolaion (ὑπερβόλαιον). The consonances that the human voice can produce, called symphonies (συμφωνίαι) in Greek, are six: diatessaron, diapente, diapason, disdiatessaron, disdiapente and disdiapason. Note — Bk. 5.4 (harmonics). Vitruvius here summarizes the musical theory of Aristoxenus of Tarentum (4th c. BC): the three genera—enharmonic (ἁρμονία), chromatic (χρῶμα), and diatonic (διάτονον)—the eighteen sounds (φθόγγοι) per genus (eight fixed and ten movable), and the five tetrachords (hypaton, meson, synemmenon, diezeugmenon, hyperbolaion) of the Greater Perfect System (systema teleion). It is the earliest Latin source for Greek harmonics; its highly technical, partly Hellenizing terminology requires collation with Aristoxenus (Elementa harmonica) and Ptolemy. Cf. Barker, Greek Musical Writings. 8. ideoque et a numero nomina ceperunt, quod cum vox constiterit in una sonorum finitione ab eaque se flectens mutaverit et pervenerit in quartam terminationem, appellatur diatessaron, in quintam diapente [in sextam diapason, in octavam et dimidiam diapason et diatessaron, in nonam et dimidiam diapason diapente, in XII disdiapason]. These consonances take their names from number. When the voice starts at a definite note and moves to the fourth position, the interval is called diatessaron; when it reaches the fifth, diapente. [The following numerical sequence is excluded from the constituted Latin text: at the sixth, diapason; at the eighth and a half, diapason and diatessaron; at the ninth and a half, diapason and diapente; at the twelfth, disdiapason.] 574

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 9. non enim inter duo intervalla, cum chordarum sonitus aut vocis cantus factus fuerit, nec inter tria aut sex aut septem possunt consonantiae fieri, sed uti supra scriptum est, diatessaron et diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason convenientiae ex natura vocis congruentis habent finitiones, et ei concentus procreantur ex coniunctione sonituum [qui graece φθόγγοι dicuntur]. Consonance does not arise at the second or third interval, or at the sixth or seventh, whether produced by strings or by the singing voice. Rather, as explained above, the fourth and fifth and the sequence extending to the double octave have limits determined by the natural agreement of the voice. These consonances arise from the combination of notes [called phthongoi in Greek]. Critical and musical note — V.4. Harmonice denotes harmonic theory and the passage expressly invokes Aristoxenus. Diatessaron, diapente, diapason, disdiapason, tonos and diesis, together with the enharmonic, chromatic and diatonic genera, retain their specialized meanings. Greek spelling or transliteration can be normalized only where the musical identification is secure; an uncertain reading remains marked. 575

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V Chapter 5 1. Ita ex his indagationibus mathematicis rationibus fiant vasa aerea pro ratione magnitudinis theatri eaque ita fabricentur ut cum tangantur, sonitum facere possint inter se diatessaron diapente et ex ordine ad disdiapason. postea inter sedes theatri constitutis cellis, ratione musica ibi conlocentur ita uti nullum parietem tangant circaque habeant locum vacuum et ab summo capite spatium, ponanturque inversa et habeant in parte quae spectat ad scaenam suppositos cuneos ne minus altos semipede, contraque eas cellas relinquantur aperturae inferiorum graduum cubilibus longae pedes duo, altae semipede. On these principles, bronze vessels should be made by mathematical calculation in proportion to the size of the theater. They must be fashioned so that, when struck, they sound in relation to one another at a fourth, a fifth and successively up to the double octave. Vaulted chambers should then be built among the seats and the vessels placed in them according to musical principles. Each vessel must touch none of the surrounding walls and must have free space around it and above. Set the vessels upside down, supported on wedges at least half a foot high on the side facing the stage. Opposite the chambers, leave openings in the beds of the lower seating steps, two feet long and half a foot high.159 Editorial note. — The bronze vessels (echea, from the Greek ἠχεῖα) were resonating jars set in niches beneath the theater’s seats and tuned to the intervals of Greek musical theory — the enharmonic, chromatic and diatonic genera that Vitruvius takes from Aristoxenus of Tarentum — so that they would vibrate in sympathy with the actor’s voice and reinforce its clarity. It is one of the few passages where Vitruvius sets out a precise acoustic application of Greek harmonics. It should be noted, however, that the archaeological evidence for such vessels is scant and disputed: niches and, in some theaters, jars that might have served the purpose have been found, but no assemblage that confirms the full system described here. 159Vitruvius describes tuned bronze sounding vessels, vasa aerea or ἠχεῖα, in De architectura 5.5. The acoustic pots found in some medieval churches belong to a different historical and material context. Their intended function and any connection with Vitruvian practice require separate archaeological assessment. 576

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 2. designationes autem eorum, quibus in locis constituantur, sic explicentur. si non erit ampla magnitudine theatrum, media altitudinis transversa regio designetur et in ea tredecim cellae duodecim aequalibus intervallis distantes confornicentur, uti ea echea quae supra scripta sunt ad neten hyperbolaeon sonantia in cellis, quae sunt in cornibus extremis, utraque parte prima conlocentur, secunda ab extremis diatessaron ad neten diezeugmenon, tertia diatessaron ad paramesen, quarta ad neten synhemmenon, quinta diatessaron ad mesen, sexta diatessaron ad hypaten meson, in medio unum diatessaron ad hypaten hypaton. Their positions should be laid out as follows. In a theater of modest size, mark a transverse line halfway up the seating and construct thirteen vaulted chambers along it, separated by twelve equal intervals. On each side, place first in the outermost chamber a vessel sounding nete hyperbolaeon. In the next chamber inward, place one a fourth away, sounding nete diezeugmenon; in the third, one a fourth away at paramese; in the fourth, one at nete synhemmenon; in the fifth, one a fourth away at mese; and in the sixth, one a fourth away at hypate meson. With this arrangement, the voice spreading from the stage as from a center strikes the hollow of each vessel and acquires greater clarity, producing through resonance a consonance in harmony with itself. Anyone wishing to carry this arrangement through accurately should consult the musical diagram at the end of this book, which Aristoxenus established with great care and effort by distinguishing the melodic genera. Attention to that diagram and these calculations will make it easier to complete theaters that give pleasure to their listeners. 578

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 7. Dicet aliquis forte multa theatra quotannis Romae facta esse neque ullam rationem harum rerum in his fuisse, sed errabit in eo, quod omnia publica lignea theatra tabulationes habent complures, quas necesse est sonare. hoc vero licet animadvertere etiam ab citharoedis, qui superiore tono cum volunt canere, avertunt se ad scaenae valvas et ita recipiunt ab earum auxilio consonantiam vocis. cum autem ex solidis rebus theatra constituuntur, id est ex structura caementorum, lapide, marmore, quae sonare non possunt, tunc echeis hae rationes sunt explicandae. Someone may object that many theaters are built in Rome each year without any provision of this kind. The objection overlooks the many boarded surfaces in public wooden theaters, which necessarily resonate. The same effect can be observed in cithara players: when they wish to sing in a higher register, they turn toward the stage doors and obtain support for the resonance of their voices. When theaters are built of solid materials—rubble masonry, stone or marble— which do not resonate in this way, the system of sounding vessels must be employed. 8. sin autem quaeritur in quo theatro ea sint facta, Romae non possumus ostendere sed in Italiae regionibus et in pluribus Graecorum civitatibus, etiamque auctorem habemus Lucium Mummium, qui diruto theatro Corinthiorum ea aenea Romam deportavit et de manubiis ad aedem Lunae dedicavit. multi etiam sollertes architecti, qui in oppidis non magnis theatra constituerunt, propter inopiam fictilibus doliis ita sonantibus electis hac ratiocinatione compositis perfecerunt utilissimos effectus. If one asks in which theaters this arrangement has been used, we cannot point to an example at Rome, but there are examples in the regions of Italy and in many Greek cities. We also have the testimony of Lucius Mummius, who, after the destruction of the theater at Corinth, brought its bronze vessels to Rome and dedicated them from the spoils at the temple of Luna. Many resourceful architects working in small towns, unable to afford bronze, have selected earthenware jars with the appropriate tones and arranged them on these principles, obtaining highly useful results. Editorial note. — The echea (ἠχεῖα, Chapter 5) are among the most celebrated — and most disputed — passages of the treatise. Vitruvius prescribes tuned bronze vessels, set in niches among the seats and proportioned to the size of the 579

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V theater, to gather and clarify the voice from the stage; he distributes them by the notes of the three Greek genera (enharmonic, chromatic and diatonic), following the harmonic theory of Aristoxenus, to whose diagram — in the nowlost end of the book — he refers. No vessels that are certainly Vitruvian survive, and their efficacy has been questioned since the Renaissance; yet the resonating niches found in several ancient theaters, and the acoustic jars built into medieval church walls, attest the persistence of the idea. Whatever their practical effect, this remains the fullest account of architectural acoustics to come down from antiquity (cf. the theory of consonance in 5.4 and the Conspectus of Greek Terms). Critical and archaeological note — V.5. The vasa aerea or ἠχεῖα are presented as tuned resonant vessels intended to improve the clarity and consonance of the voice. Comparison with a modern resonator is heuristic and requires dimensions, material and context before identity of mechanism can be asserted. The reference to Aristoxenus’s diagramma remains essential; a reconstructed diagram is identified as a reconstruction rather than incorporated as a surviving Vitruvian original. 580

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V Chapter 6 1. Ipsius autem theatri conformatio sic est facienda uti quam magna futura est perimetros imi, centro medio conlocato circumagatur linea rotundationis, in eaque quattuor scribantur trigona paribus lateribus ⟨quae paribus⟩ intervallis, extremam lineam circinationis tangant, quibus etiam in duodecim signorum caelestium <⟨astrologia⟩> astrologi ex musica convenientia astrorum ratiocinantur. ex his trigonis cuius latus fuerit proximum scaenae, ea regione qua praecidit curvaturam circinationis, ibi finiatur scaenae frons, et ab eo loco per centrum parallelos linea ducatur, quae disiungat proscaenii pulpitum et orchestrae regionem. 2. The configuration of the theater itself is to be made in such a way that, however large the perimeter will be, a line of the rounding (rotundatio) is described about the center placed in the middle, and four triangles are inscribed in it with equal sides and intervals, which touch the outermost line of the circumference, by which astrologers also reason from the concordance of the stars in the twelve celestial signs. From these triangles, the side of which is closest to the stage, in the region where it intersects the curvature of the circumference, the front of the stage is to end there, and from that place a parallel line is drawn through the center, which separates the stage platform of the proscenium and the region of the orchestra. Note — Bk. 5.6.1 (the geometry of the theater). The plan of the Roman theater is set out by inscribing in the circle of the orchestra four equilateral triangles that touch it at twelve points—as astrologers dispose the twelve signs of the zodiac by the musical consonance of the stars. The sides of these triangles fix the front of the stage, the direction of the stairs (scalaria), and the axes of the seating. It is an exact geometric construction, akin to the analemma method (see Book IX); Vitruvius refers its drawing to a figure at the end of the book. The Greek theater (5.7) instead uses three squares. Comparative note — Bk. 5.6–5.7 (plan of the theater). The geometrical setting-out of the theater is one of the most studied passages of Book V. Catherine Saliou's Budé (2009) weighs the alternatives of restitution cautiously and warns that the Vitruvian scheme —four equilateral triangles inscribed in 581

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER V the circle of the orchestra, like the twelve signs of the zodiac— is rarely verified exactly in surviving theaters; only the relation of the pulpitum to the diameter of the orchestra proves checkable. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the typological difference (the Roman pulpitum, deeper and lower, with the orchestra reserved for senators, against the Greek, with its wide orchestra); the Nexus Network Journal has re-examined the 'twelve-pointed star' and J. B. Small's hypothesis of a system of circles. This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice; the musicalastral analogy with the zodiac is Vitruvius's own, not an interpolation. 2. ita latius factum fuerit pulpitum quam Graecorum, quod omnes artifices in scaena dant operam, in orchestra autem senatorum sunt sedibus loca designata. et eius pulpiti altitudo sit ne plus pedum quinque, uti qui in orchestra sederint, spectare possint omnium agentium gestus. cunei spectaculorum in theatro ita dividantur uti anguli trigonorum, qui currunt circum curvaturam circinationis, dirigant ascensus scalasque inter cuneos ad primam praecinctionem, supra autem alternis itineribus superiores cunei medii dirigantur. 2. The stage-platform (pulpitum) should be made wider than that of the Greeks, because all the artists work on the stage. Places are designated for the seats of the senators in the orchestra. And the height of the stage platform should not exceed five feet, so that whoever sits in the orchestra can watch the movements of all the actors. The wedges of the spectacles in the theater should be divided in such a way that the corners of the triangles, which run around the curvature of the circumference, direct the ascents and stairs between the wedges to the first enclosure, and above all, the upper wedges in the middle should be directed by alternate routes. Thus, the stage-platform (pulpitum) was made wider than that of the Greeks, because all the performers act on the stage, but in the orchestra there are designated places for the senators' seats. And the height of their audience should not be more than five feet, so that those sitting in the orchestra can observe the movements of all the performers. The seating sections in the theater are so divided that the angles of the triangles, which trace the curvature of the circle, direct the ascents and staircases between the sections to the first chamber; and above, the upper middle sections are directed by alternative routes. 582

Nec tamen in omnibus theatris symmetriae ad omnes rationes et effectus possunt respondere, sed oportet architectum animadvertere quibus proportionibus necesse sit sequi symmetriam et quibus ad loci naturam aut magnitudinem operis temperari. sunt enim res quas et in pusillo et in magno theatro necesse est eadem magnitudine fieri propter usum, uti gradus diazomata pluteos itinera ascensus pulpita tribunalia et si qua alia intercurrunt ex quibus necessitas cogit discedere ab symmetria ne inpediatur usus. non minus si qua exiguitate copiarum, id est marmoris, materiae reliquarumque rerum quae parantur, in opere defuerint, paulum demere aut adicere, dum id ne nimium inprobe fiat sed cum sensu, non erit alienum. hoc autem erit si architectus erit usu peritus, praeterea ingenio mobili sollertiaque non fuerit viduatus. 7. Yet in all theaters symmetries cannot correspond to all reasons and effects, but the architect must observe with what proportions it is necessary to follow symmetry and with which to temper it to the nature of the place or the size of the work. For there are things which in both a small and a large theater it is necessary to make the same size for the sake of use, such as steps, diazomata, shelves, itinerant ascents, pulpits, tribunals, and if there are such things which intersect from which necessity compels a departure from symmetry lest use be hindered. Not less, if there is any scarcity of supplies, that is, of marble, materials, and other things which are prepared, in the work, a little should be taken away or added, provided that this is not done too improperly but with sense, it will not be out of place. This will be the case if the architect is skilled in use, and moreover is not deprived of mobile talent and skill. Not all theaters can be designed with symmetry to suit every reason and effect, but the architect must observe the proportions that necessitate symmetry and that must be moderated according to the nature or size of the venue. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V 9. genera autem sunt scaenarum tria, unum quod dicitur tragicum, alterum comicum, tertium satyricum. horum autem ornatus sunt inter se dissimili disparique ratione, quod tragicae deformantur columnis et fastigiis et signis reliquisque regalibus rebus, comicae autem aedificiorum privatorum et maenianorum habent speciem prospectusque fenestris dispositos imitatione, communium aedificiorum rationibus, satyricae vero ornantur arboribus speluncis montibus reliquisque agrestibus rebus in topeodis speciem deformati. 9. There are three kinds of scenes, one which is called tragic, the other comic, the third satirical. Now, the ornaments of these are different from each other and in a disparate way, because the tragic ones are deformed by columns and pinnacles and signs and other real things; but the domes of private buildings and mansions have the appearance of frames and windows arranged in imitation of the plans of common buildings; the satyrs, on the other hand, are adorned with trees, caves, mountains, and other wild things, deformed in the form of a topoid. Critical and geometrical note — V.6. The Latin theater plan begins with four inscribed equilateral triangles. In Graecorum theatris non omnia isdem rationibus sunt facienda, quod primum in ima circinatione ut in latino trigonorum IIII, in eo quadratorum trium anguli circinationis lineam tangunt, et cuius quadrati latus est proximum scaenae praeciditque curvaturam circinationis, ea regione designatur finitio proscaenii. et ab ea regione ad extremam circinationem curvaturae parallelos linea designatur, in qua constituitur frons scaenae, per centrumque orchestrae proscaenii regioni parallelos linea describitur et qua secat circinationis lineas dextra ac sinistra in cornibus hemicycli centra signantur, et circino conlocato in dextra ab intervallo sinistro circumagitur circinatio ad proscaenii sinistram partem, item centro conlocato in sinistro cornu ab intervallo dextro circumagitur ad proscaenii dextram partem. Comparative note — Bk. 5.7 (the Greek theater). Unlike the Roman theater—set out with four triangles (5.6)—the Greek is ordered with three squares inscribed in the circle of the orchestra. Hence its distinctive features: a wider orchestra, used by the chorus; a more recessed stage; and a platform (logeîon, λογεῖον) narrower and higher, of ten to twelve feet, since the actors perform on the proscaenium while the chorus moves below. The editions keep the Greek terminology; Rowland and Howe (Cambridge, 1999) specify the reconstruction of the platform; Gros (Budé) relates it to the surviving Hellenistic theaters. The present edition keeps the Graecisms and translates in its own words. [Historical-architectural note] The Roman/Greek distinction reflects different scenic uses: at Rome, senators in the orchestra and the show on the pulpitum; in Greece, the chorus in the orchestra. In Greek theaters, not everything should be done according to the same principles, because first, in the lower circle, as in the Latin trigon IV, the squares of the three corners touch the line of the circle, and the side of the plaza that is next to the stage and cuts the curvature of the circle, in that region, the end of the proscenium is designated. And from that region to the end of the circle, a line parallel to the curvature is drawn, in which the front of the stage is formed, and through the center of the orchestra, a line parallel to the proscenium region is described, and because it cuts the lines of the circle, the right and left lines are marked in the centers of the horns of the hemicycle. And having been placed on the right, from the left interval, the circle moves 588

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V towards the left side of the proscenium; likewise, placed in the center of the left wing, it moves from the right interval towards the right side of the proscenium. 2. ita tribus centris hac descriptione ampliorem habent orchestram Graeci et scaenam recessiorem minoreque latitudine pulpitum, quod λογεῖον appellant, ideo quod ⟨apud⟩ eos tragici et comici actores in scaena peragunt, reliqui autem artifices suas per orchestram praestant actiones, itaque ex eo scaenici et thymelici graece separatim nominantur. eius logei altitudo non minus debet esse pedum X, non plus duodecim. gradationes scalarum inter cuneos et sedes contra quadratorum angulos dirigantur ad primam praecinctionem, a praecinctione inter eas iterum mediae dirigantur, et ad summam quotiens praecinguntur, altero tanto semper amplificantur. In the Greek arrangement, these three centers produce a larger orchestra, a stage front set farther back, and a narrower stage platform, called the logeion. When all this has been set out with the utmost care and skill, then still greater vigilance is needed to ensure that a site is chosen on which the voice settles gently and is not thrown back in such a way as to carry uncertain meanings to the ears. There are, indeed, places that by their nature hinder the movement of the voice: the dissonant, called in Greek κατηχοῦντες (katechountes); the circumsonant, which they name περιηχοῦντες (periechountes); the resonant, called ἀντηχοῦντες (antechountes); and the consonant, which they call συνηχοῦντες (synechountes). The dissonant are those in which the first voice, rising aloft, strikes solid bodies above and, driven back, settles below and smothers the rise of the voice that follows. Nomenclature note — Bk. 5.8 (the four acoustic classes). Vitruvius classifies sites by their acoustic behavior with four Graecisms, retained here with transliteration: dissonantes / κατηχοῦντες (katechountes), places that smother the voice; circumsonantes / περιηχοῦντες (periechountes), which scatter it around; resonantes / ἀντηχοῦντες (antechountes), which double it in echo; and consonantes / συνηχοῦντες (synechountes), which reinforce it with clarity. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER V emendatus erit prudentia ad utilitatem in theatris vocis effectus. formarum autem descriptiones inter se discriminibus his erunt notatae uti quae Graecorum habent usus ex quadratis designentur,, latina e paribus lateribus trigonorum. ita his praescriptionibus qui voluerit uti, emendatas efficiet theatrorum perfectiones. The circumsonant are those in which the voice, forced to wander round, dissolves in the middle and, sounding there without its final syllables, dies away in an uncertain meaning of the words. The resonant are those in which, striking against a solid body, it rebounds and, forming echoes, doubles the last syllables to the ear. The consonant are those in which the voice, supported from below, rises with increasing strength and reaches the ears with distinct clarity of words. Thus, if due attention is given to the choice of site, prudence will secure, to good effect, the sound of the voice in theaters. The layouts of the plans will be marked by this difference between them: those designed from squares serve Greek usage; the Latin, from triangles of equal sides. Whoever chooses to follow these prescriptions will achieve theaters of finished perfection. Historical-architectural note — Bk. 5.8.2. The chapter's close condenses the typological distinction: the Greek plan is set out from squares (three inscribed squares, 5.7) and the Latin from equilateral triangles (four triangles, 5.6). Vitruvius's acoustic classification—unique in ancient literature—anticipates notions of modern architectural acoustics (reflection, echo, reinforcement), and has guided the analysis of ancient theaters since the Renaissance. Critical and acoustic note — V.8. Dissonantes, circumsonantes, resonantes and consonantes, with their Greek equivalents, constitute an ancient classification of places by the behavior of the voice. Modern echo, reverberation and resonance are useful comparative terms, but are not exact substitutes for all the ancient categories. 591

Editorial note. — Chapter 10 gives the earliest detailed account of the Roman bath. Its technical core is the hypocaust: the floor of the hot rooms is raised on small pillars of tile (suspensurae) so that the hot gases from a furnace (hypocausis) circulate beneath it and, through flues, up the walls; the bronze tanks (testudines alveolorum) are heated from the same source. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VI — On the private house: the influence of climate and latitude on the arrangement of buildings, the proportions of atriums, tablinums, peristyles and triclinia, the differences between the Greek and Roman house, and the suitability (decor) of each room to its use and the condition of its owner. Notice. — Book VI treats the private house. After a preface on the worth of learning above fortune, it relates domestic architecture to climate and latitude, sets out the proportions of the atrium, tablinum, peristyle and the several oeci, distinguishes the Greek house from the Roman, and turns to the working farmstead (villa rustica). It closes with the principles of sound construction — foundations, retaining walls and substructures. The book is the chief ancient evidence for the Roman domus and its social use of space. Theophrastus develops the same idea, urging people to become learned rather than to put their trust in wealth. The educated person alone is not a stranger in foreign lands or left without friends when family and companions are lost; in every city such a person is a citizen and can face the hazards of fortune without fear. By contrast, one who trusts in good luck rather than learning walks on slippery paths and struggles through a fragile, uncertain life. These, then, are the true protections of life, beyond the reach of adversity, political upheaval or war. Theophrastus extends the point: learning, not wealth, is the more secure resource. Epicurus likewise says that fortune grants the wise relatively little, whereas the greatest and most necessary matters are governed by thought and judgment. Many other philosophers held the same view. The authors of ancient Greek comedy — Crates, Chionides, Aristophanes and, above all, Alexis — expressed similar ideas on stage. Alexis praises the Athenians because, whereas Greek laws generally require children to support their parents, the Athenians impose that duty only in respect of parents who have taught their children an art. Fortune may take away everything it has given; learning, once joined to the mind, remains steadfast to the end of life. Epicurus makes a similar argument: fortune bestows few benefits on the wise, while the greatest needs are governed by the mind. The comic poets Crates, Chionides, Aristophanes and Alexis expressed the same principle. Alexis praised the Athenians for requiring children to support only those parents who had provided them with training in the arts, rather than imposing that obligation without distinction. The central courts of houses, or cava aedium, are divided into five types: Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate and testudinate. In the Tuscan type, beams spanning the width of the atrium carry the cross-members and valleys that run from the corners of the walls to the corners of the beams; the rafters direct the rain toward the central compluvium. In the Corinthian type, the beams and compluvium are arranged on the same principles, but the beams are set back from the walls and supported on columns around the opening. The tetrastyle type has columns beneath the beams at the corners, giving practical support and stability: the beams need neither span so great a distance nor bear the load of the intervening members unsupported. Explanatory note — Bk. 6.3. Vitruvius distinguishes five forms of the central court by their roof construction. The Tuscan type spans the atrium without columns; the Corinthian uses a colonnade around the opening; the tetrastyle places four columns at its corners. The displuviate sheds water outward and, in Vitruvius’s account, is vulnerable to overflowing gutters. The testudinate is fully covered and permits accommodation above it. The identification of an excavated house with one of these literary categories requires its own architectural evidence; the word testudinatum alone does not establish the material or geometry of a masonry vault. We shall now explain with what properties the several kinds of building should be suited to their use and to the quarters of the sky they face. Winter dining-rooms and baths should look towards the winter sunset, because the evening light is needed, and because the setting sun, casting its glow full upon them, gives off a warmth that makes the quarter milder towards evening. Bedrooms and libraries should face the east, for their use demands the morning light, and in libraries the books will not rot; whereas in those rooms that face south and west the books are spoiled by worms and damp, since the moist winds that rise from those quarters breed and nourish the worms and, spreading their damp breath, corrupt the rolls with mold. Now we will explain what properties buildings should have according to their use and climatic regions. Winter dining rooms and bathrooms should face west, so as to take advantage of the afternoon light, and also because the sun, when it shines in the west, gives off heat, making the region warmer at night. Halls and libraries should face east; because morning use requires light, and in the same way, books will not rot in libraries. Editorial note. — The Greek house, as Vitruvius describes it, is divided into two quarters: the gynaeconitis (women’s apartments, set about the first peristyle, where the mistress sat with her wool-workers) and the andronitis (men’s apartments, about a second and grander peristyle, where the men dined and received guests). The arrangement reflects the seclusion of women in classical Greek domestic life, in contrast to the more open Roman atrium house. Within these places large oeci are installed, in which the matrons gather with the wool-spinners. On the right and left of the prostas there are rooms, one of which is called the thalamus and the other the amphithalamus. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VI Explanatory note — Bk. 6.7 (the Greek house). Vitruvius describes the Greek house by contrast with the Roman: the Greeks use no atrium. From the gate a passage —the thyroreion (θυρωρεῖον), between the two doors, with the stable on one side and the porter's rooms on the other— leads to the peristyle, porticoed on three sides; on the south side two antae carry beams and form a recess called prostas (προστάς) or parastas. Within lies the great oecus where the mistress sits with the wool-spinners, flanked by the thalamus and the amphithalamus; around the porticoes are triclinia, bedchambers, and servants' quarters: this is the gynaeconitis (γυναικωνῖτις), the women's area. Adjoining it is a larger house with a more spacious peristyle (four equal porticoes, or the southern one higher —the 'Rhodian peristyle'—), with cyzicene oeci, triclinia, and picture-galleries: the andronitis (ἀνδρωνῖτις), reserved for men, since women did not recline at table. Between the two peristyles run the mesaulae, which the Romans call andrones. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 6.7 (Greek house). In the Budé, Louis Callebat (2004) treats this chapter as a key witness to the Greco-Latin domestic vocabulary and discusses the terminological mismatches Vitruvius himself flags (andron, xystus, prothyrum/diathyron). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) recall that the Vitruvian account served as the basis for reconstructions of the Greek house before excavation, and that the finds at Delos, Priene, and Olynthus show plans more open and less rigid in the separation of the sexes than the text implies (as recent studies of the gynaeconitis and the andron, e.g. by S. Weir and H. Franks, have qualified). This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the Greek spelling of the technical terms; the gynaeconitis/andronitis division is presented as a Vitruvian category, not as secure archaeological fact. And to these are added larger houses that have more elaborate peristyles, in which there are four porticoes of equal height, or one facing south formed by taller columns. Now that peristyle, which has a taller portico, is called a Rhodo. For it cannot always be with the same weight as it usually is during the summer, but in winter times, receiving a multitude of water from the rains, it increases in weight and size and bursts and pushes out the partitions of the structures. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VI buttresses (anterides, or in Greek erismae) are built, set apart from one another by as much space as the height of the substructure will be, and of the same thickness as the substructure itself. They are carried out from the bottom by as much as the thickness fixed for the structure, and then drawn in so that the part standing in the face is as thick as a fourth part of the height. Explanatory note — Bk. 6.8 (foundations and retaining walls). The chapter treats substructiones: foundations carried down to solid ground and, above all, retaining walls able to resist the thrust of the earth. Vitruvius prescribes thickening the wall in proportion to the mass retained and, on its outer face, raising with it counterforts —the anterides, which the Greeks call erismae (ἐρείσματα)— spaced at intervals equal to the wall's height, projecting at the base and tapering upward. On the earth side he adds saw-tooth projections and diagonal walls at the corners, so that the thrust does not bear on the wall as a single mass but is distributed: the same principle as the 'comb-like' rampart of 1.5.7. It is one of the few passages of ancient soil statics, today corroborated by the structural analysis of Roman theater substructures (Augst, Avenches). The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 6.8 (counterforts, anterides sive erismae). In the Budé, Book VI is the work of Louis Callebat (2004), who comments on the passage with the engineering of terraces and substructures. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) —whose plate labels it 'Retaining Walls and Buttresses (Anterides sive Erismae)'— stress Vitruvius's anticipation of the counterfort and of the distribution of thrust; Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (anterides, erismae, congestio). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice; H and the codices collated by the Budé offer no variant here that alters the sense. Therefore, to remedy this defect, it will be necessary to first determine the thickness of the structure in proportion to the mass of earth to be retained. Likewise, in the extreme corners, when there is a recess from the inner corner by the space of the height of the substructure, let diagonals be marked on both sides and from these marks the structure is placed, and from that the other side connected to the corner of the wall. Thus the teeth and diagonals of the structure will not be allowed to press the wall with all their force, but will dissipate the impact of the congestion by retaining it. Furthermore, the interior parts must be constructed toothed against the earth, attached to the wall, so that each tooth is as far from the wall as the height of the substructure. However, the thickness of the tooth structure must be equal to that of the walls. Likewise, at the extreme corners, when the interior corner of the space has been removed to the height of the substructure, it is marked on both sides, and from these marks the structure is placed diagonally, and from this the other half is attached to the corner of the wall. Thus, the teeth and diagonal structures will not be able to press against the wall with their full force, but will dissipate it to avoid the attack of congestion. 8. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VI 10. haec autem recte constituuntur, cum is et a fabris et ab idiotis patiatur accipere se consilia. namque omnes homines, non solum architecti, quod est bonum possunt probare, sed inter idiotas et eos hoc est discrimen quod idiota nisi factum viderit, non potest scire quid sit futurum, architectus autem simul animo constituerit, antequam inceperit et venustate et usu et decore quale sit futurum habet definitum. Quas res privatis aedificiis utiles putavi et quemadmodum sint faciundae quam apertissime potui perscripsi. de expolitionibus autem eorum uti sint elegantes et sine vitiis ad vetustatem <>, insequenti volumine exponam. 10. But these things are rightly established, since he allows himself to be advised by both craftsmen and laymen. For all men, not only architects, can approve what is good, but the difference between laymen and architects is this: a layman cannot know what will be until he sees it done, while an architect, having already established it in his mind, has defined before he begins what it will be in terms of beauty, use, and decorum. I have described as clearly as I could what things are useful for private buildings and how they should be made. But I will explain their refinements, so that they are elegant and without defects for old age, in the following volume. Editorial note. — Chapter 8 closes Book VI with the principles of sound construction (firmitas): foundations carried to solid ground; relieving arches (fornicationes) and voussoirs (cunei) to lighten the load over lintels and openings; the strict perpendicular of every wall. Its most technical passage concerns substructures and retaining walls against the thrust of earth: Vitruvius prescribes buttresses on the face — anterides, in Greek erismae — and, on the inner side, counterforts toothed into the wall (serratim), each spaced from it by a distance equal to the height of the substructure, so that the earth’s pressure is resisted as if by the teeth of a saw. The chapter ends with the famous maxim that the architect should take counsel from craftsmen and laymen alike, for the layman cannot judge a work until it is built, whereas the architect foresees its grace, utility and propriety before it is begun. Textual note — Book VI. The running Latin is checked against Krohn (1912), and the authorial Spanish translation provides the basis for the English rendering. Climate, optical adjustment, domestic arrangements and structural stability belong to distinct stages of the book’s argument. Greek technical terms 673

These aims are properly achieved when the architect accepts advice from craftsmen and laypeople alike. Everyone can judge a completed work, but a layperson cannot know its future form before seeing it built. The architect, by contrast, conceives in advance how it will answer to beauty, use, and propriety. I have described as clearly as I can the arrangements useful for private buildings and how they should be made. In the next book I shall explain their finishes, so that they remain elegant and free from defects over time. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VII — On finishes: the preparation of pavements and stuccos, lime plasters, ceiling moldings; natural and artificial colors and pigments (ochre, vermilion, purple, verdigris, ceruse) and their correct application. Notice. — Book VII, after a learned preface on plagiarism and the history of writing on architecture, treats the finishing of buildings: pavements and their bedding, the preparation of stucco and the technique of fresco, and the pigments — the natural earths and the manufactured colors, among them the synthetic Egyptian blue (caeruleum) and the lead and copper pigments. It is the most important ancient source on the technique of painting and the chemistry of pigments. Critical and structural note — VI.8. Foundations and substructures, uprights, vaults, wedges, piers and anterides or erismae are presented as an ancient constructional system. Modern distinctions between vertical loading, lintel bending, arch thrust and retaining-wall action belong to the explanatory note. Continuity of support can clarify Vitruvius’s principle without attributing elastic theory or stress calculation to him. Buttress and tooth proportions remain the prescriptions of the text. 674

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Preface 1. Maiores cum sapienter tum etiam utiliter instituerunt, per commentariorum relationes cogitata tradere posteris, ut ea non interirent sed singulis aetatibus crescentia voluminibus edita gradatim pervenirent vetustatibus ad summam doctrinarum subtilitatem. itaque non mediocres sed infinitae sunt his agendae gratiae, quod non invidiose silentes praetermiserunt, sed omnium generum sensus conscriptionibus memoriae tradendos curaverunt. 2. The ancients, both wisely and usefully, instituted the transmission of their thoughts to posterity through the reports of their commentaries, so that they would not perish, but, published in increasing volumes in each age, would gradually reach the highest subtlety of their doctrines. Therefore, the merits of this work are not moderate but infinite, because they did not pass over it in envious silence, but took care to transmit to memory all kinds of thoughts in writings. 2. namque si non ita fecissent, non potuissemus scire quae res in Troia fuissent gestae, nec quid Thales Democritus Anaxagoras Xenophanes reliquique physici sensissent de rerum natura quasque Socrates Platon Aristoteles Zenon Epicurus aliique philosophi hominibus agendae vitae terminationes finissent seu Croesus Alexander Darius ceterique reges quas res aut quibus rationibus gessissent fuissent notae, nisi maiores praeceptorum comparationibus omnium memoriae ad posteritatem commentariis extulissent. 2. For if they had not done so, we would not have been able to know what things had been done in Troy, nor what Thales, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, and the other natural philosophers had thought about the nature of things, nor what Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Epicurus, and other philosophers had concluded the ends of life for men, nor what things Croesus, Alexander, Darius, and the other kings had done, or for what reasons, would have been known, unless the elders had brought forth the memory of all things in their commentaries by comparisons of precepts for posterity. 3. itaque quemadmodum his gratiae sunt agendae, contra qui eorum scripta furantes pro suis praedicant sunt vituperandi, quique non propriis cogitationibus 675

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII scriptorum nituntur, sed invidis moribus aliena violantes gloriantur, non modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam quia impio more vixerunt, poena condemnandi. nec tamen haec res non vindicatae curiosius ab antiquis esse memorantur. quorum exitus iudiciorum qui fuerint, non est alienum quemadmodum sint nobis traditi explicare. Just as gratitude is owed to those who transmit their thoughts, so those who steal others’ writings and proclaim them their own deserve condemnation. Those who claim glory by violating the work of others, instead of relying on their own ideas, merit not merely reproach but punishment for acting dishonourably. Such offenses, it is reported, did not go unpunished among the ancients. It is therefore appropriate to recount the outcomes of those judgments as they have been handed down to us. 4. reges Attalici magnis philologiae dulcedinibus inducti cum egregiam bybliothecam Pergami ad communem delectationem instituissent, tunc item Ptolomaeus infinito zelo cupiditatisque incitatus studio non minoribus industriis ad eundem modum contenderat Alexandriae comparare. cum autem summa diligentia perfecisset, non putavit id satis esse nisi propagationibus inseminando curaret augendam. itaque Musis et Apollini ludos dedicavit et quemadmodum athletarum sic communium scriptorum victoribus praemia et honores constituit. 4. Explanatory note — Bk. 7, preface (intellectual honesty). The preface to Book VII is Vitruvius's manifesto on intellectual property. He thanks his predecessors and condemns those who steal others' work 'by changing the titles of other men's books and inserting their own name.' He illustrates it with a famous Alexandrian anecdote: at a poetic contest the king appoints six judges and, for the seventh, the librarians recommend Aristophanes of Byzantium; while the crowd acclaims the popular reciters, Aristophanes rewards the one true poet and exposes the rest as plagiarists, recalling from memory the exact volumes of the library from which they had copied. He then tells of Zoilus of Amphipolis, nicknamed Homeromastix ('scourge of Homer'), who attacked the Iliad and Odyssey before the king; fallen into poverty, he asked for help, and the king replied that Homer, dead a thousand years, still fed thousands. Archaeological note — Bk. 7.1 (pavements). Vitruvius transmits the ancient recipe for the layered Roman floor, which archaeology confirms across the Empire (from Fishbourne in Britain to Lod in Israel, from Zippori to Braga). From the bottom up: the statumen (large stones forming the base and draining ground moisture); the rudus or ruderatio (a mortar of broken brick and lime, more than 20 cm thick, rammed down —three parts lime to one if fresh, five if recycled—); the nucleus (a fine layer of three parts crushed potsherd to one of lime, some 15 cm); and above it the setting bed where the tesserae of the pavimentum were fixed. On upper floors the whole is laid over the joists. A key material here is opus signinum (cocciopesto): lime with crushed terracotta, waterproof, of Punic North African origin, spread through Sicily and Italy and used both for floors and for cisterns. The Vitruvian stratigraphy remains the reference framework for the archaeometry of mosaics. 2. But if the whole or part of the place is congested, it is solidified with great care by fusing. In floors, however, it is to be diligently observed that no wall which does not come out to the top is built under the pavement, but rather has a loose coaxation hanging above it. Critical and constructional note — VII.1. Statumen, rudus and nucleus designate different layers. In reused rudus, two parts of lime are mixed with five of aggregate; exterior rudus has a minimum thickness of one foot, tesserae are about two fingers, and the stated fall is two fingers over ten feet. After the construction of pavements, lime finishing must be explained. Soak the best lumps of lime well before they are needed. Later, painters began to imitate the forms of buildings and the projecting members of columns and pediments.
