But these subjects, once drawn from real things, are now condemned by a depraved taste. For upon the plaster are painted monstrosities rather than truthful images of definite things: reeds are set up in place of columns; in place of pediments, fluted scrolls with curling leaves and volutes; candelabra bearing the figures of little shrines; and, above their pediments, springing from roots, a multitude of slender stalks with volutes, bearing for no reason little seated figures, and other stalks half-human and half-animal in their heads. 4. haec autem nec sunt nec fieri possunt nec fuerunt.. quemadmodum enim potest calamus vere sustinere tectum aut candelabrûm ornamenta fastigii seu coliculus tam tenuis et mollis sustinere sedens sigillum aut de radicibus et coliculis ex parte flores dimidiataque sigilla procreari? at haec falsa videntes homines non reprehendunt sed delectantur, neque animadvertunt si quid eorum fieri potest necne. ergo ita novi mores coegerunt, uti inertiae mali iudices convincerent artium virtutes. iudiciis autem infirmis obscuratae mentes non valent probare quod potest esse cum auctoritate et ratione decoris. neque enim picturae probari debent quae non sunt similes veritati, nec si factae sunt elegantes ab arte, ideo de his statim debet recte iudicari, nisi argumentationis certas rationes habuerint sine offensionibus explicatas. Yet such things do not exist, cannot exist and have never existed. How can a reed truly support a roof, a candelabrum the ornaments of a pediment, or a stalk so slender and soft a seated figure? How can flowers and half-figures grow from roots and stalks? Yet people look at these falsehoods without criticism and take 702

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII pleasure in them, never considering whether any of them could exist. New fashions have thus led bad judges to condemn artistic excellence as ineptitude. Minds obscured by unsound judgment cannot recognize what may properly exist in accordance with the principles of decor. Paintings that bear no resemblance to reality should not be approved; nor, merely because they are elegantly executed, should they immediately be judged sound unless their subjects can be explained by coherent reasoning without inconsistency. Explanatory note — Bk. 7.5 (the critique of wall-painting). This is one of the most cited passages in the history of ancient art. Vitruvius condemns the pictorial fashion of his own day —the so-called 'Second' and above all 'Third' Pompeian style in August Mau's modern classification—: instead of images drawn from real things, monstra ('monsters') are painted. He lists the fantasies: reeds in place of columns; instead of pediments, curling stalks with leaves and volutes; candelabra supporting little shrines; stalks from which figurines sprout for no reason, half-figures with human or animal heads. His reproach is one of truth and decorum: 'such things neither are, nor can be, nor have been' (haec autem nec sunt nec fieri possunt nec fuerunt), since a reed cannot hold up a roof. In time these very fantasies, found in the Domus Aurea, would inspire the Renaissance grottesche. [The author's personal hermeneutic proposal: to read the passage as proof of a general decline of taste belongs to interpretation, not to the datum.] The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 7.5 (wall-painting). In the Budé, Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Marie-Thérèse Cam, and Michel Zuinghedau, whose commentary links the passage with Pompeian painting and the theory of decor. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) set it within the debate over the four Pompeian styles (Mau) and Vitruvius's relation to art criticism; Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary (monstra, tectoria, coliculi). Modern scholarship has debated whether Vitruvius is a reliable observer or a conservative moralist; this edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense. Editorial note. — This passage (7.5.3–4) is the locus classicus of ancient art criticism. Vitruvius condemns the fanciful wall-painting of the Third Pompeian Style — impossible architectures, hybrid figures, vegetal scrolls — as untruthful. When such Roman decoration was rediscovered underground (in “grottoes”) at 703

I have said enough to warn against mistakes in plasterwork. I shall now discuss the materials, beginning with marble, since lime has already been treated. Marble does not occur in the same form in every region. In some places lumps containing translucent particles like grains of salt are found; crushed and ground, they are useful in building. Where such supplies are unavailable, the fragments or chips discarded by marble-workers are crushed, ground and, once sifted, used in the work. Elsewhere, as in the territory between Magnesia and Ephesus, a ready-made powder is quarried. It needs neither grinding nor sifting, being as fine as material crushed and sifted by hand. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Chapter 7 1. Colores vero alii sunt qui per se certis locis procreantur et inde fodiuntur, nonnulli ex aliis rebus tractationibus aut mixtionum temperaturis compositi perficiuntur, uti praestent eandem in operibus utilitatem. primum autem exponemus quae per se nascentia fodiuntur, uti sil, quod graece ὤχρα dicitur. haec vero multis locis ut etiam in Italia invenitur, sed quae fuerat optima, attica ideo nunc non habetur quod Athenis argentifodinae cum habuerunt familias, tunc specus sub terra fodiebantur ad argentum inveniendum. cum ibi vena forte inveniretur, nihilominus uti argentum persequebantur, itaque antiqui egregia copia silis ad politionem operum sunt usi. item rubricae copiosae multis locis eximuntur, sed optimae paucis, uti Ponto Sinope, et Aegypto, in Hispania Balearibus, non minus etiam Lemno, cuius insulae vectigalia Atheniensibus senatus populusque Romanus concessit fruenda. paraetonium vero ex ipsis locis unde foditur habet nomen. eadem ratione melinum, quod eius metallum in sola cycladi Melo dicitur esse. 2. Some colors occur naturally in particular places and are mined there; others are produced by processing materials or adjusting mixtures to serve the same purpose in building. First I shall describe those extracted in their natural state, such as sil, called ὤχρα in Greek. It is found in many places, including Italy, but the Attic variety, once the best, is no longer available. When the Athenian silver mines employed slave gangs, underground galleries were driven in search of silver. If a vein of ochre was encountered, it was pursued as eagerly as silver, and the ancients consequently had an excellent supply for finishing their buildings. Red ochres are also extracted abundantly in many places, but the finest come from only a few: Sinope in Pontus, Egypt, the Balearic Islands in Hispania and Lemnos, whose revenues the Roman Senate and people granted to the Athenians. Paraetonium takes its name from the place where it is quarried; similarly, melinum is so called because its deposit is said to occur only on Melos in the Cyclades. 4–5. creta viridis item pluribus locis nascitur, sed optima Zmyrnae. hanc autem Graeci θεοδοτεῖον vocant, quod Theodotus nomine fuerat cuius in fundo id genus cretae primum est inventum. auripigmentum, quod ἀρσενικόν graece dicitur, foditur Ponto. sandaraca item pluribus locis, sed optima Ponto proxime flumen Hypanim habet metallum. 708

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII 4–5. Green earth also occurs in several places, but the best is found at Smyrna. The Greeks call it theodoteion after Theodotus, on whose estate that kind of earth was first discovered. Orpiment, called ἀρσενικόν in Greek, is mined in Pontus. Sandaraca occurs in several places too, but its finest deposit is in Pontus near the river Hypanis. Critical and material note — VII.7. Sil/ὤχρα, rubrica, paraetonium, melinum, creta viridis, auripigmentum/ἀρσενικόν and sandaraca belong to ancient categories of color, provenance and trade. Modern mineralogical equivalents are not always unique. A probable chemical identification belongs in commentary rather than entering the translation as certainty; sandaraca in particular must not automatically be identified with the later substance called red lead. 709

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Chapter 8 1. Ingrediar nunc minii rationes explicare. id autem agris Ephesiorum Cilbianis primum esse memoratur inventum, cuius et res et ratio satis magnas habet admirationes. foditur enim glaeba quae dicitur, antequam tractationibus ad minium perveniant, vena uti ferrum, magis subrufo colore, habens circa se rubrum pulverem. cum id foditur, ex plagis ferramentorum crebras emittit lacrimas argenti vivi, quae a fossoribus statim colliguntur. 2. 1. I shall now explain minium. It is said to have been discovered first in the Cilbian fields belonging to the Ephesians. Both the substance and its treatment are remarkable. Before processing yields minium, the material is extracted as a lump from a vein resembling iron ore, but more reddish in color and surrounded by red dust. When it is mined, the blows of the tools release frequent drops of quicksilver, which the miners immediately collect. 2. hae glaebae cum collectae sunt, in officina propter umoris plenitatem coiciuntur in fornacem ut interarescant, et is qui ex his ab ignis vapore fumus suscitatur cum resedit in solum furni, invenitur esse argentum vivum. exemptis glaebis guttae eae quae residebunt propter brevitates non possunt colligi, sed in vas aquae converruntur et ibi inter se congruunt et una confunduntur. id autem cum sint quattuor sextariorum, mensurae cum expenduntur, invenientur esse pondo centum. 2. Because these lumps contain much moisture, they are taken to the workshop and put into a furnace to dry. The fumes raised by the heat of the fire, when deposited on the furnace floor, prove to be quicksilver. After the lumps have been removed, the remaining droplets are too small to gather individually. They are swept into a vessel of water, where they unite into a single mass. When the quantity reaches four sextarii, it will be found on weighing to amount to one hundred pounds. 3. cum in aliquo vase est confusum, si supra id lapideum centenarium pondus inponatur, natat in summo neque eum liquorem potest onere suo premere nec elidere nec dissipare. centenario sublato si ibi auri scripulum inponatur, non natabit sed ad imum per se deprimetur. ita non amplitudine ponderis sed genere singularum rerum gravitatem esse non est negandum. 710

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII 3. When a liquid is mixed in a vessel, if a hundred-year-old stone weight is placed on top of it, it floats on top and cannot press down on the liquid with its own weight, nor can it remove or dissipate it. If a gold coin is placed there after the hundred-year-old stone weight is removed, it will not float but will sink to the bottom by itself. Thus it cannot be denied that gravity is not due to the magnitude of the weight but to the nature of individual things. 4. id autem multis rebus est ad usum expeditum. neque enim argentum neque aes sine eo potest recte inaurari. cumque in veste intextum est aurum eaque vestis contrita propter vetustatem usum non habeat honestum, panni in fictilibus vasis inpositi supra ignem comburuntur. is cinis coicitur in aquam, et additur eo argentum vivum. id autem omnes micas auri corripit in se et cogit secum coire. aqua defusa cum id in pannum infunditur et ibi manibus premitur, argentum per panni raritates propter liquorem extra labitur, compressione coactum aurum intra purum invenitur. 4. But this is for many things for ready use. For neither silver nor brass can be properly gilded without it. When gold is woven into a garment, and that garment, worn out because of its age, is no longer fit for honest use, the cloths are placed in earthenware vessels and burned over a fire. The ashes are thrown into water, and quicksilver is added to it. This, however, seizes all the gold flakes in itself and forces them to coalesce. When the water is poured into the cloth and pressed there with the hands, the silver slides out through the rarefied nature of the cloth because of the liquid, while the gold, forced inside by compression, is found pure. Editorial note. — Vitruvius’s minium is true vermilion (cinnabar, mercuric sulphide), not the red lead with which the word was later confused. This chapter (VII.8) gives the earliest detailed account of mining cinnabar and of distilling argentum vivum (quicksilver, mercury) from it, together with the use of mercury to recover gold from worn cloth-of-gold by amalgamation — a technique still employed in later metallurgy. Critical and metrological note — VII.8. Minium and argentum vivum retain their ancient names before a modern identification is offered. Heating, condensation, crushing and washing are treated as historical procedures. Libra, centenarium, scripulum and sextarius remain visible as ancient units; any modern conversion is approximate and requires its metrological basis. 711

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Chapter 9 1. Revertar nunc ad minii temperaturam. ipsae enim glaebae cum sunt aridae, contunduntur pilis ferreis, et lotionibus et cocturis crebris relictis stercoribus efficiuntur ut adveniant colores. cum ergo emissae sint ex minio per argenti vivi relictionem quas in se naturales habuerat virtutes, efficitur tenera natura et viribus inbecillis. 2. 1. I return now to the preparation of minium. Once dry, the lumps are crushed with iron pestles. Repeated washing and heating remove the impurities and bring out the color. Applied to the finished plaster of covered rooms, it therefore retains its color without deterioration. A more discerning owner who wishes a minium finish to retain its color should, once the wall is polished and dry, brush it with Pontic wax melted over 712

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII a fire and mixed with a little oil. Then place coals in an iron vessel and heat the wax together with the wall, causing it to sweat and spread evenly. Finally work it with a wax taper and clean linen, as bare marble statues are treated. This process is called γάνωσις in Greek. Explanatory note — Bk. 7.8–7.9 (minium, quicksilver, and ganosis). Vitruvius describes minium, which for him is cinnabar (mercuric sulphide, the ancient vermilion), not the red lead (minium secundarium) with which the name was later confused. He calls the clod from which it is drawn anthrax; he explains its working —drying, grinding, washing, and heating to bring out the color— and its source (the Spanish deposits of Sisapo, alongside Ephesus). From cinnabar comes hydrargyrum or argentum vivum, 'quicksilver,' which he describes as gathered in 'tears' and used to recover gold by amalgam. He warns that vermilion is unstable in light: exposed to the sun it blackens. Hence ganosis (7.9): over the dry color, Punic wax melted with a little oil is applied, warmed with coals, and polished with a cloth, sealing the surface as was done with the marble of statues. It is a key chapter for the history of painting technique and of ancient toxicology (mercury is poisonous). The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 7.8–7.9 (minium and quicksilver). In the Budé, Book VII is the work of Bernard Liou, Michel Zuinghedau, and Marie-Thérèse Cam (1995), whose commentary collates the passage with Theophrastus (De lapidibus 58), Pliny (Natural History 33.37–40), and Dioscorides (5.94). Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress the distinction, crucial for archaeometry, between Vitruvius's cinnabar (HgS) and red lead; Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (anthrax, hydrargyrum, ganosis). Modern physico-chemical analysis of Pompeian frescoes confirms both the use of cinnabar and its photochemical darkening —precisely the problem ganosis sought to prevent. This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. 4. ita obstans cerae ponticae lorica non patitur nec lunae splendorem nec solis radios lambendo eripere ex his politionibus colorem. quae autem in Ephesiorum metallis fuerunt officinae, nunc traiectae sunt ideo Romam quod id genus venae postea est inventum Hispaniae regionibus, e quibus metallis glaebae portantur et 713

Thus the breastplate of Pontic wax, standing firm, does not suffer either the brilliance of the moon or the rays of the sun to lick away the color from these polishes. But the workshops which were in the metals of the Ephesians have now been transferred to Rome, because that kind of vein was later discovered in the regions of Spain, from which metals the slabs are brought and treated by the publicans in Rome. Now those workshops are between the temple of Flora and Quirinus. 5. Vitiatur minium admixta calce. itaque si qui velit experiri id sine vitio esse, sic erit faciendum. ferrea lamna sumatur, eo minium inponatur, ad ignem conlocetur donec lamna candescat. cum e candore color mutatus fuerit eritque ater, tollatur lamna ab igni et sic refrigeratum si restituatur in pristinum colorem, sine vitio esse probabitur, sin autem permanserit nigro colore, significabit se esse vitiatum. 5. Let the minium be tainted with lime. Therefore, if anyone wishes to test whether it is without taint, this is what must be done. Quae succurrere potuerunt mihi de minio dixi. chrysocolla adportatur a Macedonia, foditur autem ex îs locis qui sunt proximi aerariis metallis. armenium et indicum nominibus ipsis indicatur quibus in locis procreatur. 6. I have spoken of those things which could have helped me concerning minium. Chrysocolla is brought from Macedonia, and is mined from those places which are nearest to the precious metals. Armenian and indigo are indicated by the very names in which they are produced. Critical and technical note — VII.9. The modern correlation of minium here with cinnabar or mercuric sulphide belongs in commentary. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII nomenclature; the technical reconstruction does not independently determine the transmitted word. 715

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Chapter 10 1. Ingrediar nunc ad ea quae ex aliis generibus tractationum temperaturis commutata recipiunt colorum proprietates, et primum exponam de atramento, cuius usus in operibus magnas habet necessitates, ut sint notae quemadmodum praeparentur certis rationibus artificiorum ad id temperaturae. 2. I will now proceed to those things which receive the properties of colors when changed by other types of treatment temperatures, and I will first explain about ink, the use of which in works has great needs, so that it may be known how it is prepared by certain methods of artificers at that temperature. 2. namque aedificatur locus uti laconicum et expolitur marmore subtiliter et levigatur. ante id fit fornacula habens in laconicum nares, et eius praefurnium magna diligentia comprimitur ne flamma extra dissipetur. in fornace resina conlocatur. hanc autem ignis potestas urendo cogit emittere per nares intra laconicum fuliginem, quae circa parietem et camerae curvaturam adhaerescit. inde collecta partim componitur ex gummi subacta ad usum atramenti librarii, reliquum tectores glutinum admiscentes in parietibus utuntur. 2. Build a room like a Laconian hot room, finish its interior with fine marble plaster, and polish it smooth. In front of it, construct a small furnace with vents opening into the room, and seal the firing chamber carefully so that the flame cannot escape outside. Place resin in the furnace. As it burns, the fire drives soot through the vents into the room, where it adheres to the walls and the curved vault. Collect this soot: work part of it with gum to make writing ink; plasterers mix the remainder with glue for use on walls. 3. Si autem hae copiae non fuerint paratae, ita necessitatibus erit administrandum, ne expectatione morae res retineatur. sarmenta aut taedae schidiae comburantur, cum erunt carbones extinguantur, deinde in mortario cum glutino terantur. 3. But if these supplies are not ready, then the necessities must be managed in this way, so that the matter is not held up by the expectation of delay. The twigs or splinters of firewood are burned, when the coals are extinguished, they are then ground in a mortar with glue. 716

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII 4. ita erit atramentum tectoribus non invenustum. non minus si faex vini arefacta et cocta in fornace fuerit et ea contrita cum glutino in opere inducetur, atramenti suavitatis superque efficiet colorem, et quo magis ex meliore vino parabitur, non modo atramenti sed etiam indici colorem dabit imitari. 4. Thus the ink will be not unattractive to the painters. No less so if the dregs of wine have been dried and cooked in a furnace and this crushed together with the glue are introduced into the work, on which it will produce a color of the sweetness of the ink, and the more it is prepared from the best wine, it will imitate not only the color of the ink but also of the indicator. Critical note — VII.10. Atramentum includes blacks obtained by different processes: soot from resin, charcoal from vine shoots or resinous timber, and calcined wine lees. Lacus, laconicum, fornacula, nares and glutinum are interpreted within the manufacturing apparatus. The similarity to indicum mentioned by Vitruvius concerns color and does not prove identity of material. 717

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII Chapter 11 1. Caeruli temperationes Alexandriae primum sunt inventae, postea item Vestorius Puteolis instituit faciundum. ratio autem eius e quibus est inventa satis habet admirationis. harena enim cum nitri flore conteritur adeo subtiliter ut efficiatur quemadmodum farina, ea aes cyprum limis crassis uti scobis facta mixta conspargitur ut conglomeretur. deinde pilae manibus versando efficiuntur et ita conligantur ut inarescant. aridae componuntur in urceo fictili, urcei in fornace. ita aes et ea harena ab ignis vehementia confervescendo cum coaluerint, inter se dando et accipiendo sudores a proprietatibus discedunt suisque viribus per ignis vehementiam confectis caeruleo rediguntur colore. 2. Blue (caeruleum) was first compounded at Alexandria, and afterwards Vestorius set up its manufacture at Puteoli. The method of its discovery is well worth admiration. Sand is ground together with flowers of natron so finely that it becomes as it were flour; copper is filed with coarse files into shavings and sprinkled over it; the mixture is moistened, rolled by hand into balls, dried, and packed in an earthen jar, and the jars are placed in a furnace. So, when the copper and the sand grow incandescent together by the fierceness of the fire, by giving and receiving their properties from one another they take on a blue color. Explanatory note — Bk. 7.11 (Egyptian blue, caeruleum). Vitruvius transmits the only ancient recipe for the first synthetic pigment in history: caeruleum or Egyptian blue (from caelum, 'sky'; hence 'cerulean'). Its formula was invented at Alexandria and then established at Puteoli by Vestorius —a Puteolan banker, correspondent of Cicero and Atticus—, whence the 'caeruleum Vestorianum.' The recipe: sand (harena) is ground with flower of natron until it is as fine as flour; filings of Cyprian copper are sprinkled in; balls are rolled by hand, dried, and fired in earthenware jars in a furnace, until copper and sand, fused by the fire, take on the blue color. Modern chemistry identifies the product as a calcium copper silicate (cuprorivaite, CaCuSi₄O₁₀), sintered at about 850–1000 °C; the calcium comes from the sand itself, which Vitruvius does not mention. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 7.11 (Egyptian blue). The Budé of Liou, Zuinghedau, and Cam (1995) comments on the recipe in the light of the pigment's archaeometry; Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress that it is the only ancient textual source on its manufacture. Corso– 718

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VII Romano fix the terms (harena, nitri flos, aes cyprium). Verification is today experimental: laboratory trials reproduce Egyptian blue by sintering siliceous sand, an alkaline flux, and a copper compound at 850–1000 °C, confirming the Vitruvian procedure —though the text omits quantities and temperatures. This edition translates in its own voice and keeps the transmitted text, with no variant affecting the sense. 3. Editorial note. — The caeruleum here described is Egyptian blue (calcium copper silicate), the earliest synthetic pigment known, manufactured since the third millennium BC. Vitruvius gives the recipe — silica, a copper compound, and an alkaline flux fired together — that modern analysis has confirmed; its production at Puteoli by Vestorius gave it the name caeruleum Vestorianum. 2. usta vero, quae satis habet utilitatis in operibus tectoriis, sic temperatur. glaeba silis boni coquitur ut sit in igni candens. ea autem aceto extinguitur et efficitur purpureo colore. 2. But the burnt clay, which is quite useful in roofing works, is tempered in this way. A lump of good clay is cooked until it is glowing in the fire. The recipe involving sand, nitri flos, copper filings and firing can be compared archaeometrically with Egyptian blue, but that modern identification belongs in the note. Incipiam nunc de ostro dicere, quod et carissimam et excellentissimam habet praeter hos colores aspectus suavitatem. id autem excipitur e conchylio marino, e quo purpura efficitur, cuius non minores sunt quam ceterarum <rerum> naturae considerantibus admirationes, quod habet non in omnibus locis quibus nascitur unius generis colorem, sed solis cursu naturaliter temperatur. 2. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VII 3. By what means and things the firmness of refinements is reached, and by what means beautiful pictures should be made, and likewise what powers all colors have in themselves, as could be of assistance to me, I have written down in this book. Therefore all the perfections of buildings, which they should have the opportunity of reasoning, are finished in seven volumes, but in the following I will explain about water, if in what places it is not, how it is found and by what means it is drawn, and for what purposes it will be proved wholesome and suitable. ARGUMENTUM LIBRI VIII — On water: the search for springs, the properties of different waters, the qualities of famous rivers and fountains, the methods of conveyance by channels, lead and clay pipes, and leveling by means of instruments. Notice. — Book VIII is devoted to water. Its preface argues, with the natural philosophers, that water is the first principle of all things; the book then treats the finding of springs, the qualities of different waters and famous rivers, the leveling of conduits with the chorobates, and conduction by masonry channels, lead pipes and earthenware tubes — with the prescient warning against the harm of lead. It is a foundational text in the history of hydraulic engineering and public health. Critical note — VII.14. Substitution colors made from rubia, hysginum, violets, vaccinium, luteum and other materials reveal an economy of architectural finishing. Ancient plant names remain where botanical identification is uncertain. The supplement ⟨ita⟩ is marked, and the historical practice of imitation is distinguished from a modern legal or commercial category of forgery. 724

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII Preface [1] De septem sapientibus Thales Milesius omnium rerum principium aquam est professus, Heraclitus ignem, Magorum sacerdotes aquam et ignem, Euripides, auditor Anaxagorae, quem philosophum Athenienses scaenicum appellaverunt, aera et terram, eamque e caelestium imbrium conceptionibus inseminatam fetus gentium et omnium animalium in mundo procreavisse, et quae ex ea essent prognata, cum dissolverentur temporum necessitate coacta in eandem redire, quaeque de aere nascerentur, item in caeli regiones reverti neque interitiones recipere et dissolutione mutata in eam recidere, in qua ante fuerant, proprietatem. Pythagoras vero, Empedocles, Epicharmos aliique physici et philosophi haec principia esse quattuor proposuerunt: aerem, ignem, terram, aquam, eorumque inter se cohaerentiam naturali figuratione e generum discriminibus efficere qualitates. Among the Seven Sages, Thales of Miletus held that water was the first principle of all things; Heraclitus favored fire, and the priests of the Magi both water and fire. Euripides, a pupil of Anaxagoras whom the Athenians called “the philosopher of the stage”, proposed air and earth: the latter, fertilised by rain from the heavens, brought forth human beings and other living creatures. What arose from earth would return to it when dissolved by time, while what arose from air would return to the regions of the sky, not perishing but reverting through dissolution to its former nature. Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus and other natural philosophers proposed four principles — air, fire, earth and water — whose natural combination produces different qualities. [2] Animadvertimus vero non solum nascentia ex his esse procreata, sed etiam res omnes non ali sine eorum potestate neque crescere nec tueri. Namque corpora sine spiritus redundantia non possunt habere vitam, nisi aer influens cum incremento fecerit auctus et remissiones continenter. Caloris vero si non fuerit in corpore iusta comparatio, non erit spiritus animalis neque erectio firma, cibique vires non poterunt habere coctionis temperaturam. Item si non terrestri cibo membra corporis alantur, deficient et ita a terreni principii mixtione erunt deserta. 725

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII We observe that the elements not only produce living things: without their power nothing can be nourished, grow or be sustained. Bodies cannot live without a sufficient supply of breath, as incoming air maintains the continual expansion and contraction of breathing. Unless the body has the proper measure of heat, it lacks vitality and strength, and food cannot be digested at the necessary temperature. Unless its members are nourished by food from the earth, they fail, deprived of the contribution of the earthly element. 3. Animalia vero si fuerint sine umoris potestate, exsanguinata et exsucata [a principiorum liquore] interarescent. Igitur divina mens, quae proprie necessaria essent gentibus, non constituit difficilia et cara, uti sunt margaritae, aurum, argentum ceteraque, quae neque corpus nec natura desiderat, sed sine quibus mortalium vita non potest esse tuta, effudit ad manum parata per omnem mundum. Itaque ex his, si quid forte defit in corpore spiritus, ad restituendum aer adsignatus id praestat. Apparatus autem ad auxilia caloris solis impetus et ignis inventus tutiorem efficit vitam. Item terrenus fructus escarum praestans copiis supervacuis desiderationibus alit et nutrit animales pascendo continenter. Aqua vero non solum potus sed infinitas usu praebendo necessitates, gratas, quod est gratuita, praestat utilitates. Animals deprived of moisture would likewise lose their blood and bodily fluids and dry up. The divine mind therefore did not make the necessities of human life difficult and costly to obtain, as are pearls, gold, silver and other things that neither the body nor nature requires. Instead, it made readily available throughout the world the things without which mortal life cannot be sustained. If the body lacks breath, air restores it. The warmth of the Sun and the use of fire provide the heat that makes life more secure. The produce of the earth supplies abundant food, continually feeding and sustaining living creatures. Water provides not only drink but countless other necessities, and its usefulness is all the more welcome because it is freely available. [4] Ex eo etiam qui sacerdotia gerunt moribus Aegyptiorum, ostendunt omnes res e liquoris potestate consistere. Itaque cum hydria aqua ad templum aedemque casta religione refertur, tunc in terra procumbentes manibus ad caelum sublatis inventionis gratias agunt divinae benignitati. Those who hold priestly office according to Egyptian custom likewise show that all things depend on the power of water. When water is brought in a hydria to a 726

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII temple or sanctuary with due reverence, they prostrate themselves on the ground and raise their hands to heaven, giving thanks to divine beneficence for its discovery. Cum ergo et a physicis et philosophis et ab sacerdotibus iudicetur ex potestate aquae omnes res constare, putavi, quoniam in prioribus septem voluminibus rationes aedificiorum sunt expositae, in hoc oportere de inventionibus aquae, quasque habeat in locorum proprietatibus virtutes, quibusque rationibus ducatur, et quemadmodum ante probetur, scribere. Since natural philosophers, philosophers and priests all hold that everything depends on the power of water, and since the preceding seven books have set out the principles of building, I have decided to devote this book to finding water, to the qualities it acquires in different places, to the methods of conveying it and to the tests by which it is assessed. Therefore, since both physicists and philosophers and priests judge that all things are evident by the force of water, I thought that, as in the seven previous volumes the accounts of buildings were set forth, in this one it was necessary to deal with the discoveries of water, and the virtues it has in the properties of places, and by what accounts it is led, and how, before being tested, to write. Critical note — VIII, preface. The accounts of Thales, Heraclitus, the Magian priests, Euripides and Anaxagoras, and Egyptian tradition form an ancient philosophical frame for the discussion of water. Attributed doctrine, the history of philosophy and modern physical explanation are kept separate, without retrospectively harmonizing Vitruvius’s doxography. 727

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII Chapter 1 [1] Est enim maxime necessaria et ad vitam et ad delectationes, et ad usum cotidianum Ea autem erit facilior, si erunt fontes aperti et fluentes. Sin autem non profluent, quaerenda sub terra sunt capita et colligenda. Quae sic erunt experienda, uti procumbatur in dentes, antequam sol exortus fuerit, in locis, quibus erit quaerendum, et in terra mento conlocato et fulto prospiciantur eae regiones; sic enim non errabit excelsius quam oporteat visus, cum erit inmotum mentum, sed libratam altitudinem in regionibus certa finitione designabit. Tunc, in quibus locis videbuntur umores concrispantes et in aera surgentes, ibi fodiatur; non enim in sicco loco hoc potest signum fieri. [1] For water is most necessary both for life and for its pleasures, and for daily use. It will be the easier to obtain if there are open and flowing springs. But where none flow forth, the sources must be sought and gathered underground. The search is to be made thus: let a man lie face downward, before the sun has risen, in the places in which it is to be sought, and with the chin placed and supported on the ground, those regions are to be looked for; for in this way the sight will not err higher than it should be, when the chin is motionless, but will designate a balanced height in the regions with a certain boundary. Then, in those places where moistures are seen to be bubbling and rising into the air, there is to be dug; for this sign cannot be made in a dry place. [2] Item animadvertendum est quaerentibus aquam, quo genere sint loca; certa enim sunt, in quibus nascitur. In creta tenuis et exilis et non alta est copia; ea erit non optimo sapore. Item sabulone soluto tenuis, sed inferioris loci invenietur; ea erit limosa et insuavis. Terra autem nigra sudores et stillae exiles inveniuntur, quae ex hibernis tempestatibus collectae in spissis et solidis locis subsidunt; haec habent optimum saporem. Glarea vero mediocres et non certae venae reperiuntur; hae quoque sunt egregia suavitate. Item sabulone masculo harenaque carbunculo certiores [et stabiliores] sunt copiae; eaeque sunt bono sapore. Rubro saxo et bonae et copiosae, si non per intervenia dilabantur et liquescant. Sub radicibus autem montium et in saxis silicibus uberiores et afÒuentiores; eaeque frigidiores sunt et salubriores. Campestribus autem fontibus salsae, graves, tepidae, non suaves, nisi quae ex montibus sub terra submanantes erumpunt in medios campos ibique arborum umbris contectae praestant montanorum fontium suavitatem. 728

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII Those searching for water should also examine the nature of the ground, since different kinds occur in particular formations. In clay the supply is slight, shallow and poor in taste. In loose sand it is likewise scanty, though found at a greater depth, and it is muddy and unpleasant. In black earth, small seepages and droplets collect from winter rain and settle in dense, compact ground; these have an excellent taste. Gravel contains moderate and uncertain veins, also of excellent sweetness. In coarse sand and carbunculus, supplies are more reliable [and more constant], and their taste is good. In red rock the supply is abundant and good, provided that it does not escape and disperse through intervening fissures. Beneath mountain slopes and in siliceous rock it is more plentiful, colder and more wholesome. Springs in the plains, by contrast, are saline, heavy, lukewarm and unpleasant, except where water runs underground from the mountains and emerges in the middle of a plain: shaded there by trees, it retains the sweetness of mountain springs. [3] Signa autem, quibus terrarum generibus supra scriptum est, ea invenientur nascentia: tenuis iuncus, salix erratica, alnus, vitex, harundo, hedera aliaque, quae eiusmodi sunt, quae non possunt nasci per se sine umore. Solent autem eadem in lacunis nata esse, quae sidentes praeter reliquum agrum excipiunt ex imbribus et agris per hiemem propterque capacitatem diutius conservant umorem. Quibus non est credendum, sed quibus regionibus et terris, non lacunis, ea signa nascuntur, non sata, sed naturaliter per se procreata, ibi est quaerenda. [3] The signs, which are written above, will be found growing in the following types of land: the slender rush, the wandering willow, the alder, the vitex, the reed, the ivy, and other such plants, which cannot grow by themselves without moisture. But they are usually grown in lakes, which, when they sit in them, receive more moisture from the rains and fields than from the rest of the land, and because of their capacity, they retain moisture longer during the winter. We must not believe these, but we must seek in which regions and lands, not lakes, these signs grow, not sown, but naturally produced by themselves. [4] In quibus si eae significabuntur inventiones, sic erunt experiundae. Fodiatur quoquoversus locus latus ne minus pedes <tres, altus pedes> quinque, in eoque conlocetur circiter solis occasum scaphium aereum aut plumbeum aut pelvis. Ex his quod erit paratum, id intrinsecus oleo ungatur ponaturque inversum, et 729

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII summa fossura operiatur harundinibus aut fronde, supra terra obruatur; tum postero die aperiatur, et si in vaso stillae sudoresque erunt, is locus habebit aquam. Where these signs indicate water, test the ground as follows. Dig a pit at least three feet across in each direction and five feet deep. At about sunset place in it a bronze or lead vessel, or a basin, whichever is available, first coating its inner surface with oil and setting it upside down. Cover the opening of the pit with reeds or leaves and lay earth over them. Open it the following day: if droplets of condensation appear in the vessel, the place contains water. [5] Item si vasum ex creta factum non coctum in ea fossione eadem ratione opertum positum fuerit, si is locus aquam habuerit, cum apertum fuerit, vas umidum erit et iam dissolvetur ab umore. Vellusque lanae si conlocatum erit in ea fossura, insequenti autem die de eo aqua expressa erit, significabit eum locum habere copiam. Non minus si lucerna concinnata oleique plena et accensa in eo loco operta fuerit conlocata et postero die non erit exusta, sed habuerit reliquias olei et enlychnii ipsaque umida invenietur, indicabit eum locum habere aquam, ideo quod omnis tepor ad se ducit umores. Item in eo loco ignis factus si fuerit et percalefacta terra et adusta vaporem nebulosum ex se suscitaverit, is locus habebit aquam. An unfired clay vessel placed in the pit and covered in the same way will, if water is present, be found damp and beginning to disintegrate. A fleece of wool from which water can be squeezed the following day likewise indicates an abundant supply. A lamp, prepared with oil and lit before being enclosed there, will indicate water if it has not burnt out by the next day, still contains oil and wick, and is found damp: warmth attracts moisture. Similarly, if a fire lit there heats the earth and causes a misty vapor to rise, water is present. [6] Cum haec ita erunt pertemptata et, qua supra scripta sunt, signa inventa, tum deprimendus est puteus in eo loco, et si erit caput aquae inventum, plures circa sunt fodiendi et per specus in unum locum omnes conducendi. Once these tests have been made and the signs described above have been found, sink a well at that place. If a source of water is discovered, dig several more wells around it and connect them by underground galleries so that the water gathers at a single point. Haec autem maxime in montibus et regionibus septentrionalibus sunt quaerenda, eo quod in his et suaviora et salubriora et copiosiora inveniuntur. 730

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII Aversi enim sunt solis cursui, et in his locis primum crebrae sunt arbores et silvosae, ipsique montes suas habent umbras obstantes et radii solis non directi perveniunt ad terram nec possunt. These are to be sought especially in the mountains and northern regions, because in these they are found both sweeter, more wholesome, and more abundant. For they are turned away from the course of the sun, and in these places trees and woods are first abundant, and the mountains themselves have their shadows that block them, and the rays of the sun do not reach the earth directly, nor can they burn the moisture. These, however, should be sought mainly in the mountains and northern regions, because there they are sweeter, healthier, and more abundant. For they are contrary to the course of the sun, and in these places trees and forests abound first, and the mountains themselves have their shadows, and the sun's rays are not directed towards the earth and cannot scorch the moisture. [7] Intervallaque montium maxime recipiunt imbres et propter silvarum crebritatem nives ab umbris arborum et montium ibi diutius conservantur, deinde liquatae per terrae venas percolantur et ita perveniunt ad infimas montium radices, ex quibus profluentes fontium erumpunt ructus. Campestribus autem locis contrario non possunt habere copias. Nam quaecumque sunt, non possunt habere salubritatem, quod solis vehemens impetus propter nullam obstantiam umbrarum eripit exhauriendo fervens ex planitie camporum umorem, et si quae sunt aquae apparentes, ex his, quod est levissimum tenuissimumque et subtili salubritate, aer avocans dissipat in impetum caeli, quaeque gravissimae duraeque et insuaves sunt partes, eae in fontibus campestribus relinquuntur. The valleys between mountains receive the most rain. Dense woodland and the shade of trees and mountains preserve the snow there for longer; when it melts, it filters through veins in the earth and reaches the lowest mountain slopes, where it gushes out in springs. In the plains, by contrast, supplies cannot be abundant or wholesome. With no shade to obstruct it, the Sun’s fierce heat draws moisture from the exposed ground. Of any water that remains visible, the air carries away and disperses the lightest, finest and most wholesome parts, leaving the heaviest, hardest and least pleasant components in the springs of the plains. 731

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII Critical note — VIII.1. Water prospecting combines topographical, botanical and atmospheric signs. Creta, sabulo, glarea and saxum are translated according to their function in the passage without imposing excessively precise modern geological classifications. The excavation-test supplement ⟨tres, altus pedes⟩ remains visible as an editorial intervention. 732

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII Chapter 2 [1] Itaque, quae ex imbribus aqua colligitur, salubriores habet virtutes, quod eligitur ex omnibus fontibus levissimis subtilibusque tenuitatibus, deinde per aeris exercitationem percolata tempestatibus liquescendo pervenit ad terram. Etiamque non crebriter in campis confluunt imbres, sed in montibus aut ad ipsos montes, ideo quod umores ex terra matutino solis ortu moti cum sunt egressi, in quamcumque partem caeli sunt proclinati, trudunt aera; deinde, cum sunt moti, propter vacuitatem loci post se recipiunt aeris ruentis undas. [1] Therefore, the water that is collected from the rains has more salubrious virtues, because it is selected from all the lightest and most subtle springs, and then, filtered by the exercise of the air, it reaches the ground, liquefied by storms. Moreover, the rains do not often flow in the plains, but in the mountains or on the mountains themselves, for this reason that the moistures, when they have emerged from the earth at the morning sunrise, are moved by the air in whatever part of the sky they are inclined to; then, when they are moved, because of the emptiness of the place, they receive the waves of the rushing air behind them. [2] Aer autem, qui ruit, trudens quocumque umorem per vim spiritus impetus et undas crescentes facit ventorum. A ventis autem quocumque feruntur umores conglobati ex fontibus, et fluminibus et paludibus et pelago, cum tepores solis colligunt et exhauriunt et ita tollunt in altitudinem nubes. Deinde cum aeris unda nitentes, cum perventum ad montes, ab eorum offensa et procellis propter plenitatem et gravitatem liquescendo disparguntur et ita diffunditur in terras. [2] But the air, which rushes, pushing moisture wherever it is by the force of the breath, creates the gusts and rising waves of the winds. But wherever the winds carry the moisture gathered from springs, from rivers and marshes and the sea, they collect and drain it with the time of the sun and thus lift the clouds to a height. Then, shining with the wave of the air, when it reaches the mountains, it is dispersed by their impact and storms because of its fullness and gravity, melting and thus it is spread over the lands. [3] Vaporem autem et nebulas et umores ex terra nasci haec videtur efficere ratio, quod ea habet in se et calores fervidos et spiritus inmanes refrigerationesque et aquarum magnam multitudinem. Ex eo, cum refrigeratum noctu sol oriens impetu tangit orbem terrae et ventorum flatus oriuntur per tenebras, ab umidis 733

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII locis egrediuntur in altitudinem nubes. Aer autem cur a sole percalefactus cum rationibus tollit ex terra umores, licet ex balineis exemplum capere. The following explanation appears to account for the generation of vapor, mist and moisture from the earth: the earth contains intense heat, powerful currents of air, cold and great quantities of water. When the rising Sun strikes its surface, cooled during the night, and winds arise in the darkness, clouds rise from damp places into the air. The way air heated by the Sun lifts moisture from the earth may be understood by considering baths. [4] Nullae enim camerae, quae sunt caldariorum, supra se possunt habere fontes, sed caelum, quod est ibi ex praefurniis ab ignis vapore percalefactum, corripit ex pavimentis aquam et aufert secum in camararum curvaturas et sustinet, ideo quod semper vapor calidus in altitudinem se trudit. Et primo non remittit propter brevitatem, simul autem plus umoris habet congestum, non potest sustinere propter gravitatem, sed stillat supra lavantium capita. Item eadem ratione caelestis aer, cum ab sole percepit calorem, ex omnibus locis hauriendo tollit umores et congregat ad nubes. Ita enim terra fervore tacta eicit umores, ⟨ut⟩ etiam corpus hominis ex calore emittit sudores. The vaults over the hot rooms of baths cannot have springs above them. Instead, the air inside, heated by the fire at the furnaces, draws water from the floors, carries it up into the curved vaults and holds it there, because hot vapor always rises. At first, while the quantity is small, it does not release the moisture. Once more has accumulated, however, it can no longer support the weight, and water drips onto the bathers’ heads. In the same way, atmospheric air warmed by the Sun draws moisture from every place and gathers it into clouds. Heat causes the earth to give off moisture just as it causes the human body to sweat. [5] Indices autem sunt eius rei venti, ex quibus qui a frigidissimis partibus veniunt procreati, septentrio et aquilo, extenuatos siccitatibus in aere flatus spirant; auster vero et reliqui, qui a solis cursu impetum faciunt, sunt umidissimi et semper adportant imbres, quod percalefacti ab regionibus fervidis adveniunt, et omnibus terris lambentes eripiunt umores et ita eos profundunt ad septentrionales regiones. [5] But the indications of this are the winds, which, when they come from the coldest parts, are born from the north and the north-east, and breathe in the air, weakened by the dryness; but the south and the others, which come from the 734

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII course of the sun, are very humid and always bring rain, because they arrive very hot from the hot regions, and, sliding down, they snatch the moisture from all the lands and thus carry it deeper to the northern regions. [6] Haec autem sic fieri testimonio possunt esse capita fluminum, quae orbe terrarum chorographiis picta itemque scripta plurima maximaque inveniuntur egressa ad septentrionem. Primumque in India Ganges et Indus ab Caucaso monte oriuntur; Syria Tigris et Euphrates; Asiae item, Ponto Borysthenes, Hypanis, Tanais; Colchis Phasis; Gallia Rhodanus; Celtica Rhenus; citra Alpis Timavos et Padus; Italia Tiberis; Maurusia, quam nostri Mauretaniam appellant, ex monte Atlante Dyris, qui ortus ex septentrionali regione progreditur per occidentem ad lacum Eptagonum et mutato nomine dicitur Agger, deinde ex lacu Eptabolo sub montes desertos subterfluens per meridiana loca manat et influit in Paludem quae appellatur, circumcingit Meroen, quod est Aethiopum meridianorum regnum, ab hisque paludibus se circumagens per flumina Astansobam et Astoboam et alia plura pervenit per montes ad cataractam ab eoque se praecipitans per septentrionalem pervenit inter Elephantida et Syenen Thebaicosque in Aegyptum campos et ibi Nilus appellatur. The river sources shown on maps and described in accounts of the world provide evidence for this explanation: many of the greatest rivers emerge in northern regions. In India the Ganges and Indus rise from the Caucasus; in Syria, the Tigris and Euphrates; in Asia, in the region of Pontus, the Borysthenes, Hypanis and Tanais; in Colchis, the Phasis; in Gaul, the Rhône; in Celtic territory, the Rhine; on this side of the Alps, the Timavus and Po; and in Italy, the Tiber. In Maurusia, which our people call Mauretania, the river Dyris rises from Mount Atlas, flows from the northern region westwards to Lake Eptagonus and changes its name to Agger. From Lake Eptabolus it passes beneath the desert mountains, flows through southern regions and enters the marshes that surround Meroë, the kingdom of the southern Ethiopians. From these marshes it winds through the Astansobas, Astoboa and several other rivers, crosses the mountains to the cataract, plunges down and flows northwards between Elephantine and Syene through the Theban plains into Egypt, where it is called the Nile. [7] Ex Mauretania autem caput Nili profluere ex eo maxime cognoscitur, quod ex altera parte montis Atlantis alia capita item profluentia ad occidentem 735

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII Oceanum, ⟨petunt⟩ ibique nascuntur ichneumones, crocodili, aliae similes bestiarum pisciumque naturae praeter hippopotamos. [7] But it is best known that the head of the Nile flows from Mauretania, because from the other side of the mountain of Atlantis other heads also flow towards the western Ocean, and there are born ichneumons, crocodiles, and other similar animals and fish, besides hippopotamuses. [8] Ergo cum omnia flumina magnitudinibus in orbis terrarum descriptionibus a septentrione videantur profluere Afrique campi, qui sunt in meridianis partibus subiecti solis cursui, latentes penitus habeant umores nec fontes crebros amnesque raros, relinquitur, uti multo meliora inveniantur capita fontium, quae ad septentrionem aut aquilonem spectant, nisi si inciderint in sulphurosum locum aut aluminosum seu bituminosum. Tunc enim permutantur <et> aut calidae aquae aut frigidae odore malo et sapore profundunt fontes. [8] Therefore, since all rivers seem to flow from the north in their magnitudes in descriptions of the world, the plains of Africa, which are in the southern parts subject to the course of the sun, have completely hidden moisture, and neither frequent springs nor rare rivers, it remains that much better sources should be found which face the north or northeast, unless they fall into a sulphurous or aluminous or bituminous place. For then they are exchanged <and> either hot waters or cold ones deepen the springs with a bad smell and taste. [9] Neque enim calidae aquae est ulla proprietas, sed frigida aqua, cum incidit percurrens in ardentem locum, effervescit et percalefacta egreditur per venas extra terram. Ideo diutius non potest permanere, sed brevi spatio fit frigida. Namque si naturaliter esset calida, non refrigeraretur calor eius. Sapor autem et odor et color eius non restituitur, quod intinctus et commixtus est propter naturae raritatem. [9] For hot water has no property, but cold water, when it falls as it flows into a burning place, boils and, being very hot, comes out through the veins outside the earth. Therefore it cannot remain longer, but in a short space becomes cold. For if it were naturally hot, its heat would not be cooled. But its taste, smell and color are not restored, because it is mixed and mixed, due to the rarity of nature. Historical and critical note — VIII.2. The chain linking rain, vapor, clouds, mountains and river sources is translated as Vitruvius’s causal explanation. Assertions about the northern origins of major rivers and the Nile belong to 736
THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII ancient physical geography; a modern correction should be made in the commentary rather than inserted into his argument. 737

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII Chapter 3 [1] Sunt autem etiam nonnulli fontes calidi, ex quibus profluit aqua sapore optimo, quae in potione ita est suavis, uti nec fontalis ab Camenis nec Marcia saliens desideretur. Haec autem ab natura perficiuntur his rationibus. Cum in imo per alumen aut bitumen seu sulphur ignis excitatur, ardore percandefacit terram, quae est supra se; item fervidum emittit in superiora loca vaporem, et ita, si qui in îs locis, qui sunt supra, fontes dulcis aquae nascuntur, offensi eo vapore effervescunt inter venas et ita profluunt incorrupto sapore. [1] There are also some hot springs, from which flow water of excellent taste, which is so sweet in drink, that neither the spring of the Camenae nor the Marcian water (the Aqua Marcia) is desired. But these are accomplished by nature in these ways. When fire is excited at the bottom by alum or bitumen or sulphur, it scorches the earth above it with its heat; and it emits a hot vapor into the higher places, and so, if in any of these places, which are above, springs of sweet water arise, offended by that vapor they boil between the veins and thus flow forth without any corrupting taste. [2] Sunt etiam odore et sapore non bono frigidi fontes, qui ab inferioribus locis penitus orti per loca ardentia transeunt et ab eo per longum spatium terrae percurrentes refrigerati perveniunt supra terram sapore odore coloreque corrupto, uti in Tiburtina via flumen Albula et in Ardeatino fontes frigidi eodem odore, qui sulphurati dicuntur, et reliquis locis similibus. Hi autem, cum sunt frigidi, ideo videntur aspectu fervere, quod, cum in ardentem locum alte penitus inciderunt, umore et igni inter se congruentibus offensa vehementi fragore validos recipiunt in se spiritus, et ita inflati vi venti coacti bullientes crebre per fontes egrediuntur. Ex his autem qui non sunt aperti, sed ⟨grumis⟩ aut saxis continentur, per angustas venas vehementia spiritus extruduntur ad summos grumorum tumulos. [2] There are also cold springs with a bad smell and taste, which, rising from deep below, pass through burning places and from there, running over a long distance of land, reach the surface of the earth cooled with a spoiled smell and color, as in the Tiburtine road the river Albula and in the Ardeatine cold springs with the same smell, which are called sulphurous, and in other similar places. But these, when they are cold, seem to boil to the eye because, when they have fallen deeply into a burning place, the moisture and fire, which are in harmony 738

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII with each other, are struck with a violent crash and receive strong spirits into themselves, and thus, being inflated by the force of the wind, they frequently come out bubbling through the springs. But from those which are not open, but are contained by rocks, the spirits are forced out through narrow veins to the highest mounds of the cairns by the force of the wind. [3] Itaque qui putant se altitudine, qua sunt grumi, capita fontium posse habere, cum aperiunt fossuras latius, decipiuntur. Namque uti aeneum vas non in summis labris plenum sed aquae mensurae suae capacitatis habens ⟨e⟩ tribus duas partes operculumque in eo conlocatum, cum ignis vehementi fervore tangatur, percalefieri cogit aquam, ea autem propter naturalem raritatem in se recipiens fervoris validam inflationem non modo implet vas, sed spiritibus extollens operculum et crescens abundat, sublato autem operculo emissis inflationibus in aere patenti rursus ad suum locum residit: ad eundem modum ea capita fontium cum sunt angustiis compressa, ruunt in summo spiritus aquae bullitus, simul autem sunt latius aperti, exanimati per raritates liquidae potestatis residunt et restituuntur in libramenti proprietatem. [3] Therefore, those who think that they can have the heads of springs from the height of the clods, when they open the trenches wider, are deceived. For as a brass vessel, not filled to the very brim, but having two-thirds of its capacity of water, and a lid placed in it, when the fire is touched with intense heat, forces the water to become very hot, but the water, due to its natural rarefaction, receiving within itself a strong inflation of heat, not only fills the vessel, but also lifts the lid with spirits and increases in abundance, but when the lid is lifted, the inflations are released and it returns to its place in the open air. In the same way, when those heads of springs are compressed by narrow spaces, the boiling spirits of the water rush in at the top, but at the same time they are opened wider, tested by the rarities of the liquid power, they settle and are restored to their property of balance. [4] Omnis autem aqua calida ideo [quod] est medicamentosa, quod in pravis rebus percocta aliam virtutem recipit ad usum. Namque sulphurosi fontes nervorum labores reficiunt percalefaciendo exurendoque caloribus e corporibus umores vitiosos. Aluminosi autem, cum dissoluta membra corporum paralysi aut aliqua vi morbi receperunt, fovendo per patentes venas refrigerationem contraria caloris vi reficiunt, et hoc continenter restituuntur in antiquam membrorum 739

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII curationem. Bituminosi autem interioris corporis vitia potionibus purgando solent mederi. [4] But all hot water is medicinal because it receives its healing power for use in bad cases. For sulphurous springs relieve the labors of the nerves by heating them and burning away the foul humours from the bodies with their heat. But aluminous springs, when the limbs of the body have become weak due to paralysis or some disease, by warming them through the open veins they relieve the body by the opposite force of heat, and this continually restores the limbs to their former health. But bituminous springs are wont to cure the vices of the interior of the body by cleansing them with potions. [5] Est autem aquae frigidae genus nitrosum, uti Pinnae Vestinae, Cutiliis aliisque locis similibus, quae potionibus depurgat per alvumque transeundo etiam strumarum minuit tumores. Ubi vero aurum, argentum, ferrum, aes, plumbum reliquaeque res earum similes fodiuntur, fontes inveniuntur copiosi, sed hi maxime sunt vitiosi. Habent enim uti aquae calidae sulphur alumen bitumen, faecem, quae, per potiones cum in corpus iniit et per venas permanando nervos attingit et artus, eos durat inflando. Igitur nervi inflatione turgentes e longitudine contrahuntur et ita aut nervicos aut podagricos efficiunt homines, ideo quod ex durissimis et spissioribus rigidissimisque rebus intinctas habent venarum raritates. [5] There is also a kind of cold water, nitrous, as in Pinnae Vestinae, Cutilii, and other similar places, which purifies by drinking and, passing through the bowels, also reduces the swellings of the goiters. But where gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, and other similar things are mined, springs are found in abundance, but these are especially vitiated. For hot vitriolic waters contain sulphur, alum, and bitumen, and when these enter the body through drinks and continue through the veins, they reach the nerves and joints, hardening them by swelling them. Therefore, the nerves, swelling by swelling, contract in length and thus make men neurasthenic or gouty, because they have the rarefied veins soaked in the hardest and thickest and coldest things. [6] Aquae autem species est, quae cum habeat non satis perlucidas et ipsa uti flos natat in summo, colore similis vitri purpurei. Haec maxime considerantur Athenis. Ibi enim ex eiusmodi locis et fontibus in asty et ad portum Piraeum ducti sunt salientes, e quibus bibit nemo propter eam causam, sed lavationibus et 740

Troezeni non potest id vitari, quod omnino aliud genus aquae non reperitur, nisi quod cibdeli habeant; itaque in ea civitate aut omnes aut maxima parte sunt pedibus vitiosi. Cilicia vero civitate Tarso flumen est nomine Cydnos, in quo podagrici crura macerantes levantur dolore. [6] But there is a kind of water which, though not sufficiently transparent, and which itself floats like a flower on the top, is of a color similar to purple glass. These are most highly regarded in Athens. For there, from such places and springs, springs have been brought to Asty and to the port of Piraeus, from which no one drinks for that reason, but they use washings and other things, but they drink from wells and thus avoid their vices. This cannot be avoided in the Troezen, for no other kind of water is found at all, except as many as they have; and therefore in that city either all or the greater part are defective in their feet. But in the Cilician city of Tarsus there is a river called Cydnus, in which gouty sufferers, soaking their legs, are relieved of their pain. [7] Sunt autem et alia multa genera, quae habent suas proprietates, ut in Sicilia flumen est Himeras, quod a fonte cum est progressum, dividitur in duas partes; quae pars profluit contra Etruriam, quod per terrae dulcem sucum percurrit, est infinita dulcedine, quae altera parte per eam terram currit, unde sal foditur, salsum habet saporem. Item Paraetonio et quod est iter ad Ammonem et Casio ad Aegyptum lacus sunt palustres, qui ita sunt salsi, ut habeant insuper se salem congelatum. Sunt autem et aliis pluribus locis et fontes et flumina <et> lacus, qui per salifodinas percurrentes necessario salsi perficiuntur. [7] But there are also many other kinds, which have their own properties, as in Sicily there is a river called Himeras, which, when it has advanced from its source, is divided into two parts; the part which flows towards Etruria, which runs through the sweet juice of the land, is of infinite sweetness, while the other part which runs through that land, from which salt is mined, has a salty taste. Likewise, in Paraetonium and on the road to Ammon and Cassius in Egypt there are marshy lakes, which are so salty that they have frozen salt on top of them. But there are also in many other places springs and rivers <and> lakes, which, running through salt mines, are necessarily made salty. [8] Alii autem per pingues terrae venas profluentes uncti oleo fontes erumpunt, uti Solis, quod oppidum est Ciliciae, flumen nomine Liparis, in quo natantes aut 741

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII lavantes ab ipsa aqua unguntur. Similiter Aethiopiae lacus est, qui unctos homines efficit, qui in eo nataverint, et India, qui sereno caelo emittit olei magnam multitudinem, item Carthagini fons, in quo natat insuper oleum, odore uti scobe citreo; quo oleo etiam pecora solent ungere. Zacyntho et circa Dyrrachium et Apolloniam fontes sunt, qui picis magnam multitudinem cum aqua evomunt. Babylone lacus amplissima magnitudine, qui λίμνη ἀσφάλτιτις appellatur, habet supra natans liquidum bitumen; quo bitumine et latere testaceo structum murum Samiramis circumdedit Babyloni. Item Iope in Syria Arabiaque Nomadum lacus sunt inmani magnitudine, qui emittunt bituminis maximas moles, quas diripiunt qui habitant circa. [8] But others, flowing through the veins of the earth, burst forth with oilanointed springs, as at Solis, a town in Cilicia, a river called Liparis, in which those who swim or wash are anointed by it. Similarly, there is a lake in Ethiopia which makes men anointed who swim in it, and India, which, when the sky is clear, emits a great quantity of oil, as well as a spring in Carthage, in which oil also floats, with a smell like that of lemon grass; with which oil they also anoint cattle. At Zacynthus and around Dyrrachium and Apollonia there are springs which spew out a great quantity of pitch with water. At Babylon a lake of very large size, which is called λίμνη ἀσφαλτῖτις, has liquid bitumen floating on it; with which bitumen and earthenware brick wall was built at Sameramis surrounding Babylon. Likewise at Joppa in Syria and Arabia there are lakes of the Numidians of enormous size, which emit the greatest quantities of bitumen, which those who live around plunder. [9] Id autem non est mirandum; nam crebrae sunt ibi lapidicinae bituminis duri. Cum ergo per bituminosam terram vis erumpit aquae, secum extrahit et, cum sit egressa extra terram, secernitur et ita reicit ab se bitumen. Etiamque est in Cappadocia in itinere, quod est inter Mazaca et Tyana, lacus amplus, in quem lacum pars sive harundinis sive alii generis si demissa fuerit et postero die exempta, ea pars, quae fuerit exempta, invenietur lapidea, quae autem pars extra aquam manserit, permanet in sua proprietate. [9] But this is not to be wondered at; for there are frequent stony deposits of hard bitumen there. Therefore, when the force of the water bursts through bituminous soil, it draws it with it, and when it has gone out of the ground, it is separated and thus throws the bitumen from itself. And there is also in 742

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII Cappadocia, on the road, which is between Mazaca and Tyana, a large lake, into which lake if a piece of reed or of some other kind is dropped and taken out the next day, that part which was taken out will be found to be stony, but the part which remained outside remains in its own right. [10] Ad eundem modum Hierapoli Phrygiae effervet aquae calidae multitudo, e quibus circum hortos et vineas fossis ductis inmittitur; haec autem efficitur post annum crusta lapidea. Ita quotannis dextra ac sinistra margines ex terra faciundo inducunt eam et efficiunt his crustis in agris saepta. Hoc autem ita videtur naturaliter fieri, quod in îs locis et ea terra, quibus is nascitur, sucus subest coaguli naturae similis; deinde cum commixta vis egreditur per fontes extra terram, a solis et aeris calore cogitur congelari, ut etiam in areis salinarum videtur. [10] In the same way, at Hierapolis in Phrygia, a multitude of hot waters boil, from which they are let in through ditches around the gardens and vineyards; but this becomes a crust of stone after a year. Thus every year on the right and left they introduce it by making the edges of the earth and make fences in the fields in these crusts. But this seems to happen naturally, because in these places and the land in which it is born, the juice is under the nature of a clot; then when the mixed force comes out of the earth through springs, it is forced to freeze by the heat of the sun and the air, as is also seen in the air of salt lakes. [11] Item sunt ex amaro suco terrae fontes exeuntes vehementer amari, ut in Ponto est flumen Hypanis. ⟨is⟩ A capite profluit circiter milia XL sapore dulcissimo; deinde, cum pervenit ad locum, qui est ab ostio ad milia CLX, admiscetur ei fonticulus oppido quam parvulus. Is cum in eum influit, tunc tantam magnitudinem fluminis facit amaram, ideo quod per id genus terrae et venas, unde sandaracam fodiunt, ea aqua manando perficitur amara. [11] Likewise, there are springs issuing from the bitter juice of the earth, which are exceedingly bitter, as in Pontus is the river Hypanus. From its head it flows about 40 miles with a very sweet taste; then, when it reaches a place which is 160 miles from the mouth, a small spring is mixed with it, which is very small. When it flows into it, then by the greatness of the river it becomes bitter, for this reason, because through that kind of earth and the veins from which they dig sandaraca, the water is made bitter by flowing. 743

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII [12] Haec autem dissimilibus saporibus a terrae proprietate perficiuntur, uti etiam in fructibus videtur. Si enim radices arborum aut vitium aut reliquorum seminum non ex terrae proprietatibus sucum capiendo ederent fructus, uno genere essent in omnibus locis et regionibus omnium sapores. Sed animadvertimus insula Lesbo vinum protropum, Maeonia Catacecaumeniten, Lydia Tmoliten, Sicilia Mamertinum, Campania Falernum, Terracina et Fundis Caecubum reliquisque locis pluribus innumerabili multitudine genera vini virtutesque procreari. Quae non aliter possunt fieri, nisi, cum terrenus umor suis proprietatibus saporis in radicibus sit infusus, enutrit materiam per quam egrediens ad cacumen profundat proprium loci et generis sui ⟨in⟩ fructus saporem. [12] But these are perfected with dissimilar flavors by the properties of the earth, as is also seen in fruits. For if the roots of trees or vines or other seeds did not produce fruit by drawing juices from the properties of the earth, the flavors of all would be of one kind in all places and regions. But we observe that the island of Lesbos produces protropous wine, Maeonia Catacecaumene, Lydia Tmolite, Sicily Mamertine, Campania Falerno, in Terracina and Fundis Caecubus and many other places in an innumerable multitude, kinds of wine and virtues are produced. Which cannot be done otherwise, unless, when the earthly moisture is infused with its properties of flavor in the roots, it nourishes the matter through which, rising to the top, it deepens the flavor proper to the place and kind of fruit. [13] Quodsi terra generibus umorum non esset dissimilis et disparata, non tantum in Syria et Arabia in harundinibus et iuncis herbisque omnibus essent odores, neque arbores turiferae, neque piperis darent bacas, nec murrae glaebulae, nec Cyrenis in ferulis laser nasceretur, sed in omni terra regionibus eodem genere omnia procrearentur. Has autem varietates terrae umoris qualitatis regionibus et locis inclinatio mundi et solis impetus propius aut longius cursum faciendo tales efficit nec solum in his rebus, sed etiam in pecoribus et armentis haec non ita similiter efficerentur, nisi proprietates singularum terrarum ⟨umorum⟩ in regionibus ad solis potestatem temperarentur. [13] But if the earth were not dissimilar and disparate in the kinds of moisture, not only would there be odours in the reeds and rushes and all the herbs in Syria and Arabia, nor would frankincense trees, nor peppercorns yield berries, nor myrrh clusters, nor would Cyrene produce a laser in its canes, but in every region 744

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII of the earth everything would be produced in the same kind. Now these varieties in regions and places are produced by the inclination of the world and by the influence of the sun, by making its course nearer or farther, such are the qualities of the earth and the moisture, and not only in these things, but also in cattle and herds, these would not be produced in such a similar way, unless the properties of the individual lands in the regions were tempered to the power of the sun. [14] Sunt enim Boeotiae flumina Cephisos et Melas, Lucanis Crathis, Troia Xanthus inque agris Clazomeniorum et Erythraeorum et Laodicensium fontes. Ad ⟨ea⟩ flumina cum pecora suis temporibus anni parantur ad conceptionem partus, per id tempus adiguntur eo cotidie potum, ex eoque, quamvis sint alba, procreant aliis locis leucophaea, aliis locis pulla, aliis coracino colore. Ita proprietas liquoris, cum inît in corpus, proseminat intinctam sui cuiusque generis qualitatem. Igitur quod in campis Troianis proxime flumen armenta rufa et pecora leucophaea nascuntur, ideo id flumen Ilienses Xanthum appellavisse dicuntur. [14] For the rivers of Boeotia are Cephisos and Melas, of Lucania Crathis, of Troy Xanthus, and in the fields of the Clazomenians and Erythraeans and Laodiceans springs. At the rivers with their cattle at their proper times of the year they are prepared for conception and birth, during that time they are driven to drink it daily, and from it, although they are white, in some places they produce white, in others a fawn, in others a raven-colored. Thus the property of the liquid, when it is in the body, reveals the inherent quality of each of its kinds. Therefore, because in the Trojan plains red cattle and white cattle are born near the river, the Ilians are said to have called that river Xanthus. [15] Etiamque inveniuntur aquae genera mortifera, quae per maleficum sucum terrae percurrentia recipiunt in se vim venenatam, uti fuisse dicitur Terracinae fons, qui vocabatur Neptunius, ex quo qui biberant inprudentes, vita privabantur; quapropter antiqui eum obstruxisse dicuntur. Et Chrobsi Thracia lacus ex quo non solum qui biberint, moriuntur, sed etiam qui laverint. Item in Thessalia fons est profluens, ex quo fonte nec pecus ullum gustat nec bestiarum genus ullum propius accedit; ad quem fontem proxime est arbor florens purpureo colore. [15] And there are also found kinds of waters that are deadly, which, flowing through the earth through the malefic juice, receive within themselves a 745
