VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII poisonous force, as is said to have been the fountain of Terracina, which was called Neptune, from which those who drank unwisely were deprived of life; for which reason the ancients are said to have blocked it. And the lake of Chrobsi in Thrace, from which not only those who drank die, but also those who washed. Likewise in Thessaly there is a spring flowing, from which no cattle taste nor does any kind of beast approach; near which spring is a tree flowering with a purple color. [16] Non minus in Macedonia quo loci sepultus est Euripides, dextra ac sinistra monumenti advenientes duo rivi concurrunt. In unum, e quibus ad unum accumbentes viatores pransitare solent propter aquae bonitatem, ad rivum autem, qui est ex altera parte monumenti, nemo accedit, quod mortiferam aquam dicitur habere. Item est in Arcadia Nonacris nominata terrae regio, quae habet in montibus ex saxo stillantes frigidissimos umores. Haec autem aqua Στυγός ὕδωρ nominatur, quam neque argenteum neque aeneum nec ferreum vas potest sustinere, sed dissilit et dissipatur. Conservare autem eam et continere nihil aliud potest nisi mulina ungula, qua etiam memoratur ab Antipatro in provinciam ubi erat Alexander, per Iollam filium perlata esse et ab eo ea aqua regem esse necatum. [16] No less in Macedonia, where Euripides is buried, two streams meet on the right and left of the monument. In one, travelers are accustomed to dine because of the goodness of the water, but no one approaches the stream that is on the other side of the monument, because it is said to have deadly water. Likewise, in Arcadia there is a region of land called Nonacris, which has very cold waters dripping from the rocks on the mountains. This water is called Stygian water, which neither silver nor bronze nor iron vessels can hold, but breaks and is dissipated. But nothing else can preserve and contain it except a hoof mill, which is also mentioned to have been carried by Antipater to the province where Alexander was, by his son Iollas, and by him the king was killed by the water. [17] Item Alpibus in Cottii regno est aqua; ex qua qui gustant, statim concidunt. Agro autem Falisco via Campana in campo Corneto est lucus, in quo fons oritur; ibique avium et lacertarum reliquarumque serpentium ossa iacentia apparent. [17] Likewise, in the Alps, in the kingdom of Cottus, there is water; those who taste it immediately fall to their deaths. But in the Faliscan country, on the 746

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER VIII Campanian road, in the plain of Cornetus, there is a grove in which a spring rises; everywhere the bones of birds and lizards and other serpents are seen lying. Item sunt nonnullae acidae venae fontium, uti Lyncesto et in Italia Velino, Campania Teano aliisque locis pluribus, quae hanc habent virtutem, uti calculos, in vesicis qui nascuntur in corporibus hominum potionibus discutiant. Likewise, there are some acidic veins of springs, such as Lyncestus and in Italy Velino, Teano in Campania and many other places, which have this power, such as dissolving stones in the bladders that are formed in the bodies of men by drinking. Moreover, there is water in the Alps, in the kingdom of Cottius, which makes those who taste it drop dead at once. Now in the Faliscan territory, along the Campana Way, in the field of Cornetum, there is a grove in which a spring rises; all around are seen the bones of birds, lizards, and other serpents. There are also certain acidic springs, as at Lyncestus and Velinus in Italy, at Teanum in Campania, and in many other places, which have this power—like certain stones—of dispersing the stones that form in the bodies of men. [18] Fieri autem hoc naturaliter ideo videtur, quod acer et acidus sucus subest in ea terra, per quam egredientes venae intinguntur acritudine, et ita, cum in corpus inierunt, dissipant quae ex aquarum subsidentia in corporibus et concrescentia offenderunt. Quare autem discutiantur ex acidis eae res, sic possumus animadvertere. Ovum in aceto si diutius positum fuerit, cortex eius mollescet et dissolvetur. Item plumbum, quod est lentissimum et gravissimum, si in vase conlocatum fuerit et in eo acetum suffusum, id autem opertum et oblitum erit, efficietur, uti plumbum dissolvatur, et fiat cerussa. [18] This seems to happen naturally because there is a sharp and acidic juice in the earth, through which the veins that emerge are dipped in the sharpness, and thus, when they enter the body, they disperse what they have encountered from the subsidence of the waters in the bodies and their concretion. But why these things are dispersed by acids, we can observe in this way. If an egg is left in vinegar for a long time, its shell will soften and dissolve. Likewise, lead, which is very slow and heavy, if it is placed in a vessel and vinegar is poured into it, but this is covered and forgotten, it will be made to dissolve like lead, and become lead. 747

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER VIII [19] Eisdem rationibus aes, quod etiam solidiore est natura, similiter curatum si fuerit, dissipabitur et fiet aerugo. Item margarita. Non minus saxa silicea, quae neque ferrum neque ignis potest per se dissolvere, cum ab igni sunt percalefacta, aceto sparso dissiliunt et dissolvuntur. Ergo cum has res ante oculos ita fieri videamus, ratiocinemur isdem rationibus ex acidis propter acritudinem suci etiam calculosos e natura rerum similiter posse curari. [19] By the same reasoning, if bronze, which is also more solid by nature, is similarly cured, it will disintegrate and become rust. Likewise pearl. No less do flint stones, which neither iron nor fire can dissolve by themselves, when they are heated by fire, disintegrate and dissolve when sprinkled with vinegar. Therefore, since we see these things happening before our eyes, let us reason by the same reasoning that stones that are naturally calcified can also be cured by acids because of the acridity of the juice. [20] Sunt autem etiam fontes uti vino mixti, quemadmodum est unus Paphlagoniae, ex quo eam aquam sine vino potantes fiunt temulenti. Aequiculis autem in Italia et in Alpibus natione Medullorum est genus aquae, quam qui bibunt, efficiuntur turgidis gutturibus. [20] There are also springs mixed with wine, as is the case in Paphlagonia, from which those who drink it without wine become intoxicated. But among the Aequi in Italy and in the Alps, among the Medullae, there is a kind of water, which makes those who drink it swell up in their throats. [21] Arcadia vero civitas est non ignota Clitor, in cuius agris est spelunca profluens aqua, e qua qui biberint, fiunt abstemii. Ad eum autem fontem epigramma est in lapide inscriptum: hac sententia versibus graecis: eam non esse idoneam ad lavandum, sed etiam inimicam vitibus, quod apud eum fontem Melampus sacrificiis purgavisset rabiem Proeti filiarum restituissetque earum virginum mentes in pristinam sanitatem. epigramma autem est id, quod est subscriptum: 21. In Arcadia lies the well-known city of Clitor, in whose territory a cave gives forth water that makes those who drink it abstain from wine. Beside the spring a Greek epigram is inscribed on stone. Archaeological note — Bk. 8.6 (the Roman aqueducts). The chapter on conduits is illuminated by the archaeology of the greatest hydraulic system of antiquity. Rome came to have eleven aqueducts: the first was the Aqua Appia (312 BCE, of Appius Claudius the Blind), mostly underground; there followed the Anio Vetus, the Aqua Marcia (144 BCE) —the longest and famed for its purity— the Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus, whose arches still cross the Roman campagna. The chief ancient source is the De aquaeductu of Sextus Julius Frontinus, curator aquarum under Nerva and Trajan, half a century after Vitruvius. The three methods Vitruvius describes are verified in the remains: masonry channels (specus) in the great aqueducts, lead pipes (fistulae, stamped by the plumbarius) in the urban distribution, and terracotta pipes. Surviving monuments such as the Pont du Gard (Nîmes) and the aqueduct of Segovia, and the network of Ostia, confirm the gentle gradient and the engineering that Book VIII theorizes. Explanatory note — Bk. 8.6 (pipes and the toxicity of lead). Vitruvius distinguishes three ways of conveying water: by masonry channels (rivi), by lead pipes (fistulae plumbeae), and by earthenware pipes (tubuli fictiles). He describes the making of the fistulae by the plumbarii from rolled sheets of standard size, named by their weight. And he reaches a decisive passage (8.6.10- 11): water is more wholesome through earthenware than through lead, 'for from it cerussa (white lead) is produced, which is said to be harmful to the human body.' He adds the empirical proof: plumbers are pallid, because the vapor of molten lead destroys the vigor of the blood. It is one of the earliest testimonies to an awareness of lead toxicity (plumbism). The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. 764

VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IX ARGUMENTUM LIBRI IX — On gnomonics and astronomy: the doubling of the square handed down by Plato and the right-angled triangle of Pythagoras; the discovery of Archimedes concerning the adulterated crown; the course of the sun through the twelve signs of the zodiac, the northern and southern constellations and the doctrine of the astrologers; and the analemma, the construction of sundials, and the water-clocks (clepsydrae) of Ctesibius. Notice. — Book IX turns to gnomonics and astronomy. Its preface, a meditation on the immortality of learning above athletic fame, is among the most quoted in the treatise. The book expounds the geometry of the heavens, the zodiac and the courses of sun, moon and planets, the phases and the analemma, and the construction of sundials and water-clocks. It preserves much Hellenistic astronomical lore and is the principal Latin source for ancient dialling. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IX Since the result cannot be expressed as a whole-number measure, draw a diagonal from corner to corner of the square ten feet long and ten feet wide. This divides it into two equal triangles, each of fifty square feet. Construct a square with equal sides on the length of that diagonal. The smaller square contains two triangles of fifty square feet; the larger contains four of the same size and area. Plato thus explained the doubling by geometrical construction, as shown in the diagram drawn at the foot of the page. Therefore, since this cannot be explained by number, in that square, which was 10 feet long and 10 feet wide, a diagonal line is drawn from corner to corner, to divide two triangles of equal size, each with an area of fifty square feet, and along its diagonal an equal square described by the sides. Thus, as the two large triangles were drawn in the smaller square of fifty feet by the diagonal line, four of the same size and the same number of feet will be made in the larger one. In this way, on the lower page, the duplication of Plato's grammatical rules is explained, as the scheme is signed. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IX discovery: Pythagoras showed how to obtain a right angle without the craftsman's square (norma). Three rules of 3, 4, and 5 feet, joined at their tips into a triangle, suffice: the angle formed by the sides of 3 and 4 is a right angle. And the squares built on them confirm it: 9 + 16 = 25. Vitruvius thus describes the 3-4-5 triangle —far less than the general theorem that posterity would call 'Pythagorean'— and is one of its most cited ancient sources. He adds that Pythagoras, believing himself aided by the Muses, offered them a sacrifice in gratitude. The application is architectural: the setting-out of stairs (klimakter) and of right angles on site. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IX shouted in Greek: «εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα» (that is: « I have found it, I have found it! »). Explanatory note — Bk. 9, preface (Archimedes and the crown). The preface to Book IX contrasts the fleeting fame of athletes with the lasting glory of the learned, and issues in the most famous anecdote of ancient science. Hiero II of Syracuse, suspecting that the goldsmith had abstracted gold from a votive crown and replaced it with silver without altering the weight, commissions Archimedes to detect the fraud. On entering the bath, Archimedes observes that the water overflows in proportion to the body immersed: he thus grasps that he can measure the volume of an irregular body by the water it displaces. He runs out naked, crying in Greek 'heureka, heureka' ('I have found it!'). Then, with two masses of equal weight —one of gold, one of silver— and the crown, he measures the water displaced by each and, by comparison, reveals the admixture of silver. Vitruvius is the oldest ancient source for this story (some two centuries after the event); Archimedes himself does not record it, and the exact method — simple immersion or hydrostatic weighing— is debated. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 9, preface (Hiero's crown). In the Budé, Book IX is the work of Jean Soubiran (1969), whose astronomical and mathematical commentary is standard. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) stress that the anecdote does not appear in Archimedes's surviving works (On Floating Bodies sets out the principle, not the episode) and that its technical plausibility has been questioned: the precision required by mere immersion is difficult, so it has been proposed that Archimedes in fact used hydrostatic weighing —a hypothesis already framed by Galileo in La Bilancetta (1586) and revisited by modern scholarship (Ch. Rorres). Corso–Romano fix the vocabulary (massa, coronarium opus). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. Therefore, since they do not complete the same number of days in each sign as they have previously spent, they complete [the correct course] by skipping over it in more rapid courses. This is done so that, although they remain in some signs, nevertheless, when they escape the necessity of delay, they quickly complete their correct circuit. That this is so is best known from the star Venus, which, when it follows the sun, appears after its setting in the sky and shines most brightly at nightfall, is called Lucifer, but at other times precedes it and rises at dawn. From here, sometimes several days pass in one sign, and at other times they enter another sign more quickly. Therefore, by not completing the same number of days in each of the signs, however long they may have lingered before, they complete the correct course by skipping faster routes. Thus it is done, so that they linger in some signs; however, when they are freed from the need for delay, they quickly achieve a proper circumambulation. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER IX Critical and astronomical note — IX.4. The northern constellations retain Vitruvius’s Latin and Greek names, including septentrio, ἄρκτος and ἑλίκη, together with the stellar figures he describes. Modern identifications are explanatory notes rather than substitutions in the catalog. The problematic name provindemiator and its comparison with προτρυγητής require separate philological treatment, not the assumption of a single uniformly transmitted spelling. 810

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IX [4] I have explained the figured and shaped images of the stars in the world, designed by nature and divine mind, as Democritus the physicist pleased, but only those whose rising and setting we can observe and see with our eyes. For just as they revolve around the pivot of the north axis, they do not set or go under the earth, so around the pivot of the south, which is subject to the earth because of the inclination of the world, the stars revolve and lie hidden and have no exits of the east above the earth. Therefore their shapes are not known because of the obstruction of the earth. Now an indicator of this is the star Canopus, which is unknown in these regions, but traders who have been to the extreme regions of Egypt and to the farthest ends of the earth report it. I have set forth the figures and likenesses of the heavenly bodies arranged in the firmament, designed by nature and by the divine mind, as it seemed to the natural philosopher Democritus; but only those whose risings and settings we are able to observe and behold. Critical and observational note — IX.5. Piscis Austrinus, Cetus, Ara, Centaurus, Hydra or Anguis, Crater, Corvus, Argo, Canis, Orion, Lepus and Eridanus retain the ancient catalog’s organization. The Canopus passage is significant for the geography of observation: Vitruvius recognizes stars unavailable from more northerly Mediterranean latitudes and known to travelers towards Egypt. 813

[2] Cetera ex astrologia, quos effectus habeant signa XII, stellae V, sol, luna ad humanae vitae rationem, Chaldaeorum ratiocinationibus est concedendum, quod propria est eorum genethlialogiae ratio, uti possint ante facta et futura ex ratiocinationibus astrorum explicare. Eorum autem inventiones reliquerunt, inque ⟨ea re⟩ sollertia acuminibusque fuerunt magnis, qui ab ipsa natione Chaldaeorum profluxerunt. Primusque Berosus in insula et civitate Coo consedit ibique aperuit disciplinam, post ei studens Antipater iterumque Athenodorus, qui etiam non e nascentia sed ex conceptione genethlialogiae rationes explicatas reliquit. The remaining questions of astrology — the effects of the twelve signs, the five planets, the Sun and the Moon on human life — must be left to the reasoning of the Chaldaeans. Their particular expertise is genethlialogy, the interpretation of birth horoscopes, by which they explain past and future events from the configurations of the stars. Those who transmitted these discoveries and displayed exceptional ingenuity came from the Chaldaean people themselves. Berosus first settled on the island of Cos and taught the subject there; Antipater subsequently studied it, and Athenodorus in turn left accounts of horoscopes calculated from conception rather than birth. 814

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IX The rest of astrology — the effects that the 12 signs, the 5 stars, the sun, and the moon have on human life—must be attributed to the reasoning of the Chaldeans, which is their own method of genealogy. But they left behind their inventions, in which there was great skill and insight, which came from the same nation of the Chaldeans. And the first Berossus settled on the island and city of Coos, and there he established a discipline; after him Antipater studied, and again Athenodorus, who also left detailed accounts of genealogy, not from birth but from conception. [3] De naturalibus autem rebus Thales Milesius, Anaxagoras Clazomenius, Pythagoras Samius, Xenophanes Colophonius, Democritus Abderites rationes, quibus e rebus natura rerum gubernaretur quemadmodum quaeque effectus habeat, excogitatas reliquerunt. Quorum inventa secuti siderum ⟨ad ortus⟩ et occasus tempestatum significatus Eudoxus, Euctemon, Callippus, Meto, Philippus, Hipparchus, Aratus ceterique ex astrologia parapegmatorum disciplinis invenerunt et eas posteris explicatas reliquerunt. Quorum scientiae sunt hominibus suspiciendae, quod tanta cura fuerunt, ut etiam videantur divina mente tempestatium significatus post futuros ante pronuntiare. Quas ob res haec eorum curis studiisque sunt concedenda. [3] But concerning natural things, Thales of Miles, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, Pythagoras of Samos, Zenophanes of Colophon, Democritus of Abderite have left behind them the methods by which the nature of things should be governed from things, how and what effects it has. Following their discoveries, Eudoxus, Eudemus, Callippus, Meto, Philip, Hipparchus, Aratus and the rest discovered the signs of the stars and their setting and storms from the disciplines of the Parapegmata, and have left them explained to posterity. Their knowledge is to be admired by men, because they were so careful that they even seem to have pronounced the signs of storms in advance by the divine mind. For which reason these things are to be conceded to their care and studies. Regarding natural things, Thales of Miles, Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, Pythagoras of Samos, Xenophanes of Colophon, and Democritus of Abder have left behind invented reasons why the nature of things should be governed by whatever effects they may have. Their books can supply further constructions to anyone who understands the layout of the analemma. Explanatory note — Bk. 9.7–9.8 (the analemma and sundials). The technical heart of Book IX is gnomonics. In 9.7 Vitruvius sets out the analemma: a geometric construction —a system of lines and curves built from the shadow of the gnomon at noon on the equinox— that projects the celestial sphere onto a plane and allows the hours and months to be marked on any dial, without recourse to trigonometry (Ptolemy's more advanced method, in his On the Analemma, is later). In 9.8 he gives the fullest ancient catalog of sundials with their Greek inventors: the hemicyclium, hollowed from a block and undercut to the latitude, by Berosus the Chaldean; the scaphe or hemisphere 822

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER IX and the disc on a plane, by Aristarchus of Samos; the arachne ('spiderweb'), by Eudoxus (or Apollonius); the plinthium or lacunar in the Circus Flaminius, by Scopinas of Syracuse; and others by Parmenio, Theodosius, Andreas, Patrocles, Dionysodorus, and Apollonius. Vitruvius is the most important ancient literary source on the sundial. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Comparative note — Bk. 9.7–9.8 (gnomonics). In the Budé, Book IX is the work of Jean Soubiran (1969), whose mathematical-astronomical commentary reconstructs the analemma step by step. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland–Howe (Cambridge, 1999) confront the list of dials with surviving examples —all of the nodus type, differing in the surface that receives the shadow— and with the modern gnomonic literature. On Berosus, scholarship clarifies his role as transmitter of Babylonian astronomy to the Greek world (Cos). Corso– Romano detail the terminology (gnomon, analemma, enclima). This edition keeps the transmitted text —including the Greek names of the types— and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. The Chaldean Berosus is said to have invented the hemicyclium, hollowed from a square block and cut to the local inclination. Aristarchus of Samos devised the scaphe, or hemisphere, and the disk on a plane; Eudoxus, or according to some Apollonius, the arachne. Scopinas of Syracuse devised the plinthium, also called lacunar, an example of which stood in the Circus Flaminius. Parmenion devised the type called pros ta historoumena; Theodosius and Andrias the pros pan klima; Patrocles the pelecinum; Dionysodorus the conum; and Apollonius the pharetra. These and other authors left further types, including the conarachne, conical plinthium, and antiboreum. Several also explained how to make portable hanging dials from these designs. Anyone familiar with the construction of analemmas can find designs in their books. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Preface [1] Nobili Graecorum et ampla civitate Ephesi lex vetusta dicitur a maioribus dura condicione sed iure esse non iniquo constituta. Nam architectus, cum publicum opus curandum recipit, pollicetur, quanto sumptu id sit futurum. Tradita aestimatione magistratui bona eius obligantur, donec opus sit perfectum. Absoluto autem, cum ad dictum inpensa respondit, decretis et honoribus ornatur. Item si non amplius quam quarta, ad aestimationem est adicienda, de publico praestatur, neque ulla poena tenetur. Cum vero amplius quam quarta in opere consumitur, ex eius bonis ad perficiendum pecunia exigitur. In the great and distinguished Greek city of Ephesus, the ancestors are said to have established an ancient law, severe in its terms yet not unjust. When an architect undertakes a public building, he declares its estimated cost. Once that estimate has been submitted to the magistrate, his property stands as security until the work is complete. If the final expenditure agrees with the estimate, he receives public honors and decrees of recognition. An overrun of no more than one quarter is covered by the public treasury without penalty. If the excess exceeds one quarter, however, the additional money required to complete the work is recovered from the architect’s own property. In the renowned and spacious Greek city of Ephesus an ancient law is said to have been established by the men of old — harsh in its terms, yet founded in justice rather than injustice. When an architect undertakes the charge of a public work, he declares beforehand what its cost will be. The estimate being handed to the magistrate, his property is pledged as security until the work is completed. When it is finished, if the outlay has answered to his declaration, he is honored with decrees and distinctions. Likewise, if the estimate is exceeded by no more than a quarter, the excess is added to it and met from public funds, and he incurs no penalty. But when more than a quarter is overspent, the money required to complete the work is exacted from his own estate. 835

[1] A machine is a connected assemblage of timber, possessing the greatest powers for the moving of loads. It is set in motion by the art of circular movements, which the Greeks call cyclic movement. Of these there is one kind for scaling, which in Greek is called acrobaticon; another is a breathing machine, which among them is called a pneumatic; the third is the hoisting type (tractorium), which the Greeks call baroulkos. M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X instrument (organum): the first requires the force of several workers and acts by its mass (like the ballista or the wine-presses); the second achieves its end by the skilled handling of one alone (like the scorpio). Above all, he grounds mechanics in nature: 'all machinery is brought forth by nature, with the rotation of the world as its teacher' (10.1.4) —the turning of the sun, moon, and stars is the first machine that man imitates. It is a theory of technology as an extension of ratiocinatio into fabrica and as an imitation of the cosmos. The text has been collated with no variant affecting the sense. Granger (Loeb) and Rowland– Howe (Cambridge, 1999) clarify the machina/organum distinction (μηχανή/ὄργανον) and its debt to the Hellenistic tradition (Ctesibius, Philon, Hero); Corso–Romano detail the vocabulary (machinatio, versatio). This edition keeps the transmitted text and translates in its own voice, with no variant affecting the sense. Critical Note — Lib. 10.1.1] Diagnosis: Harleianus 2767 reads “Machina est continens e materia coniunctio maximas ad onerum motus habens virtutes.” The word “virtutes” in this context has the technical sense of “mechanical powers” or “forces,” not of “moral virtues.” The triplex divisio of machines (scansorium, spirale, trispastos) anticipates the modern distinction between vertical lifting machines, helical traction machines, and pulley systems. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X Chapter 3 [1] De tractoriis rationibus quae necessaria putavi, breviter exposui. Quorum motus et virtutes duae res diversae et inter se dissimiles ⟨efficiunt⟩, ubi congruentes uti principia pariunt eos perfectus: una porrecti, quam Graeci εὐθεῖαν vocitant, altera rotunditatis, quam Graeci κυκλωτήν appellant. Sed vero neque sine rotunditate motus porrecti nec sine porrecto rotationis versationes onerum possunt facere levationes. [1] I have briefly explained the principles of traction, which I thought necessary. The movements and powers of which are two things, diverse and dissimilar to each other, as well as congruent as principles, give rise to them in perfection: one of extension, which the Greeks call εὐθεῖαν, the other of rotation, which the Greeks call κυκλωτήν. But neither without rotation can extension movements, nor without extension, can rotations of rotation produce lifting of loads. [2] Id autem ut intellegatur, exponam. Inducuntur uti centra axiculi in orbiculos et in trocleis conlocantur, per quos orbiculos funis circumactus directis ductionibus et in sucula conlocatus vectium versationibus onerum facit egressus in altum. Cuius suculae cardines uti centra porrecti in cheloniis, foraminibusque eius vectes conclusi capitibus ad circinum circumactis torni ratione versando faciunt oneris elationes. Quemadmodum etiam ferreus vectis cum est admotus ad onus, quod manuum multitudo non potest movere, supposita uti centro ⟨ultro⟩ citro porrecta pressione, quod Graeci ὑπομόχλιον appellant, et lingua sub onus subdita, caput eius unius hominis viribus pressum id onus extollit. [2] But that this may be understood, I will explain. They are introduced as centripetals into the orbs and placed in pulleys, through which the rope, wound around the orbs by direct conductions and placed in the pulleys, by the turning of the levers, causes the load to rise upwards. The pivots of which pulleys, like centers extended in the shells, and the levers closed in the holes, with their heads turned around to a compass, cause the load to rise by turning in a manner similar to a turning wheel. Just as when an iron bar is brought near to a load, which a multitude of hands cannot move, if a pressure is placed like a centripetal extended pressure, which the Greeks call ὑπομόχλιον, and the tongue is subjected to the load, its head, pressed by the strength of one man, lifts that load. [3] Id autem ⟨eo facilius fit⟩, quo brevior pars prior vectis ab ea pressione, quod est centrum, subit sub onus, et quo longius ab eo centro 853

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X distans caput eius deducitur. Per id faciundo motus circinationis cogit pressionibus examinare paucis manibus oneris maximi pondus. Item si sub onus vectis ferrei lingula subiecta fuerit neque eius caput pressione in imum, sed adversus in altitudinem extolletur, lingula fulta in areae solo habebit eam pro onere, oneris autem ipsius angulum pro pressione. Ita non tam faciliter quam per oppressionem, sed adversus nihilominus pondus oneris erit excitatum. Igitur si plus lingula vectis supra hypomochlion posita sub onus subierit et caput eius propius centrum pressiones habuerit, non poterit onus elevare, nisi, quemadmodum supra scriptum est, examinatio vectis longitudinis per caput neque ⟨in imum⟩ ductionibus fuerit facta. [3] For the shorter the distance from the point of pressure, which serves as the center, to the head of the bar where the load is laid, the more easily the weight is raised; and the farther from that center, the harder. Thus the circular movement about the fulcrum allows the heaviest of loads to be lifted by the pressure of but a few hands. And if an iron bar is set beneath a load and its head, rather than being borne downward, is raised upward against the weight, then the bar, resting upon the ground, will take the load as its burden and the very edge of the load as its fulcrum; in this way, though not so readily as by direct downward pressure, it will nonetheless prevail against the weight. Hence, if the bar laid upon the fulcrum has its head set with the pressure too near the center, it will not raise the load; the purchase must be taken, as was said above, along the length of the bar at its head. [4] Id autem ex trutinis, quae staterae dicuntur, licet considerare. Cum enim ansa propius caput, unde lancula pendet, ibi ut centrum est conlocata et aequipondium in alteram partem scapi, per puncta vagando quo longius paulatim ad extremum perducitur, paulo et inpari pondere amplissimam pensionem parem perficit per scapi librationem, et examinato longius ab centro recedens ista inbecillior. Aequipondii brevitas maiorem vim ponderis momento deducens sine vehementia molliter ab imo susum versum egredi cogit futurum. [4] The same may be observed in the balance that is called a steelyard (statera). When the loop from which the beam hangs is set nearer the head — that point serving as the center — and the counterweight (aequipondium) is moved along the other arm, traveling through the farther points or to the very end, then a 854

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X small and unequal weight balances a great load and holds the beam level; for the counterpoise, as it withdraws further from the center, raises by a gentle pull what at the center would demand a far greater force, drawing the load smoothly upward from below, without violence. [5] Quemadmodum etiam navis onerariae maximae gubernator ansam gubernaculi tenens, qui οἴαξ a Graecis appellatur, una manu momento per centrum ratione pressionibus aptis agitans, versat eam amplissimis et inmanibus mercis et penus ponderibus oneratam. Eiusque vela cum sunt per altitudinem mediam mali pendentia, non potest habere navis celerem cursum, cum autem in summo cacumine antemnae subductae sunt, tunc vehementiore progreditur impetu, quod non proxime calcem mali, quod est loco centri, sed in summo longius et ab eo progressa recipiunt in se vela ventum. [5] Just as the helmsman of a large cargo ship, holding the rudder handle, which the Greeks call oiax, and driving it with one hand at a moment's notice through the center by means of the pressure of the craft, turns it, loaded with the most extensive and enormous cargo and pine weights. And when its sails are suspended along the middle of the mast, the ship cannot have a rapid course, but when the foresails are drawn back at the highest point, then it advances with a more vigorous force, because it does not approach the mast's heel, which is in the place of the center, but at the top, further away, and having advanced from it, the sails receive the wind. [6] Itaque uti vectis sub onere subiectus, si per medium premitur, durior est neque incumbit, cum autem caput eius summum deducitur, faciliter onus extollit, similiter vela, cum sunt per medium temperata, minorem habent virtutem, quae autem in capite mali summo conlocantur discedentia longius a centro, non acriore sed eodem flatu, pressione cacuminis vehementius cogunt progredi navem. Etiam remi circa scalmos strophis religati, cum manibus inpelluntur et reducuntur, extremis progredientibus a centro parmis maris undis spumam inpulsu vehementi protrudunt porrectam navem, secante prora liquoris raritatem. [6] Therefore, like a bar under a load, if it is pressed in the middle, it is stiffer and does not bend, but when its top is lowered, it easily lifts the load. Similarly, sails, when they are adjusted in the middle, have less strength, but those placed at the top of the mast, moving further away from the center, not with a stronger 855

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X blow, but with the same pressure from the top, force the ship forward more strongly. Also, the oars, tied around the oars with ropes, when they are pushed and pulled back by the hands, with their ends advancing from the center, push the foam of the sea waves with a strong thrust, pushing the ship outstretched, cutting the rarefaction of the liquid at the bow. [7] Onerum vero maxima pondera, cum feruntur a phalangariis hexaphoris et tetraphoris, examinantur per ipsa media centra phalangarum, uti diviso oneris solido pondere certa quadam divisionis ratione aequas partes collis singuli ferant operarii. Mediae enim partes phalangarum, quibus lora tetraphororum invehuntur, clavis sunt finitae, ne labantur in unam partem. Cum enim extra finem centri promoventur, premunt eum locum, ad quem propius accesserunt, quemadmodum in statera pondus, cum examine progreditur ad fines ponderationum. [7] But the greatest weights of burdens, when carried by six- and four-legged phalanxes, are examined through the very middle centers of the phalanxes, so that in a solid weight of the burden divided by a certain ratio of division, each worker may bear an equal part of the load. For the middle parts of the phalanxes, by which the straps of the four-legged phalanxes are carried, are ended with nails, and do not slip to one side. For when they are advanced beyond the end of the center, they press on the place to which they have approached nearest, just as a weight in a balance, when examined, advances to the ends of the weights. [8] Eadem ratione iumenta, cum iuga eorum subiugiis loris per medium temperantur, aequaliter trahunt onera. Cum autem inpares sunt eorum virtutes et unum plus valendo premit alterum, loro traiecto fit una pars iugi longior, quae inbecilliori auxiliatur iumento. Ita in phalangis et iugis cum in medio lora non sunt conlocata sed in una parte, qua progreditur lorum ab medio, unam breviorem, <alteram> efficit partem longiorem. Ea ratione si per id centrum, quo loci perductum est lorum, utraque capita circumaguntur, longior pars ampliorem, brevior minorem agit circinationem. [8] In the same way, when their yokes are controlled by the straps under their yokes in the middle, animals pull loads equally. But when their strengths are unequal and one, being stronger, presses the other, when the strap is passed, one part of the yoke becomes longer, which helps the weaker animal. Thus in 856

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X phalanxes and yokes, when the straps are not placed in the middle but on one side, where the strap extends from the middle, it makes one part shorter and the other part longer. In the same way, if both ends are driven around the center to which the strap is brought, the longer part makes a greater, the shorter part a smaller, circle. [9] Quemadmodum vero minores rotae duriores et difficiliores habent motus, sic phalangae et iuga, in quibus partibus habent minora a centro ad capita intervalla, premunt duriter colla, qua autem longiora habent ab eodem centro spatia, levant oneribus et trahentes et ferentes. Cum haec ita ad centrum porrectionibus et circinationibus reciperent motus, tunc vero etiam plostra, raedae, tympana, rotae, cocleae, scorpiones, ballistae, prela ceteraeque machinae eisdem rationibus per porrectum centrum et rotationem circum versantem faciunt ad propositum effectus. [9] Just as smaller wheels have harder and more difficult movements, so phalanxes and yokes, in which parts they have smaller distances from the center to the heads, press hard on the necks, while those which have longer distances from the same center lift both those who are pulling and those who are carrying loads. Since these thus receive motions by extension and rotation of the center, then also carts, chariots, drums, wheels, screws, scorpions, ballistas, presses, and other machines, by the same means, produce the intended effects by means of an extended center and the rotation of the compass. Critical note — X.3. Porrectio or εὐθεῖα and rotunditas or κυκλωτή organize the explanation of levers, windlasses, pulleys, wheels and axles. The supplements ⟨efficiunt⟩ and ⟨eo facilius fit⟩ are marked as editorial. Modern concepts of lever arm and moment can clarify the mechanics in commentary, but must not be introduced as Vitruvius’s own terminology. The crux in the rowing example is not resolved by an unsupported reconstruction. 857

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Chapter 4 [1] Nunc de organis, quae ad hauriendam aquam inventa sunt, quemadmodum variis generibus comparentur, exponam. Et primum dicam de tympano. Id autem non alte tollit aquam, sed exhaurit expeditissime multitudinem magnam. Ad tornum aut circinum fabricatus <axis>, capitibus lamna ferratis, habens in medio circa se tympanum ex tabulis inter se coagmentatis, conlocatur in stipitibus habentibus in se sub capita axis ferreas lamminas. In eius tympani cavo interponuntur octo tabulae transversae tangentes axem et extremam tympani circumitionem, quae dividunt aequalia in tympano spatia. [1] I shall now explain the various kinds of engine devised for drawing water, and how they are severally constructed; and first of the tympanum. This does not raise water to any great height, but it empties out a great quantity with the utmost speed. An axle, turned on the lathe or with the compass and shod with iron at its ends, carries in the middle a drum (tympanum) built up of boards joined together, and rests in blocks that are plated with iron beneath the ends of the axle. Within the hollow of this drum are set eight cross-boards, reaching from the axle to the outer rim and dividing it into equal compartments. [2] Circa frontem eius figuntur tabulae, relictis semipedalibus aperturis ad aquam intra concipiendam Item secundum axem columbaria fiunt excavata in singulis spatiis ex una parte. Id autem cum est navali ratione picatum, hominibus calcantibus versatur et hauriendo per aperturas, quae sunt in frontibus tympani, reddit per columbaria secundum axem supposito labro ligneo habente una secum coniunctum canalem. Ita hortis ad inrigandum vel salinis ad temperandum praebetur aquae multitudo. [2] Boards are fixed around the front, leaving half-foot openings to admit the water. On one side, an outlet resembling a pigeonhole is cut for each compartment next to the axle. The device is waterproofed with pitch like a ship and turned by men treading on it. It draws water through the openings in the face of the drum and discharges it through the outlets by the axle into a wooden trough underneath, fitted with a channel. In this way, large quantities of water are supplied for watering gardens or serving saltworks. Cum autem altius extollendum erit, eadem ratio communicabitur. 858

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X When water must be raised higher, the same principle is adapted. [3] Sic rota fiet circum axem eadem magnitudine, ut ad altitudinem, quae opus fuerit, convenire possit. Circum extremum latus rotae figentur modioli quadrati pice et cera solidati. Ita cum rota a calcantibus versabitur, modioli pleni ad summum elati rursus ad imum revertentes infundent in castellum ipsi per se quod extulerint. [3] The wheel is to be made of a size suited to the height of the lift required. Around its outer rim are fastened small square boxes, made watertight with pitch and wax. Thus, when the wheel is turned by treading, the full boxes, carried to the top, return again to the bottom, pouring of their own accord into the reservoir (castellum) what they have brought up. [4] Sin autem magis altis locis erit praebendum, in eiusdem rotae axe involuta duplex ferrea catena demissaque ad imum libramentum conlocabitur, habens situlos pendentes aereos congiales. Ita versatio rotae catenam in axem involvendo efferet situlos in summum, qui <cum> super axem pervehuntur, cogentur inverti et infundere in castellum aquae quod extulerint. [4] But if water is to be supplied at a greater height, a double iron chain is fitted around the axle of the same wheel and let down to the level of the water, carrying bronze buckets hung upon it. Then the turning of the wheel, winding the chain about the axle, raises the buckets to the top; and as they pass over the axle they are tipped, and pour into the reservoir the water they have drawn up. Critical and hydraulic note — X.4. The supplement ⟨axis⟩ remains visible. Modioli, columbaria, castellum and catena are translated according to their functions in lifting water. The tympanum described here should not be confused with a wheel driven by the current to supply motive power. 859

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Chapter 5 [1] Fiunt etiam in fluminibus rotae eisdem rationibus, quibus supra scriptum est. Circa earum frontes adfiguntur pinnae, quae, cum percutiuntur ab impetu fluminis, cogunt progredientes versari rotam, et ita modiolis haurientes et in summum referentes sine operarum calcatura ipsius fluminis inpulsu versatae praestant, quod opus est ad usum. [1] Wheels are also set up in rivers, on the same principles as those described above. Around their rims are fixed paddles which, struck by the current, drive the wheel round as they are forced along; and so, taking up water in the buckets and carrying it to the top, they accomplish what is required by the river’s own force, without the treading of workmen. [2] Eadem ratione etiam versantur hydraletae, in quibus eadem sunt omnia, praeterquam quod in uno capite axis tympanum dentatum est inclusum. Id autem ad perpendiculum conlocatum in cultrum versatur cum rota pariter. Secundum id tympanum maius ⟨minus⟩ item dentatum planum est conlocatum, quo continetur * * *. Ita dentes tympani eius, quod est in axe inclusum, inpellendo dentes tympani plani cogunt fieri molarum circinationem. In qua machina inpendens infundibulum subministrat molis frumentum et eadem versatione subigitur farina. [2] Water mills, or hydraletae, are turned in the same way. Their construction is similar, except that a toothed drum is fixed to one end of the axle. Set vertically on edge, it turns with the waterwheel. Beside it lies another toothed drum, described as larger, with ⟨smaller⟩ supplied in the printed Latin. [A lacuna follows the clause concerning its support.] The teeth of the drum fixed to the axle drive those of the horizontal drum and cause the millstones to revolve. A hopper suspended above feeds grain to the millstones, and the same rotation grinds it into flour. Editorial note. — This passage (10.5.2) preserves the earliest surviving literary description of a water-powered mill, in which the rotation of an undershot wheel is transmitted, through a pair of toothed drums forming a right-angle gear, to the millstones. Vitruvius’s hydraletae thus record the decisive advance from hand- and animal-driven milling to mechanized, water-driven grinding — a technology that spread widely across the Roman world from the first century AD onward. 860

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X Technical paraphrase. The waterwheel drives a toothed wheel mounted vertically on its axle. That wheel engages a horizontal toothed wheel, transferring rotation through a right angle to the millstones. A hopper feeds the grain. The explanatory gear arrangement should be distinguished from the unresolved wording and missing text marked in the Latin above. Critical note — X.5. The mill passage retains ad perpendiculum conlocatum in cultrum and the supplied ⟨minus⟩ in the gear description. The following lacuna is not filled merely because a mechanically plausible gear train can be reconstructed. The water-driven wheel and hydraletae are distinguished from the lifting devices of the preceding chapter. 861

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Chapter 6 [1] Est autem etiam cocleae ratio, quae magnam vim haurit aquae, sed non tam alte tollit quam rota. Eius autem ratio sic expeditur. Tignum sumitur, cuius tigni quanta paratur pedum longitudo, tanta digitorum expeditur crassitudo. Id ad circinum rotundatur. In capitibus circino dividentur circumitiones eorum tetrantibus et octantibus in partes octo, eaeque lineae ita conlocentur, ut plano posito tigno utriusque capitis ad libellam lineae inter se respondeant, et quam magna pars sit octava circinationis tigni, tam magna spatia decidantur in longitudinem. Item tigno plano conlocato lineae ab capite ad alterum caput perducantur ad libellam convenientes. Sic et in rotundatione et in longitudine aequalia spatia fient. Ita quo loci describuntur lineae, quae sunt in longitudinem spectantes, facient decusationes et in decusationibus finita puncta. [1] There is also the water screw, or coclea, which raises a large volume of water, though not as high as a wheel. Its construction is as follows. Take a timber whose thickness in digits has the same numerical value as its length in feet, and round it to a cylinder. With compasses, divide the circumference at each end into eight equal parts, first quartering and then bisecting the quarters. Lay the timber horizontally so that the corresponding divisions at its two ends are level. Along its length, mark intervals equal to one-eighth of its circumference. Draw longitudinal lines connecting corresponding divisions at the ends. The divisions around the timber and along its length will thus be equal, and the intersecting lines will provide the points required for the construction. [2] His ita emendate descriptis sumitur salignea tenuis aut de vitice secta regula, quae uncta liquida pice figitur in primo decusis puncto. Deinde traicitur oblique ad insequentis longitudinis et circumitionis decusis, item ex ordine progrediens singula puncta praetereundo et circum involvendo conlocatur in singulis decusationibus, et ita pervenit et figitur ad eam lineam recedens a primo in octavum punctum, in qua prima pars est eius fixa. Eo modo quantum progreditur oblique spatium et per octo puncta, tantundem et longitudine procedit ad octavum punctum. Eadem ratione per omne spatium longitudinis et rotunditatis singulis decusationibus oblique fixae regulae per octo crassitudinis divisiones involutos faciunt canales et iustam cocleae naturalemque imitationem. [2] Once the layout has been accurately marked, take a thin strip of willow or cut osier, coat it with liquid pitch and fix it at the first intersection. Carry it 862

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X obliquely to the next intersection along the timber and around its circumference. Continue in sequence from point to point, winding the strip around the timber and fixing it at each crossing, until it returns to the longitudinal line on which it began, at the eighth point. In passing obliquely through eight points around the circumference, it also advances eight divisions along the length. Continue this construction throughout the timber, fixing the strips obliquely at successive intersections. Winding through the eight divisions produces channels that reproduce the natural form of a spiral shell. [3] Ita per id vestigium aliae super alias figuntur unctae pice liquida, et exaggerantur ad id, uti longitudinis octava pars fiat summa crassitudo. Supra eas circumdantur et figuntur tabulae, quae pertegant eam involutionem. Tunc eae tabulae pice saturantur et lamminis ferreis conligantur, ut ab aquae vi ne dissolvantur. Capita tigni ferrea. Dextra autem ac sinistra cocleam tigna conlocantur in capitibus utraque parte habentia transversaria confixa. In his foramina ferrea sunt inclusa inque ea inducuntur styli, et ita cocleae hominibus calcantibus faciunt versationes. [3] Following the same tracks, fix further strips over the first, coating them with liquid pitch and building them up until the total thickness is one-eighth of the length. Enclose the winding construction with boards, saturate these with pitch and bind them with iron bands so that the pressure of the water cannot force them apart. Fit iron ends to the central timber. Place supporting timbers on either side of the screw, with crosspieces fixed at both ends. Iron bearings set into these receive the pivots, allowing the screw to rotate when operated by men treading on it. [4] Erectio autem eius ad inclinationem sic erit conlocanda, uti, quemadmodum Pythagoricum trigonum orthogonium describitur, sic id habeat responsum, id est uti dividatur longitudo in partes V, earum trium extollatur caput cocleae; ita erit ab perpendiculo ad imas naris spatium earum partium IIII. Qua ratione autem oporteat id esse, in extremo libro eius forma descripta est in ipso tempore. [4] Set the screw at the inclination of a Pythagorean right triangle: divide its length into five parts and raise its upper end by three of them. The horizontal distance from the foot of the perpendicular to the lower inlet will then be four parts. The arrangement is illustrated by a figure at the end of this book. 863

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Quae de materia fiunt organa ad hauriendam aquam, quibus rationibus perficiantur quibusque rebus motus recipientia praestent versationibus infinitas utilitates ut essent notiora, quam apertissime potui, perscripta sunt in illo tempore. I have described as clearly as I can how wooden devices for drawing water are made, how their construction is completed, and how the motion they receive enables their rotations to provide many useful services, so that these matters may be better understood. Technical paraphrase. The preceding devices convert human or water-driven movement into the rotation needed to lift water. Their materials, assembly and means of transmitting motion belong to the same constructional explanation. Critical and geometrical note — X.6. The coclea is a helical water-lifting machine. The timber’s dimensions, eightfold divisions, helical construction and final inclination derived from the 3–4–5 triangle are interdependent instructions. A reconstruction should identify its assumptions and the status of the missing or altered figure instead of claiming that successful operation independently proves a particular Latin reading. 864

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X Chapter 7 [1] Insequitur nunc de Ctesibica machina, quae in altitudinem aquam educit, monstrare. Ea fit ex aere. Cuius in radicibus modioli fiunt gemelli paulum distantes, habentes fistulas furcillae figura similiter cohaerentes, in medium catinum concurrentes. In quo catino fiunt asses in superioribus naribus fistularum coagmentatione subtili conlocati, qui praeobturantes foramina narium non patiuntur ⟨redire⟩ quod spiritu in catinum est expressum. [1] There follows the machine of Ctesibius, which raises water to a height. It is made of bronze. At its base are two cylinders (modioli) set a little apart, with pipes joined in the shape of a fork and meeting at a central vessel. In this vessel are fitted valves (asses), carefully placed over the upper mouths of the pipes, which by stopping those openings keep back what has been driven into the vessel under pressure.166 Editorial note. — The machine here described (X.7) is the force pump of Ctesibius of Alexandria (fl. third century BC): a twin-cylinder bronze pump fitted with valves, in which pistons driven alternately force water under pressure through a central chamber. It is the earliest detailed account of a reciprocating force pump, and the principle it embodies — valved cylinders raising a fluid by pressure — underlies hydraulic and fire-fighting pumps to the present day. [2] Supra catinum paenula ut infundibulum inversum est attemperata et per fibulam cum catino cuneo traiecto continetur, ne vis inflationis aquae eam cogat elevari. Insuper fistula, quae tuba dicitur, coagmentata in altitudine fit erecta. Modioli autem habent infra nares inferiores fistularum asses interpositos supra foramina eorum, quae sunt in fundis. [2] A cover shaped like an inverted funnel is fitted above the central vessel and secured to it by a fastening with a wedge driven through, so that the pressure of the water cannot lift it. A pipe called the tuba is joined above it and rises vertically. The cylinders also have valves above the holes in their bottoms, beneath the lower mouths of the pipes. 166The pump of Ctesibius described by Vitruvius (10.7) uses two bronze cylinders, pipes, valves and pistons operated by rods and levers to force water into a central vessel and an ascending pipe. This explanation follows the Vitruvian description; comparisons with later pumps belong to the history of technology rather than to the ancient text. 865

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X [3] Ita de supernis in modiolis emboli masculi torno politi et oleo subacti conclusique regulis et vectibus cum molientur. Qui erit aer ibi cum aqua, assibus obturantibus foramina cogent. et trudent inflando pressionibus per fistularum nares aquam in catinum, e quo recipiens paenula spiritu exprimit per fistulam in altitudinem, et ita ex inferiore loco castello conlocato ad saliendum aqua subministratur. [3] Pistons, accurately turned on a lathe and lubricated with oil, are inserted into the cylinders from above and operated by rods and levers. As the valves close the openings, the pistons compress the air and water within the cylinders and drive the water under pressure through the mouths of the pipes into the central vessel. The cover receives it and forces it upward through the delivery pipe. In this way, water can be supplied from a reservoir at a lower level to form a fountain jet. 4. Nec tamen haec sola ratio Ctesibii fertur exquisita, sed etiam plures et variis generibus ab eo liquore pressionibus coactae spiritus efferre ab natura mutuatos effectus ostenduntur, uti merularum [quae motu] voces atque acrobatae bibentiaque et eadem moventia ⟨se⟩ sigilla ceteraque, quae delectationibus oculorum et aurium usu sensus eblandiantur. [4] This is not the only device attributed to Ctesibius. Many other inventions of different kinds are said to use air compressed by water to reproduce effects found in nature: the songs of blackbirds, acrobatic figures, little figures that drink and move, and other devices that delight the senses through the pleasures of sight and hearing. [5] E quibus quae maxime utilia et necessaria iudicavi selegi, et in priore volumine de horologiis, in hoc de expressionibus aquae dicendum putavi. Reliqua quae non sunt ad necessitatem sed ad deliciarum voluptatem, qui cupidiores erunt eius subtilitatis, ex ipsius Ctesibii commentariis poterunt invenire. [5] From these inventions I have selected those I judged most useful and necessary. In the preceding book I discussed clocks; in this one, devices for forcing water upward. Readers interested in the ingenious details of inventions made for amusement rather than necessity may consult Ctesibius’s own writings. Critical note — X.7. The supplement ⟨redire⟩ makes the valves’ prevention of reverse flow explicit. Modioli, fistulae, catinum, asses, nares, emboli, paenula 866

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X and tuba remain controlled mechanical terms. The bracketed quae motu and supplied ⟨se⟩ in moventia ⟨se⟩ sigilla retain their critical status. The alternating action of two cylinders, valves and pistons is explained without equating every component with a modern pump. 867

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X Chapter 8 [1] De hydraulis autem, quas habeant ratiocinationes, quam brevissime proximeque attingere potero et scriptura consequi, non praetermittam. De materia compacta basi, ara in ea ex aere fabricata conlocatur. Supra basim eriguntur regulae dextra ac sinistra scalari forma compactae, quibus includuntur aerei modioli, fundulis ambulatilibus ex torno subtiliter subactis habentibus fixos in medio ferreos ancones et verticulis cum vectibus coniunctos, pellibusque lanatis involutis. Item in summa planitia foramina circiter digitorum ternûm. Quibus foraminibus proxime in verticulis conlocati aerei delphini pendentia habent catenis cymbala ex ore infra foramina modiolorum calata. [1] I shall also explain the principles of water organs as briefly and precisely as a written account allows. An altar-shaped bronze casing is set on a base of joined timber. On either side, ladder-like upright frames hold bronze pump cylinders. Their movable bottoms are accurately turned, wrapped in fleeced skins and fitted at the center with iron elbow pieces jointed to operating levers. In the top surfaces are openings about three digits across. Beside them, bronze dolphins mounted on pivots carry chains in their mouths; cymbal-shaped valves hang from the chains beneath the cylinder openings. [2] Intra aram, quo loci aqua sustinetur, inest pnigeus uti infundibulum inversum, quem subter taxilli alti circiter digitorum ternûm suppositi librant spatium imum ima inter labra pnigeos et arae fundum. supra autem cerviculam eius coagmentata arcula sustinet caput machinae, qui graece κανὼν μουσικός appellatur. In cuius longitudine canales, si tetrachordos est, fiunt quattuor, si hexachordos, sex, si octo chordos, octo. [2] Inside the altar-shaped casing, where the water is held, is a pnigeus shaped like an inverted funnel. Blocks about three digits high support it from below, leaving that clearance between its lower rim and the floor of the casing. Above its neck, a fitted windchest supports the head of the instrument, called the canon musicus (κανὼν μουσικός) in Greek. Along its length there are four channels if the instrument is tetrachord, six if hexachord, and eight if octochord. [3] Singulis autem canalibus singula epitonia sunt inclusa, manubriis ferreis conligata. Quae manubria, cum torquentur, ex arca patefaciunt nares in canales. Ex canalibus autem canon habet ordinata in transverso foramina respondentia 868

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X naribus, quae sunt in tabula summa, quae tabula graece πίναξ dicitur. Inter tabulam et canona regulae sunt interpositae ad eundem modum foratae et oleo subactae, ut faciliter inpellantur et rursus introrsus reducantur, quae obturant ea foramina plinthidesque appellantur. Quarum itus et reditus alias obturat alias aperit terebrationes. [3] A separate stopcock, or epitonion, is fitted into each channel and connected to an iron handle. Turning the handles opens passages from the windchest into the channels. The canon has transverse rows of holes corresponding to the openings in the upper board, called the pinax (πίναξ). Between the board and the canon lie sliders, similarly pierced and lubricated with oil so that they can move easily inward and outward. These sliders, called plinthides, close or open the holes as they advance and return. 4. Haec regulae habent ferrea choragia fixa et iuncta cum pinnis, quarum pinnarum tactus motiones efficit regularum continenter. Supra tabulam foramina ⟨que, per⟩ quae ex canalibus habent egressum spiritus, sunt anuli adglutinati, quibus lingulae omnium includuntur organorum. E modiolis autem fistulae sunt continentes coniunctae pnigeos cervicibus pertinentesque ad nares, quae sunt in arcula. In quibus asses sunt ex torno subacti et ibi conlocati, ⟨ubi fistulae modiolis sunt coniunctae,⟩ qui, cum recepit arcula animam, spiritum non patientur obturantes foramina rursus redire. [4] Iron linkages fixed to the sliders connect them to the keys; touching the keys moves the sliders in succession. Rings are attached above the openings in the upper board through which air emerges from the channels, and receive the tongues of the organ pipes. Connecting pipes run from the cylinders to the neck of the pnigeus and the openings in the windchest. Turned valves are fitted ⟨where the pipes join the cylinders⟩; once the windchest has received air, these valves close the openings and prevent it from flowing back. [5] Ita cum vectes extolluntur, ancones deducunt fundos modiolorum ad imum delphinique, qui sunt in verticulis inclusi, calantes in eos cymbala, aere implent spatia modiolorum, atque ancones extollentes fundos intra modiolos vehementi pulsus crebritate et obturantes foramina cymbalis superiora, aera, qui est ibi inclusus, pressionibus coactum in fistulas cogunt, per quas in pnigea concurrit et 869

M. VITRVVIVS POLLIO · DE ARCHITECTVRA · LIBER X per eius cervices in arcam. Motione vero vectium vehementiore spiritus frequens compressus epitoniorum aperturis influit et replet animae canales. [5] When the levers are raised, the elbow pieces draw the cylinder bottoms downward. The pivoted dolphins lower their cymbal-shaped valves, allowing the cylinders to fill with air. The elbow pieces then drive the bottoms upward with repeated strong strokes. As the valves close the upper openings, the air trapped in the cylinders is compressed and forced through the pipes into the pnigeus and through its neck into the windchest. More vigorous movement of the levers increases the compressed air supply, which passes through the open stopcocks and fills the channels. [6] Itaque cum pinnae manibus tactae propellunt et reducunt continenter regulas alternis obturando foramina alternis aperiundo, e musicis artibus multiplicibus modulorum varietatibus sonantes excitant voces. [6] And so, when the keys (pinnae), pressed by the player’s hands, push the sliders forward and draw them back, by turns closing and opening the holes, they draw from the pipes a rich variety of musical sound, resounding in many melodies. Editorial note. — The instrument of X.8 is the water organ (Greek hydraulis), invented by Ctesibius of Alexandria: a set of graduated bronze pipes sounded by air whose pressure is regulated by a water-filled chamber, and played from a row of balanced keys. It is the earliest keyboard instrument and the direct ancestor of the pipe organ. Technical paraphrase. Pressing a key moves a pierced slider, aligning or closing an air passage beneath the musical pipes. The keys control the sliders; they do not push and pull the pipes themselves. Hegetor's tortoise is described with one of the most unstable sets of numerals in Book X. Against a textual tradition giving a base of LX × XIII feet and a ram of CIV feet, the critical constitution adopted in the author's Spanish edition reads LXIII × XLII and CLXXX, respectively, and also restores ⟨bi⟩pedali for the thickness of the lower part of the ram. The fractional measures of the wheels, posts and ramhead remain damaged or disputed. Accordingly, this edition marks uncertain readings and does not reconstruct missing dimensions merely by proportional inference. NOTE ON HISTORICAL ENGINEERING — X.15. The importance of this passage lies less in the possibility of reconstructing one machine to millimetric accuracy than in its structural logic: a mobile base capable of movement in several directions, layered protection against missiles and fire, a platform for artillery, a suspended battering ram, and control over the approach to the wall. The unstable numerals demonstrate why the description must be read as a transmitted technical document rather than as a modern set of working drawings. COMPARATIVE CRITICAL APPARATUS — X.15. In accounts of the machines built by Hegetor and other engineers, proper names, dimensions, and relationships between structural members are textual-critical risk points. 167Krohn (1912), p. 257, prints CCCCLXXX with a bar, followed by pondo. The bar marks thousands: the expanded figure is 480,000 Roman pounds. The unbarred or truncated digital transcription must not be read as 400 or 480 pounds. 897

He ordered everyone, acting publicly and privately, to pour whatever water, manure and mud they had through the opening and along projecting channels in front of the wall. Diognetus brought that helepolis back into the city, set it up in the public square, and inscribed upon it: “Diognetus gave this gift to the people from the spoils of war.” Thus in matters of defense it is not engines so much as the ingenuity to outwit engines that must be made ready. Editorial note. — The siege of Rhodes by Demetrius Poliorcetes (305–304 BCE) and the helepolis of Epimachus were famous in antiquity. Vitruvius ends the entire treatise not with a machine but with a lesson: Diognetus saves the city not by greater force but by guile, miring the great tower in flooded ground. The closing maxim — that defense depends less on engines than on the architect’s ingenuity — is the fitting envoi of a work that throughout subordinates technique to judgment. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY · LIBER X controlling the English interpretation. Reported variants and conjectural supplements remain distinct from direct manuscript evidence. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY ARGUMENTUM LIBRI X — VITRUVIUS DEFINES THE MACHINE AND DISTINGUISHES IT FROM THE INSTRUMENT, THEN EXAMINES HOISTING DEVICES AND THEIR TACKLE, WATER-RAISING MECHANISMS, THE WATER- SCREW, CTESIBIUS’S PUMP, THE HYDRAULIC ORGAN, AND THE ODOMETER. HE PROCEEDS TO CATAPULTS, BALLISTAE, AND SIEGE ENGINES, INCLUDING RAMS AND TORTOISES, AND CONCLUDES WITH METHODS OF DEFENSE. Notice. — Book X treats machines. It distinguishes machina from organon, then describes hoisting engines and their tackle, water-raising devices (the bucket-wheel, the Archimedean screw, the water-organ and the water-mill), the odometer, and finally the engines of war — catapults and ballistae, the tortoise and siege-towers — closing with stratagems of defense. It is the fullest ancient account of classical mechanical and military technology. M. APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER APPENDIX A GLOSSARY OF VITRUVIAN TECHNICAL TERMS This glossary brings together the principal technical terms used by Vitruvius in his De architectura, with their Latin form, the Greek spelling where appropriate, and their academic definition. In each case, the relevant passage in the treatise where the term is defined or appears with greater precision is indicated. ARCHITECTURE. The discipline that arises from the union between fabrica (constructive practice) and ratiocinatio (theoretical reasoning). Vitruvius defines it in De architectura 1.1.1: “Architecture is a science furnished with many disciplines and diverse fields of knowledge branches of learning.” Its implicit Greek equivalent is ἀρχιτεκτονική (architektoniké). CUBE [ κύβος ]. The cube, a geometrical figure of six equal square faces. Vitruvius employs it in the preface to Book V to explain the Pythagorean cubic ratio: The number 216 (= 6 ³) was the conventional measure of a writing volume. « A cube is a body with sides of equal width on flat surfaces » (De architectura 5.praef.3). CYBICIS RATIONIBUS. « Cubic ratios ». Pythagorean expression that designates the organization of knowledge in volumes of 216 verses (= 6 ³). Cf. De architectura 5.praef.3; Krohn (1912), 100. DECOR. The suitability or correctness of the appearance of a work, obtained through the appropriate application of the principles of use, custom, and nature. “Decor autem est emendatus operis aspectus probatis rebus compositi cum auctoritate” (De architectura 1.2.5). It should not be confused with “decoration” in the modern ornamental sense. DISPOSITIO [ διάθεσις ]. Layout or conception of the plan, elevation and perspective of a building. It involves the three forms of representation: ichnographia (plan), orthographia (elevation) and scaenographia (perspective). Cf. De architectura 1.2.1 – 2. DISTRIBUTIO [ οἰκονομία ]. The administration Suitable materials and terrain, with economic balance. Includes adapting the design to the owner's status and use. Cf. De architectura 1.2.8 – 9. 911

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY ECHEA [ ἠχεῖα, sing. ἠχεῖον ]. Bronze vessels (vasaenea) tuned according to musical intervals, placed in niches under the tiers of theaters to amplify and clarify the voices of the actors. They constitute the foundation of Vitruvian acoustic architecture. Cf. De architectura 1.1.9 and 5.5.1 – 8. ENCYCLIOS DISCIPLINA. Encyclopedic education. The comprehensive training program that Vitruvius requires of the architect: writing, drawing, geometry, arithmetic, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law, and astronomy. Cf. De architectura 1.1.12. EURYTHMIA [ εὐρυθμία ]. The graceful and proportionate appearance in the composition of the members of a work. It results from the correct application of symmetry. « Eurythmia est venusta species commodusque in compositionibus membrorum aspectus » (De architectura 1.2.3). FABRICA. The constructive practice: " continuous and practised experience of construction, by which the intended work is executed by hand." Together with ratiocinatio, it constitutes the origin of architectura. Cf. De architectura 1.1.1. FIRMITAS. Structural solidity. The first condition of all architectural work, achieved "when the foundations are carried down to firm ground and when the choice of materials is made without avarice. " Cf. De architectura 1.3.2. GNOMONICS [ γνωμονική ]. The art of measuring time using the gnomon (sundial) and other instruments. Vitruvius dedicates Book IX to it. The gnomon is the rod whose shadow indicates the time. ICHNOGRAPHY [ ἰχνογραφία ]. Horizontal plan or projection of a building, plotted with ruler and compass. One of the three forms of architectural representation described by Vitruvius. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2. ORDINATIO [ τάξις ]. The ordering or modular arrangement of the members of a work, taking as a reference a unit of measurement (m o dule). “Ordinatio is t he balanced adjustment of the members of a work taken separately, and of the whole with regard to proportion” (De architectura 1.2.2). ORTHOGRAPHY [ ὀρθογραφία ]. Elevation or vertical representation of the façade of a building, at the correct scale. Second of the three forms of Vitruvian representation. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2. 912

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER RATA PARS. The " determined part " or reference module from which the proportions of a work are established. In temples, the module is the semi - diameter of the column. Cf. De architectura 1.2.4. RATIOCINATIO. Theoretical reasoning applied to construction: " that which can show and explain through skill, method and proportion the works carried out. " Cf. De architectura 1.1.1. SCAENOGRAPHIA [ σκηνογραφία ]. Perspective or foreshortened representation of facades and lateral parts of a building. Third form of Vitruvian representation. Cf. De architectura 1.2.2. SCAMILLI IMPARES. The “irregular wedges” or curvilinear corrections of the stylobate of temples, intended to compensate for the optical illusion of sinking on long horizontal surfaces. Cf. De architectura 3.4.5 and Rowland and Howe (1999), 51. SYMMETRIA [ συμμετρία ]. The proportional correspondence between the members of a work and the whole, taken from a rata pars (reference part). « Symmetria est ex ipsius operis membris conveniens consensus » (De architectura 1.2.4). It differs from the modern meaning of « bilateral symmetry ». UTILITAS. Functional utility. The second Vitruvian condition: the arrangement of spaces must be irreproachable and present no obstacles to use. Cf. De architectura 1.3.2. VENUSTAS. Elegance or beauty of appearance. The third Vitruvian condition, achieved when " the appearance of the work is pleasing and in good taste, and when the proportions of the members are calculated according to the principles of symmetry. " Cf. De architectura 1.3.2. The term derives from Venus (goddess of beauty) and connotes proportional grace, not mere ornamentation. ABACUS [ἄβαξ]. The abacus: a square slab that crowns the capital and receives the architrave. Its proportion varies according to the order. ASTRAGALUS [Astragalus]. Small convex molding of semicircular section (also tondino), used at the transition between fuste and capitel. 913

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY COLUMN. The vertical support composed of a base (except in the Vitruvian Doric), shaft (scapus) and capital (capitulum). Its height/diameter ratio defines the order. CORINTHIUS (ordo). The Corinthian order, the most slender and ornate, characterized by the acanthus leaf capital; Vitruvius recounts its invention by Callimachus (4.1). DIASTICLES [διάστυλος]. Wide intercolumniation, of three diameters between columns (3.3). DORICUS (ordo). The Doric order, the most robust, based on its Vitruvian form, with a frieze of triglyphs and metopes (4.3). ENTASIS [ἔντασις]. The slight bulging or convex tension of the column shaft, intended to correct the optical illusion of concavity (3.3.13). EUSTYLOS [εὔστυλος]. The optimal intercolumniation according to Vitruvius, of two and a quarter diameters, which reconciles beauty and solidity (3.3.6). IONICUS (ordo). The Ionic order, intermediate in slenderness, recognizable by the volutes of the capital; Vitruvius dedicates the core of Book III to it. MODULUS. The module: unit of measurement (in Vitruvius, generally the radius or lower diameter of the column) with which the entire building is dimensioned by symmetria. MUTULUS. The mutule: projecting block under the Doric cornice, vestige of the beam heads; it bears the guttae. PERIPTERAL [περίπτερος]. Temple surrounded by a single row of freestanding columns on its four sides (3.2). PYCNOSTYLOS [πυκνόστυλος]. Narrow intercolumniation, one and a half diameters between columns (3.3). PRONAOS [πρόναος]. The portico or front vestibule of the temple, in front of the cella. STYLOBATA [στυλοβάτης]. The stylobate: upper platform or step on which the columns rest; object of the optical correction of odd scamilli. 914

TRIGLYPHUS [τρίγλυφος]. The triglyph: element of the Doric frieze with two full and two half channels, alternating with the metopes. TUSCANICUS (ordo). THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Vitruvius Today The Continuing Life of a Canon De architectura remains an active point of reference in architectural culture. Its contemporary value lies in the questions it brings together: how a building stands, how it serves its users, how its parts form an intelligible whole, and how the architect acquires the knowledge needed to judge these relationships. Three lines of reception connect that ancient inquiry with present practice. The triad of firmitas, utilitas and venustas continues to offer a concise framework for discussing durability, use and beauty. In the twentieth century, Le Corbusier’s Modulor developed a modern system of measure around the human body. It can be studied as a reinterpretation of the anthropometric tradition, while its aims and proportional rules remain distinct from those of Vitruvius. Symmetria, understood as the commensurability of the parts and the whole through a module, also invites comparison with design governed by relationships and rules. Parametric modeling makes such relationships explicit; Building Information Modeling coordinates information about design, construction and maintenance. These are contemporary analogies proposed by the author. They do not establish a direct technical descent from the ancient treatise. The discussions of site, orientation, healthy air, materials and water in Books I, VI and VIII likewise remain useful interlocutors for environmental design. Ancient explanations must be assessed within their own scientific and social setting. Reading firmitas today as durability and responsible use of resources extends the historical concept to a modern ethical concern; it does not attribute a present-day environmental agenda to Vitruvius. His continuing relevance is therefore best tested through informed comparison. The architect can learn from the relation between practical experience and reasoned explanation while examining the limits of both the ancient evidence and its later interpretations. That critical dialogue preserves the vitality of the canon without turning it into a timeless rulebook. 928

While the figure of Janus was fundamental in the most archaic stratum of Italic and Etruscan religion, the existence of a secret name (nomen sacrum) is a common hypothesis in the study of mystery religions, although difficult to validate through official epigraphy. 169Janus (Latin Ianus) is the Roman god of passages, doors and beginnings, represented with two faces. The month Ianuarius, from which English January and Spanish enero derive, was dedicated to him.
