This edition stems from an extended study of the symbols, archetypes, and technical traditions linked to architecture and the art of building in classical antiquity. Through the figure of Marcus Vitruvius Pollio and his treatise De architectura, an attempt has been made to offer a comprehensive approach that combines historical and philological analysis with a hermeneutical reading of the symbolic dimensions present in the Greco -Roman architectural tradition. Vitruvius is not only the only architectural theorist whose complete works have survived from antiquity, but he also embodies a comprehensive conception of technical knowledge in which *fabricatio* and *ratiocinatio * — practice and theoretical reflection — are inextricably linked. His treatise, structured in ten books, constitutes a true encyclopedic corpus that reflects both the technical knowledge of his time and a vision of the architect as an intellectual versed in the liberal arts. The influence of De architectura far transcends its value as a construction manual. Its rediscovery and dissemination from the 15th century onwards decisively contributed to shaping the architectural thought of the Renaissance and the Modern Age. From Leon Battista Alberti to Andrea Palladio and Le Corbusier, by way of Leonardo da Vinci, the Vitruvian tradition has served as a guiding thread linking Antiquity with modernity. I arranged its distribution so that whoever is looking for a specific topic does not have to search for it in different parts, but rather has in each of the volumes a complete explanation of the different styles or genres, all in a single set. Vitruvius mentions that in Greece the number six was considered the emblem of physical nature and the generator of the cosmos. In this chapter, he recovers the Chaldean tradition which, since antiquity, attributed to the number six the representation of creation, considering it a perfect number. The Chaldeans classified their deities according to the number six, assigning the number 6 to minor gods and to wise men or teachers. The principal god, Anu, was represented by the number 60. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY 1. Commensurability as a governing principle Vitruvius relates the proportional organization of a temple to that of a wellformed human body. The analogy concerns the commensurable relation of parts to the whole, rather than bilateral symmetry alone. He gives the following ratios: • The face: The face, from the chin to the top of the forehead (where the hair grows), should measure one - tenth of the man's total height. • The hand: The length of the hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, is also equal to one - tenth of the total height. • The head: From the chin to the crown, it represents one-eighth of the total height. • The upper chest: The distance from the upper chest to the hairline is one-sixth of the body’s height; the distance from the upper chest to the crown is one-quarter. 2. The circle and the square Vitruvius postulates that the human body has two inscribed geometric forms that demonstrate its proportional perfection: • The square: If a man stands with his arms extended horizontally, the distance between his fingertips (his wingspan) is equal to his total height. Thus, inscribing the body in a square results in a figure with equal sides. • The circle: If a man lies on his back with his legs and arms outstretched, his navel is the center point of his body. If a circle is drawn by placing a compass on his navel, the circumference will touch the tips of his fingers and toes. 3. The body as a unit of measurement (The module) Vitruvius insists that the measurements of the human body should be the basis for establishing "modules" in architecture: • The foot: It is equivalent to one sixth of the total height of a man. • The cubit (distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger): Represents one-quarter of the height. 4. XXXVI.54–56: the working of the marble quarries of Luna (Carrara) under Augustus. Cicero De officiis I.150–151: the moral censure of the mechanical arts and manual trades held unworthy of the senatorial citizen — the background to Vitruvius’s effort to dignify his profession. APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER APPENDIX I Testimonia veterum (Ancient Testimonies about Vitruvius) Antiquity and the early Middle Ages that mention Vitruvius or use his work are gathered. They constitute the documentary basis for reconstructing his biography and the fortune of De architectura, and explain why the treatise, far from being completely forgotten, enjoyed continuous transmission. Pliny the Elder, Natural History, indexes of books XVI and XXXV. He includes Vitruvius among the sources (auctores) he uses for the chapters on materials and pigments; it is the oldest testimony of the use of the work, barely one or two generations after its composition. Frontinus, De aquaeductu urbis Romae. The curator aquarum of Rome (c. 97 CE) agrees with Vitruvius in the measurements of the pipes (fistulae) and in the hydraulic doctrine, which proves the technical circulation of the treatise in the field of public administration. Faventino, De diversis fabricis architectonicae. Compendium from the 3rd-4th century AD that summarizes and transmits large portions of Vitruvius; It is the main late antique link in the tradition. Palladius, Opus agriculturae. He collects, through Faventinus, Vitruvian prescriptions on rural construction, disseminating them in medieval agronomic literature. Servius, Commentarii in Vergilii Aeneidem. The grammarian quotes Vitruvius on matters of architecture and religion, a sign of his authority in late antique teaching. Sidonius Apollinaris, Epistulae IV.3. He mentions Vitruvius as a model of technical knowledge, proof of his prestige in 5th century Gaul. Cassiodorus, Variae VII.5; Institutiones. He recommends the reading of Vitruvius to the officials in charge of the public works of the Ostrogothic kingdom (6th century), guaranteeing its survival. Einhard, Epistulae. Charlemagne's biographer uses Vitruvian vocabulary and concepts, reflecting the circulation of the text in the Carolingian Renaissance that produced the Codex Harleianus. 973

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix K · Apparatus fontium: Vitruvius’ Greek sources Vitruvius states in the preface to Book VII (7.praef.11-14) that his treatise is based on the works of the Greek architects and theorists who preceded him, most of whose works are now lost. This appendix lists, book by book, the principal Hellenic sources that scholars recognize as underlying Vitruvian doctrine, distinguishing those Vitruvius himself names from those inferred from the content. Unless otherwise indicated, the attributions follow Gros (Budé) and Rowland-Howe. Book I — Principles and training of the architect The doctrine of principles (ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, distributio) and the encyclopedic ideal of the architect reflect Hellenistic architectural theory and Greek paideia. Vitruvius cites Pytheos of Priene as an authority on the architect's comprehensive training (1.1.12). The philosophical background refers to the Pythagorean tradition and the pre-Socratic physiologoi (Thales, Democritus), invoked in the proems. Book II — Materials and Origins of Construction The history of the origin of architecture and the primitive hut is linked to Greek evolutionary theories (Democritus, Epicurus, and the Peripatetic tradition). For the doctrine of the elements and matter, Vitruvius follows Thales, Heraclitus, Democritus, and the Greek physics that he himself summarizes (2.2). Books III-IV — Temples and the Orders This is the most densely Greek core of the work. Vitruvius relies primarily on Hermogenes of Alabanda (2nd century BC), architect of the pseudodipteral temple of Artemis at Magnesia on the Meander and the monopteral temple of Dionysus at Teos, from whom he takes the rules of the Ionic order, the eustyle, and the critique of the dipteral (3.2-3.3; 4.3). Also contributing are Pytheos, author of the temple of Athena at Priene and, with Satyrus, of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus; Arcesius, on Corinthian proportions; and the archaic writers whom Vitruvius 979

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY himself lists in 7.praef.12 (Silenus, Theodorus, Chersiphron and Metagenes, Ictinus and Carpio, Philo of Athens). Book V — Public Buildings, Theater and Acoustics For the theory of the acoustic vessels of the theater (echea) and the harmonic arrangement of the seating, Vitruvius adapts the Greek musical theory of Aristoxenus of Tarentum (5.4-5.5), whose doctrine of tetrachords he explicitly summarizes. The design of the Greek theater compared to the Latin one (5.7) derives directly from Hellenic models. Book VI — Private Buildings and Climate The theory of the suitability of housing to latitudes and climates (6.1) is based on Greek ethnography and scientific geography, particularly on the Hippocratic tradition (On Airs, Waters and Places) and on Posidonius. Book VII — Finishes, stucco and painting His preface is the main source for reconstructing Vitruvius's library: it lists the Greek authors on proportions and machines. For stage perspective (scaenographia) he cites the works of Agatharchus of Samos and the commentaries of Democritus and Anaxagoras on optics (7.praef.11). Book VIII — Water The doctrine on the search, properties and conduction of water follows the Greek authors of natural sciences; Vitruvius invokes Thales (water as a principle) and gathers material from the Peripatetic and Hippocratic tradition on the qualities of waters (8.3). Book IX — Gnomonics and Astronomy The most dependent on Greek scientific sources. Vitruvius follows Berossus the Chaldean (who introduced astrology to Greece), Aristarchus of Samos (to whom he attributes the sundial and heliocentrism), Eudoxus of Cnidus, Eratosthenes (measurement of the meridian), and Archimedes (9.praef.; 9.1-9.8). The anecdote about the crown comes from the tradition surrounding Archimedes. 980

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Book X — Machines Vitruvian mechanics rests on the Alexandrian school. For pumps, the hydraulic organ, and the water-lifting machine, Vitruvius follows Ctesibius of Alexandria (10.7-10.8); for artillery and catapults, Philo of Byzantium and Ctesibius; for the lifting screw, Archimedes (10.6); and for siege engines, Diades (Alexander's engineer), Agesistratus, and the Hellenistic siegecraft tradition (10.13-10.16). Note. The works of these authors have been almost entirely lost; they are known primarily through Vitruvius himself, Pliny the Elder (Natural History), and the surviving Greek mechanical treatises (Heron of Alexandria, Philo). This appendix does not aim to be exhaustive, but rather to guide the reader towards the profound Hellenic roots of De architectura. 981

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Appendix L · Critical editions of Vitruvius: overview and assessment The editions and translations that form the basis of the study of Vitruvius today are listed here in chronological order, along with a brief assessment of their usefulness. This list expands upon and formalizes what was presented in the Preliminary Note. Valentin Rose (Teubner, 1867; 2nd ed. 1899) An important modern critical edition of the Latin text, without a facing translation. Rose’s recension and apparatus remain valuable for comparison. In the present edition, Krohn (1912) is the declared reference text; a quotation following a different reading requires an explanation at its locus. Fritz Krohn (Teubner, 1912) Krohn’s critical edition is the declared reference text of this reading edition. It gives substantial weight to H while distinguishing the four principal witnesses H, S, E and G. Its constitution and apparatus should be compared with Rose and the relevant Budé volume at disputed passages, rather than reduced to a mechanical rule of following the oldest witness. APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix M · Stemma Codicum and the Manuscript Transmission This appendix sets out the genealogy of the surviving manuscripts of the De architectura, traces the principal stages of its transmission from Antiquity to the editio princeps, and explains the reasoning — the recensio — by which the two main branches of the tradition are reconstructed. The classification rests not on any single isolated error but on shared conjunctive errors (errores coniunctivi): when two or more codices preserve the same improbable corruption, a common ancestor may be inferred. 1. Chronology of the transmission (1st c. BC – 15th c. AD) c. 27–23 BCE — Composition. Marcus Vitruvius Pollio composes the ten books of the De architectura under Augustus, to whom the work is dedicated. It is the only complete treatise on architecture to survive from classical Antiquity. 1st–3rd c. CE — Ancient circulation. The work was transmitted through successive copies; the author’s autograph has not survived. The surviving witnesses do not establish when it was lost. Late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages — The text passed through copies that are now lost. Shared lacunae and textual disturbances allow editors to infer a common exemplar behind the surviving witnesses; neither its physical form nor an exact date is established by that inference alone. 6th–8th c. — The dark age of transmission. Documentation is extremely scarce. The survival of the De architectura through these centuries is one of the most remarkable episodes in the preservation of Roman literature. 9th c. — Carolingian Renaissance. Under Carolingian patronage, many ancient works were copied afresh. Harley MS 2767 (H) is an important early witness to De architectura. Its age and textual value do not establish that every surviving manuscript descends from it. Krohn distinguishes the H–S grouping from the Gudianus witnesses E and G; their relationships must be assessed through shared readings, corrections and losses. 10th–13th c. — Monastic and scholastic preservation. The work circulates in monastic libraries and cathedral schools. New copies appear; errors of 985

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY transcription, omissions and interpolations multiply, and some witnesses show contamination through the collation of different exemplars. 14th–15th c. — Humanist rediscovery. Italian scholars revive their interest in the technical literature of Antiquity; Poggio Bracciolini and others recover and diffuse dispersed manuscripts. Vitruvius becomes essential reading for Alberti, Francesco di Giorgio Martini and Leonardo da Vinci. Humanistic copies circulate widely. 1486 — Editio princeps. The first printed edition of the De architectura, published in Rome by Fra Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli, marks the passage from manuscript to print and opens the modern editorial tradition. 2. General scheme of the transmission The surviving witnesses are commonly referred to a lost archetype, but the relationships between their branches must be stated according to a named critical edition. Krohn’s preface (1912, VIII) distinguishes H and S from E and G. The age and authority of H do not justify treating every other witness as its direct descendant. Lost common exemplar (Ω): inferred from shared lacunae and textual disturbance. H–S: Harleianus 2767 and Selestadiensis. E–G: Gudianus 132 and Gudianus 69. These paired witnesses summarize Krohn’s grouping; they do not assign direct descent to every copy. The manuscript tradition passes into print in the Roman editio princeps prepared by Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli in the 1480s. 3. Stemma codicum of the De architectura The grouping is visualized in Figure 22 and cataloged in Table 9. The diagram reports H–S and E–G as distinguished by Krohn; it is not a complete stemma of all extant manuscripts. 4. Mechanisms of textual change and their stemmatic value The following examples illustrate how textual changes can arise. They are methodological examples, not reported readings assigned to named Vitruvian witnesses. A change acquires stemmatic significance only when its distribution, probability, and relation to contamination have been established from the apparatus or the manuscripts. I. Omission by homoeoteleuton. A scribe’s eye may pass between similar endings and omit the intervening text. A shared, unlikely omission may 986

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER indicate common ancestry, provided independent recurrence and later correction have been considered. II. Dittography. A word or phrase may be copied twice. The same repetition in several witnesses can be significant, but a common copying error may also arise independently. III. Corruption of Greek terminology. An unfamiliar Greek expression may be altered, transliterated inconsistently, or replaced. Its evidential value depends on the precise reading and its distribution among identified witnesses. IV. Explanatory substitution. A technical expression may be replaced by a more familiar one. Such a substitution must be documented before it is attributed to a particular witness or branch. V. Transposition. Words, clauses, or larger units may change position. Shared unusual dislocations can be valuable evidence, particularly where they reveal the arrangement of an earlier exemplar. VI. Grammatical normalization. A copyist or editor may regularize an unfamiliar construction or spelling. An assimilated spelling is not inherently preferable to an unassimilated one, and common normalizations alone rarely establish a unique genealogy. VII. Numbers and proportions. Numerals, fractions, and dimensional signs are especially vulnerable in technical texts. Agreement must be assessed at a specific locus; a plausible reconstructed dimension does not independently establish the transmitted figure. VIII. Suppression of repetition. A passage judged redundant may be shortened. The editor must distinguish deliberate abbreviation from accidental omission and from an author’s own repetition. IX. Explanatory additions. A marginal or interlinear gloss may enter the running text. Its origin and date cannot be inferred from brackets alone; the relevant edition’s editorial signs must be read in context. 987

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY X. Contamination. Consultation of more than one exemplar can produce a witness that shares readings with different groups. A stemma therefore requires an account of corrections and mixed readings as well as a diagram of descent. 5. The primacy of H and the constitution of the text Harley MS 2767 (H), copied in the first quarter of the ninth century, is the oldest known surviving witness. Krohn distinguishes its side of the tradition, with S, from the Gudianus witnesses E and G. The precise genealogy remains an editorial reconstruction; neither the age of H nor a simplified stemma proves that all later manuscripts descend directly from it. The constitution of the text requires comparison of readings, not a presumption that all witnesses descend directly from H. Krohn’s printed text supplies the principal control for the running Latin in this edition. The explanatory notes below discuss the adopted wording and its interpretation; an attribution to an individual manuscript requires an identifiable apparatus entry or direct examination of that witness. 6. Textual commentary: selected passages The following notes explain five passages important for the language and interpretation of the treatise. The wording cited is checked against Krohn (1912). They are explanatory commentary, rather than a newly established manuscript apparatus; the text of an edition, an editorial conjecture and the reading of a particular witness must be distinguished. 1. Dedication and political ideology — De architectura I, preface. parenti tuo — I, preface 2. Krohn prints parenti tuo and subsequently imperium parentis. The dedication presents continuity between Caesar and the emperor addressed by Vitruvius. The political and legal implications of parens require interpretation in that context; the wording alone does not establish the precise date of composition. in tuam potestatem transtulisset — I, preface 2. This is the wording printed by Krohn. Potestas is important to the dedication’s representation of imperial authority, but an alternative wording should not be assigned to the recentiores without an identified critical source. 988

Its relation to the person of the architect matters to the argument; the abstract paraphrase ‘architecture is a science’ should not be substituted for a diplomatic quotation. fabrica — I.1.1. Krohn’s text defines fabrica as continuata ac trita usus meditatio. The term concerns sustained practical activity and must be read alongside ratiocinatio. A modern explanatory gloss is distinct from an attested medieval reading. ratiocinatione — I.1.1. Krohn prints ea nascitur ex fabrica et ratiocinatione. In the following definition, ratiocinatio explains and demonstrates what has been made through knowledge and reasoning. Reducing the term to numerical calculation alone would narrow its meaning; that semantic point does not establish the readings of H, G or later witnesses. 3. The Greek aesthetic vocabulary — De architectura 1.2.1. The Greek words suffered grave degradation in the manual transmission, since the Western medieval copyists of the Carolingian scriptoria did not know the Greek alphabet (Graeca sunt, non leguntur). τάξις — I.2.1. Krohn prints τάξις as the Greek counterpart of ordinatio. The explanatory discussion concerns order and the measured organization of the work. Claims about a blank in H, the form tasis in G, or a first restoration by Turnebus require separate documentary support and are not adopted as established variants here. διάθεσιν — I.2.1. It should not be reduced to bilateral symmetry. An anonymous scholium or the wording of a later manuscript cannot be treated as evidence without a source and location. 4. Pozzolana and the geology of concrete — De architectura 2.6.1. genus pulveris — II.6.1. Krohn prints Est etiam genus pulveris and locates the material in the districts around Vesuvius. Vitruvius describes its mixture with lime and aggregate and its hardening under water. This is a technical account of volcanic building material; the alleged variant arenae is not assigned to a manuscript family here. circa Vesuvium montem — II.6.1. The phrase locates the volcanic material geographically. The received historical dating of Vitruvius places the work before the eruption of 79 CE, but this phrase alone cannot prove that a later copyist or interpolator would necessarily have mentioned that eruption. 5. The figure of man and the genesis of proportion — De architectura 3.1.3. The well-proportioned body — III.1.1–3. Krohn’s text relates the design of temples to the proportional relations of a well-formed human body, hominis bene figurati. The circular and square constructions are both described in III.1.3. They should not be presented as a Renaissance addition to an otherwise non-geometrical ancient passage. item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus — III.1.3. Krohn prints the navel as the center of the circle traced around the outstretched body. The same section then describes the square derived from height and arm span. Leonardo’s later distinction of centers belongs to the reception and graphic interpretation of the passage; it is not a textual conjecture in Vitruvius’s Latin. 990

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix N · Restitutio vocabulorum Graecorum Vitruvius frequently uses Greek technical vocabulary, sometimes in Greek script and sometimes in Latinised forms. This glossary supplies lexical forms, equivalents and explanations. A Latin transliteration is not automatically a corruption, and a dictionary lemma need not be the inflected form printed in the treatise. The entries do not establish individual manuscript readings without an identified critical source. Appendix D provides selected page references. I. Aesthetic and modular concepts (Book I, chapter 2) 1. τάξις (taxis) Textual form: τάξις in Krohn, I.2.1. Restitution: τάξις (nominative singular, from τάσσω, ‘to set in order’, ‘to arrange in a row’). Vitruvian equivalent: ordinatio. Note: not to be confused with the mere placing of objects. In Aristotle and Hellenistic usage τάξις implies a mathematical and quantitative ordering. Vitruvius defines it as the measure of the members of a work in relation to the whole through the module (modulus): the establishment of the basic metric pattern. 2. διάθεσις (diathesis) Textual form: διάθεσιν, accusative singular, in Krohn, I.2.1. Restitution: διάθεσις (Vitruvius uses the accusative διάθεσιν; from διατίθημι, ‘to dispose’, ‘to arrange effectively’). Vitruvian equivalent: dispositio. Note: the expression of the τάξις in design. It is made visible through three modes of graphic representation (ideae): ichnographia (plan), orthographia (elevation) and scaenographia (perspective). 3. οἰκονομία (oikonomia) Textual form: οἰκονομία in Krohn, I.2.1; oeconomia is a Latin transliteration. Restitution: οἰκονομία (from οἶκος, ‘house’, and νόμος, ‘law, management’). 991

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Vitruvian equivalent: distributio. Note: under Augustus the term carries a double, technical and financial nuance. It implies the prudent management of materials and budget (sumptus), but also the fitting of the building to the owner according to social status, and the pragmatic adaptation of the architecture to the local climate. 4. εὐρυθμία (eurythmia) Corrupt reading: eurithmia, euritmia (direct Latinisation). Lexical form: εὐρυθμία, with the prefix εὖ and the noun ῥυθμός, ‘rhythm’ or ‘ordered movement’. Note: a qualitative concept of visual perception. Whereas τάξις is purely mathematical and objective, εὐρυθμία is the aesthetic result perceptible to the human eye: the graceful and harmonious appearance of the whole when contemplated. 5. συμμετρία (symmetria) Latinised form: symmetria. The Greek lemma explains the technical vocabulary; variants such as simetria require an identified source before they can be assigned to a witness. Restitution: συμμετρία (from σύν, ‘with’, and μέτρον, ‘measure’). Note: a critical point for collation. In late and medieval Latin the term degraded semantically to ‘bilateral symmetry’. The classical sense used by Vitruvius must be recovered: modular symmetry or commensurability — the exact proportional relation that binds a single element (for instance, the diameter of a column) to all the other parts and to the whole. It is included here as explanatory vocabulary, without asserting that σκιαθήρας is a verified manuscript reading at I.1.4. Restitution: σκιαθήρας (accusative plural; from σκιά, ‘shadow’, and θηράω, ‘to hunt, to capture’). Definition: literally ‘the hunters of shadows’. Restitution: λογεῖον (from λόγος, the place from which speech is delivered). Definition: in the Greek-type theater, the raised wooden platform above the proskenion on which the actors performed. Vitruvius contrasts the Greek λογεῖον (narrower and higher) with the Roman pulpitum (wider and lower), since in the Roman theater the senators and magistrates occupied the orchestra. 8. ἀναλογία (analogia) Greek lemma: ἀναλογία. Definition: the lyric, musical and dancing performers (musicians, flautists, chorus members) who, unlike the tragic and comic actors, performed below, on the area of the orchestra, in keeping with the ritual conventions of the Hellenic spectacle. 993

Restitution: σκηνικοί (nominative plural, from σκηνή, ‘tent, booth’ and later the ‘scene’). Definition: the dramatic actors (the interpreters of the dialogues of tragedy, comedy and satyr-play). VITRUVIUS TODAY: SURVIVAL OF A CANON De architectura is not a museum piece. Its categories continue to operate, sometimes explicitly, in contemporary architectural culture, and it is 997

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY appropriate to conclude this study by pointing out three lines of enduring influence. The Triad and the Modulor. The celebrated triad firmitas, utilitas, venustas— solidity, utility, beauty—continues to be the implicit framework by which built works are judged. Its most direct descendant in the 20th century is Le Corbusier's Modulor (1948), a system of proportions based on the measurements of the human body and the golden section, which reinterprets, in modern language, the ancient Vitruvian doctrine of the body as measure (homo bene figuratus, De architectura 3.1). Le Corbusier consciously acknowledged himself as the heir to this tradition: the Modulor is, in essence, a reinterpretation of Vitruvius's anthropometric canon in light of industrial standardization. Proportion, Parametrization, and BIM. The Vitruvian idea of symmetria—the commensurability of the parts with the whole based on a module— conceptually prefigures current parametric design, where the geometry of the building is governed by relationships and rules rather than fixed dimensions. Building Information Modeling (BIM) methodologies, which integrate design, construction, and maintenance information into a single model, also revive Vitruvius's ambition of an architecture understood as a holistic knowledge that articulates materials, technique, function, and understanding. Firmitas and Sustainability. Finally, Vitruvius's concern for site selection, orientation, air quality, and the use of local resources (Books I, VI, and VIII) resonates strongly with the contemporary agenda of sustainability and bioclimatic architecture. Firmitas, as understood today, is not only structural solidity but also durability and environmental responsibility: the building that endures and is wisely integrated into its surroundings. In this sense, Vitruvius remains a relevant voice twenty centuries later. Comparative Table: The Proportions of the Orders, from Vitruvius to the Treatise Writers. APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER Appendix Q · Status quaestionis: a survey of modern Vitruvian scholarship The study of De architectura has been transformed over the past century by new critical editions, philological commentary, and—most recently—archaeology. The following survey outlines the principal questions that continue to occupy specialists, so that the reader may situate the present edition within the living debate. On the text and its transmission. The editions of Valentin Rose (1867; 1899) and Fritz Krohn (1912) remain central to the constitution of the Latin text. Harley MS 2767 is the oldest known surviving copy and a witness of substantial authority. Krohn distinguishes H and S from E and G; the later witnesses cannot all be dismissed as a single contaminated group. The weight of each reading must be considered at its locus. On the date and unity of the work. The treatise is generally dated between 27 and 23 BCE and dedicated to Augustus. While some scholars have detected signs of stratified composition or later interpolation in particular passages, the substantial unity of the ten books is now broadly accepted. On the author’s identity. Almost nothing is known of Vitruvius’s life beyond what the prefaces disclose: military service under Caesar and a pension obtained through the mediation of Octavia. The cognomen Pollio rests on slender and late evidence, and the older identification of the author with Mamurra (proposed by Thielscher) is now generally rejected. On the foundational categories. The interpretation of ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, and distributio is a central crux. Following the commentary of Pierre Gros in the Budé edition and the philological studies of Louis Callebat, symmetria is now understood as commensurability—modular proportion—rather than modern bilateral symmetry. In the Anglophone sphere, the translation and commentary of Ingrid D. Rowland and Thomas Noble Howe (1999) and the work of Indra Kagis McEwen on the Vitruvian body have reframed much of the discussion. On the Greek sources and reception. Vitruvius drew on lost Greek treatises, including those of Hermogenes and Pytheos and the authors cataloged in Book 1001

Apparatus fontium (selective). Vitruvius acknowledges his debts —above all in the preface to Book VII—, though all his sources are lost. The principal authorities he names are, by field: in architecture and proportions, Pythius and Hermogenes of Priene, Silenus, Theodorus, Arcesius, and Philo (and the less celebrated Nexaris, Theocydes, Demophilos, Pollis, Leonides, Silanion, Melampus, Sarnacus, and Euphranor); in mechanics (7 pr. 14), Diades, Archytas, Archimedes, Ctesibius, Nymphodorus, Philo of Byzantium, Diphilus, Democles, Charidas, Polyidus, Pyrrus, and Agesistratus; in music, Aristoxenus of Tarentum; in scene-painting and perspective, Agatharchus of Samos, with Democritus and Anaxagoras; in astronomy and gnomonics, Berosus the Chaldean, Aristarchus of Samos, Eudoxus, Apollonius, Scopinas, Thales, and Anaximander; in philosophy and science, Plato (the doubling of the square, 9 pr.) and Pythagoras. Among the Latins he cites Fuficius (the first to write on architecture in Latin), Terentius Varro (who included architecture among his Disciplinae), and Publius Septimius. Modern scholarship (Granger, Gros) accepts that Vitruvius selected what was useful from these works, partly through Varro, partly at first hand. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Stemma codicum — the genealogical tree of the manuscripts, showing which copies depend on which and so which readings are likeliest to go back to Ω. Apparatus criticus — the band of notes printed beneath the Latin text recording the variant readings of the witnesses and the reasons for the editor’s choice; what may look like “mere grammar” is in fact the recovery of the original sense. Lectio difficilior potior — “the more difficult reading is the stronger”: between two readings the harder is the likelier original, since copyists tend to simplify an unfamiliar text — and Vitruvius’s technical Latin was often unfamiliar. Lectio facilior — the “easier” reading, frequently a later simplification or a fifteenth-century humanist “correction” that smoothed the grammar at the cost of authenticity. Contaminatio — the mixing of readings from two or more manuscript families in a single copy (as in the Selestadiensis), producing a hybrid text that the editor must disentangle. Crux desperationis (†) — the “cross of despair”, placed in the text where a passage is so corrupt that it cannot be restored with certainty — a mark of editorial honesty rather than of failure. The oldest codices and their history The transmission of De architectura rests almost entirely on the work of Carolingian copyists. When, around the year 800, the cultural renaissance fostered by Charlemagne and his teachers — Alcuin of York, Theodulf of Orléans — promoted the systematic copying of ancient authors, Vitruvius's treatise was one of the technical texts that escaped oblivion. The essential testimony of the entire tradition dates from that period. H · Codex Harleianus 2767 Harley MS 2767, copied in Caroline minuscule in the first quarter of the ninth century, is the oldest known surviving copy of De architectura. The British Library gives Cologne or Aachen as possible places of origin and treats the palace-scriptorium association as uncertain. Its documented medieval provenance includes St Pantaleon in Cologne. Two leaves are now in Oxford, 1008

It is worth remembering, contrary to the common notion of Vitruvius being " rediscovered " during the Renaissance, that the treatise never completely fell out of use: it was known and cited by medieval scholars such as Alcuin, Einhard, Hugh of Saint Victor, Vincent of Beauvais, and Hildegard of Bingen. Poggio's discovery in 1416 did not rescue the text from oblivion, but rather returned its finest testimony to scholarly circulation. 1009

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Theses on Vitruvius This chapter gathers, in concise form, the principal scholarly positions that underlie the present edition. They are offered as theses for discussion: where a statement rests on textual, archaeological, or philological evidence it is presented as such; where it belongs to the editor’s interpretive proposal, it is expressly marked as the author’s hypothesis and not as established consensus. The chapter is deliberately brief and may be expanded in subsequent editions. 1. A single complete witness, not the “first architect.” De architectura is not the earliest architecture ever written but the only complete treatise on the subject to survive from classical antiquity. Vitruvius’s historical importance lies in this completeness and in the systematic ambition of his ten books, not in any claim to have founded the discipline. The Greek treatises of Hermogenes, Pytheos and others that Vitruvius cites as his sources are lost; what survives of the ancient theory of building survives largely through him, so the claim this edition defends is one of transmission and completeness, not of priority. 2. The triad is a system, not a checklist. firmitas, utilitas, and venustas (De architectura 1.3.2) are neither optional nor separable. In Vitruvius’s conception, beauty arises from, and is inseparable from, sound construction and fitness for use; the same proportional reasoning that makes a building stand also makes it pleasing. Read in this way the three terms are not a checklist to be satisfied in turn but a single requirement seen from three sides, and the later reception that treated them as separable departs from Vitruvius’s own emphasis on their interdependence. 3. symmetria is modular commensurability, not modern symmetry. Vitruvian symmetria (συμμετρία) denotes the proportional correspondence of the parts to one another and to the whole through a common module; it must not be read as the modern, post-eighteenth-century notion of bilateral or mirror symmetry. The confusion is consequential, for rendering symmetria as “symmetry” imports a modern visual idea of balance that the Latin does not carry and obscures the modular reasoning — the use of a common module (modulus) — on which the whole proportional system rests. 1012

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER 4. The homo bene figuratus is not the “Vitruvian Man.” Vitruvius (3.1) describes a well-proportioned human figure inscribed within circle and square as a canon of proportion; he does not give the celebrated phrase or image later associated with Leonardo. The Renaissance “Vitruvian Man” is an interpretive elaboration, not a quotation of the text. His concern is to derive the proportions of the temple from those of the well-formed body; the image of a single figure simultaneously inscribed in circle and square, with its famous shifting of centers, is Leonardo’s graphic solution to a problem the text poses but does not itself resolve. 5. Pythagorean number-symbolism is the author’s hypothesis. Vitruvius names Pythagoras and the practice of composing precepts in “cubes” of 216 verses (6³) in the preface to Book V; his use of number is technical. Any further reading of 216 or of the cube as a carrier of cosmic or sacred meaning is advanced here explicitly as the author’s interpretive proposal, not as Vitruvius’s stated intention. The distinction is methodological: the technical use of proportion is documented and defended philologically, whereas the symbolic resonance of particular numbers is offered as a separate and clearly labeled interpretive layer. 6. The transmission preserves collateral witnesses. The text descends through a complex medieval manuscript tradition in which the Carolingian Harleianus 2767 (H) is a major witness and Gudianus 69 (G) preserves an important collateral line. The Latin in this edition follows Krohn (1912), checked against Rose (1899) and the Budé volumes. Greek technical terminology, sometimes corrupted or transliterated in transmission, is normalized in the present text according to the critical editions and discussed in Appendix N and the Conspectus of Greek Terms. 7. The Basilica at Fano is the one work Vitruvius claims — and a current test case. The basilica at Fanum Fortunae is the building Vitruvius explicitly says he designed and supervised (5.1.6–10). On 19 January 2026 the Italian Ministry of Culture announced the identification of the remains in Piazza Andrea Costa as that basilica, and further archaeological investigation continued. The survival of a canon. The afterlife of De architectura — from its Carolingian copying and humanist rediscovery to the editio princeps of 1486 and the treatises of the Renaissance — is itself part of its meaning: Vitruvius matters not only for what he records of Roman practice but for the canon of proportion and decorum that later ages built upon his text. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Appendix · Glossarium Vitruvianum A philological and technical dictionary of Vitruvius’s fundamental terms. Each entry gives the Latin lemma, the English equivalent used uniformly throughout this edition, a brief philological note, the chief loci in De architectura, and, where instructive, parallels in other Latin authors (Cicero, Varro, Pliny) and cross-references. Its purpose is to guarantee terminological consistency, to forestall the false friends that have dogged earlier translations, and to justify the renderings adopted. It complements the existing Glossary, the Restitutio vocabulorum Graecorum (Appendix N) and the Conspectus of Greek Terms; it may be expanded in future editions towards a full lexicon. Book I — principles, the architect, the city Architectura — architecture. The discipline (scientia) that Vitruvius founds at 1.1.1 upon fabrica and ratiocinatio — practice and reasoning together. For the underlying distinction between ars and scientia cf. Cicero, De oratore 1.144. Cross-refs: fabrica, ratiocinatio. Fabrica — practice. 1.1.1: the continued and habitual exercise of the hand upon the material; the executant side of the art, inseparable from its reasoning. Cross-ref: ratiocinatio. Ratiocinatio — reasoning. 1.1.1: the power to expound and demonstrate by proportion what is wrought by skill; the theoretical side of architecture. Cf. the Ciceronian ratio. Cross-ref: fabrica. Ordinatio (τάξις) — modular ordering. 1.2.2: the apt adjustment of the members of a work taken severally, and their arrangement for proportion as a whole, by a chosen unit (quantitas). A calque of Greek τάξις; cf. its military and philosophical use in Varro and Caesar. Cross-refs: modulus, symmetria. Dispositio (διάθεσις) — disposition. 1.2.2: the fit placing of the parts and the elegant effect of the whole in its arrangement, realized in the three “ideas” — ichnographia, orthographia, scaenographia. Compare the rhetorical dispositio of Cicero, De oratore 1.142. Cross-refs: ichnographia, orthographia, scaenographia. Eurythmia (εὐρυθμία) — graceful proportion. 1.2.3: the comely look that arises when the members answer one another in height, breadth and length — the visible grace that follows the right application of symmetria. A Hellenism; 1018

Symmetria (συμμετρία) — commensurability (modular proportion). 1.2.4 and 3.1.1–3.1.9: the agreement of the parts among themselves and with the whole through a common module; never bilateral “symmetry” in the modern sense. The central mathematical principle of Vitruvian design, and the most frequently misunderstood term in the treatise; to render it “symmetry” distorts the whole system. THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY Excursus · The Querelle of Proportion: Vitruvius, Palladio, and Perrault No question runs deeper through the reception of the De architectura than this one: are the proportions that Vitruvius records grounded in nature, and therefore binding upon every architect in every age, or are they conventions — beautiful because they are familiar, authoritative because they are old? On the answer hangs the whole status of Vitruvius’ canon. If proportion is a law of nature, the treatise is a body of science; if it is custom, the treatise is a record of taste. The debate came to a head in seventeenth-century France, but its terms are already latent in Vitruvius himself. Vitruvius grounds beauty in symmetria — the commensurability of every part with a fixed module — and derives that commensurability from the proportions of the well-formed human body (3.1) and, by analogy, from the consonances of music (5.4). For him the orders are not arbitrary: the Doric carries the proportions of a man, the Ionic those of a matron, the Corinthian those of a maiden (4.1). Proportion is thus a natural and quasi-mathematical fact, discovered rather than invented. Andrea Palladio (1508–1580) inherited this conviction and gave it its most influential modern form. In the I quattro libri dell’architettura (Venice, 1570) he prescribes seven “most beautiful” room-shapes whose ratios — the square, the diagonal of the square, and the simple musical proportions 2:3, 3:4, 3:5 — echo the harmonic intervals. For Palladio, as for Alberti before him (De re aedificatoria, 1452), the architect who follows these ratios does not impose a private preference but obeys a harmony written into the cosmos. This is the doctrine that Rudolf Wittkower named the “harmonic” or “musical” theory of proportion. Claude Perrault (1613–1688), physician, anatomist and member of the Académie des Sciences, also participated in the Louvre colonnade project. His French translation, Les dix livres d’architecture de Vitruve (Paris, 1673; revised 1684), brought together commentary and engraved illustrations. His criticism of proportional authority must be read in the context of that close engagement with the treatise. 1028

APPENDICES AND REFERENCE MATTER In the preface to that translation, and at length in the Ordonnance des cinq espèces de colonnes selon la méthode des anciens (Paris, 1683), Perrault distinguished two kinds of architectural beauty. Positive beauty (beauté positive) rests on causes that convince everyone — richness of material, precision and cleanness of execution, bilateral regularity, and magnitude. Arbitrary beauty (beauté arbitraire), by contrast, comprises the proportions of the orders; these please us, Perrault argued, not because reason or nature compels them but because custom and association have accustomed the eye to them. There is no single ratio that nature dictates: the proof, he observed, is that the proportions admired by the ancients themselves vary from building to building and from author to author. From this premise Perrault drew a practical method as radical as his theory. Rather than seek the one true proportion, he proposed a mean or averaged system, derived by reconciling the divergent measures of the most admired ancient buildings into a simple, memorable rule. Proportion, for Perrault, was to be regulated by reasonable convention — by the architect’s judgment and the consensus of taste — not deduced from a law of nature. The challenge did not go unanswered. François Blondel (1618–1686), first director of the Académie Royale d’Architecture, defended the older view in his Cours d’architecture (1675–1683), insisting that proportion possesses an objective foundation in number, in music, and in nature, exactly as Vitruvius had taught. The exchange between Perrault and Blondel became the architectural front of the wider querelle des anciens et des modernes: Blondel for the ancients and the absolute, Perrault for the moderns and the conventional. The quarrel was never settled, and that is its importance. It exposed, once and for all, that the Vitruvian canon can be read in two incompatible ways, and that a reader must choose. Later theory has oscillated between the poles. The harmonic tradition revived in the proportional systems of the nineteenth century and in Le Corbusier’s Modulor (1948), which sought once more to anchor design in the measures of the body; the conventionalist tradition fed the historicism and, ultimately, the proportional skepticism of much modern practice. For the present edition the controversy carries a precise consequence. When Vitruvius states that a column shall be of such-and-such a diameter, or that the 1029

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY eustyle intercolumniation shall measure two and a quarter diameters, the modern reader is entitled to ask whether such figures record a discovered law or a codified habit. This edition takes no side in the metaphysical question. It renders the proportions faithfully, as Vitruvius gives them, and leaves to the architect — as Perrault would have wished, and as Palladio would have resisted — the freedom to regard them either as nature’s rule or as the accumulated wisdom of a tradition. The text is law for those who read it as law, and counsel for those who read it as counsel. Select references. The Fano basilica: the case of direct verification The basilica of Fanum Fortunae is the only building Vitruvius claims to have designed and supervised himself (conlocavi curavique faciendam, 5.1.6), and so it offers an exceptional test of the text against material remains. In January 2026 the Italian authorities (the Marche Region, the Municipality of Fano and the Soprintendenza) announced the identification, in Piazza Andrea Costa at Fano, of the remains of a monumental basilica attributed to this work. The features made public correspond strikingly to the Vitruvian description: a rectangular 1038

THE ARCHITECT OF THEORY EPILOGUE The figure of Vitruvius presents a paradox characteristic of many foundational authors: while we know remarkably little about his life, his De architectura has shaped architectural thought for more than two thousand years. This disproportion between the obscurity of the author and the enduring legacy of his work is not accidental: it is the very nature of foundational texts, which survive precisely because they cease to belong to their author and become the heritage of their readers. Vitruvius’s treatise has come down to us mutilated, deprived of its original figures. The illustrations that accompanied the text — the diagrams of the orders, the plans of the temples, the layouts of the machines — were lost somewhere in the chain of copies, and the Renaissance had to reconstruct them with ruler and compass from the words alone. This loss, far from impoverishing the work, made it fruitful: it forced Alberti, Cesariano, Palladio, and Barbaro to read Vitruvius with pencil in hand, transforming philology into a project and commentary into architecture. If this journey through the Ten Books teaches us anything, it is that the triad Vitruvius enunciated — firmitas, utilitas, venustas — does not describe three separable qualities, but rather three facets of the same measure. Solidity without utility is premature ruin; utility without beauty, mere construction; beauty without solidity, ephemeral scenery. For Vitruvius, architecture begins where the three converge, and this conviction — that number, matter, and form obey a single reason — remains the core of any architectural theory worthy of the name. This edition has sought to uphold a twofold commitment: historical and philological rigor, on the one hand, and openness to the symbolic dimension of the treatise, on the other, always maintaining the distinction between what the sources allow us to affirm and what belongs to the author's interpretation. Perhaps this is the most faithful way to honor Vitruvius, who wrote convinced that the architect should master both the square and astronomy, construction and reasoning, the hand and number. A debt and a hope remain. Every edition of a classical work is provisional: further collation, closer translation and a more precise apparatus can always 1040
